## 1. Your understanding: right, with 2 small fixes

**Right:** the label line marks the spots to skip with 65535. The loss kernel skips every spot whose label is 65535. **Every other spot gets a loss and a gradient.**

**Fix 1: the model doesn't learn *which* spots to skip.** **We** decide that in step 4 by writing 65535 in the label line. The model just isn't graded at those spots.

**Fix 2: the question still matters.** The model never learns to *write* the question. But it still *reads* it: every answer token looks back at the question tokens. So the model still learns how to *use* the question. Only the padding is truly useless.

## 2. The note you remembered: yes, it's documented

It's in the **SFT doc §33** ("Immediate future task: remove the redundant lm_head matmul on ignored rows", decided 2026-09-29), and in the task list (loss doc §26, line 2614).

**The waste, in simple words:**
- The model's last step (the **lm_head**) is a big multiplication. It makes **50,304 scores at every spot**.
- At a skipped spot (label 65535) those scores are **never used**. Our loss kernel already skips the softmax there (`LossKernels.cu:211-219`), but the multiplication **before** it still runs, plus 2 more in backward.
- Cost: the lm_head is **6.3%** of the model's work per token (0.695 of 11.0 GFLOP). It also needs memory for all the scores.

**How much we'd save:** in today's real Tülu sample, only **12.0%** of spots are answer spots. So with one example per row, about 88% of the lm_head work is for skipped spots. That's roughly 5-6% of total work. **This is my estimate, not measured.**

**Only the last step can be skipped.** The 26 layers must still run on the question tokens, because the answer looks at them. Padding is waste in **every** layer; bucketing (v1.5) and packing (v2) fix that later.

**Who already does it** (from the local clones, §33):

| Library | Scores for skipped spots |
|---|---|
| **TRL** | **not made at all, by default** (`loss_type="chunked_nll"`, `sft_trainer.py:122-232`): picks only the spots with a real label, then runs the lm_head only on those |
| Liger-Kernel | made |
| Megatron-LM | made |
| torchtitan | made |
| BluTrain today | made |

**Our plan (§33):**
1. Pick out only the answer spots.
2. Run the lm_head and the loss on them only.
3. Put the gradients back in their places (zeros everywhere else).
4. Round the count up to a multiple of 256, so the matmul doesn't get endless new shapes.

**When:** right after the first SFT run. Then measure 6 cases (v1, v1.5, v2, each with and without) in **answer tokens per second**, step time and memory.

Here is step 6, the dataloader, from zero.

## What the dataloader is

It's the part of the trainer that, **before every micro-step**:
1. takes the next pieces of data from the files on disk;
2. puts them on the GPU as **two tensors**: `input` (what the model reads) and `target` (the labels).

The training loop asks for them here: `Batch batch = train_loader.next_batch();` (`bluscript_zero_ckpt.cpp:2240`).

## Which loader our trainer uses

**`MixedDataLoaderLite`**, in `Tensor-Implementations/include/MixedDataloader.h`, created at `bluscript_zero_ckpt.cpp:1829`.
- "Mixed" means it can read **several datasets at once**, each with a share. Its own example is web text 70%, code 20%, math 10%.
- For each batch it picks which dataset to take from, so the shares stay exact.

## What it does today (pretraining), step by step

A pretraining file is **one very long line of tokens, with no rows**:
```
file: t0 t1 t2 t3 t4 t5 t6 t7 t8 t9 ...   (100,000,000 tokens)
```

Every micro-step, for each GPU:
1. **Take 32,769 tokens** from where it stopped last time: 8 rows × 4096 = 32,768, **plus 1 extra** (`need = BT + 1`, line 538).
2. **Input** = the first 32,768. **Target** = the same tokens **moved over by one** (lines 578-579: `tokens` and `tokens + 1`). This is the pretraining shift: every token's label is simply the next token.
3. **Copy both to the GPU** (line 609).
4. **Move forward.** Each GPU starts at a **different place** (line 530: start = 32,768 × GPU number). After each batch it jumps over the other GPUs' parts (line 621). So two GPUs **never read the same tokens**:
   ```
   GPU 0 reads: [ tokens 0 to 32,767 ]                    then [ 65,536 to ... ] ...
   GPU 1 reads:                       [ 32,768 to 65,535 ]                    ...
   ```
5. **At the end of a file**, go to the next file. After the last file, start again from the first. **It never stops.**
6. **Optional id check:** if you set `BLU_TOKEN_MAX=50304`, it checks every id of every batch and **prints** an error for bad ids. It doesn't stop the run (lines 580-607). It's off by default.

## What SFT needs instead

SFT files are different. They have **rows** (4096 each), and the labels are a **separate file** that already has the shift and the 65535s.

| | Today (pretraining) | SFT needs |
|---|---|---|
| files | 1 long line of tokens | **2 files with rows**: `inputs.bin`, `labels.bin` |
| how to read | 32,769 tokens, then shift by one | **row r from both files**, exactly 4096 each, **no shift, no +1** (step 4 already did it) |
| order | in file order | **shuffle the rows every epoch**, so the model doesn't see the same order each time |
| GPUs | each takes different tokens | each takes **different rows** |
| counting | none | count the labels that are not 65535: per micro-batch, and for the whole step. That's the denominator (task 6), read from the metadata file's per-row counts |
| id check | optional, prints only | **always on, once per file, stops the run**: inputs below 50,304; labels below 50,304 **or** exactly 65535 |
| end | loops forever | **stop after 1-2 epochs** (an epoch = one full pass over all the examples) |

## Who writes it

**You** (C++, the trainer side). The plan is a new SFT loader class next to `MixedDataLoaderLite`. It would reuse that class's machinery for copying to the GPU, and change only how it reads, shuffles, counts and checks.

**Two corrections from checking the code** (both written into the task list, loss doc §26, item 4):
1. The report's §3.9 says the trainer uses `dist/dataloader_dist.h`. It really uses `MixedDataLoaderLite`.
2. An id check already exists (`BLU_TOKEN_MAX`). The SFT check will build on it.

The bug is real, and I've found the exact cause. It is **not** in Navin's Muon code. It is one line in the Tensor-Implementations library, and I reproduced it outside the test.

**What happens, simply:**
- Before Newton-Schulz, the code divides the matrix by its size (the Frobenius norm). To get that size it adds up all the squared values.
- For the 96×96 tensor the GPU splits that sum across 9 workers (blocks). Each worker adds its part into one shared number with `atomicAdd` ([MuonKernels.cu:77](Tensor-Implementations/src/Kernels/cuda/optimizer/MuonKernels.cu#L77), on the box clone).
- The workers finish in a different order each time. With floats, `(a+b)+c` and `a+(b+c)` can differ in the last bit. So the total sometimes comes out 1 bit higher.
- That 1-bit difference changes the scale. 5 rounds of bf16 Newton-Schulz then grow it. That gives the 7,077 different elements, max 2.7e-5, that the test reports.

**Proof (three separate tests, all on GPU 2):**

| Test | Result |
|---|---|
| Fingerprint every value in both modes, 3 commits × 10 runs | Weights, gradient, momentum and Newton-Schulz input are bit-identical in both modes, at every step, in all 3 commits. The first value that differs is the norm-scaled matrix. |
| Same input, add the 9 block sums in all 362,880 orders | Only 3 totals are possible. Exactly one of them (reached by 29,736 orders) gives the test's odd value `309adc…`. The other two give the normal value `b3f448…`. |
| Real library function alone on the same input, 200 calls per condition | Idle GPU: 0/200 odd. L2 cache flushed first: 16/200 odd. Other work running on the GPU: 38/200 odd. |

**Why it only shows in REDUCE_BROADCAST mode, and only from Navin's commit:**
- The odd value appeared 17/20 times in REDUCE_BROADCAST mode on HEAD and 11/20 on a3aba3e. It never appeared in RS/AG mode (0/40), and never on e6eaeba.
- Navin's change alters what the GPU did just before this step: what is in the cache, and which parts of the GPU are busy. That changes the finishing order. His change does not cause the bug; it exposes it. Test 3 shows any change like that can do the same.
- I did not find which single line of a3aba3e shifts the order. Turning off his in-place change alone (S3) still failed 4/10, so no single line is "the switch".

**I got two things wrong earlier today:**
- "Introduced by a3aba3e" was too strong. Exposed by it, yes; caused by it, no. Our F4 is cleared: a3aba3e alone fails 7/10.
- In the last status I said the `atomicAdd` was not the cause. That was wrong. The idle-GPU test always gave the same result only because an idle GPU always finishes in the same order. Under load it changes, as test 3 shows.

**Answer to your earlier question ("is the test wrong, not the actual code?"):**
- Navin's Muon code computes the same thing in both modes.
- The test is right to expect identical results, but the library's norm is not repeatable bit for bit.
- The real fix is in the library: write the 9 block sums to a small buffer and add them in one fixed order. That costs almost nothing and also makes training runs repeatable bit for bit. Only loosening the test would hide the problem.
- For training this is rounding-size noise, not wrong math. But the same seed will not give exactly the same weights twice.

Yes, we can fix it today. It is a small change: one function in one library file (`MuonKernels.cu`), about 30 lines. Below is the fix, the analysis of how it affects precision and speed, and the plan. The GPU measurement is written and ready, but not run yet.

## The fix, simply

Today, 9 blocks each throw their part into one box, in whatever order they finish.

The fix: each block writes its part into **its own numbered slot**. Then the slots are added **in one fixed order**: same order, same tree, every time. Arrival order stops mattering, so the same input always gives the same bits, whatever the GPU is doing.

## Four ways to build it (the GPU test decides which)

| Version | How | GPU steps per matrix | Notes |
|---|---|---|---|
| V0 (today) | clear box → 9 blocks `atomicAdd` → scale | 3 | not repeatable |
| V1 | blocks write slots → one small block adds slots in order → scale | 3 | same design Navin already uses in his new W=1 norm (`ZeroKernels.cu:131-182`) |
| V2 | blocks write slots → the **last** block to finish adds them in order → scale | 2 | one step fewer; needs a counter and a memory fence (trickier) |
| V3 | blocks write slots → **each** scale block adds the slots itself, in order | 2 | one step fewer, simplest; a little repeated reading |
| V3n | V3, with the block count depending only on matrix size, not on the GPU's SM count | 2 | bonus: this step gives the same bits on H200 and B300 |

I lean towards **V3** (simplest, one step fewer) or **V1** (copies Navin's proven design). The measurement picks.

## Precision

- **What changes:** only the step that adds the 9 parts. How each thread and each block adds stays exactly the same.
- **It is never worse, and usually better.** Adding P parts one by one can be off by up to (P−1) roundings. A fixed tree is off by at most about log₂(P) roundings.
  - Tensor 15: worst case 8 → 4.
  - The biggest matrices (about 1,000 parts): about 1,000 → about 12.
- **Our real tensor-15 numbers** (computed exactly on the laptop): the exact sum is 46.8725519.

  | Total | Distance from exact |
  |---|---|
  | today, possible total 1 | −1.25 ulp |
  | today, possible total 2 | −0.25 ulp |
  | today, possible total 3 (the bad one) | +0.75 ulp |
  | **the fix, every time** | **−0.25 ulp** |

  So the fix always gives the float **closest to the exact answer**, which is also today's "normal" result.
- **Effect on Muon:** none that matters. After the sum come `rsqrtf` (its own error is up to 2 ulp) and then bf16, which keeps about 3 digits. bf16 rounding is about 10,000 times bigger than this sum's error. Newton-Schulz only needs the norm to be big enough, and the Frobenius norm is big enough by a wide margin.
- **What you will see:** the weights' last bits change once compared to today, at rounding level. After that, results are the same every run. That is the point of the fix.

## Speed

- **Size of this step:** the Frobenius part is 3 tiny GPU steps per matrix. The rest of Newton-Schulz is 15 matrix multiplications plus their helper steps. So this is a small slice either way.
- **V1:** same number of steps (the "clear the box" step becomes a "1-block add"), so expected about the same speed.
- **V2/V3:** one step fewer, so expected a few microseconds **faster** per matrix per step.
- **Extra work in V3:** each scale block re-reads the parts. For the biggest matrix that is about 4 MB of fast cache reads, against the 235 MB the matrix itself moves.
- **Training step:** expected ≈ 0% change. A few µs per matrix, while a training step takes hundreds of milliseconds or more. This is my expectation, not yet measured; the probe will give real numbers.

## I checked whether other kernels have the same problem

| Kernel | Status |
|---|---|
| `multi_tensor_grad_norm` (grad clipping in the trainer) | **already safe**: block parts, then 1 block adds them, then one single add per call |
| Navin's W=1 norm (`sumsq_accumulate`) | **already safe**: two-step, fixed order |
| `GradNormKernels.cu:51` | same unsafe pattern, but **nothing calls it** (dead code); leaving it alone |
| **`MuonKernels.cu:77`** | **the only live one** in the optimizer path |

## Plan and time (about 1-1.5 hours)

1. **Measure (about 2 minutes on GPU 2):** `ns_probe6` runs all 5 versions on 8 matrix sizes, from our real tensor 15 up to 4096×14336. For each version it reports:
   - how many different totals it gives over 400 calls, on an idle GPU, with the cache flushed, and with busy SMs;
   - its error against an exact sum;
   - its µs per call.

   The kernels are copied verbatim from the library and built with the library's own flags (`--use_fast_math -O3`). The files are ready: [ns_probe6.cu](profiling_reports/muon_bug_2026_10_05/ns_probe6.cu) and [run_probe6.sh](profiling_reports/muon_bug_2026_10_05/run_probe6.sh).
2. **Patch the library** with the winning version.
3. **Test the real library** in a scratch copy on the box:

   - repeat the stress test on the real patched function;
   - run the other Muon tests to check nothing else broke.
4. **Hand-over:** I give you the diff. You commit it to the TI branch `dist_side_merge_BLUCCL` and bump the submodule pointer in BluTrain. Then we tell Navin and Kathir.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-05 21:27 IST]

**Go with Navin's design.** That is V1, plus one more piece of his design: the number of blocks depends only on the matrix size. Call it **V1n**. It is the most robust and the easiest to keep in sync later. Its precision is the same as the other fixes, and its speed should be the same as today.

## Precision: all the fixes are equal

V1, V2 and V3 add exactly the same parts in exactly the same fixed order, so they give **bit-identical** results by construction. All of them are as accurate as today's best case or better. On our real tensor 15 they all give the float closest to the exact sum. Precision does not decide this.

V1n can differ from V1 in the last bit, and only for matrices above about 1 million numbers, because the sum is split into slightly different pieces. That is the same accuracy, just a different rounding. In return, it gives the same bits on H200 and B300.

## Speed: only a tiny difference

- **V1:** about the same as today. It still has 3 steps; the "clear the box" step becomes a "1-block add".
- **V2/V3:** one step fewer, so maybe a few µs faster per matrix per step.
- **Rough estimate:** GPT-2 small has about 48 Muon matrices × ~3 µs ≈ 0.15 ms per step, which is roughly 0.1% or less. With ZeRO each GPU only handles its own matrices, so even less. This is an estimate; the probe will measure it.

## Robustness and future changes: V1n wins clearly

| | V1n (Navin's design) | V2 (last block) | V3 (sum inside scale) |
|---|---|---|---|
| Already used in our code | **yes, twice**: Navin's `sumsq_accumulate` and TI's `multi_tensor_grad_norm` | no | no |
| Hidden state | none | a counter that must be back to 0 after every launch | none |
| What breaks if someone edits it later | nothing subtle | if a block ever exits early, the counter is left wrong. The next call **silently** uses a stale norm. | the sum kernel's block count must be passed exactly right to the scale kernel, or the scale is silently wrong |
| Scale kernel | **unchanged** | unchanged | rewritten |
| Norm stored as one value in memory (for logging, NaN checks) | yes | yes | no, it is never stored |
| Same result on any GPU model | **yes** | no | only as V3n |
| Size of the diff (easy to merge with others' edits) | smallest | medium | medium |

V2 saves a few µs but adds a trap for the next person who edits the kernel. V3 saves a few µs but spreads the logic across two kernels. V1n keeps each piece simple and separately testable. It matches the pattern the codebase already uses, so there is one way of doing this everywhere.

**One detail:** we copy Navin's *pattern*, not his code. TI cannot call `dist/zero` code, because dist is built on top of TI, not the other way round. Later, one shared deterministic-sum helper in TI that both use would be the cleanest. That touches Navin's code, so it is not for now.

**One existing limit we keep:** the scratch buffer is one static buffer, the same as today's `s_muon_norm`. So the function assumes one stream at a time, as it does today. I'll write that in a comment and not change it.

## Probe updated so it also measures V1n
> tool `Bash`: Add V1n variant to probe6 locally

I recommend we go with **V1n, Navin's design**. Precision is the same for every fix. Speed should match today, while V2/V3 would save only a few µs. And V1n is the safest for anyone editing this code later.

## How the fix works, and does it cost time?

**Before (3 steps):**
1. Clear the box (set it to 0).
2. Many blocks (9 for our test tensor, up to 792 for big matrices) each add up their own share of the numbers. **This is the heavy part.** Then each block does `atomicAdd` into the one box.
3. Scale the matrix.

**After (3 steps):**
1. The **same** blocks do the **same** heavy part, in parallel, exactly as before. Each writes its result into its own slot. A plain write is even cheaper than an atomic.
2. **New:** one block of 256 threads adds the slots (at most 768 numbers, 3 KB). Each thread adds about 3 slots, then a tree of 8 levels finishes it.
3. Scale the matrix (unchanged).

**Is it serialized?** No.
- **The heavy part is unchanged:** reading and squaring all the numbers, which is thousands to 58 million of them, is still fully parallel on all blocks.
- **Only the final combining step changed.** And `atomicAdd` was already one-at-a-time there: when many blocks add into the **same** address, the GPU's memory unit applies the adds one after another. So we replaced "one at a time, in random order" with "a small tree, in fixed order". No new serialization.

**The real cost** is the small "add the slots" step. It must wait for step 1 to finish, and starting a step on the GPU takes about 2 µs. The old "clear the box" step was cheaper.

| Matrix | Extra time per call (measured) |
|---|---|
| small (96×96 to 2048×2048) | +0.3 to +0.7 µs |
| big (4096×4096, 4096×14336) | +2.4 to +2.8 µs (+1.3% on the biggest) |
| per training step, GPT-2 small (≈48 Muon matrices, estimate) | ≈ 17 µs |

That is tiny next to the Newton-Schulz matrix multiplications. If it ever matters, the V3 version measured faster than today, so we can switch later. We chose V1n for safety.

## Precision: only benefit, yes

- **Same parts, better combining:** each thread's and each block's math is exactly the same as before. Only the final combining changed, from a random-order chain to a fixed tree. A chain's error grows with the number of pieces; a tree's grows only with the number of levels.
- **Measured:** today the worst error was up to **18 ulp** on big matrices. The fix stays within **about 1 ulp** of the exact answer, and gives the same answer every time.
- **Two honest notes:**
  - "Within about 1 ulp" is not always the exact closest float. For example, 768×3072 came out 0.94 ulp off.
  - The weights' last bits change once compared with old runs. After that, they repeat exactly.

---first , on the sft side , i went through the sft report page by page and checked every claim against the original papers (instructgpt , zephyr , deepseek-r1 , chu et al) with the exact lines and page numbers , and corrected the two zephyr numbers that were wrong (mt-bench 7.34 → 7.00 , alpacaeval 90.60% → 86.07%) ,,, , then i walked through the whole sft data flow step by step , from the chat template to the loss : one chat becomes one token string with the gpt-2 tokenizer , the labels are the same tokens shifted by one , every position the model should not learn from (the prompt and the padding) is marked 65535 so the loss kernel skips it , the input side is padded with 50256 , and the loss is divided by the number of trained tokens across all gpus , not per micro-batch ,,, , the decisions are written down with file and line numbers : the token-range check goes into the sft dataloader using the vocab size , the loss gets the global token count , and the loss kernel stays as it is with only a comment , the next step on this side is a sample run on the h200 starting from navin's step-8000 checkpoint ,,, ,

---second , the muon bug , a small background first so it makes sense : muon is the optimizer that updates the model's weight matrices , and navin's test test_muon_rsag runs the same 4 training steps twice , once with each of the two ways sharded muon moves data between gpus (reduce_broadcast and reduce_scatter_all_gather) , and demands the two final results be identical to the last bit , that is how it catches a silent data-layout bug ,,, , since navin's commit a3aba3e this test failed in 17 of 20 runs on 1 gpu , always on the same 96x96 tensor , with 7,077 of 82,120 numbers different by at most 2.7e-5 , and randomly , the same binary sometimes passed ,,, ,

---third , how i found the cause : i built debug copies of the optimizer that print a fingerprint of every value at every stage , in both modes , every step , and the weights , gradient , momentum and the input to newton-schulz were bit-identical in both modes at every step and in 3 different commits , so navin's code is correct and our own f4 change is not involved ,,, , the first value that differed was inside the library's newton-schulz , in the step that divides the matrix by its size (the frobenius norm) , that size is a sum of all the squared numbers , and the library splits it across 9 gpu blocks that each add their part into one shared number with atomicadd , in whatever order they finish ,,, , computer numbers keep only about 7 digits , so the order of adding can change the last digit , like a 3-digit calculator where (1000+4)+4 gives 1000 but 1000+(4+4) gives 1010 ,,, , i tried all 362,880 possible orders of those 9 parts : they give only 3 totals , and exactly one of them produces the odd result the test saw , and i reproduced it outside the test with the real library function just by flushing the gpu cache (16 of 200 calls) or keeping some sms busy (38 of 200 calls) ,,, , navin's commit only changed what the gpu was doing just before this sum , which made the bad order show up , memory checks with the cuda sanitizer were clean ,,, ,

---fourth , the fix : instead of all blocks adding into one shared number , each block now writes its part into its own slot , and one small block adds the slots in one fixed order , so the total is the same every time whatever the gpu is doing , this is the same two-step pattern navin already uses in his zero kernels , and the number of blocks now depends only on the matrix size (capped at 768 , which fits in one round on the h200) ,,, , i measured 5 ways of doing it and chose this one as the safest for future edits , it lives in one library file (muonkernels.cu) with the full reason written in its code comments ,,, , "ulp" below means the smallest possible step of a number :

| matrix (400 calls each , h200) | old : different totals | old : worst error | fixed : different totals | fixed : worst error | extra time per call |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 96x96 (the test's tensor) | 3 | 1.28 ulp | 1 | 0.72 ulp | +0.3 us |
| 768x768 | 20 | 9.76 ulp | 1 | 0.24 ulp | +0.4 us |
| 768x3072 | 21 | 13.1 ulp | 1 | 0.94 ulp | +0.3 us |
| 4096x14336 | 26 | 18.4 ulp | 1 | 0.40 ulp | +2.4 us (+1.3%) |

---so the fix gives the same answer every time , it is 10-45x more accurate in the worst case , and it costs only a few microseconds per matrix ,,, , then i rebuilt the library in a scratch copy and ran the same test binary with the old and the fixed library , changing nothing else :

| check (same test binary) | old library | fixed library |
|---|---|---|
| test_muon_rsag , 20 runs each | 19 failed | 0 failed |
| norm under gpu stress , 800 calls | odd result 54 times | odd result 0 times |
| newton-schulz on the test's own inputs | 4 normal outputs | the same 4 outputs |

---finally , the fix is pushed with only the needed changes , and anyone pulling needs git submodule update and a libtensor rebuild (only this one file recompiles) ,,, , one more thing i noticed : the cuda sanitizer also shows shared-memory race warnings inside the library's own bf16 matmul kernel , they never changed a result in more than 12,000 calls here , but it is worth a separate look later , and the plain dist_side_merge branch still has the old norm code ,,, , tomorrow i will tell navin and kathir about the fix , and start the sft sample run on the h200 with navin's step-8000 checkpoint ,,, ,

| repo | branch | commit | what changed |
|---|---|---|---|
| tensor-implementations | dist_side_merge_bluccl | a60099b → a9bc08c | muonkernels.cu only |
| blutrain | dist_side_merge_bluccl | b9b567f → 35df307 | the library pointer only |

## The 2 commands

**1. `scp …` (on the laptop)**
- Copied your edited `bluscript_zero_ckpt.cpp` (154 KB) from the laptop's `~/Downloads/BluTrain_sft/` to the same place in the box's fresh clone.

**2. `md5sum … && git diff --stat` (on the box)**
- `md5sum` makes a fingerprint of the file's bytes. `ad7c5f68…` is the same as on the laptop, so the copy is byte-for-byte identical.
- `git diff --stat` asks git what differs from the commit we cloned (`909ab75`, GitHub's `dist_side_merge`). The answer: only this file, with 80 lines added and 1 removed.
- So the box now holds exactly **GitHub's `dist_side_merge` + your task-2 change**, and nothing else.

## What `bluscript_zero_ckpt.cpp` is

It's BluTrain's **main training program**: one C++ file, 2,748 lines. Running it trains the model. In order, it does this:

1. **Model settings** (lines 128-137): 26 layers, width 2304, FFN 6144, context 4096, rope_theta 500000, vocab 50304. That is our 1.59B model.
2. **Precision settings**, such as `BLU_ALL_BF16`.
3. **GPU setup**: MPI + NCCL.
4. **Our new block (line 1030)**: load the weights from a checkpoint.
5. **Optimizers**: ZeRO-1 AdamW / Muon. Each copies the weights into its own fp32 "master" copy.
6. **Data**: the mixed loader (commoncrawl / code / math under `BLU_MIX_ROOT`).
7. **Checkpointing**: save every N steps, auto-resume.
8. **The training loop**:
   - validation (at step 0, then every 250 steps);
   - the training step: forward, loss, backward over 32 micro-batches, clip, optimizer update;
   - a per-step report;
   - a checkpoint save.

## What your 80 lines add (task 2)

**Why it's needed:** SFT must start from Navin's trained model (step 8000), not from random numbers. But his checkpoint also holds his optimizer state, step number and data position. For SFT we want **only the weights**, and everything else fresh: step 0, a new learning-rate schedule, a new optimizer.

**How it works, step by step:**
1. **Only if `BLU_INIT_FROM=<folder>` is set.** Otherwise the block is skipped and the trainer behaves exactly as before. So it's safe for colleagues.
2. It names our 262 weights `param_000000 … param_000261`, the same names the checkpoint uses.
3. On 1 GPU, it creates a one-GPU communication group, because the checkpoint loader needs one.
4. **`DistCheckpoint::load(…, optimizer = nullptr)`** reads `metadata.bin` (the table of contents) and copies each weight out of `data_rank_0.bin`. `nullptr` means: don't load the optimizer.
5. **`sync_back_to_model()`** puts the weights into the model's tensors. It does nothing extra when the dtypes match, which is why we run with `BLU_ALL_BF16=1`, as Navin did.
6. **With `BLU_INIT_VERIFY=1`:** for each of the 262 weights it copies the weight from GPU to CPU, computes its CRC32 checksum, and compares it with the checksum Navin's run stored. It prints `262/262 weights match`. Any mismatch stops the run with an error.
7. It prints `[init] weights only from … (its step 8000, loss 2.009818) …`.

**Why it sits before the optimizers:** each optimizer copies the model's weights into its fp32 master copy when it's created. If we loaded after that, the masters would still hold random numbers, and the first update would write them back over Navin's weights.

**The other small changes:**
- the 2 new `#include` lines at the top bring in the metadata reader and the CRC32 checker;
- the 1 changed line (2009) makes the checkpoint-saving code on 1 GPU reuse the group from point 3, instead of creating a second one with the same name.

> tool `Bash`: Show where print_run_ld_path is defined and who added it

I didn't add it anywhere, and I changed no file. It's part of **BluTrain's own `Makefile`**.

## Where it is
- **`Makefile` line 782:** `print_run_ld_path:` with one command, `@echo "$(RUN_LD_PATH)"`.
- **Who added it:** **kathir-23s on 2026-07-31**, commit `475bd30` ("naive run - week 1"). It's been in the team's Makefile since then.
- **Our copy is unchanged:** `git diff` shows no change to the Makefile on the laptop, and the box has the same file from GitHub.

`make print_run_ld_path` **builds nothing**. It only prints one value from the Makefile and exits.

## What it prints

`RUN_LD_PATH` (line 263) is 4 folders joined with `:`.

| Folder | Holds | Makefile line |
|---|---|---|
| `/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu` | NCCL (GPU communication library) | 181 |
| `…/BluTrain_sft/Tensor-Implementations/lib` | `libtensor.so` (the library we just built) | 160 |
| `…/BluTrain_sft/Profiler/lib` | `libprofiler.so` | 158 |
| `…/BluTrain_sft/dist/lib` | `libdist.so` | 162 |

On the box it prints `/usr/lib/x86_64-linux-gnu:/home/operator/gautam_k/BluTrain_sft/Tensor-Implementations/lib:…/Profiler/lib:…/dist/lib`.

## Why we need it
- **`_runner_` isn't a standalone program.** When it starts, it loads `libtensor.so`, `libprofiler.so`, `libdist.so` and NCCL.
- **Linux only searches standard system folders** for these files. `LD_LIBRARY_PATH` is the list of extra folders to search. Without it, the run fails at once with `error while loading shared libraries: libtensor.so: cannot open shared object file`.
- **`-x LD_LIBRARY_PATH`** in the `mpirun` command passes that same setting to the trainer process `mpirun` starts.

## Why this exact way
- **The Makefile itself tells us to launch like this.** Line 589 prints, at the end of `build-mpi`: `launch: LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$(RUN_LD_PATH):$LD_LIBRARY_PATH mpirun -np <N> -x LD_LIBRARY_PATH ./_runner_`.
- **Our step-5 line is that same recipe:**
  ```bash
  export LD_LIBRARY_PATH=$(make --no-print-directory print_run_ld_path):$LD_LIBRARY_PATH
  ```
  The only difference is that the Makefile works out the 4 folders instead of us typing them. `--no-print-directory` just stops make from adding "Entering directory…" text to what it prints.

If you want to see it first, run this alone on the box:

The check itself already exists in the library's code. Let me show exactly where, and who wrote it:
> tool `Bash`: Show where BLU_TOKEN_MAX is read and who added it

Same as before: **no file changed**, only a setting on the run command. The check is old library code written by colleagues.

## Where the check lives
| File (in `Tensor-Implementations`) | Lines | Used by | Added in |
|---|---|---|---|
| `include/MixedDataloader.h` | **581-607** | **our trainer's loader** (`MixedDataLoaderLite`) | `c6f0dbb`, 2026-09-18, "Mixed dataloader" |
| `include/DataLoader.h` | 429-462 | the older single-source loader | `6242c68`, 2026-08-07, "dataloader for zero1 v2" |

The library on the laptop has no local changes, and the box has the same commit (`d96b991`) from GitHub. Both commits show the author as `root`, meaning they were committed from a box with no git name set.

## How a setting like this works
- An environment variable is a named setting a program receives when it starts. The code reads it at line 586: `getenv_int("BLU_TOKEN_MAX", 0)`.
- **Not set:** the value is 0, so the check is **skipped**. That's the default, so nobody else is affected.
- **`BLU_TOKEN_MAX=50304`:** the check is **on**.

## What the check does when on
- For **every batch** the loader reads (B×T+1 tokens), it looks at every token id.
- The model has **50,304 rows** (ids 0-50303). If any id is **≥ 50304**, it prints a line such as:
  `[MixedLoader] OUT-OF-RANGE token ids: N of M in domain 'commoncrawl' shard … at token offset … (max id …)`
- It **only prints**. It never stops the run, and it costs microseconds.

## Why I want it on for this test
- **The loss kernel has no bounds check.** The comment at `DataLoader.h:430-439` warns that a wrong token id makes the loss silently read the wrong numbers, giving a garbage but normal-looking loss with no error at all.
- **Our flux files came from your laptop (June).** I haven't verified they were tokenized for this exact vocab.
- **If the files were bad,** the step-0 validation loss could look wrong, and we'd wrongly blame the checkpoint loading.
- **With the check on:** no warning means clean data, and then the validation number really tells us whether the weights loaded correctly.

Step 5 stays exactly as I gave it. Paste me the output when you've run it.

Yes, all bf16 includes the embedding. Today's log says `precision: resid bfloat16 | logits bfloat16 | embed bfloat16`. Only the 52 q/k-norm scales stay fp32 (6,656 numbers), because the attention kernel requires it.

But the **embedding is not where most of the memory is saved.** Here are the sizes:

**The embedding table is small:** 50,304 × 2,304 = 115.9 million numbers.

| What bf16 changes for the embedding | Saving |
|---|---|
| the table itself (4 → 2 bytes per number) | ~221 MiB |
| its gradient | ~221 MiB |
| the extra bf16 copy the output layer needed when the table was fp32 | ~221 MiB |
| the lookup output at B=8 (32,768 × 2,304) | ~144 MiB |
| **total** | **~0.8 GiB** |
| optimizer memory | **no change**: AdamW keeps fp32 master + 2 states either way (18,176 MB in both logs) |

**The bigger parts:**
1. **bf16 logits:** about **9.2 GiB** at B=8, measured on 09-24 (−4,716 MiB at B=4, which doubles at B=8). Note the earlier ~88 GiB run already had this on.
2. **bf16 residual stream** (the "resid" part of `BLU_ALL_BF16`): every one of the 26 layers keeps residual-stream tensors for the backward pass, and bf16 halves them. That's several GiB at B=8. I haven't measured the exact amount.

## One correction first

**Today's run was not an SFT run.** It only tested task 2, loading Navin's weights. The trainer still trains like pretraining: no answer-only masking, no SFT learning rate. The real "sample SFT runs" come after tasks 3-6.

## How much SFT data does a 1.5B model need?

**There's no fixed number.** It depends mostly on:
1. **How many skills you want.** Format alone needs little; each extra skill (math, code, instruction-following, safety) needs its own data.
2. **How strong the base model is.**

| Paper | Model size | SFT examples | What for |
|---|---|---|---|
| LIMA | 65B | 1,000 | format/style only |
| InstructGPT | up to 175B | ~13k | format + quality |
| Llama 2 | 7-70B | 27,540 | quality-focused |
| Tülu 3 | 8B, 70B | 939k | many skills |
| OLMo 3 Instruct | 7B, 32B | 2.15M | many skills |

Our base is small and briefly trained (1.5B on 8.4B tokens, report §8.5), so it knows less, and the papers' numbers may not carry over. **Your idea of measuring it ourselves is the right one.** It is exactly the data-size and data-mix study already in the report (§5.6, §8.3).

## Which of those datasets we can actually use (checked on Hugging Face today)

| Dataset | Size | Can we use it? |
|---|---|---|
| LIMA (`GAIR/lima`) | 1,000 | ⚠️ gated: needs a Hugging Face login and accepting its license ("other"). Check the license before use |
| Llama 2's SFT set | 27,540 | ❌ never released |
| InstructGPT's SFT set | ~13k | ❌ never released |
| Tülu 3 (`allenai/tulu-3-sft-mixture`) | 939,343 | ✅ public, ODC-BY |
| OLMo 3 Instruct (`allenai/Dolci-Instruct-SFT`) | 2,152,112 | ✅ public, ODC-BY |
| OLMo 3 Think (`allenai/Dolci-Think-SFT-7B`) | 2,268,178 (36 GB) | ✅ public, but long reasoning beyond our 4,096-token limit, so it's for the think model later |
| SmolTalk (`HuggingFaceTB/smoltalk`) | ~1.1M | ✅ public, built for small models |

## The experiment design I'd suggest (after the first runs work)

1. **Size curve, one source:** Tülu 3 at 1k → 10k → 100k → full. This answers how much is enough for 1.5B.
2. **Source comparison at the same size (100k):** Tülu 3 vs OLMo 3 Instruct vs SmolTalk.
3. **Hand-picked vs random:** LIMA 1k vs a random 1k from Tülu 3, if LIMA's license is OK.
4. **Skill removal:** drop math, instruction-following or safety data, and see which benchmark falls. This is how Tülu 3 proved each skill needs its own data.

Every arm uses the same learning rate, the same checkpoints and the same tests, plus a comparison with the base model.

**Cost:** at today's measured ~45k tokens/s on 1 GPU, 100k examples take ~2.5 h per epoch. Full Tülu 3 takes ~24 h per epoch on 1 GPU, so the big arms need GPUs 5+6 or length bucketing.

**One blocker for benchmarks at checkpoints:** BluTrain can't generate text yet (report gap 8).
- **Without generation** we can measure held-out loss and multiple-choice benchmarks (HellaSwag, MMLU, ARC).
- **With generation** we can also run IFEval, GSM8K, AlpacaEval and MT-Bench.
- Building generation is **report decision 4**, and needs your call: now, or after the first runs.

All three numbers are confirmed in the papers. Now the second part of your question: what each paper says about **releasing its data**.
> tool `Bash`: Find what each paper says about releasing its data

Here are the proofs, quoted word for word from the official papers (arXiv PDFs; page = PDF page).

## 1. LIMA: 1,000 examples
**Paper:** *LIMA: Less Is More for Alignment*, Meta AI, 2023, [arXiv 2305.11206](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.11206)

- **p.1:** *"…training LIMA, a 65B parameter LLaMa language model fine-tuned with the standard supervised loss on only **1,000 carefully curated prompts and responses**, without any reinforcement learning or human preference modeling."*
- **p.1:** *"…responses from LIMA are either equivalent or strictly preferred to GPT-4 in **43%** of cases; this statistic is as high as **58%** when compared to Bard and **65%** versus DaVinci003… these results strongly suggest that **almost all knowledge in large language models is learned during pretraining, and only limited instruction tuning data is necessary to teach models to produce high quality output.**"*
- **p.2:** *"We define the **Superficial Alignment Hypothesis**: A model's knowledge and capabilities are learnt almost entirely during pretraining, while alignment teaches it which subdistribution of formats should be used when interacting with users."*
- **Data released?** The paper text has **no release statement**. The 1,000 examples are on Hugging Face as [`GAIR/lima`](https://huggingface.co/datasets/GAIR/lima), but **gated**: you must log in and accept its license (marked "other"). I checked the Hugging Face API today.

## 2. Llama 2: 27,540 examples
**Paper:** *Llama 2: Open Foundation and Fine-Tuned Chat Models*, Meta, 2023, [arXiv 2307.09288](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.09288)

- **p.9:** *"**Quality Is All You Need.** Third-party SFT data is available from many different sources, but we found that many of these have insufficient diversity and quality…"*
- **p.9:** *"We found that SFT annotations in the order of **tens of thousands** was enough to achieve a high-quality result. We stopped annotating SFT after collecting a total of **27,540 annotations**. Note that we do not include any Meta user data."*
- **Data released? No.** The release list on **p.4** names **only models**: *"We are releasing the following models to the general public for research and commercial use: 1. Llama 2… 2. Llama 2-Chat…"*. The 27,540 annotations are not in it.

## 3. InstructGPT: ~13k examples
**Paper:** *Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback*, OpenAI, 2022, [arXiv 2203.02155](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)

- **p.7:** *"The **SFT dataset contains about 13k training prompts** (from the API and labeler-written), the RM dataset has 33k training prompts (from the API and labeler-written), and the PPO dataset has 31k training prompts (only from the API)."*
- **p.1:** *"…outputs from the **1.3B** parameter InstructGPT model are preferred to outputs from the **175B** GPT-3, despite having **100x fewer parameters**."*
- **Data released? No.** The only release it mentions is model outputs, **p.10**: *"We are releasing **samples from our models** on all of the sampling-based NLP tasks."* The training data includes prompts from OpenAI API customers.

## Also checked: Tülu 3 (open)
**Paper:** [arXiv 2411.15124](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124), **p.12, Table 7:** *"Total 23,327,961 | **939,344** | 425,145"*. The middle column is the SFT set. The Hugging Face copy has **939,343** rows, one fewer than the paper.

**In short:**
- LIMA's 1,000 can be used only after accepting its gated license.
- Llama 2's 27,540 and InstructGPT's ~13k were never released. Their papers release only models, or model samples.
- Tülu 3 (and OLMo 3) are fully public.

- It trains on **all tokens** (prompts too), so don't copy that. Hugging Face's **real** SmolLM3 recipe trains only the answer plus the end-of-turn token, the **same as our plan**.

**2. OpenThoughts**
- It's **long reasoning ("think") data**: OT-114k, OT2 (1.14M rows), OT3 (1.2M rows), all Apache-2.0.
- Almost none of it fits our **4,096-token** limit. OT3 averages about 11,600 tokens, and 62% of its rows are cut off with no final answer.
- Their own paper measured that keeping only short traces costs **−22%**.
- So it's for the **think model later**, once we have longer context.
- Their paper is still useful **now** for designing our data-size experiments, especially its size ladder 316 → 1K → 3.16K → 10K → 31.6K → 100K.

**3. Nvidia Llama-Nemotron post-training dataset**

- The useful part for our instruct model is small: **~22.6k single-turn chats** and **~15.7k safety examples** (the "reasoning off" rows).
- Rows generated by Llama models bring **Llama licence conditions** if we ever release a model trained on them.

Short answers.

**1. Why fastText's language model?** Only to **drop non-English rows** from the Tülu 3 sample, because our model and tokenizer are English.
- My first simple rule (count ASCII characters) couldn't catch Spanish, French or Turkish, since they're mostly ASCII too. It also wrongly dropped English tables and code.
- fastText's `lid.176` is the standard language detector used in big data pipelines. It caught 917 non-English rows (59 languages) and didn't drop English math or code.
- It runs only on the laptop, inside the preprocessing script. Nothing else uses it.

**2. The research is finished.** All 4 agents completed before my last message. **Nothing is running now**, neither the research nor any data build.

**3. Why a separate SFT dataloader?** Both loaders give the trainer the same shape, `B × 4096` uint16 on the GPU. But the **content is different**, so changing only the file names would silently break SFT:

| | Current loader (pretraining) | What SFT needs |
|---|---|---|
| Files | **one** token stream | **two** files: `inputs.bin` + `labels.bin` |
| Target | computed as **input shifted by one** | **read from `labels.bin`**, with 65535 on the prompt and padding |
| Reading | a sliding window over one long stream | **whole rows**, one example per row, always starting at position 0 |
| Order | sequential, never ends | **shuffled examples**, stops after N epochs |
| Counts | none | **valid-token count per micro-batch**, for the global denominator |

If we just pointed the old loader at our files, it would make the target "input shifted by one" again. Then **nothing would be masked**: it would train on prompts and padding, and rows would misalign at their edges. That is exactly the "SFT run that is secretly pretraining" the report warns about, and nothing would report it.

**Your choice:**
- **A (my recommendation):** a separate small loader in BluTrain (`sft/SftDataLoader.h`). The pretraining loader and the library stay untouched.
- **B:** add an "SFT mode" to the existing loader. That loader lives in the library repo (Tensor-Implementations), so it means changing shared pretraining code plus a library commit.

Which one?

### CLAUDE [2026-10-06 15:29 IST]

Here's the exact code of the existing loader, so you can see the difference for yourself:
> tool `Bash`: Show the existing loader's input/target code

Your intuition is mostly right: the loading is the same, `B × 4096` uint16 numbers onto the GPU. **The one real difference is where the target comes from.** In the existing loader (`DataLoader.h:507-508`):

```cpp
std::memcpy(x_buf_.data(), tokens,     BT * sizeof(u_int16_t));   // input  = tokens[pos ... pos+BT)
std::memcpy(y_buf_.data(), tokens + 1, BT * sizeof(u_int16_t));   // target = the SAME file, shifted by 1
```

The target is always "the same file, shifted by one". It **never reads a labels file**, so 65535 can never appear in the target and nothing can be masked.

A small example, one row:

| | position 1 | 2 | 3 | 4 | 5 | 6 | 7 | 8 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| input (`inputs.bin`) | `<\|user\|>` | Hi | `\n` | `<\|assistant\|>` | Hello | . | EOS | PAD |
| **existing loader's target** (input shifted) | Hi ✗ | `\n` ✗ | `<\|assistant\|>` ✗ | Hello ✓ | . ✓ | EOS ✓ | PAD ✗ | first token of the **next row** ✗ |
| **SFT target** (`labels.bin`) | – | – | – | Hello | . | EOS | – | – |

With the existing loader, the model would also train on the **prompt** and on **padding**, and it would cross into the **next example**. Our `labels.bin` would simply be ignored.

**So the only extra things needed:**
1. **Read the target from `labels.bin`** instead of shifting. This is the whole point of SFT masking.
2. **Count the valid (non-65535) tokens** per micro-batch, for the global denominator.

Shuffling isn't needed for the sample run, because the preprocessing already wrote the rows in random order.

**Two ways to do exactly that:**
- **Change the existing loader:** add "use a labels file instead of shifting". It's in the library (`Tensor-Implementations`). Two code paths in it need the change (the fast prefetch path and the fallback), plus how it finds its files. It's opt-in, so pretraining stays the same.
- **A small separate loader** in BluTrain that does only these two things. No library change.

Which one do you prefer?

### CLAUDE [2026-10-06 15:36 IST]

Yes, you're correct. One small word fix: by "validation" you mean the **target** (the token the loss compares against), not the validation set.

| | Pretraining (today) | SFT |
|---|---|---|
| Input at position t | token t of `tokens.bin` | token t of `inputs.bin` |
| Target at position t | token **t+1 of the same file** (the loader shifts it) | position **t of `labels.bin`** |
| What's in the target | always the next token | **the next token (t+1)** where the next token is part of the answer or the end token, otherwise **65535** (prompt and padding) |

So the "t+1" is still there, but it's **already done inside `labels.bin`** by the preprocessing script (`labels = ids[1:]`, then masked). The loader reads input and target at the **same position t**, with no shift in the loader.

The only other addition is the **count of non-65535 targets** per micro-batch, which feeds the global denominator.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-06 15:58 IST]

Not quite. **Nothing is divided by 8 anywhere.** Here is what the global denominator is.

**1. What we count:** in every row, the **valid tokens** are the labels that are not 65535: the answer tokens plus the EOS after each answer. You're right about that part. The script already stored this count per row in `valid_counts.bin`.

**2. The global denominator** = the valid tokens of the **whole optimizer step**: all micro-steps **and** all GPUs, added up. That's one number per step.

**3. Every micro-step's loss kernel** then does:
`loss = (sum of the per-token losses in this micro-batch) / (the step's total)`

The same total is used in every micro-step. Gradient accumulation then adds the micro-steps up, so the step's gradient is the **mean over every answer token of the step**.

**A small example:** 1 GPU, 2 micro-steps, 2 rows each.

| | rows' valid tokens | micro-batch total |
|---|---|---|
| micro-step 1 | 100 + 300 | 400 |
| micro-step 2 | 50 + 50 | 100 |
| **step total** | | **500** |

| Method | weight of each token in micro-step 1 | weight of each token in micro-step 2 |
|---|---|---|
| **Today** (each micro-batch divides by its own count, then × 1/2) | 1/800 | **1/200: 4× more** |
| **Global denominator** (both divide by 500, then add) | **1/500** | **1/500: equal** ✅ |

Today, a micro-batch with short answers gets too much weight. With the global denominator, **every answer token counts the same**.

**So what changes in the trainer (task 6):**
1. **Before the first micro-step of a step:** the loader gives the valid count of the next 8 micro-batches (`valid_tokens_ahead(8)`). Sum it across GPUs (all-reduce SUM) to get one number, and put it in a 1-element GPU tensor.
2. **In every micro-step:** `sparse_cross_entropy_loss(logits, target, 65535, &total)`.
3. **Backward seed:** change `1/8` to `W` (the number of GPUs, so 1 on one GPU). The `1/8` is no longer needed because the total already covers all 8 micro-steps. The `W` cancels ZeRO, which averages the gradients across GPUs, while our total already counts all GPUs.

About your second guess: on one GPU, "total ÷ 8" with the old `1/8` seed gives the same number. But "total, seed W" is the clean form, and it stays correct on several GPUs.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-06 16:05 IST]

Here it is step by step, with tiny numbers.

## Step 1: what the loss is

For every **answer token**, the model gives one number: **how wrong it was** (its token loss). Prompt and padding tokens give no number, because they're ignored (65535).

For one optimizer step we want **the average wrongness over all answer tokens the step saw**:

> **average = (add up all the answer-token losses) ÷ (how many answer tokens there are)**

The weight update (the gradient) is computed from this average. Whatever weight a token has in the average is the weight it has in the update.

## Step 2: why it's done in pieces

One optimizer step uses **8 micro-batches** (gradient accumulation), because the GPU can't hold all of them at once.
- It runs micro-batch 1, computes its gradient, and **adds it into a buffer**.
- Then micro-batch 2, and adds it in.
- After all 8, it updates the weights **once**.

So the average has to be built from 8 pieces, and each piece only sees its own tokens.

## Step 3: a tiny example (1 GPU, 2 micro-batches)

| | answer-token losses | sum | count |
|---|---|---|---|
| micro-batch 1 | 2, 2, 2, 2 | 8 | 4 |
| micro-batch 2 | 6 | 6 | 1 |
| **whole step** | | **14** | **5** |

**Correct average** = 14 ÷ 5 = **2.8**

**Today's method:** each micro-batch averages itself, then the two are averaged.
- micro 1: 8 ÷ 4 = 2
- micro 2: 6 ÷ 1 = 6
- result: (2 + 6) ÷ 2 = **4.0** ❌

The **single token** of micro-batch 2 counted as much as **all 4 tokens** of micro-batch 1.

**Global denominator:** first count all answer tokens of the step, 4 + 1 = **5**. Then:
- micro 1 computes 8 ÷ **5** = 1.6
- micro 2 computes 6 ÷ **5** = 1.2
- they are **added** in the buffer: 1.6 + 1.2 = **2.8** ✅

**That 5 is the global denominator.** Every micro-batch divides by the same 5, and every token gets the same weight (1/5).

## Step 4: why we must know the 5 before micro-batch 1 runs

Micro-batch 1 divides by 5 **while it runs**, and its gradient goes into the buffer right away. We can't go back and change it later. So we count first. That's easy, because the loader knows each row's count from `valid_counts.bin`, and it adds up the next 8 micro-batches' counts before running them.

## Step 5: with 2 GPUs

Each GPU sees different micro-batches.

| | sum of losses | answer tokens |
|---|---|---|
| GPU 0 | 14 | 5 |
| GPU 1 | 30 | 15 |
| **both** | **44** | **20** |

**Correct average** = 44 ÷ 20 = **2.2**

1. The GPUs **exchange their counts and add them**: 5 + 15 = **20**, now known on both GPUs. This exchange is the "all-reduce SUM".
2. Each GPU divides by **20**: GPU 0 gets 14 ÷ 20 = 0.7, GPU 1 gets 30 ÷ 20 = 1.5.
3. These should be **added**: 0.7 + 1.5 = **2.2** ✅

But **ZeRO combines the GPUs by averaging**: (0.7 + 1.5) ÷ 2 = 1.1, which is **half** ❌. So at the start of backward each GPU multiplies by **W = 2**, the number of GPUs: 1.4 and 3.0, then ZeRO's average (1.4 + 3.0) ÷ 2 = **2.2** ✅. That multiplier is the "backward seed = W".

**Why today's seed is 1/8:** today each micro-batch averages itself, so the 8 micro-batches then need averaging (÷ 8). With the global denominator, the 20 already covers all 8 micro-batches and all GPUs, so the ÷ 8 must go, and the seed becomes **W**. On one GPU, W = 1.

## The 3 trainer changes (task 6)

| | Today | SFT |
|---|---|---|
| Before a step | nothing | count the answer tokens of the next 8 micro-batches, add across GPUs, put the total in a GPU tensor |
| Loss call in each micro-step | `loss(logits, target)` | `loss(logits, target, 65535, &total)` |
| Backward seed | `1/8` | `W` (the number of GPUs) |

### CLAUDE [2026-10-06 17:04 IST]

**1. One division at the end vs. dividing in each micro-step**

**Mathematically they're identical.** But note what actually gets added up across micro-steps: **not the loss numbers, but the gradients.**
- After micro-step 1's backward, its gradients (one number per parameter, **1.59 billion numbers**) are added into the gradient buffer. The micro-step's loss number has done its job and is only logged.
- "Divide once at the end" would mean: run the micro-steps undivided, then multiply all **1.59 billion** gradient numbers by 1/total before the optimizer step. That's an **extra pass over every gradient**, plus new code in the optimizer path.
- Dividing inside each micro-step costs **nothing extra**. The loss kernel already divides by something (today 8 × 4096), so we just give it a different number, the global total. The library's loss op was built for exactly this (`denom`), and torchtitan does the same thing.
- **Precision:** about the same either way. bf16 has the same exponent range as fp32, so nothing overflows.

So it's not that "at the end" is bad. Ours just fits the existing code with **zero extra work**.

**2. Yes: one loss number produces a gradient for every parameter.**
- The loss is **one number** at the top of the computation.
- **Backward** (backpropagation) asks, for **every parameter**: "if I nudge this parameter a little, how much does that loss number change?" That's the gradient: **one gradient number per parameter number**.
- The chain rule passes it back through every layer: logits → output layer → each transformer block → embedding.
- Backward **starts from the "seed"**, the number the loss's own gradient begins with (normally 1). Everything is multiplied through from there, which is why changing the seed (`1/8` → `W`) scales every gradient.

**With 8 micro-steps:** each micro-step has its own loss number, which produces gradients for all parameters, and these are **added** into the buffer. Since the gradient of a sum equals the sum of the gradients, after 8 micro-steps the buffer holds exactly the gradients of **one step loss** (the 8 micro losses added up). And because each micro loss was divided by the global total, that step loss **is the average over every answer token of the step**.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-06 17:07 IST]

Right: **the global denominator divides the loss, not the gradients.** You understood it correctly.

**Where it's used:** in the loss kernel, for each micro-batch:

> loss = (sum of the token losses of the answer + EOS tokens) ÷ **global total**

**Why the gradients come out divided too, automatically:** dividing by a fixed number passes straight through the backward. If loss = (sum) ÷ D, then the gradient of the loss = (gradient of the sum) ÷ D. So during backward, every gradient automatically carries the same ÷ D, and nobody touches the gradients separately.

Inside the kernel, the backward for each answer token's logits is `(softmax − one-hot) ÷ D`, and it's **0** for ignored tokens. The library's loss backward already takes the same `denom` tensor for exactly this.

**Why I talked about gradients before:** across the 8 micro-steps, the thing that **accumulates in the buffer** is the gradients, not the loss values. The "divide once at the end" alternative would have meant dividing that gradient buffer. **Our method divides the loss in each micro-step**, and the gradients simply follow.

## There are 2 methods

**Method 1, "average of averages"**: each micro-batch divides by its **own** token count, then the result is divided by the number of micro-steps. **This is what BluTrain does today.**

**Method 2, "global token count"**: count the tokens of the **whole step** (all micro-steps, all GPUs) and divide by that one number. **This is our SFT plan.**

## Who does what (with proof)

| Framework | Method | Proof (file:line) |
|---|---|---|
| **PyTorch itself** (`CrossEntropyLoss`) | it only averages **one call** (one micro-batch); gradient accumulation is left to your training loop | `torch/nn/modules/loss.py:1278-1280`: *"ignore_index … the loss is averaged over non-ignored targets"* |
| **nanoGPT** (Karpathy, pretraining) | **Method 1** | `train.py:292,301`: `for micro_step in range(gradient_accumulation_steps):` … `loss = loss / gradient_accumulation_steps` |

| **Hugging Face Transformers Trainer** | **Method 2, for every run** (pretraining or SFT) whenever labels exist | `trainer.py:1855-1859` takes `gradient_accumulation_steps` batches per step; `:2318` `num_items_in_batch = sum(labels.ne(-100).sum() …)`; `:2325` sums it over GPUs; `:1892` passes it to every micro-step. `loss/loss_utils.py` `fixed_cross_entropy`: `reduction = "sum"` … `loss = loss / num_items_in_batch` |

| Hugging Face | multiplies the loss by the **number of GPUs**, exactly like our seed W | `trainer.py:2183-2190`: `loss *= loss_scale` (= `num_processes`) |

## Answers to your questions

1. **For pretraining, is Method 1 fine?** **Yes.** Every micro-batch has exactly the same number of tokens (nothing ignored), so the average of averages equals the true average. That's why nanoGPT, Megatron's default and today's BluTrain are all correct for pretraining.
2. **Do they use the SFT method for pretraining too?** **torchtitan and Hugging Face: yes, always.** For pretraining it gives the same result. **Megatron:** it's an optional flag (required for packing). **nanoGPT:** no.
3. **Are they doing the same as us?**
   - Our **arrangement** (pretraining unchanged, SFT uses the global count) matches **Megatron's** (default vs flag).
   - Our **way of dividing** (each micro-step divides its loss by the global count, seed = W) matches **torchtitan and Hugging Face**.
   - The other valid way, dividing the gradients once at the end, is what **Megatron's flag** does.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-06 18:18 IST]

Let's use small numbers. One thing to fix first: **the first average does not get bigger because a micro-batch has fewer tokens.** An average shows how wrong the tokens are *on average*, whatever their number. What the token count changes is the **weight** in the second average. That's the whole problem.

## The example: 1 GPU, 2 micro-batches

| | answer tokens counted | loss of each token | sum | 1st average |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Micro-batch A** (long answers) | 8 | 1.0 each | 8 | 8 ÷ 8 = **1.0** |
| **Micro-batch B** (one short answer) | 2 | 4.0 each | 8 | 8 ÷ 2 = **4.0** |
| **whole step** | **10** | | **16** | |

B's average is higher because **its tokens are harder** (loss 4.0), not because there are fewer of them. If B's 2 tokens had loss 1.0, its average would also be 1.0.

## Case 1: average of averages (today's method, used for SFT)

> second average = (1.0 + 4.0) ÷ 2 = **2.5**

Each micro-batch gets **half** the total, whatever its size. So how much does **each token** count?

| token | share of the final loss |
|---|---|
| each of A's 8 tokens | 50% ÷ 8 = **6.25%** `█▎` |
| each of B's 2 tokens | 50% ÷ 2 = **25%** `█████` |

## Case 2: one global average (correct)

> (8 + 8) ÷ 10 = **1.6**

| token | share of the final loss |
|---|---|
| each of A's 8 tokens | 1 ÷ 10 = **10%** `██` |
| each of B's 2 tokens | 1 ÷ 10 = **10%** `██` |

## Side by side

```
                    A tokens (8 of them)                 B tokens (2)
Correct (global):   ██ ██ ██ ██ ██ ██ ██ ██              ██ ██          -> loss 1.6
Avg of averages:    █▎ █▎ █▎ █▎ █▎ █▎ █▎ █▎              █████ █████    -> loss 2.5
```

**What goes wrong with the average of averages:**
1. **The update is skewed.** The weights decide how hard the model is pushed to fix each token. Each token of the **short** answer is pushed **4× harder** than each token of the long answers (25% vs 6.25%). The model over-learns short answers and under-learns long ones.
2. **The reported loss is wrong:** 2.5 instead of the true 1.6. The training curves would mislead us.

## Why this never mattered in pretraining

Every micro-batch has **exactly 8 × 4,096 = 32,768 tokens**, and none are ignored. Each micro-batch's half is split over the same number of tokens, so every token gets the same share. Both methods give **exactly the same number**.

In SFT, micro-batches can easily differ a lot. For example, one has 400 answer tokens (8 short answers) and another has 8,000 (8 long ones). Then each short-answer token would count **20×** more than each long-answer token. **The global average fixes that: every answer token counts the same.**

### CLAUDE [2026-10-06 18:32 IST]

Good question, and the answer is reassuring: **"equal share" does not mean every token gets the same loss or the same update.** It means every token gets the **same multiplier** (1/N). Each token **keeps its own loss**, so a more-wrong token still counts more.

## Same example (A: 8 tokens with loss 1.0 · B: 2 tokens with loss 4.0)

**Global average:** each token's contribution = its own loss × 1/10.

| token | own loss | × multiplier | = contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| each A token | 1.0 | × 1/10 | **0.1** |
| each B token | 4.0 | × 1/10 | **0.4**, so **4× more**, because it's 4× more wrong ✅ |

**Average of averages:**

| token | own loss | × multiplier | = contribution |
|---|---|---|---|
| each A token | 1.0 | × 1/16 | **0.0625** |
| each B token | 4.0 | × 1/4 | **1.0**, so **16× more**: 4× because it's more wrong (real) **× 4× from the unequal multiplier (fake)** ❌ |

So with the global average, **the only reason one token counts more than another is that it's more wrong**. That is exactly the "correct update" you're describing. The average of averages adds a fake extra factor that depends on which micro-batch a token happened to land in.

## And the update itself follows each token's own error

For cross-entropy, a token's gradient is **(the model's predicted probabilities) − (the right answer)**.
- **Model already right** (gives the right token high probability): the difference is ≈ 0, so a **tiny** update.
- **Model very wrong** (gives the right token low probability): the difference is large, so a **big** update.

So "each token is updated according to its own loss" is **built into the cross-entropy math already**. The 1/N is just one shared scale, like the learning rate, applied equally to everyone.

**Are there methods that deliberately weight tokens differently?** Yes, as a research choice: for example **DFT** (weights tokens by the model's confidence, arXiv 2508.05629, already in our report's §8.3 experiment list) and focal loss (pushes hard tokens extra). Plain SFT (Tülu 3, Hugging Face, torchtitan) uses equal multipliers, and we can test DFT later as an experiment.

## 1. Your backward picture is correct

1. In the global average, backward starts each answer token at the **same share, 1/N**. Ignored tokens get 0.
2. Each token then multiplies that share by **its own error**, (predicted probabilities − the right answer):

| how sure the model was of the right token (p) | that token's loss | its push (error size) |
|---|---|---|
| 0.9 (almost right) | 0.105 | **0.1** (small) |
| 0.1 (quite wrong) | 2.303 | **0.9** (big) |
| 0.01 (very wrong) | 4.605 | **0.99** (it can't go past 1) |

3. Backprop carries each token's push through every layer, so each weight's gradient = **the sum of all tokens' pushes on it**.
4. The optimizer then moves each weight a lot or a little based on that.

✅ So the **equal 1/N is only the shared scale**, and each token's own error decides how much it moves the weights. One precision: a bigger loss means a bigger push, but **not in exact proportion**. The push tops out near 1, while the loss keeps growing.

## 2. What DFT and focal loss change (from their papers)

They multiply each token's loss by an **extra weight that depends on p**, on purpose:

| loss | per token | what it does | hard token (p=0.1) vs easy (p=0.9) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **plain cross-entropy** (our v1) | −log p | every token the same multiplier | **22×** more |
| **focal loss** (Lin et al. 2017, arXiv 1708.02002) | −(1−p)² · log p | *"down-weights the loss assigned to well-classified examples"*, so hard tokens dominate. Built for object detection, where *"the vast number of easy negatives"* would overwhelm training | **~1,770×** more |
| **DFT** (Wu et al. 2025, arXiv 2508.05629) | −p · log p, with p treated as a fixed number (no gradient through it) | *"rescaling the objective function with the probability of this token"*. **The opposite of focal:** tokens the model finds unlikely count **less**. They argue plain SFT's gradient *"implicitly encode[s] a problematic reward structure"* that hurts generalization, and report better math and code results from *"a single-line change"* | only **2.4×** more |

## 3. "If ours is correct, how can they be correct too?"

They answer **different questions**.
- **Our global average is correct** in the sense that it computes exactly the objective we chose (plain cross-entropy, every token equal), **without the accidental micro-batch bias**. Plain cross-entropy = "make the training answers as likely as possible", and it's what Tülu 3, Hugging Face and torchtitan use.
- **Focal and DFT deliberately pick a different objective.** It's not an accident, it's a design choice with a goal: focal focuses on hard tokens, DFT aims for better generalization.
- They even **pull in opposite directions** (focal up-weights hard tokens, DFT down-weights them). So they're **trade-offs to test**, not one "right answer". Both would still use our global token count for normalization.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-06 19:02 IST]

**1. Is the final loss number just for reference? Yes, mostly.**

- **Its value** (for example 1.6) is **not used anywhere in the backward**. The cross-entropy gradient for a token is (predicted probabilities − right answer) × (its multiplier), and the loss value doesn't appear in it. So the number is for **logging and monitoring**: training curves, validation, spotting NaN.
- **What backward does need is the "÷ N" part**, the derivative of the average. Averaging N token losses means each token starts its backward with **1/N**.
- **So yes, backprop can start "before the average":** give each answer token a starting gradient of 1/N (and 0 to ignored tokens) and you get **exactly the same gradients**. Our loss kernel's backward already works this way: it computes every token's gradient directly as `(softmax − one-hot) × 1/N × seed`, without needing the scalar's value. Frameworks only keep the scalar as the **starting point** of autograd (you call `.backward()` on it).
- **One caution:** if you start each token with **1** instead of 1/N (a sum, not an average), every gradient becomes **N times bigger**. That acts like an N-times bigger learning rate, which changes training. So the 1/N must be there, either through the average or in the per-token start.

**2. With the global average, are DFT and focal different from ours? Yes, still different.**

All three divide by the **same global N**. They differ in the **weight on each token**:

| | step loss |
|---|---|
| ours (plain) | Σ ( −log p ) ÷ N |
| focal | Σ ( (1−p)² · −log p ) ÷ N |
| DFT | Σ ( p · −log p ) ÷ N, with p treated as a constant in backward |

The ÷ N normalization is the same. The per-token weight differs, so the gradients differ, so the training differs.

**3. Do we need to test them, and how? Two kinds of test:**

| What we want to know | How | Needs the training script? |
|---|---|---|
| **Is the implementation right?** (loss values and gradients match the formula; ignored tokens get 0; the global N is used) | a **standalone test**: random logits and labels, compare the GPU kernel against a simple CPU/NumPy reference. Exactly like our 136-case loss test, and fine on the laptop GPU | ❌ no |
| **Does it give a better model?** | real **SFT runs** with the training script: same data, same LR, same steps, comparing held-out loss and benchmarks for plain vs DFT vs focal | ✅ yes, nothing replaces this |

So: standalone tests prove they're **built correctly**, and training runs prove whether they **help**. Both are future tasks (saved), to do after v1 SFT works.

The doc is done. All three of your questions are checked in the code, and the first one also in PyTorch.

## 1. Is 1/N applied twice? No.

- **Backward never uses the loss value.** The backward kernel computes, for each token, `(softmax − one-hot) × seed ÷ N` (`LossKernels.cu:704`). The loss number, for example 1.204, is not an input to the backward at all.
- **The seed is not the loss value.** Today it is 1/32: one over the number of micro-steps, set at `bluscript_zero_ckpt.cpp:1796`. That is a different factor from 1/N. So each token gets 1/32 × 1/N, one of each.
- **How far it carries:** you're right that the 1/N belongs to the step from "one number" to "per-token losses". It is put in only there. From there it is carried to every weight, because each layer of the backward only multiplies by its own factor. Nothing applies 1/N again.
- **PyTorch run:** I used p = 0.9 and p = 0.1 for the right token, with N = 2.
  - The gradients on the right logits are −0.05 and −0.45.
  - The loss value 1.204 appears nowhere in them.
  - With a seed of 1/32, they come out exactly 32 times smaller.

## 2. For SFT, does the loss backward use the global N? The library does; the trainer doesn't yet.

- **Library: checked, correct.** Your tensor holding the global count (`denom`) is used for both passes:
  - the forward divides by it;
  - the same tensor is saved for the backward (`LossOps.cpp:493-495`);
  - the backward kernel divides by it (`:704`).
  
  So the forward and the backward can never use different N values.
- **Trainer: not wired yet.** It still calls the loss with 2 arguments (`:2164`), so each micro-batch divides by its own 32,768. Changing that is task 6.
- **Risk:** don't plug in the SFT loader without the 65535 loss call. A label of 65535 is beyond the 50,304 vocabulary, and the kernel has no bounds check, so it reads out of bounds. Both must go in the same change.

## 3. Does the F1 NaN fix check the final loss? No, it checks the gradient norm.

There are two checks in each step:
- **Old check, the loss number** (`:2270`): runs after backward and before the update. It stops the run with exit code 2.
- **F1, the gradient norm:** runs inside the optimizer's step, before any weight changes. It stops the run with exit code 4.

**Before F1, your guess was right.** A NaN gradient with a normal-looking loss:
1. passed through clipping, because a NaN norm made the clip factor 1.0, i.e. no clipping;
2. made AdamW write NaN into the weights;
3. got saved to disk if that step saved a checkpoint;
4. turned the next step's forward into a NaN loss, where the old check stopped the run, one step late.

Muon's 2-D matrices never stopped: they silently stopped learning.

## The doc

- **Files:** `~/Downloads/sft_research/loss_calculation_in_pretraining_and_sft.md`, copied to `work_docs`. Both copies are identical.
- **Name:** I fixed the typo and the space from "los_calculation_in pretraining_and_sft.md".
- **Contents:** shapes, all the share examples and bars, the framework proofs, the NaN flow, DFT and focal loss, and how to test them.
- **New real-data number:** in our stage-0 data, the answer-token count of a micro-batch varies within one step, by 2.5× typically and up to 4.1×. So the "average of averages" would weigh some tokens up to 4× more than others.
- **One correction to what I told you earlier:** "starting each token with 1 instead of 1/N acts like an N-times bigger learning rate" is only true for plain SGD. AdamW and Muon mostly cancel an overall scale. It still matters for clipping and Adam's epsilon. Fixed in §6.8.
- **Found while reading** (§12):

Yes to both. Both checks run after backward and before the weight update. The difference is which number each one checks.

```
one optimizer step
 ├─ zero the gradients                                     :2155
 ├─ 32 micro-steps: forward → loss → backward              :2160-2213
 │      (gradients are added up; each micro loss is added up on the GPU, :2183)
 ├─ loss for the log: copy to CPU, ÷32, add the other GPUs, ÷W        :2216-2224
 ├─ CHECK 1 (old): is that loss NaN/Inf?  → exit 2                    :2270
 ├─ for each optimizer group, smallest first                          :2386
 │    step():
 │     ├─ combine the gradients of all GPUs
 │     ├─ grad norm² = sum of g² over the group's gradients, all GPUs added
 │     ├─ CHECK 2 (F1): is the norm² NaN/Inf?  → exit 4      ShardedOptimizer.cpp:1285
 │     ├─ clip
 │     └─ AdamW/Muon update (weights, m, v), then all-gather
 └─ checkpoint save (every ckpt_freq steps)                           :2566-2591
```

## Check 1 (old): the loss number

- **What it checks:** the step's loss, one number.
- **How it gets it:**
  1. each micro-step's loss is added on the GPU (`:2183`);
  2. after the last micro-step, the 4 bytes are copied to the CPU and divided by 32;
  3. the GPUs add their values together (MPI all-reduce), then divide by W (`:2216-2224`).
- **How it detects:** `std::isnan(loss) || std::isinf(loss)`. One bad token is enough, because NaN spreads: NaN + anything = NaN.
  - Example micro losses: 2.1, 2.3, **NaN**, 2.2 … → the sum is NaN → caught.
  - Every GPU sees the same summed value, so every GPU stops.

## Check 2 (F1): the gradient norm

- **What it checks:** one number per optimizer group, the sum of the squares of all its gradient numbers. The optimizer already computes this every step for clipping and for the logged grad norm.
- **How it gets it:**
  1. after the gradients of all GPUs are combined, a GPU kernel runs `total_sq += val * val` over every gradient number (`MultiTensorKernels.cu:137`);
  2. the GPUs add their parts (`:1243`), so every GPU has the same number;
  3. it is copied to the CPU (`:1253`).
- **How it detects:** `!std::isfinite(nsq)` (`:1285`). One bad gradient number anywhere ruins the sum:

| gradients | squares | sum | result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0.1, −0.2, 0.3 | 0.01, 0.04, 0.09 | 0.14 | continue |
| 0.1, **NaN**, 0.3 | 0.01, NaN, 0.09 | **NaN** | stop |
| 0.1, **Inf**, 0.3 | 0.01, Inf, 0.09 | **Inf** | stop |
| 0.1, **3e20**, 0.3 | 0.01, 9e40, 0.09 | 9e40 is above float's max (3.4e38), so **Inf** | stop (a real explosion) |

So one number checks all ~1.6 billion gradient numbers, at the cost of a single comparison on the CPU. It then throws, the trainer catches it (`:2411`), and the run exits with code 4.

## Why both are needed, even though both run at the same point

- **The loss is made in the forward.** If a NaN is created in the backward (for example, a value too big for the number format in one layer's backward; in our test we put a NaN straight into one gradient), this step's loss is still finite, so check 1 passes.
- **Before F1, nothing stopped it:**
  1. the update wrote the NaN into the weights;
  2. the next step's forward produced a NaN loss;
  3. check 1 caught it there, one step late.
- **F1 looks at the gradients themselves**, so it catches the NaN in the same step.

## One correction to what I said

I said F1 stops the run "before any weight changes". To be exact, it's before **that group's** update.
- The optimizer groups (one per parameter dtype; with Muon, the Muon groups plus the AdamW groups) are stepped one at a time, smallest first (`:1490-1497`).
- If only a later group has the NaN, the earlier groups have already updated in GPU memory, using their own finite gradients.
- That's harmless, because the run is killed at once and no checkpoint is written.
- Muon and v2 are the same: their checks (`ShardedMuon.cpp:1225`, `SymmetricShardedOptimizer.cpp:1045`) run before their updates. In Muon's case that is before the momentum write that used to freeze matrices silently.
