**1. The fused-kernel problem.** It appears whenever the number of tokens in a micro-batch changes. Not only with bucketing:

| Method | Tokens per micro-batch | Fused kernel's fixed N |
|---|---|---|
| v1 (pad every chat to 4096) | always 8 × 4096 | ✅ fine |
| v1.5 (bucketing) | 8 × T, T changes | ❌ breaks |
| v2, packed into fixed [8, 4096] rows | always 8 × 4096 | ✅ fine |
| v2 "padding-free" (all chats in one flat stream, variable size) | changes | ❌ breaks |

**2. Which is fastest.** I simulated it on our real 5,000 stage-0 chats (mean 1,238 tokens, median 1,154, longest 4,069), with our model's work per token and per attention pair:

| Method | Useful tokens (not padding) | Total work vs v1 | Speed-up (upper bound) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **v1** (today) | 30.2% | 100% | ×1.00 |
| **v1.5** realistic (shuffle, sort each 64-chat step, pad to the longest ×256) | 79.8% | 35.2% | **×2.84** |
| v1.5 ideal (whole dataset sorted; not usable in practice) | 90.5% | 30.7% | ×3.26 |
| **v2** packing + block-diagonal mask | **99.6%** | **27.8%** | **×3.60** |
| v2 without the mask | 99.6% | 30.3% | ×3.30, and **wrong**: chats see each other |

- **v2 is the fastest and most efficient.** Almost no padding, and attention is cheapest because each chat only attends inside itself.
- Without the mask, packing is both slower (attention runs over the whole 4096 row) and wrong.
- **These are upper bounds.** The optimizer step and gradient all-reduce happen once per step and don't shrink, so the real speed-ups will be somewhat lower.

**3. Cost to build each one:**

| | v1.5 | v2 |
|---|---|---|
| Attention kernel | no change (T must be a multiple of 256) | **new**: block-diagonal mask in forward and backward, plus a guard for fully-masked tiles |
| RoPE | no change | positions must restart at 0 for each chat |
| Loader | sort inside each step, pad per micro-batch | pack chats into rows, pass chat boundaries |
| GEMMs | **new shapes** (M = 8·T changes), so the BluBLAS dispatch must be checked | same shapes as today |
| Risk | low | high: a mask bug gives no error, the loss still goes down |

**What I'd do:**
- **v1.5 first.** It gets most of the gain (×2.84 of a possible ×3.60) with no kernel change.
- **v2 later**, for the extra ~27% on top of v1.5 (35.2% → 27.8% work).
- v2 becomes a must for think-model SFT with long traces.

Both are fine with our loss, because we already divide by the global trained-token count. Each token keeps the same weight however the chats are grouped.

The simulation script is `scratchpad/pack/pack_sim.py`, if you want to re-run it on other data.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-08 16:22 IST]

Yes, **v2 is the most efficient**. I mixed two things together earlier, so here they are separately.

## The row length (T) and padding in each method

| | Chats per row | Row length T | Padding | Attention change? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **v1** (today) | 1 | always 4096 | lots (~70%) | no |
| **v1.5** (bucketing) | 1 | **changes per micro-batch** (the longest chat in it, rounded up to 256) | some (~20%) | no |
| **v2** (packing) | many | **always 4096** | tiny (~0.4%) | **yes**: each chat may see only itself |

So the row length changes in **v1.5**, not in v2. The "variable size" I mentioned for v2 was a different style, "padding-free" (all chats in one flat stream with no rows). We don't need that. Packing into fixed 4096 rows is the right choice for us.

## v1.5: still one chat per row, just shorter rows

Sort the chats inside each step by length, put similar lengths in the same micro-batch, and pad only up to the longest one in that micro-batch:

```
v1 (today), every row padded to 4096:
row 1: [chat A 1,200][pad ......................................... 2,896]

v1.5, micro-batch of 8 similar chats, T = 1,280 (longest 1,250 → rounded up to 1,280):
row 1: [chat A 1,200][pad 80]
row 2: [chat B 1,250][pad 30]
row 3: [chat C 1,180][pad 100]
 ...
```

- Still one chat per row, padding at the end. Attention only looks back, so no attention change is needed, same as v1.
- Padding still exists, just much less: on our data, 79.8% of tokens are real vs 30.2% in v1.

## v2: several chats in one 4096 row

```
row (T = 4096):
tokens:     [ chat A: 1,200 ][ chat B: 1,500 ][ chat C: 1,380 ][pad 16]
positions:   0 … 1,199        0 … 1,499        0 … 1,379        (RoPE restarts per chat)
labels:      A's own labels    B's own labels   C's own labels   65535
             (65535 on A's     (65535 on B's    (65535 on C's
              prompt)           prompt)          prompt)
```

The attention mask has to be **block-diagonal**: each chat sees only itself, and only backwards.

```
            A A A   B B B   C C C   pad
A           ■
A           ■ ■
A           ■ ■ ■
B                   ■
B                   ■ ■
B                   ■ ■ ■
C                           ■
C                           ■ ■
C                           ■ ■ ■
pad                                  ■   (its own block; label 65535, so no loss either way)
```

- Without this mask, chat B would read chat A. The loss would still go down and nothing would warn us.
- The skipped blocks are also why v2's attention is the cheapest: a chat of 1,500 tokens costs 1,500², not 4,096².

## "Must we fill exactly 4096?" No. A small leftover is padded

Chats rarely add up to exactly 4096. The usual method is **best-fit decreasing**:

1. Sort the chats from longest to shortest.
2. Put each chat into the row where it fits best, with the least space left over.
3. If it fits nowhere, start a new row.
4. Fill whatever space is left at the end of each row with pad tokens (label 65535).

```
row 1: [ 2,000 ][ 1,500 ][ 580 ][pad 16]   = 4,096
row 2: [ 3,100 ][ 990 ][pad 6]             = 4,096
```

- **Measured on our 5,000 chats:** 1,517 rows, an average of **16 pad tokens per row**, 99.6% real.
- **Never split one chat across two rows.** The answer would lose its prompt, or the end token would land in another row. TRL has a split option (`bfd_split`), but it isn't for SFT.
- A chat longer than 4096 is dropped, same as today.
- The pad tail sits at the end of the row and only looks back, so it's harmless, same as in v1.

## Two small things that change with v2

- **The number of chats per row varies** (here 1–5). So a "step" should be counted in tokens or chats, not rows. Our loss already divides by the global trained-token count, so every token keeps the same weight.
- **Tokens per micro-batch stay 8 × 4096**, so Kruthik's fused embedding kernel (fixed N) still works with v2. With v1.5 it doesn't, until it takes the real count.

one doubt , now in the v1 padding techique , what will happen to those padded tokens ? those will be processed aah ? like causal mask will process all the previous tokens right ? then that padded tokens too willsee all the one example right ? so that computed aah wasted right ? still that padded tokens will see that one example right ?

### CLAUDE [2026-10-08 16:44 IST]

**Yes.** In v1 every pad position is fully computed, and it does "see" the whole chat. That compute is wasted. It doesn't change the result.

**Forward: pads are processed like real tokens.**

```
row:    [ chat: positions 0 … 1,237 ][ pad: positions 1,238 … 4,095 ]

pad at position 3,000, attention reads positions 0 … 3,000:
        [■■■■■■■■ whole chat ■■■■■■■■][■■■ earlier pads ■■■]
```

- Every pad position goes through every layer: embedding lookup (id 50256), norms, Q/K/V, attention, MLP, and its 50,304 logits.
- Causal attention lets a pad read everything before it: the whole chat and the earlier pads.
- The kernels don't know which rows are pads (no length or mask is passed), so they compute all 4,096 rows.

**Why the result doesn't change:**
- **Nobody uses a pad's output.** Its label is 65535, so it has 0 loss. No real token reads it, because pads come *after* the chat.
- **The chat doesn't get anything back from the pads in backward.** Gradient flows from a position to the positions it *read*. A pad's gradient is exactly 0, so it sends exactly 0 back to the chat.
- **Measured (Q9 test):** pad rows had gradient 0 at every layer. Replacing the pads with random tokens changed the weight gradients by **0.0**, bit-for-bit.

**Backward is wasted too.** The GEMMs and the attention backward still run over all 4,096 rows. For pad rows they just multiply zeros. Their activations are also stored for the backward, so memory is wasted as well.

**How much is wasted (our data, average chat 1,238 of 4,096 tokens):**
- **Linear layers:** ~70% of rows are pads.
- **Attention:** a pad near the end reads ~3,000–4,000 positions, while a chat token reads at most ~1,238. So pads take about **90%** of the attention work.
- **Overall: ~73%** of each step's work goes to tokens that change nothing.

This is exactly the waste v2 removes. Packing fills those ~2,900 pad slots with other chats, so ~99.6% of positions do real work.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-08 16:56 IST]

Good question. I'll test exactly your case: put the **same tokens that are used in the chat** (" France", "Paris", …) into the pad slots, and check whether the gradients change.
> tool `Bash`: Fill pad slots with chat tokens and compare gradients

**Measured just now:** I filled the 5 pad slots with tokens that *also* appear in the chat (" France", " capital", "Paris", ".", "?").

```
largest change in ANY weight gradient:            0.0
embedding row " France":  grad before 0.887154   after 0.887154   (diff 0.0)
embedding row "Paris":    grad before 2.814328   after 2.814328   (diff 0.0)
logits at chat positions 0–22:   change 0.0
logits at pad  positions 23–27:  change 0.36   ← pad outputs change, but nobody uses them
```

**Why it stays 0: gradient belongs to a *position*, not to a token id.**

The embedding row for " France" gets the sum of the gradients of every position where " France" sits:

```
grad of row " France"  =  grad at position 11   +   grad at position 23 (pad slot)
                       =  non-zero                +   0
                          (the answer read it)       (label 65535, and nobody reads it,
                                                      because it comes after the chat)
```

- **Position 23 adds 0, whatever token sits there.** Its own guess isn't scored, and no later position uses it.
- **Position 11 gives the same gradient in both runs.** Causal attention means position 11 and the answer positions can't see anything after them, so changing positions 23–27 can't change them.
- **The layer weights work the same way.** Each one gets the sum over positions of (input × gradient). Pad positions have gradient 0, so they add 0, whatever their input is.

"France" appearing somewhere else doesn't matter. Only *what the position at that place does* matters, and a pad slot at the end does nothing that anyone uses.

**Where your idea would be right: padding on the left.**

```
[pad pad pad][ chat ]   ← the chat would READ the pads
```

The chat's gradients would then depend on what's in the pad slots, so left padding needs an explicit pad mask. That's why we pad on the right.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-08 16:57 IST]
> tool `Bash`: Check whether weight decay applies to the embedding table
> tool `Bash`: See how weight decay is passed to the optimizer groups

**Only in one special case, and not in our setup.**

**1. Our pad token is 50256 (`<|endoftext|>`), and its row does change.**
- **It isn't random.** It comes from Navin's pretrained model, where 50256 is a real token (end of a document).
- **In SFT it's also the target at the end of every answer.** The table is tied (the same table is the output layer), so every step pushes this row *up* where it's the right answer.
- **In multi-turn chats, the end token of earlier answers is a real input**, read by later turns.

So only the *pad positions'* share of its gradient is 0. The row itself changes every step.

**2. If a token were used ONLY as padding (never a real input, never a target),** for example one of the 47 spare rows 50257–50303:

```
input side  (lookup):   0 from padding, forever          → never learns "what I mean"
output side (logits):   small push DOWN at every trained position (softmax pushes all
                        wrong tokens down; in the Q9 test the output side touched all 50,304 rows)
weight decay:           0.1 on all 2-D weights, wte included (only 1-D is excluded, :1267)
                        → shrinks by (1 − lr·0.1) per step; at SFT LR 2e-5, ×0.999998, tiny
```

- It doesn't stay frozen, but it only learns "never predict me". It never learns a meaning as an input.
- That's harmless, because nobody uses a pad's output.
- With an untied table (a separate output layer), its input row would stay exactly as it started, apart from weight decay. Also harmless.

**3. The same thing explains the 47 spare rows in Navin's model.** In pretraining they were never inputs and never targets. So their input meaning was never trained: they were only pushed down as outputs and shrunk by weight decay. That's why using them for new special tokens (option B in report §3.4) means SFT has to teach them from scratch.

> tool `WebFetch`: https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pytorch/torchtitan/main/torchtitan/components/loss.py
> tool `WebFetch`: https://github.com/pytorch/torchtitan

**1. The final kernel benchmark list for SFT** (v1.5 is skipped, so its GEMM-shape checks drop out; v2 keeps today's shapes):

| What | When | Compare with |
|---|---|---|
| **Loss kernel** (ignore 65535, global denominator, fp32 loss value, bf16 path) | now | PyTorch `F.cross_entropy` (fp32 and bf16), Liger CE / fused linear CE, Apple CCE |
| **v2 attention** forward + backward with the block-diagonal mask, plus RoPE restarting per chat | when v2 is built | FlashAttention-2 varlen, PyTorch FlexAttention (document mask); PyTorch SDPA with an explicit mask as the correctness reference |
| **Embedding backward** (bf16 atomicAdd) | now, for precision (the speed problem mostly goes away with v2) | our fp32 atomic-free kernel, Kruthik's fused kernel, PyTorch's embedding backward |
| **Q11** gather + lm_head GEMM with irregular M | when built | cuBLAS; also check BluBLAS at M not a multiple of 64 |

**2. PyTorch vs torchtitan: they are separate.**

```
torch  (PyTorch library: tensors, autograd, CUDA kernels = "ATen")
   ├─ F.cross_entropy(..., ignore_index=-100)    ← the CE kernel and ignore_index live HERE
   └─ FSDP2, tensor/pipeline/context parallel, torch.compile   ← also here
          ▲                 ▲                  ▲
          │ built on        │ built on         │ built on
     torchtitan         torchtune        HF transformers / TRL
     (pretraining       (fine-tuning     (SFTTrainer, …)
      reference)         recipes)
```

- **PyTorch** (`pip install torch`) is the library. The cross-entropy kernel and `ignore_index` (default −100) belong to PyTorch, not to torchtitan.
- **torchtitan** is a separate project from the PyTorch team ([github.com/pytorch/torchtitan](https://github.com/pytorch/torchtitan)), installed on its own (`pip install torchtitan` or from source). It calls itself "a PyTorch native platform… for large-scale training of generative AI models". It's a training program built *on top of* PyTorch, using PyTorch's own FSDP2, parallelism and `torch.compile`. It is not inside the `torch` package.
- **Its loss** ([`components/loss.py`](https://github.com/pytorch/torchtitan/blob/main/torchtitan/components/loss.py)):
  - calls PyTorch's `F.cross_entropy` with `reduction="sum"` and `IGNORE_INDEX = -100`;
  - then does `loss / global_loss_token_counts`.
- So the **kernel and ignore_index come from PyTorch**. The **"sum, then divide once by the whole step's token count" recipe comes from torchtitan's code**, and that recipe is what we copied in our trainer.

**What this means for our benchmarks:** the "PyTorch" baseline is just `F.cross_entropy`. Benchmarking torchtitan's loss on one GPU is the same thing, because it calls that kernel. Only with tensor parallel does torchtitan use its own split cross-entropy, written in Python on top of PyTorch ops.

I've finished the research. There are two levels of rivals:
- **kernels:** compared on the same shapes;
- **whole trainers:** compared on the same model and data.

The numbers below are each project's own claims, not measured by us.

## 1. Kernel rivals

| Our kernel | Top rivals | Their own numbers |
|---|---|---|
| **Loss** (CE forward + backward) | **PyTorch** `F.cross_entropy` (the baseline); **Liger** CE and Fused-Linear-CE (Triton); **Apple Cut Cross-Entropy** | Liger: +20% throughput, −60% memory overall; its fused linear CE cuts loss memory >4× at a 128k vocab. CCE: Gemma 2 2B loss memory 24 GB → 1 MB, "without sacrificing speed" |
| **Embedding backward** (Kruthik's fused) | **PyTorch** embedding backward: sorts the ids for large batches, which is the same idea as Kruthik's | it's the default everyone uses |
| **Attention v1 / v1.5** (causal, padded rows) | **FlashAttention-3** (Hopper, so H100/H200), FlashAttention-2, PyTorch SDPA (cuDNN) | FA3: BF16 up to 840 TFLOP/s (85% of H100 peak), 1.5–2.0× FA2 |
| **Attention v2** (block-diagonal, packed) | **FA3 / FA2 `flash_attn_varlen_func`** (takes chat boundaries as `cu_seqlens`; FA3's has forward + backward, I checked its code); **PyTorch FlexAttention** document mask; NVIDIA **Transformer Engine / cuDNN "THD"** format (used by NeMo) | FlexAttention: 90% of FA2 forward, 85% backward (A100), and +71% sample-packing throughput in torchtune |

## 2. Whole-trainer rivals, by case

| Case | Who does the same thing | Their claim |
|---|---|---|
| **v1** (pad every chat) | HF **TRL SFTTrainer** with packing off (its default), **torchtune** default | the baseline everyone starts from |
| **v1.5** (length grouping) | HF **Transformers `group_by_length=True`** (groups similar lengths, "keeping a bit of randomness") with per-batch padding; Kathir's `sft.py` (sorts inside each global batch, cuts micro-batches by a token budget) | no headline number; the gain depends on the data (ours: ×2.84 work cut) |
| **v2** (packing + boundary-aware attention) | **NVIDIA NeMo** (sequence packing with FA + Transformer Engine); **HF TRL** packing / padding-free with FA2 varlen; **torchtune** PackedDataset + FlexAttention; **Axolotl** multipack | NeMo: "up to 10× FLOPs, up to 6× training time, no impact on convergence". HF + IBM: "up to 2× training throughput" |

## 3. Who to actually benchmark against (short list)

| What | Rival 1: speed king | Rival 2: most used | Baseline |
|---|---|---|---|
| Loss kernel | Apple CCE | Liger fused linear CE | PyTorch `F.cross_entropy` |
| Attention (all cases) | **FA3** (incl. varlen for v2) | FlexAttention | PyTorch SDPA |
| Embedding backward | — | PyTorch ATen | our old atomicAdd kernel |
| Whole SFT step | **NeMo / Megatron + Transformer Engine** (NVIDIA's own, tuned for H100/H200) | **HF TRL** + FA2/FA3 | our v1 |

**How to compare fairly:**
- Use the same model (d 2304, 26 layers), the same stage-0 data, the same tokens per step, H200, bf16.
- Measure **useful tokens per second**: real non-pad tokens only, because our logged MFU counts the padding.
- Also measure step time, peak memory, and the same final val loss.
- Get the kernel times from one nsys profile per run.

Our own measured work cut from v2 on this data is ×3.60. That fits inside NeMo's "up to 6×" and HF's "up to 2×", whose gains depend on how much padding their data had.

Sources:
- [HF + IBM: packing with Flash Attention 2](https://huggingface.co/blog/packing-with-FA2) · [IBM paper 2407.09105](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.09105)

### CLAUDE [2026-10-08 18:13 IST]
> tool `WebFetch`: https://github.com/apple/ml-cross-entropy

Yes, it's really Apple's. It's not just a nickname.

- **CCE** is the method name, **Cut Cross-Entropy**. People say "Apple CCE" as short for "Apple's Cut Cross-Entropy".
- **It comes from Apple researchers:** the paper is "Cut Your Losses in Large-Vocabulary Language Models" (ICLR 2025), by Erik Wijmans, Brody Huval, Alexander Hertzberg, Vladlen Koltun and Philipp Krähenbühl.
- It's listed on Apple's official ML research site ([machinelearning.apple.com](https://machinelearning.apple.com/research/cut-your-losses)).
- **The code is Apple's open-source release** ([github.com/apple/ml-cross-entropy](https://github.com/apple/ml-cross-entropy)). The repo now sits under Apple's AI/ML research GitHub account.
- **It isn't Mac-only.** It's written in **Triton** for PyTorch and needs an **NVIDIA Ampere or newer GPU** (A100, H100, H200 work). On Mac it falls back to a `torch.compile` version.

**Short answer:** there's no score you can compute on data alone that proves it's the best. Every top lab does the same thing: **train a model on the data, then test it on a fixed set of benchmarks, keeping everything else the same.** Cheaper scoring methods (an LLM judge, length, gradients) are used to *build candidate sets*, and those candidates are then checked by training and testing too.

## 1. The standard method: train-and-test experiments ("ablations")

| Who | What they did | What they found |
|---|---|---|
| **Tülu 1, "How Far Can Camels Go?"** (Ai2, NeurIPS 2023) | trained models on **12 instruction datasets** each; tested knowledge, reasoning, multilingual, code, safety, open-ended chat | "different datasets… enhance specific skills"; **no single dataset or mix is best on everything**; judge/human scores missed differences the benchmarks showed |
| **Tülu 3** (Ai2) | removed one category at a time; a data-size curve (5%→100%); compared whole mixes; dev vs unseen test suites | each category raises its own skill (without math, GSM8K 76.2 → 64.1); the Tülu 3 mix scored 60.1 vs 48.3 for Tülu 2's on the same base |
| **OLMo 3** (Ai2) | a base mix of 100K, plus one category at a time, judged per benchmark | every category helps at least one test and often hurts another, so a mix is a trade-off |
| **SmolLM2** (HF, **1.7B, closest to our size**) | small-scale ablations, then hand-tuning the mix ratios stage by stage | built SmolTalk this way |
| **OpenThoughts** (ICLR 2026) | **1,000+ controlled experiments**: question source, mixing, filtering, answer generation, teacher model, each judged by fine-tuning and testing | the best recipe gave OpenThinker3-7B |
| **"Fixing It in Post"** (NeurIPS 2025) | **same model, same hyperparameters**: Tülu-3 mix vs SmolTalk on 14 benchmarks; tagged every sample's quality and task | their curated **TuluTalk** used 14% fewer samples than Tülu and 23% fewer than SmolTalk, with the same or better results |

## 2. Can a smaller model decide for us?

- **DataDecide** (Ai2, ICML 2025, *pretraining*): rankings at 150M parameters predicted the 1B ranking about 80% of the time. Smooth likelihood-based scores predicted better than accuracy at small scale.
- **LESS:** data picked using a small model also worked for bigger models.
- **For us this matters less.** Our model is already small. A 5,000-chat, 2-epoch run takes about **3.5 minutes on 4 H200s** (1.35 s × 156 steps), so we can run the experiments on the real model directly.

## 3. Ways to score or filter data without training on each candidate

| Method | How it scores | Their result |
|---|---|---|
| **AlpaGasus** (ICLR 2024) | ChatGPT rates each sample; keep the high ones | 9k of Alpaca's 52k beat the full 52k; 5.7× faster training |
| **Deita** (ICLR 2024) | complexity + quality scorers + a diversity filter | 6K samples ≈ the best open models of the time, with 10× less data |
| **IFD / Cherry** (NAACL 2024) | how hard the answer is for the model itself | 10% of the data gave better results |
| **LESS** (ICML 2024) | gradient similarity to a target skill | 5% often beat the full dataset |
| **Long Is More** (ICML 2024) | just keep the **1,000 longest answers** | beat LIMA and AlpaGasus; "should be the default baseline" |
| **Magpie** (2024) | synthetic data, then filtered (4M → 300K) | matched Llama-3-8B-Instruct, which used 10M examples |

**The reality check: "Rethinking Data Selection at Scale"** (EMNLP 2025):
- on pools of a million samples, almost every clever scoring method **failed to clearly beat random selection**;
- **diversity mattered more than "quality" scores**;
- **filtering by token length** was the stable win.

So **random** and **longest** must always be in our comparison.

## 4. Checks every recipe runs before training

- **Decontamination:** remove anything that overlaps a test question. Tülu 3 and OLMo 3 drop a sample if it matches ≥50% of a test question's 8-grams (your doc §5.1).
- **Deduplication, licence check, correctness:** run the code, check the math answers.

## 5. What this means for us

1. **A fixed test suite** (from Q7/Q8): answer val loss, end-token rate, IFEval, TruthfulQA MC2, PopQA, DROP, plus HellaSwag/ARC in cloze form for forgetting. Split it into dev and unseen.
2. **A fixed training recipe:** same base, LR, epochs, tokens per step. **Only the data changes.**
3. **The experiments:**
   - (a) dataset vs dataset at the same size: UltraChat vs SmolTalk vs a Tülu 3 subset;
   - (b) a base mix plus one category at a time (OLMo 3 style);
   - (c) a size curve: 1k / 5k / 20k / 100k (Tülu 3 style);
   - (d) selection methods vs **random** and **longest** at the same size.
4. **At least 2 runs per arm.** Two identical runs of our trainer already differ (doc §5.6).
5. **"Best" can't be proven absolutely.** You show it beats the alternatives at equal size and compute on your dev suite, then confirm on the unseen suite.

The generation-based tests still need the eval harness from Q7/Q8.

Sources:
- [How Far Can Camels Go? (Tülu 1, NeurIPS 2023)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2023/hash/ec6413875e4ab08d7bc4d8e225263398-Abstract.html)
- [Tülu 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124) · [SmolLM2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.02737) · [OpenThoughts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04178)
- [Fixing It in Post (NeurIPS 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06522)
- [DataDecide (ICML 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.11393)

- [Long Is More for Alignment (ICML 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04833) · [Magpie](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.08464)
- [Rethinking Data Selection at Scale (EMNLP 2025 Findings)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.09335)
- [Survey: data assessment and selection for instruction tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.02085)

### CLAUDE [2026-10-08 18:40 IST]

Okay. Let me explain it slowly, from zero, step by step.

---

## Step 1: What problem are we solving?

There are many SFT datasets: UltraChat, SmolTalk, the Tülu 3 mix, and others. We want to know:
- Which dataset makes **our** model best?
- How much data do we need?
- If we mix datasets, in what proportions?

## Step 2: Think of it like a school

- **The model is a student.**
- **The SFT data is a textbook.**
- **Benchmarks are exams.**

Question: which textbook is best?

You can't answer by just *reading* the textbooks. A book can look great and still not help this student. Another book may be great for math but bad for English. **The only real judge is the student's exam result after studying from it.**

The first Tülu paper (Ai2, 2023) showed exactly this. They taught students from 12 different textbooks. Each book made the students good at *different* subjects, and **no book was best at everything**.

## Step 3: The main method, "same student, different book, same exam"

This is what every top lab does. It's called an **ablation** experiment:

```
start:      the same base model (our step-8000 model)
                │                │                │
study from:  book A           book B           book C
            (UltraChat)      (SmolTalk)       (Tülu 3 subset)
                │                │                │
same rules:  same LR, same epochs, same amount of data
                │                │                │
same exam:   IFEval, TruthfulQA, HellaSwag, …  (the same exams for all)
                ▼                ▼                ▼
             score A          score B          score C   → compare
```

**Only one thing changes: the book.** If you also changed the LR or the number of examples, you couldn't tell what caused the difference.

## Step 4: Making the comparison fair

1. **Same amount of data.** Compare 5,000 chats against 5,000 chats, not 5,000 against 50,000.
2. **Run it twice.** The same data in a different order gives a slightly different score, like a student having a good day or a bad day. Run each book twice with a different shuffle. Only trust a difference that's bigger than this "good day / bad day" gap.
3. **Keep a secret exam.** If you keep picking whatever scores best on one exam, you slowly "study for that exam". So keep a second set of exams that you **never** use for choosing. Check the winner on it once at the end. Tülu 3 does this (a "dev" set for choosing, an "unseen" set for the final check).

## Step 5: The questions these experiments answer, and how the big labs did each

**a) "Which book is better?"** (dataset vs dataset)
- The "Fixing It in Post" paper (NeurIPS 2025) took one model and one set of training settings. It trained one copy on the Tülu 3 mix and one on SmolTalk, then gave both 14 exams.
- Each was better at different subjects.
- Then they kept the best and most varied examples from both and made a new book, "TuluTalk". It had **14–23% fewer examples** and scored **the same or better**.

**b) "Which chapters matter?"** (remove one part at a time)
- Tülu 3 trained the full mix, then the mix with one part removed:
  - math removed → the math exam (GSM8K) fell from **76.2 to 64.1**;
  - safety removed → the safety score fell from **93.1 to 74.7**.
- So **each chapter teaches its own skill**. Remove it and that skill drops.

**c) "What happens if I add a chapter?"** (add one part at a time)
- OLMo 3 started with a small base book, then added one chapter at a time.
- Adding math raised math (MATH 6.6 → 14.2) but **lowered instruction-following** (IFEval 61.7 → 54.0).
- So mixing is **balancing**. More of one thing can mean less of another.

**d) "How much data is enough?"** (size curve)
- Tülu 3 trained on 5%, 10%, 25%, 50% and 100% of its data.
- More data kept helping on average. But one exam, TruthfulQA, actually got *worse* with more data.
- So "more" isn't automatically "better" for every skill.

**e) "How should the book be written?"**
- OpenThoughts ran **over 1,000** of these train-and-test experiments: where the questions come from, how they're filtered, which teacher model writes the answers.
- Each choice was decided by an exam result.

## Step 6: Shortcuts for picking good examples without training each time

Training a student for every idea is slow, so researchers invented ways to **grade each example first** and keep only the good ones:

- **Ask a strong AI to grade each example** (AlpaGasus): ChatGPT gave every one of Alpaca's 52,000 examples a score. They kept the best 9,000. The student trained on those 9,000 beat the one trained on all 52,000, and trained 5.7× faster.
- **Grade by how complex and how good each example is, and skip near-duplicates** (Deita): 6,000 well-chosen examples were enough.
- **Ask the student how hard each example is for it** (IFD): the hard-but-learnable ones, about 10% of the data, gave better results.
- **Pick the examples most similar to the skill you want** (LESS): just 5% of the data often beat all of it.
- **The simplest trick: keep the examples with the longest answers** (Long Is More). The 1,000 longest beat the fancy methods above. The authors say this should be the default thing to compare against.

**But here is the surprise** ("Rethinking Data Selection at Scale", 2025):
- When the pile of data is huge (a million examples), almost all the fancy grading methods did **no better than picking examples at random**.
- What mattered more was **variety**: many different kinds of questions.
- Filtering by length still helped.

What this means:
1. Every comparison must include **random** and **longest** as baselines. A fancy method is only worth using if it beats both.
2. Even after a shortcut picks the examples, you still check it with **Step 3** (train and test).

## Step 7: Can we test on a smaller student to save money?

- Ai2's DataDecide (for pretraining) found that if you rank books using small students, the big students rank them the same way about 80% of the time.
- **We don't need this.** Our model is already small. A 5,000-chat run takes about 4 minutes on 4 H200s. A 100,000-chat run is roughly 70 minutes, and about 3× less once v2 packing is in. So we can test directly on the real model.

## Step 8: Clean the book before any test

1. **Remove exam questions from the book (decontamination).** If a training example is almost the same as an exam question, the student just memorizes the answer and the score is fake. Tülu 3 and OLMo 3 remove a training example if it shares half or more of a test question's 8-word chunks.
2. **Remove duplicates.**
3. **Check the licence.** We must be allowed to use the data.
4. **Check correctness:** run the code examples and check the math answers.

## Step 9: Our plan, in order

1. **Fix the exams.** These come from Q7/Q8: answer loss, whether answers stop properly, IFEval, TruthfulQA, PopQA, DROP, plus HellaSwag/ARC to check forgetting. Split them into "choosing" and "secret" sets.
2. **Fix the training rules:** same base model, LR, epochs, data size.
3. **Run the experiments:**
   - UltraChat vs SmolTalk vs a Tülu 3 subset, the same size each;
   - a size curve: 1k → 5k → 20k → 100k;
   - add or remove one category at a time;
   - our picking method vs **random** vs **longest**.
4. **Run each at least twice,** and only trust differences bigger than the run-to-run gap.
5. **Confirm the winner on the secret exams.**

One thing is needed first: the exams that need the model to *write* answers (IFEval, PopQA, DROP) need the evaluation setup from Q7/Q8.

2. **Run each setup at least twice.**
   - Training the same data in a different shuffled order gives slightly different scores.
   - Run each dataset twice with different shuffle seeds and measure how far apart the two scores are (the run-to-run variation).
   - Only trust a difference between datasets that is bigger than that variation.
3. **Keep two separate benchmark sets.**
   - **Dev set:** used for every decision.
   - **Unseen set:** never used for decisions, only to check the final choice once.
   - Why: if you keep choosing whatever scores best on the dev set, the choices slowly become tuned to those specific benchmarks. The unseen set shows whether the improvement is real.
   - Tülu 3 works this way.

## Step 5: What these experiments answer, with real results

**a) Which dataset is better? (dataset vs dataset)**
- "Fixing It in Post" (NeurIPS 2025) took one model and one set of training settings. It trained one copy on the Tülu 3 mix and one on SmolTalk, then measured both on 14 benchmarks.
- Each dataset won on different benchmarks.
- They then kept the highest-quality and most varied examples from both and built a new dataset, "TuluTalk". It was **14–23% smaller** and scored **the same or better**.

**b) Which parts of a mix matter? (remove one category at a time)**
- Tülu 3 trained the full mix, then the same mix with one category removed:
  - math data removed → GSM8K fell from **76.2 to 64.1**;
  - safety data removed → the safety score fell from **93.1 to 74.7**.
- Each category of data is responsible for its own skill. Remove it and that skill drops.

**c) What does adding a category do? (add one category at a time)**
- OLMo 3 started from a small base mix and added one category at a time.
- Adding math raised MATH from 6.6 to 14.2, but **lowered** IFEval from 61.7 to 54.0.
- So a mix is a trade-off: adding more of one category can lower another skill.

**d) How much data is enough? (size curve)**
- Tülu 3 trained on 5%, 10%, 25%, 50% and 100% of its mix.
- The average score kept rising with more data, but TruthfulQA went **down** as data increased.
- More data is not automatically better for every skill.

**e) How should the data be generated?**
- OpenThoughts ran **over 1,000** train-and-measure experiments, one for each choice in its data pipeline: where the questions come from, how they're filtered, which model writes the answers.
- Every choice was decided by the benchmark scores of a trained model.

## Step 6: Ways to score examples without training a model for each choice

Training a model for every candidate is expensive, so researchers built methods that give **each example a score** and keep only the best-scoring ones:

| Method | How it scores an example | Reported result |
|---|---|---|
| **AlpaGasus** | ChatGPT rates each example's quality | kept 9,000 of Alpaca's 52,000; the model beat the one trained on all 52,000, and trained 5.7× faster |
| **Deita** | separate scores for complexity and for quality, plus removing near-duplicates | 6,000 selected examples matched models trained on 10× more data |
| **IFD** | how much the prompt helps the model predict the answer, measured with the model itself; keeps the hard ones | 10% of the data gave better results |
| **LESS** | the gradient of each example compared to the gradient of a few examples of the target skill | 5% of the data often beat the full dataset |
| **Long Is More** | answer length only: keep the 1,000 longest answers | beat AlpaGasus and LIMA; the authors say it should be the default baseline |

**The important later finding** ("Rethinking Data Selection at Scale", 2025):
- On datasets with about a million examples, almost every scoring method above did **no better than random selection**.
- **Variety in the data** (many different kinds of prompts) mattered more than these quality scores.
- Filtering by length still gave a steady gain.

What this means for us:
1. Any selection method we try must be compared against **random selection** and **longest answers**, at the same size. It's only useful if it beats both.
2. A selection method only *proposes* a subset. The subset is still judged by Step 3: train, then measure.

## Step 7: Do we need a smaller model to save compute?

- Ai2's DataDecide (pretraining) found that dataset rankings measured with small models (150M) matched the rankings at 1B about 80% of the time. Labs use this to save compute.
- **We don't need it.** Our model is 1.5B, and the runs are cheap:
  - a 5,000-chat, 2-epoch run takes about 4 minutes on 4 H200s;
  - a 100,000-chat run takes roughly 70 minutes;
  - both drop about 3× once v2 packing is in.
- So we can run every experiment on the real model.

## Step 8: Cleaning the data before any experiment

1. **Decontamination.** If a training example is almost identical to a benchmark question, the model memorizes the answer and the score is inflated. Tülu 3 and OLMo 3 drop a training example if it shares 50% or more of a benchmark question's 8-token chunks (8-grams).
2. **Deduplication:** remove repeated examples.
3. **Licence check:** the data must be allowed for company use.
4. **Correctness:** run code answers against their tests and check math answers.

## Step 9: Our plan, in order

1. **Fix the benchmark list** (from Q7/Q8): answer-token val loss, end-token rate, IFEval, TruthfulQA, PopQA, DROP, plus HellaSwag/ARC for forgetting. Split it into a dev set and an unseen set.
2. **Fix the training settings:** same base checkpoint, LR, epochs, number of examples.
3. **Run the experiments:**
   - UltraChat vs SmolTalk vs a Tülu 3 subset, at the same size;
   - a size curve: 1k → 5k → 20k → 100k chats;
   - add or remove one category at a time;
   - any selection method vs random vs longest answers.
4. **Run each setup at least twice.** Trust only differences larger than the run-to-run variation.
5. **Check the final choice once on the unseen set.**

One dependency first: IFEval, PopQA and DROP need the model to generate answers, so they need the evaluation setup from Q7/Q8.

The Core Problem: "Information Leakage"
To understand why we need both a Dev Set and an Unseen Set, you have to understand the biggest trap in AI: Information Leakage.

When researchers are building an AI, they have to make hundreds of decisions:

"What learning rate should we use?"
"Should we include 10% math data or 20% math data?"
"How many layers should the neural network have?"
They answer these questions by running an experiment, testing the model, and picking the option that gets the highest score.

The 3 Datasets (The Big Picture)
To prevent the AI from cheating, researchers take their giant pile of data and split it into three strict buckets before they even start:

1. The Training Set (The Engine)
What it is: 99% of the data. This is what goes through the GPU. The model directly calculates gradients and updates its weights based on this data.
The flaw: If you test the model on this data, it will score 100% because it memorized it.
2. The Dev Set / Validation Set (The Steering Wheel)
What it is: A small chunk of data the model never trains on.
How it's used: After training for a bit, the researchers test the model on the Dev Set. Let's say they are testing two different data mixes for Tülu 3 (Mix A and Mix B). They train two models.
Model A scores 85% on the Dev Set.
Model B scores 88% on the Dev Set.
The researchers choose Mix B.
Why it is flawed (The Leakage): Even though the model never directly updated its weights on the Dev Set, the researchers used the Dev Set to make a design choice. Because the researchers are constantly making tweaks to get the Dev Set score higher and higher, the model indirectly becomes "overfitted" to the Dev Set. The model is essentially being tailored to be really good at whatever specific questions happen to be in the Dev Set.
3. The Unseen Set / Test Set (The Final Reality Check)
What it is: Another small chunk of data.
The Golden Rule: The researchers are forbidden from looking at the Unseen Set while building the model. They cannot use it to tune hyperparameters. They cannot use it to choose data mixtures. It sits completely idle on a hard drive for months while the AI is being built.
How it's used: Only when the model is 100% finished, frozen, and ready to be released to the public, do they test it on the Unseen Set.
Why it's crucial: Because nobody used this data to make any decisions during training, the Unseen Set score is the only mathematically pure, unbiased measurement of how the AI will perform in the real world on tasks it has never encountered.
To sum it up: Why are they different?
If the Dev Set and the Unseen Set were the same thing, the researchers would be reporting their final accuracy based on the exact same dataset they used to tune and tweak the model for months. That is bad science. It artificially inflates the model's scores.

The Dev Set is a tool for the engineers to guide the model's development (which taints the data).
The Unseen Set is a tool for the public to know how good the model actually is (because the data is pure).

## Your dev / unseen explanation: correct, with 3 fixes

The main idea is right. Choosing things by the dev score "leaks" information into those choices, so the dev score ends up too optimistic. Only a set that was never used for choosing gives an honest number.

Three fixes:
1. **For SFT, the dev and unseen sets are separate *benchmark lists*, not three slices of one data pile.**
   - The training data is the SFT chats.
   - Our 500 validation chats are a held-out slice of the same source; they only give the val loss.
   - The Tülu 3 dev suite is a list of benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, IFEval, …).
   - Its unseen suite is a *different* list (AGIEval, MMLU-Pro, GPQA, IFEval-OOD, HREF, …). It was designed separately, so it also tests tasks that are different, not just new samples of the same tasks.
2. **"Testing on training data gives 100%" is too strong.** The score is usually just higher than on new data, not 100%.
3. **"The only pure measure of real-world performance" is too strong.** The unseen score is unbiased only for those benchmarks, and only if you use it once. If you look at it, change something and look again, it starts leaking too.

Sources: [Tülu 3, §7 evaluation](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124)

Below is the full SFT-data explanation again: more detail, with the paper behind every claim, and nothing from the earlier answers left out.

## Step 1: What we have to decide

We have to make three decisions:
1. **Which dataset.** UltraChat, SmolTalk, a Tülu 3 subset, or another.
2. **How much data.** 5,000 chats, 100,000, or a million.
3. **The mix.** If we combine sources (general chat, math, code, instruction-following, safety), what share each one gets.

Each decision can only be judged by its effect on the trained model.

## Step 2: Why reading a dataset can't tell you if it's good

Two reasons:
- **Looking good is not the same as helping.** A dataset can have clean, correct, well-written answers and still not improve the model. For example, the model may already know how to produce those answers.
- **Datasets improve different skills.** A math dataset raises math scores and may do nothing for instruction-following.

**Proof: the first Tülu paper**, "How Far Can Camels Go?" (Ai2, NeurIPS 2023).
- They fine-tuned models from 6.7B to 65B parameters on **12 different instruction datasets**, one model per dataset.
- They measured each model on factual knowledge, reasoning, multilingual tasks, coding, safety and open-ended instruction following.
- Their finding, in their words: "different instruction-tuning datasets can uncover or enhance specific skills, while no single dataset (or combination) provides the best performance across all evaluations".
- They also found that scores from model judges and human preference **missed differences that the benchmarks showed**. So you need several kinds of tests, not one.
- Source: [How Far Can Camels Go? (NeurIPS 2023)](https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2023/hash/ec6413875e4ab08d7bc4d8e225263398-Abstract.html)

## Step 3: The method every lab uses, the ablation experiment

An **ablation** is a set of training runs that are identical except for one thing. You compare the results to see the effect of that one thing.

```
start:        the same base model (our step-8000 checkpoint)
                 │                 │                 │
train on:     dataset A         dataset B         dataset C
             (UltraChat)       (SmolTalk)        (Tülu 3 subset)
                 │                 │                 │
same settings: same LR, same epochs, same number of examples
                 │                 │                 │
same tests:   IFEval, TruthfulQA, HellaSwag, …  (identical list for all)
                 ▼                 ▼                 ▼
              scores A          scores B          scores C   → compare
```

**In our trainer, "same settings" means all of these are identical between runs:**
- the starting checkpoint (step 8000);
- the optimizer and its LR, warmup and decay;
- the number of epochs;
- the chats (or tokens) per step;
- the sequence length (4096);
- the chat template (`tulu-plain-v1`) and tokenizer (GPT-2);
- the precision flags (`BLU_ALL_BF16=1`).

**Only the training data changes.** If two things change at once (say, the data *and* the LR), a score difference can't be assigned to either one.

## Step 4: Rules that make the comparison trustworthy

### 4.1 Same amount of data, and the choice between examples and tokens

- Compare 5,000 chats with 5,000 chats, never 5,000 with 50,000. More data usually changes the score by itself.
- **Examples vs tokens:** datasets have different answer lengths. 5,000 chats with long answers contain more trained tokens than 5,000 with short ones. Answer length alone changes results ("Long Is More", Step 6). So if two datasets have very different lengths, also run them at **the same number of trained tokens**. That way the comparison isn't just "longer answers win".
- This is my reasoning from that paper's finding, not a rule a paper states.

### 4.2 Measure the noise, and only trust differences bigger than it

Two runs with identical settings don't give identical scores. The data order (shuffle seed) and the GPU's non-deterministic adds make small differences.

**Proof that this matters:** "Quantifying Variance in Evaluation Benchmarks" (Meta and others, 2024).
- They trained **10 identical 7B models** that differed only in the random seed.
- Benchmark scores still varied between them.
- Their point: without measuring this variance you can't tell whether a difference between two models is meaningful.
- They also found that, for smaller models, scoring multiple-choice tasks as a completion (the "cloze" form) gives less variance than the letter form. That matches Ai2's OLMES advice from Q7/Q8.
- Source: [Quantifying Variance in Evaluation Benchmarks (2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.10229)

**A second source of noise: the benchmark size.** A benchmark with few questions gives a noisy score. Simple math (one standard error at a 50% score):
- **IFEval**, 541 prompts: √(0.5 × 0.5 ÷ 541) ≈ **±2.1 points**;
- **GSM8K**, 1,319 problems: ≈ **±1.4 points**.

**The rule for us:**
1. Run each setup at least twice with different shuffle seeds, and note how far apart the two scores are.
2. Treat a difference between two datasets as real only if it's clearly bigger than both that run-to-run gap and the benchmark's own noise. Roughly, more than twice either.

### 4.3 Two benchmark lists: dev and unseen

- **Dev list:** used for every decision (which dataset, which size, which mix).
- **Unseen list:** designed separately, never used for decisions, and run once on the final choice.

**Proof: Tülu 3.**
- Its dev suite: MMLU, PopQA, TruthfulQA, HumanEval, GSM8K, MATH, BBH, DROP, IFEval, AlpacaEval 2, and safety.
- Its unseen suite was designed independently. It includes AGIEval, MMLU-Pro, GPQA, a new **IFEval-OOD** (new kinds of instructions not in IFEval) and HREF.
- The unseen suite is there "to measure overfitting and generalization".
- Source: [Tülu 3 (Ai2, 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124)

### 4.4 Measure the base model the right way (from Q7/Q8)

- The **base** model doesn't follow instructions, so it gets a few solved examples in its prompt (few-shot).
- The **SFT** model gets the plain question inside its chat template (zero-shot).
- For multiple-choice tests on a small model, use the **cloze** form: score each full answer by its probability. Don't ask for a letter (A/B/C/D).
- Source: [OLMES (Ai2, 2024)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.08446)

## Step 5: The questions ablations answer, and how the labs ran each one

### a) Which dataset is better? (dataset vs dataset)

**"Fixing It in Post" (NeurIPS 2025).** What they did:
1. Took two popular open SFT datasets, the **Tülu 3 SFT mix** and **SmolTalk**.
2. Labelled every sample with the Magpie tools: single or multi-turn, task category (math, code, …), the quality of the prompt and the quality of the answer.
3. Trained the **same model with the same hyperparameters** on each dataset and measured both on **14 benchmarks**.
4. Each dataset was stronger on different skills (coding, math, instruction following).
5. Built a new dataset, **TuluTalk**, by keeping high-quality samples while keeping all task types covered. It has **14% fewer samples than Tülu and 23% fewer than SmolTalk**, and scored the same or better on the key benchmarks.

Source: [Fixing It in Post (NeurIPS 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.06522)

### b) Which categories in a mix matter? (remove one at a time)

**Tülu 3, Table 10.** They trained the full mix, then again with one category removed each time:
- math removed: GSM8K **76.2 → 64.1**, MATH **31.5 → 23.5**;
- safety removed: safety score **93.1 → 74.7**;
- persona instruction data removed: IFEval **72.8 → 53.6**.

Each category carries its own skill. Removing it removes that skill.

Source: [Tülu 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124)

### c) What does adding a category do? (add one at a time)

**OLMo 3, Table 28.** They started from a small base mix (on an OLMo 2 model) and added one category at a time, then looked at every benchmark separately:
- adding math: MATH **6.6 → 14.2**, GSM8K **30.1 → 39.7**, but IFEval **61.7 → 54.0**;
- adding instruction-following data: IFEval **74.1**, but HumanEval **23.2 → 14.6**.

So adding one category can lower another skill. That's why a mix has to be judged per benchmark, not only by the average.

Source: [OLMo 3 (Ai2, 2025)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13961)

### d) How much data is enough? (size curve)

**Tülu 3, Figure 4.** They trained on 5%, 10%, 25%, 50%, 75% and 100% of their mix.
- The average kept rising, and the full mix was best overall.
- GSM8K gained the most from more data.
- TruthfulQA **went down** as the data grew.

"More" helps on average but not for every skill.

Source: [Tülu 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124)

### e) How should the data itself be made?

**OpenThoughts (ICLR 2026).** They ran **over 1,000 controlled experiments**, one for each step of making the data:
- where the questions come from;
- how sources are mixed;
- how questions are filtered;
- how answers are generated (one or several per question, deduplication);
- which teacher model writes the answers.

Each choice was decided by fine-tuning and measuring on AIME24, AMC23, MATH500, CodeElo, CodeForces, LiveCodeBench, GPQA Diamond and JEEBench. The final recipe produced OpenThinker3-7B: 53% on AIME 2025, 51% on LiveCodeBench, 54% on GPQA Diamond.

Source: [OpenThoughts](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.04178)

### f) The same method at our model size

**SmolLM2** (Hugging Face, **1.7B**, the closest to our 1.5B). They decided their data with small-scale ablations, plus manual updates of the mix ratios at each training stage based on the previous stage's results. Their SFT dataset, SmolTalk, came out of this process.

Source: [SmolLM2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.02737)

## Step 6: Scoring single examples without training a model for every choice

Training a model for every candidate subset is expensive. So researchers built methods that **give each example a score**, then keep the top-scoring ones. Each method below, what it computes, and what it reported:

**1. AlpaGasus: an LLM grades every example** (ICLR 2024).
- ChatGPT rated each Alpaca example (instruction, input, answer) for quality.
- Of 52,000 examples they kept about **9,000** high-rated ones.
- The model trained on those 9,000 beat the one trained on all 52,000 (judged by GPT-4 and by humans).
- Training was **5.7× faster**: 80 minutes → 14 minutes for 7B.
- Their reason: Alpaca contained many wrong or off-topic answers that hurt training.
- Source: [AlpaGasus](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.08701)

**2. Deita: complexity + quality + no near-duplicates** (ICLR 2024).
- They trained two small scorer models: one rates how complex an instruction is ("Evol Complexity"), one rates how good an answer is ("Evol Quality").
- They ranked examples by these scores and added them one by one, **skipping any that are too similar** (by embedding distance) to ones already chosen. That keeps the selection varied.
- With **6,000** selected examples, their models matched or beat open models trained on about 10× more data.
- Source: [Deita: What Makes Good Data for Alignment?](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.15685)

**3. IFD: measure how hard each example is for the model itself** (NAACL 2024).
- For each example, compare two losses on the answer: the loss *with* the prompt in front of it, and the loss of the answer *alone*.
- IFD = (loss with prompt) ÷ (loss without prompt).
- If the prompt barely lowers the loss, the ratio is near 1: the model doesn't yet know how to use this kind of instruction, so it's a hard, useful example.
- They kept high-IFD examples: about **10%** of Alpaca / WizardLM data gave better results than all of it.
- Source: [From Quantity to Quality (IFD)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.12032)

**4. LESS: pick examples that push the model toward the skill you want** (ICML 2024).
- For each training example, compute its gradient (with LoRA, then shrunk to a small vector).
- Do the same for a few examples of the target skill.
- Keep the training examples whose gradients point the **same way** as the target skill's (highest cosine similarity).
- A **5%** selection often beat training on everything.
- A selection made with a **small model also worked for larger models** and other model families.
- Source: [LESS](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04333)

**5. Long Is More: keep the longest answers** (ICML 2024).
- Keep the **1,000** examples with the longest answers, from Alpaca-52k or Evol-Instruct-70k.
- This beat LIMA and AlpaGasus (judged by GPT-4 and PaLM-2) and stayed competitive on factual-knowledge benchmarks.
- They checked that the win wasn't just the judge model preferring longer text.
- They say longest-answers selection "should be the default baseline".
- Source: [Long Is More for Alignment](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.04833)

**6. Magpie: generate data, then filter it** (2024).
- They made Llama-3-Instruct write **4 million** instructions with answers, then filtered them down to **300,000**.
- Models trained on those matched the official Llama-3-8B-Instruct, which used about 10 million SFT examples plus preference training, on AlpacaEval, ArenaHard and WildBench.
- Source: [Magpie](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.08464)

**The later result that checks all of these:** "Rethinking Data Selection at Scale: Random Selection is Almost All You Need" (EMNLP 2025 Findings).
- They tested self-scoring methods like the ones above on two datasets of about **a million examples each**.
- Almost none clearly beat **random selection**.
- **Variety in the data mattered more than quality scores.**
- **Filtering by token length gave a stable gain.**
- Why the earlier papers looked better: they mostly tested on small pools (like Alpaca's 52,000), where filtering out bad examples matters more.
- Source: [Rethinking Data Selection at Scale](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.09335)

**How these methods are grouped** (survey, 2024): every method scores examples by one of three things.
1. **Quality:** is the answer correct and well written? (AlpaGasus, Deita's quality score)
2. **Diversity:** does the set cover many kinds of prompts? (Deita's similarity filter)
3. **Importance:** does the example help the target skill? (IFD, LESS)

Source: [Survey: Data Assessment and Selection for Instruction Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.02085)

**What this means for us:**
1. Any selection method we try must be compared, at the same size, against **random selection** and **longest answers**. It's only worth using if it beats both.
2. A selection method only produces a candidate subset. That subset is still judged by Step 3: train, then measure.

## Step 7: Testing with a smaller model to save compute

**DataDecide** (Ai2, ICML 2025). This is about pretraining data, not SFT.
- They pretrained models on **25 different corpora** (up to 100B tokens), at **14 sizes up to 1B parameters**.
- Ranking the datasets with **150M** models gave the same order as the **1B** models in **about 80%** of comparisons.
- Smooth likelihood-based scores (the probability of the right answer) predicted the 1B results better than plain accuracy did at small scale.
- Source: [DataDecide](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.11393)

**LESS** (Step 6) also showed that data chosen with a small model works for bigger models.

**Why we don't need a smaller model:** ours is already small (1.5B), and our runs are cheap.
- A 5,000-chat, 2-epoch run is about **4 minutes on 4 H200s** (1.35 s per step × 156 steps, plus startup and validation).
- A 100,000-chat run is roughly **70 minutes**.
- Both drop about 3× once v2 packing is in.

So we can run every ablation on the real model.

## Step 8: Cleaning the data before any experiment

**1. Decontamination: remove training examples that match benchmark questions.**
- If a training example contains a benchmark question, the model can memorize the answer, and that benchmark's score becomes fake.
- **How Tülu 3 and OLMo 3 check:**
  1. Cut each benchmark question into all its runs of **8 consecutive tokens** (8-grams).
  2. For each training example, count how many of those 8-grams also appear in it.
  3. If **50% or more** of a question's 8-grams appear in a training example, drop that example.
- Sources: [Tülu 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124) · [OLMo 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13961)

**2. Deduplication.** Remove exact and near-exact repeats. Repeats over-weight some examples and waste compute.

**3. Licence check.** OLMo 3 removed examples "with (1) non-commercial or unclear licenses". We must check every dataset card before company use.

**4. Correctness.** OLMo 3:
- runs code answers against test cases;
- checks that instruction constraints are met;
- drops incomplete reasoning and heavy repetition.

Math answers should be checked against the known final answer.

## Step 9: Our plan, in order

1. **Fix the benchmark lists.**
   - **Dev:** answer-token val loss, end-token rate, IFEval, TruthfulQA (MC2), PopQA, DROP, and HellaSwag/ARC in cloze form to catch forgetting.
   - **Unseen:** a separate set, e.g. MMLU-Pro and AGIEval in cloze form. Chosen now, and not looked at until the final choice.
2. **Fix the training settings** (all of Step 3's list).
3. **Clean every candidate dataset** (Step 8). Decontaminate against *both* benchmark lists.
4. **Run the ablations, each at least twice:**
   - dataset vs dataset at the same size (and the same trained tokens if their lengths differ): UltraChat vs SmolTalk vs a Tülu 3 subset;
   - a size curve: 1k → 5k → 20k → 100k chats;
   - one category added or removed at a time;
   - any selection method vs **random** vs **longest answers**.
5. **Trust only differences larger than the noise** (Step 4.2).
6. **Check the final winner once on the unseen list.**

**One dependency:** IFEval, PopQA and DROP need the model to generate text, so they need the evaluation setup from Q7/Q8. The val loss and the cloze-form tests can run before that.

# What are the dev suite (development suite) and the unseen suite in evaluations?

## 1. The problem: information leakage

Building a model means making many decisions, for example:
- which learning rate to use;
- whether the data mix should be 10% math or 20% math;
- how many epochs to train;
- which saved checkpoint to keep as the final model;
- for pretraining, how many layers the network should have.

Each decision is made the same way:
1. Train one model for each option.
2. Measure every model on some evaluation data.
3. Keep the option with the highest score.

**Information leakage** happens when the data used to measure the model has also influenced how the model was built. Then the measurement is no longer independent of the model, and the score comes out higher than the model's real performance on new data.

There are two kinds of leakage. Both inflate scores.

| Kind | What happens | How it's prevented |
|---|---|---|
| **Direct leakage (contamination)** | benchmark questions, or near-copies of them, are inside the training data, so the model can memorize their answers | **decontamination:** remove those examples from the training data before training |
| **Indirect leakage (selection bias)** | a benchmark is used to *choose* between options, so the choices end up fitted to that benchmark | a **separate unseen set** that is never used for choices |

The dev / unseen split exists to deal with the second kind.

## 2. The general idea in machine learning: three separate sets

Before training starts, the data is divided into three groups that never mix.

### 2.1 The training set

- **What it is:** most of the data. How much depends on the project: 80/10/10 splits are common for small datasets, and with millions of examples the training share can be 98–99%. There is no fixed rule.
- **How it's used:** this is the only data the GPU computes gradients on. The weights are updated from it.
- **Why you can't evaluate on it:** the model was fitted to these exact examples. Its score on them is higher than on new data, often much higher. That doesn't have to mean 100%; it means the number says nothing about new data.

### 2.2 The dev set (also called the validation set)

- **What it is:** data the model never trains on. No gradients are ever computed on it.
- **How it's used:** for **every decision**. Example: comparing two data mixes for an SFT run:
  - model trained on mix A: **85%** on the dev set;
  - model trained on mix B: **88%** on the dev set;
  - so you choose mix B.
- **Why its score becomes too high (indirect leakage):** the model never trained on the dev set, but **the choices did use it**.
  - Every score has random noise. Two mixes that are equally good will still score differently by chance.
  - When you keep the higher one, you also keep part of that chance difference.
  - After many decisions made this way, the final model is partly chosen for doing well on *these particular dev questions*, including their noise and quirks.
  - So its dev score is higher than its real performance.

**A worked example with real numbers:**
- Say we compare **10 data mixes** that are all *truly equal*: each really scores 50% on IFEval.
- IFEval has 541 prompts. One run's score has random noise of about **±2.1 points** (one standard error: √(0.5 × 0.5 ÷ 541) ≈ 0.021).
- So the 10 measured scores scatter around 50%: some at 48, some at 52, one maybe at 53.
- We pick the highest. The expected highest of 10 such scores is about **1.54 standard errors above the truth: about +3.2 points.**
- So the "winner" shows about **53.2%** on the dev set, even though it is really 50%, like all the others.
- Measured on data it was never chosen with, it shows about **50%**. That gap is the leakage.
- The more options you compare on the same dev set, the bigger this inflation gets.

This effect has been studied directly. Cawley & Talbot (JMLR 2010) showed that over-fitting during model selection can be as large as the real differences between the methods being compared, so common evaluation practices are biased by it. ([paper](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html))

### 2.3 The unseen set (also called the test set)

- **What it is:** another set of data, kept fully separate.
- **The rule:** nobody uses it for any decision while building the model:
  - not for the learning rate or other hyperparameters;
  - not for choosing data or data mixes;
  - not for choosing a checkpoint.
  It stays unused until the end.
- **How it's used:** only after the model is **finished and frozen** is it measured on the unseen set, **once**.
- **Why it's needed:** no decision depended on it, so its score has no selection bias. It's an **unbiased estimate of how the final model does on that kind of task.**

Two limits on that:
1. **It is unbiased only for the tasks in the unseen set.** It doesn't measure every real-world use of the model. A model can do well on the unseen benchmarks and still fail on tasks none of them cover.
2. **It stays unbiased only while it's used once.** If you look at the unseen score, change something, and measure again, you're now making decisions with it. It has become a second dev set, and its score starts inflating too. You'd then need a fresh unseen set.

### 2.4 Why the two must be different

- If the dev set and the unseen set were the same, the final reported score would come from the same data used for months of decisions. That score would be inflated (section 2.2), and it would make the model look better than it is.
- The **dev set** is for the people building the model: it guides every choice, and because of that its score becomes biased.
- The **unseen set** is for reporting: since nothing was chosen with it, its score is an honest measure of the final model on those tasks.
- **How to read the two together:**
  - unseen score close to the dev score → the decisions generalized;
  - unseen score much lower → the decisions over-fitted the dev set, or the dev set measures different skills than the unseen set.

## 3. How this looks in LLM post-training (SFT)

LLM post-training doesn't usually split one data pile into three parts. It uses **separate things for each role**:

| Role | What it is in SFT | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **Training data** | the SFT chats the model learns from | our 5,000 UltraChat chats (`train_sft`) |
| **Validation split** | held-out chats **from the same source**; gives the validation loss (how well the model predicts answers it hasn't trained on) | our 500 UltraChat chats (`test_sft`) |
| **Dev suite** | a **list of public benchmarks** used for every decision | Tülu 3: MMLU, PopQA, TruthfulQA, HumanEval(+), GSM8K, MATH, BBH, DROP, IFEval, AlpacaEval 2, plus safety tests |
| **Unseen suite** | a **different list of benchmarks**, designed separately and never used for decisions | Tülu 3's includes AGIEval, MMLU-Pro, GPQA, **IFEval-OOD** and HREF |

### 3.1 How Tülu 3 built its unseen suite

- It was designed **independently** of the dev suite, so the unseen tests are **different tasks**, not just new questions of the same task types.
  - Example: **IFEval-OOD** uses kinds of instruction constraints that aren't in IFEval. A model that was only tuned toward IFEval's specific constraint types doesn't automatically do well on it.
- Its tests were written to look like **real use**:
  - no few-shot examples presented as a dialogue;
  - clear instructions that set the context;
  - a request to keep reasoning short;
  - a stated format for the final answer.
- Tülu 3 says the unseen evaluations are "held-out as tests to measure overfitting and generalization".
- It also has a third, separate group of **safety** evaluations.

Source: [Tülu 3 (Ai2, 2024), evaluation section](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124)

### 3.2 Decontamination has to cover both lists

If any training chat contains a dev or unseen benchmark question, those scores are inflated by direct leakage, whatever the split.
- Tülu 3 and OLMo 3 check every training example against every benchmark question using **8-grams** (runs of 8 consecutive tokens).
- If a training example contains **50% or more** of a question's 8-grams, the example is removed.

### 3.3 The validation split is also a dev measure

The validation loss on our 500 held-out chats counts as dev data as soon as we use it to choose something. We already did that:
- in the Muon learning-rate sweep, we picked **1.2e-4** partly because it had the lowest validation loss (**1.2747 at step 80**);
- choosing both the LR and the step by that same number means the 1.2747 is **optimistic**, for exactly the reason in section 2.2.

The honest check is to measure the chosen setting on tests that weren't used for the choice.

## 4. The correct order of work

1. **Before any experiment:** choose the dev list and the unseen list, and decontaminate the training data against **both**.
2. **During development:** make every decision with the dev list and the validation loss: dataset, mix, size, LR, epochs, checkpoint.
3. **Freeze** the final model.
4. **Measure it on the unseen list once.** Report the dev and unseen scores side by side.
5. **Never tune on the unseen score.** If you change anything because of it, it's now a dev measure and you need a new unseen list for an honest final number.

## 5. What we'll use

- **Validation loss:** the 500 held-out UltraChat chats (already running every 10 steps).
- **Dev list:** end-token rate, IFEval, TruthfulQA (MC2), PopQA, DROP, plus HellaSwag and ARC in cloze form to catch forgetting.
- **Unseen list:** different benchmarks chosen now and not looked at until the end. For example MMLU-Pro and AGIEval in cloze form, and IFEval-OOD once text generation works.

Sources:
- [Tülu 3 (Ai2, 2024): dev / unseen / safety suites, decontamination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124)
- [Cawley & Talbot, "On Over-fitting in Model Selection and Subsequent Selection Bias in Performance Evaluation" (JMLR 2010)](https://www.jmlr.org/papers/v11/cawley10a.html)
- [OLMo 3 (Ai2, 2025): decontamination](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13961)

# What is the dev suite (development suite) and what is the unseen suite in evaluations?

## The core problem: "information leakage"

To understand why we need both a dev set and an unseen set, you have to understand one of the biggest traps in AI: **information leakage**.

When researchers build an AI, they have to make hundreds of decisions:
- "What learning rate should we use?"
- "Should we include 10% math data or 20% math data?"
- "How many epochs should we train, and which checkpoint should we keep?"

They answer these questions by running an experiment, testing the model, and picking the option that gets the highest score.

## The 3 sets (the big picture)

To keep the scores honest, researchers keep three separate sets of data. In LLM post-training (SFT), these are usually not three slices of one data pile. The dev set and the unseen set are **separate lists of benchmarks**.

### 1. The training set (the engine)
- **What it is:** the data the model learns from. For SFT, this is the chats (for us, 5,000 UltraChat chats). This is what goes through the GPU: the model computes gradients and updates its weights on this data.
- **The flaw:** if you test the model on this data, it scores higher than it would on new data, often much higher, because it was fitted to these exact examples. The score tells you nothing about new data.

### 2. The dev set / validation set (the steering wheel)
- **What it is:** data the model never trains on. In SFT there are two kinds:
  - a **validation split**: held-out chats from the same source, which give the validation loss (for us, 500 UltraChat chats);
  - a **dev suite**: a list of benchmarks. Tülu 3's dev suite is MMLU, PopQA, TruthfulQA, HumanEval(+), GSM8K, MATH, BBH, DROP, IFEval, AlpacaEval 2 and safety tests.
- **How it's used:** after training, the researchers test the model on the dev set. For example, they test two data mixes (Mix A and Mix B) by training two models:
  - Model A scores 85% on the dev set.
  - Model B scores 88% on the dev set.
  - The researchers choose Mix B.
- **Why it is flawed (the leakage):** the model never updated its weights on the dev set, but the researchers used the dev set to make a design choice.
  - Every score has some random noise, so the option that wins is partly the one that got lucky on these particular questions.
  - Because they keep making changes to push the dev score higher, the model indirectly becomes over-fitted to the dev set. It ends up tailored to the specific questions in it.
  - So the dev score of the final model is **higher than its real performance**.

### 3. The unseen set / test set (the final reality check)
- **What it is:** another set of benchmarks, designed separately from the dev set. It tests different tasks, not just new questions of the same tasks. Tülu 3's unseen suite includes AGIEval, MMLU-Pro, GPQA, IFEval-OOD (new kinds of instructions that are not in IFEval) and HREF.
- **The golden rule:** the researchers are not allowed to use the unseen set while building the model:
  - not to tune hyperparameters;
  - not to choose data mixtures;
  - not to choose checkpoints.
  It stays unused while the model is being built.
- **How it's used:** only when the model is finished and frozen do they test it on the unseen set, **once**.
- **Why it's crucial:** nobody used this data to make any decision, so the unseen score is an **unbiased measurement of how the finished model performs on those unseen benchmarks**.
- **Two limits:**
  - it measures only the kinds of tasks in those benchmarks, not every real-world use;
  - it stays unbiased only if it's used once. If you look at the unseen score, change something and test again, it starts leaking too, and it becomes a second dev set.

## To sum up: why are they different?

If the dev set and the unseen set were the same thing, the researchers would report their final score on the exact data they used to tune and tweak the model for months. That is bad science: it artificially inflates the model's scores.

- The **dev set** is the tool the engineers use to guide the model's development. Because it's used for choices, its score becomes biased (too high).
- The **unseen set** is the tool that tells everyone how good the model actually is. Because it was never used for choices, its score is honest.
- **Reading them together:**
  - unseen close to dev → the decisions generalized;
  - unseen much lower than dev → the decisions over-fitted the dev set.

**One more rule:** the training data must not contain questions from either the dev or the unseen benchmarks. Otherwise the model memorizes answers and both scores are fake. Tülu 3 removes any training example that contains 50% or more of a benchmark question's 8-token chunks (8-grams).

Source: [Tülu 3 (Ai2, 2024), evaluation section](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124)
