Written for: your colleagues and sir, reading the Q7/Q8 section of the shared doc. This is the kernel-benchmarks part, in the same format as your SFT-DATA EVALUATION section.

---

**SFT – KERNEL BENCHMARKS —>**

**Step 1: What we have to decide**

The kernels used in pretraining are already benchmarked: the BluBLAS GEMMs, attention (forward v62 and backward Vj1d), RMSNorm, RoPE, SwiGLU, AdamW/Muon, and the gradient all-reduce. For SFT, only three groups of kernels need new benchmarks:
1. **Kernels we changed for SFT.**
2. **Kernels we didn't change, but which get different inputs in SFT.**
3. **Kernels that will be new** once we build the planned features (v1.5 bucketing, v2 packing, logits only at trained positions).

For each one we decide what to measure (speed, memory, correctness) and who to compare against.

**Step 2: Where the work goes in one SFT step today (v1, padding)**

This is my arithmetic from our model config (d_model 2304, 26 layers, ffn 6144, vocab 50,304) for one micro-batch of 8 × 4096 tokens. These are not measured kernel times.
* **Linear layers:** about 289 TFLOP, 80% of the work. About 70% of it is spent on padding rows, because the average chat is 1,238 of 4,096 tokens.
* **Attention:** about 48 TFLOP, 13% of the work. Up to about 90% of it is spent on padding. The pads sit at the end of each row, where every position reads the most earlier positions.
* **lm_head (the logits):** about 23 TFLOP, 6% of the work. About 77% of it is spent on rows with no loss (prompt + padding).
* **In total, about 73% of each step's work goes to tokens that don't change the result.**
* The logged 53% MFU counts padding as useful work (`tokens = B·T·GA·W`, `bluscript_zero_ckpt.cpp:2666`). On real tokens it is about 14% (my estimate).

So for SFT speed, the biggest gain comes from removing padding (v1.5 / v2), not from any single kernel. A one-step nsys profile on the H200 will replace these estimates with measured kernel times.

**Step 3: Kernels we changed for SFT (benchmark now)**

**Loss kernel** (`LossKernels.cu`). What changed:
* label 65535 is ignored: the forward skips the row (`:215`, `:350`), the backward writes a zero row (`:692`, `:777`), and the count skips it (`:110`);
* it can divide by the global trained-token count of the whole step;
* the loss value is always fp32;
* the bf16 vector path and the vocab%4 case are fixed.

It is tested correct on 136 cases.

What to measure:
* forward + backward time with 0%, 50%, 77% (our real share) and 95% of rows ignored;
* peak memory;
* the numerical error against an fp64 reference.

One fact to keep in mind: the backward still writes a full row of 50,304 zeros for every ignored row. That is about 3.3 GB per micro-batch, or about 0.5 ms on the H200 out of a ~660 ms micro-step. So for this kernel, correctness and memory matter more than speed.

Rivals:
* **PyTorch `F.cross_entropy`** (fp32 and bf16): the baseline. Its `ignore_index` (default −100) "does not contribute to the input gradient", and the mean is taken over the non-ignored targets only.
* **Liger Kernel** (LinkedIn, Triton): about +20% throughput and −60% memory overall. Its fused linear cross-entropy (lm_head + loss in chunks) cuts loss memory more than 4× at a 128k vocabulary.
* **Apple Cut Cross-Entropy (CCE)**: from Apple researchers, written in Triton, needs an NVIDIA Ampere or newer GPU. It never stores the full logits. On Gemma 2 (2B), loss memory went from 24 GB to 1 MB and the classifier head from 28 GB to 1 GB, with no loss in speed (their claim).

Sources: PyTorch CrossEntropyLoss docs · Liger Kernel (arXiv 2410.10989) · Cut Your Losses (Apple, ICLR 2025, arXiv 2411.09009) · apple/ml-cross-entropy

**Step 4: Kernels we didn't change, but SFT gives them different inputs (measure now)**

**Embedding backward.** Checked in our code:
* SFT runs with `BLU_ALL_BF16=1`, so the embedding table is bf16.
* The atomic-free "cooperative" kernel is fp32-only (`EmbeddingKernels.cu:415`). A bf16 table always falls back to the one-atomicAdd-per-element kernel (`:127-148`).
* The trainer passes `padding_idx = −1` (`bluscript_zero_ckpt.cpp:713`), so padding is not skipped.
* About 70% of every row is the pad id 50256. So in one micro-batch, about 22,900 pad positions × 2,304 columns ≈ **53 million atomic adds of 0.0 onto the same 2,304 memory addresses**, which all wait in line.
* For comparison, the most repeated pretraining token in our 10-01 test (`,`) appeared 1,290 times per micro-batch. The pad token appears about 18× more.

Precision:
* Adding 0.0 changes nothing, so the pads themselves don't hurt precision.
* But template tokens (`<`, `|`, `\n`, `user`, `ass`, `istant`) repeat in every chat, so the bf16 rounding problem is bigger in SFT.
* Our 10-01 local test used real token ids and made-up gradients. On the most frequent tokens, the bf16 atomicAdd lost 4.2% (random-direction gradients) to 52–55% (aligned gradients), against about 3e-8 for an fp32 table.

Decision:
* Use **Kruthik's `EmbeddingBwdFused`** (BLUCCL branch) instead of the atomicAdd kernel. It sorts the token ids, adds each token's gradients in fp32, and rounds to bf16 once. No atomics, and the same result every run.
* Its file header (their numbers, not measured by us) gives the error against fp64: atomicAdd 1.83e-3 (different each run), cooperative 1.10e-3, fused 2.44e-4 (the same every run).
* **Required fix:** it ignores the real token count. It throws away `N` (`embedding_fused.cu:1300`) and always sorts the count fixed at install, B × T (`:1189`). That's correct while every micro-batch is 8 × 4096 (v1 and v2), and silently wrong when the count changes (v1.5). The fix is to pass the real N into `run()` and size its buffer for the largest N.

What to measure:
* time and error with SFT-like ids (70% = 50256) and with pretraining ids;
* determinism: two runs must give identical results.

Rival: **PyTorch's embedding backward**. For large batches it sorts the indices and then sums each token's rows, the same idea as Kruthik's.

Sources: PyTorch embedding backward (commit #22016, "Optimization of the Embedding and Embedding-Bag CUDA Kernel") · work doc §36.2 · embedding_optimizer_zero_1_parallelism.md §6.2, §17

**Step 5: Kernels that will be new when we build the planned features (benchmark when built)**

Measured on our real stage-0 data (5,000 chats), total work compared to v1:
* **v1.5:** 35.2% (×2.84);
* **v2:** 27.8% (×3.60).

These are upper bounds, because the optimizer step and the all-reduce don't shrink.

**v1.5: length bucketing.**
* No new kernel.
* New GEMM shapes: M = 8·T, with T anywhere from 256 to 4096. The BluBLAS dispatch is tuned for M = 32,768, so each new shape must be checked against cuBLAS.
* Attention v62 needs T to be a multiple of 256 in the forward, and of 64 in the backward.
* The fused embedding kernel needs the real-N fix, because N changes every micro-batch.

**v2: packing several chats into each 4096 row.**
* Attention forward (v62) and backward (Vj1d) with a block-diagonal causal mask, so each chat sees only itself.
* A guard for fully-masked tiles (they give NaN today).
* RoPE positions restarting at 0 for each chat.
* The loader passing the chat boundaries.
* Correctness check: compare against PyTorch SDPA with an explicit mask. A mask bug gives no error, and the loss still goes down.
* Speed rivals:
  * **FlashAttention-3 `flash_attn_varlen_func`**: forward + backward, takes the chat boundaries as `cu_seqlens`. I checked its code in the hopper folder. FA3 reaches up to 840 TFLOP/s in BF16 on H100 (85% of peak), 1.5–2.0× FA2.
  * **FlashAttention-2 varlen.**
  * **PyTorch FlexAttention** document mask: 90% of FA2 forward and 85% backward (A100), and +71% sample-packing throughput in torchtune.
  * **NVIDIA Transformer Engine / cuDNN "THD" format**, used by NeMo.

**Logits only at trained positions (Q11).**
* A gather of the trained rows, then the lm_head GEMM with M = the number of trained tokens (for example 7,533 in one micro-batch), then a scatter back in the backward.
* Risk: BluBLAS silently returns wrong numbers when M or N is not a multiple of 64 with a transposed operand. We saw this on 09-26 in Muon's Newton–Schulz. So M must be padded to a multiple of 64, or a guard added.
* Saving: about 4.9% of a step's work today, but only about 1.5% after v2, because then only prompt rows are wasted.
* Rivals: Liger fused linear CE, Apple CCE.

**Long-context think SFT.**
* A chunked or fused linear + loss kernel, so the full logits are never stored. At T = 32,768, one sequence's logits take 3.3 GB in bf16.
* Rivals: Liger fused linear CE, Apple CCE.

**DFT / focal loss** (future): loss-kernel variants, compared for numbers against a PyTorch reference.

Sources: FlashAttention-3 (NeurIPS 2024, arXiv 2407.08608) · Dao-AILab/flash-attention (hopper `flash_attn_varlen_func`) · FlexAttention (PyTorch blog; arXiv 2412.05496) · NVIDIA NeMo sequence packing docs

**Step 6: What doesn't need new benchmarks**

* **RMSNorm, RoPE (v1), SwiGLU, the GEMMs at today's shapes, AdamW/Muon, the all-reduce:** same shapes and same kind of inputs as pretraining, which are already benchmarked.
* **The denominator:** no kernel. It's the CPU count from `valid_counts.bin` plus one MPI all-reduce of a single number. The library's GPU count kernel (`LossKernels.cu:104`) is not used by the trainer.

**Step 7: The rivals we compete against**

| What | Rivals |
|---|---|
| Loss kernel | Apple Cut Cross-Entropy, Liger (fused linear CE), PyTorch `F.cross_entropy` |
| Attention (v1, v1.5, and v2 packed) | FlashAttention-3 (incl. varlen), FlexAttention, PyTorch SDPA |
| Embedding backward | PyTorch's embedding backward |
| Whole SFT step | NVIDIA NeMo / Megatron + Transformer Engine, HF TRL (+ FlashAttention) |

Whole-step claims (theirs, not ours):
* NeMo sequence packing: "up to 10X performance improvement in terms of FLOPs, up to 6X … in terms of training time, and no impact on model convergence".
* HF + IBM packing with FlashAttention-2: "up to 2x improvement in training throughput".

PyTorch vs torchtitan:
* **torchtitan** is a separate project from the PyTorch team, installed on its own. It's a training platform built on top of PyTorch.
* Its loss calls PyTorch's `F.cross_entropy` with `reduction="sum"` and `ignore_index = −100`, then divides by the global trained-token count.
* So the kernel and `ignore_index` come from PyTorch. The "sum, then divide once by the whole step's token count" recipe comes from torchtitan's code, and that is the recipe we used in our trainer.

Sources: NeMo packed sequence docs · HF blog "Improving Hugging Face Training Efficiency Through Packing with Flash Attention" · IBM paper (arXiv 2407.09105) · pytorch/torchtitan (`components/loss.py`)

**Step 8: How to benchmark fairly**

1. **Same shapes as our real run:**
   * 8 × 4096 = 32,768 rows;
   * vocabulary 50,304;
   * d_model 2,304, 26 layers;
   * head_dim 128, 18 query heads and 6 key/value heads.
2. **Same conditions:** bf16, the H200, free (unlocked) clocks, which is how production runs.
3. **Correctness before speed:** compare outputs and gradients against an fp64 reference first. A fast kernel that is wrong is useless.
4. **Timing:**
   * do warm-up runs first;
   * time many repetitions and report the median and the spread;
   * repeat the whole measurement at least twice.
5. **Memory:** record the peak memory of each kernel and of the whole step.
6. **Whole step:**
   * measure **useful tokens per second** (real non-pad tokens per second), because our MFU counts padding;
   * also measure step time, peak memory, and the final val loss, which must be the same.
7. **One nsys profile of a real SFT step on the H200**, to get measured kernel time shares instead of the estimates in Step 2.

**Step 9: My plan, in order**

1. **Loss kernel** vs PyTorch, Liger and Apple CCE, at 77% ignored rows: laptop GPU first, then H200.
2. **Embedding backward:**
   * port Kruthik's fused kernel with the real-N fix;
   * compare against the atomicAdd kernel and PyTorch for time, error and determinism.
3. **One nsys profile** of a real SFT step on the H200.
4. **v1.5:**
   * loader bucketing, the GEMM shape check, and the fused embedding with real N;
   * whole-step comparison against HF `group_by_length`.
5. **v2:**
   * masked attention forward and backward, RoPE restart, packing loader;
   * correctness against SDPA;
   * speed against FA3 varlen and FlexAttention;
   * whole-step comparison against NeMo and HF TRL packing.
6. **Logits only at trained positions (Q11)** after v2, with the BluBLAS M%64 guard.

The row length (T) and padding in each method
	Chats per row	Row length T	Padding	Attention change?
v1 (today)	1	always 4096	lots (~70%)	no
v1.5 (bucketing)	1	changes per micro-batch (the longest chat in it, rounded up to 256)	some (~20%)	no
v2 (packing)	many	always 4096	tiny (~0.4%)	yes: each chat may see only itself

So the row length changes in v1.5, not in v2. The "variable size" I mentioned for v2 was a different style, "padding-free" (all chats in one flat stream with no rows). We don't need that. Packing into fixed 4096 rows is the right choice for us.
v1.5: still one chat per row, just shorter rows

Sort the chats inside each step by length, put similar lengths in the same micro-batch, and pad only up to the longest one in that micro-batch:

v1 (today), every row padded to 4096:
row 1: [chat A 1,200][pad ......................................... 2,896]

v1.5, micro-batch of 8 similar chats, T = 1,280 (longest 1,250 → rounded up to 1,280):
row 1: [chat A 1,200][pad 80]
row 2: [chat B 1,250][pad 30]
row 3: [chat C 1,180][pad 100]
 ...

    Still one chat per row, padding at the end. Attention only looks back, so no attention change is needed, same as v1.
    Padding still exists, just much less: on our data, 79.8% of tokens are real vs 30.2% in v1.

v2: several chats in one 4096 row

row (T = 4096):
tokens:     [ chat A: 1,200 ][ chat B: 1,500 ][ chat C: 1,380 ][pad 16]
positions:   0 … 1,199        0 … 1,499        0 … 1,379        (RoPE restarts per chat)
labels:      A's own labels    B's own labels   C's own labels   65535
             (65535 on A's     (65535 on B's    (65535 on C's
              prompt)           prompt)          prompt)

The attention mask has to be block-diagonal: each chat sees only itself, and only backwards.

            A A A   B B B   C C C   pad
A           ■
A           ■ ■
A           ■ ■ ■
B                   ■
B                   ■ ■
B                   ■ ■ ■
C                           ■
C                           ■ ■
C                           ■ ■ ■
pad                                  ■   (its own block; label 65535, so no loss either way)

    Without this mask, chat B would read chat A. The loss would still go down and nothing would warn us.
    The skipped blocks are also why v2's attention is the cheapest: a chat of 1,500 tokens costs 1,500², not 4,096².

"Must we fill exactly 4096?" No. A small leftover is padded

Chats rarely add up to exactly 4096. The usual method is best-fit decreasing:

    Sort the chats from longest to shortest.
    Put each chat into the row where it fits best, with the least space left over.
    If it fits nowhere, start a new row.
    Fill whatever space is left at the end of each row with pad tokens (label 65535).

row 1: [ 2,000 ][ 1,500 ][ 580 ][pad 16]   = 4,096
row 2: [ 3,100 ][ 990 ][pad 6]             = 4,096

    Measured on our 5,000 chats: 1,517 rows, an average of 16 pad tokens per row, 99.6% real.
    Never split one chat across two rows. The answer would lose its prompt, or the end token would land in another row. TRL has a split option (bfd_split), but it isn't for SFT.
    A chat longer than 4096 is dropped, same as today.
    The pad tail sits at the end of the row and only looks back, so it's harmless, same as in v1.

Two small things that change with v2

    The number of chats per row varies (here 1–5). So a "step" should be counted in tokens or chats, not rows. Our loss already divides by the global trained-token count, so every token keeps the same weight.
    Tokens per micro-batch stay 8 × 4096, so Kruthik's fused embedding kernel (fixed N) still works with v2. With v1.5 it doesn't, until it takes the real count.

| **v1.5** (bucketing) | 1 | **changes per micro-batch** (the longest chat in it, rounded up to 256) | some (~20%) | no |
| **v2** (packing) | many | **always 4096** | tiny (~0.4%) | **yes**: each chat may see only itself |

So the row length changes in **v1.5**, not in v2. The "variable size" I mentioned for v2 was a different style, "padding-free" (all chats in one flat stream with no rows). I don't need that. Packing into fixed 4096 rows is the right choice for me.

**About the padding-free style.** This is what HF TRL's `padding_free` and FlashAttention's varlen functions use: all chats of a micro-batch are joined into one flat stream, and only the chat start positions (`cu_seqlens`) are passed to attention. There are no rows at all. The number of tokens per micro-batch then changes every time, which breaks fixed-size kernels such as Kruthik's embedding kernel (Step 4). Fixed 4096 rows keep the same 8 × 4096 tokens every micro-batch.

**v1.5: still one chat per row, just shorter rows**

Sort the chats inside each step by length, put similar lengths in the same micro-batch, and pad only up to the longest one in that micro-batch:

```
v1 (today), every row padded to 4096:
row 1: [chat A 1,200][pad ......................................... 2,896]

v1.5, micro-batch of 8 similar chats, T = 1,280 (longest 1,250 → rounded up to 1,280):
row 1: [chat A 1,200][pad 80]
row 2: [chat B 1,250][pad 30]
row 3: [chat C 1,180][pad 100]
 ...
```

* Still one chat per row, padding at the end. Attention only looks back, so no attention change is needed, same as v1.
* Padding still exists, just much less: on my data, 79.8% of tokens are real vs 30.2% in v1.

Added details for v1.5:
* **Why sort only inside each step, not the whole dataset:** if the whole dataset were sorted, each step would hold only long chats or only short chats, and the order would no longer be random. So the realistic method is:
  1. shuffle;
  2. take one step's 64 chats;
  3. sort only those;
  4. cut them into 8 micro-batches of 8.

  HF Transformers' `group_by_length` does the same kind of thing: it groups similar lengths "while keeping a bit of randomness". Kathir's PyTorch script sorts inside each global batch too.
* **Why round up to 256:** the attention forward kernel (v62) needs T to be a multiple of 256 (the backward needs 64).
* **What changes for the kernels:**
  * the GEMMs get new shapes every micro-batch (M = 8·T), while the BluBLAS dispatch is tuned for M = 32,768;
  * the number of tokens per micro-batch changes, so Kruthik's fused embedding kernel needs the real-N fix.

**v2: several chats in one 4096 row**

```
row (T = 4096):
tokens:     [ chat A: 1,200 ][ chat B: 1,500 ][ chat C: 1,380 ][pad 16]
positions:   0 … 1,199        0 … 1,499        0 … 1,379        (RoPE restarts per chat)
labels:      A's own labels    B's own labels   C's own labels   65535
             (65535 on A's     (65535 on B's    (65535 on C's
              prompt)           prompt)          prompt)
```

The attention mask has to be **block-diagonal**: each chat sees only itself, and only backwards.

```
            A A A   B B B   C C C   pad
A           ■
A           ■ ■
A           ■ ■ ■
B                   ■
B                   ■ ■
B                   ■ ■ ■
C                           ■
C                           ■ ■
C                           ■ ■ ■
pad                                  ■   (its own block; label 65535, so no loss either way)
```

* Without this mask, chat B would read chat A. The loss would still go down and nothing would warn me.
* The skipped blocks are also why v2's attention is the cheapest: a chat of 1,500 tokens costs 1,500², not 4,096².

**"Must I fill exactly 4096?" No. A small leftover is padded**

Chats rarely add up to exactly 4096. The usual method is **best-fit decreasing**:
1. Sort the chats from longest to shortest.
2. Put each chat into the row where it fits best, with the least space left over.
3. If it fits nowhere, start a new row.
4. Fill whatever space is left at the end of each row with pad tokens (label 65535).

```
row 1: [ 2,000 ][ 1,500 ][ 580 ][pad 16]   = 4,096
row 2: [ 3,100 ][ 990 ][pad 6]             = 4,096
```

* **Measured on my 5,000 chats:** 1,517 rows, an average of **16 pad tokens per row**, 99.6% real.
* **Never split one chat across two rows.** The answer would lose its prompt, or the end token would land in another row. TRL has a split option (`bfd_split`), but it isn't for SFT.
* A chat longer than 4096 is dropped, same as today.
* The pad tail sits at the end of the row and only looks back, so it's harmless, same as in v1.

**Two small things that change with v2**

* **The number of chats per row varies** (here 1–5). So a "step" should be counted in tokens or chats, not rows. My loss already divides by the global trained-token count, so every token keeps the same weight.
* **Tokens per micro-batch stay 8 × 4096**, so Kruthik's fused embedding kernel (fixed N) still works with v2. With v1.5 it doesn't, until it takes the real count.

**Measured comparison on my real stage-0 data** (5,000 UltraChat chats; mean 1,238 tokens, median 1,154, longest 4,069). Work is my model's work per token plus attention, relative to v1:

| Method | Real tokens (not padding) | Total work vs v1 | Speed-up (upper bound) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **v1** (today) | 30.2% | 100% | ×1.00 |
| **v1.5** realistic (shuffle, sort each 64-chat step, pad to the longest ×256) | 79.8% | 35.2% | **×2.84** |
| v1.5 ideal (whole dataset sorted; not usable in practice) | 90.5% | 30.7% | ×3.26 |
| **v2** packing + block-diagonal mask | **99.6%** | **27.8%** | **×3.60** |
| v2 without the mask | 99.6% | 30.3% | ×3.30, and **wrong**: chats see each other |

* These are upper bounds. The optimizer step and the gradient all-reduce run once per step and don't shrink.
* **Which tokens-per-micro-batch each method gives, and whether Kruthik's fused embedding kernel works with it:**

| Method | Tokens per micro-batch | Fused kernel (fixed N = 32,768) |
|---|---|---|
| v1 | always 8 × 4096 | works |
| v1.5 | 8 × T, T changes | silently wrong until the real-N fix |
| v2 (fixed 4096 rows) | always 8 × 4096 | works |
| padding-free (flat stream) | changes | silently wrong until the real-N fix |

* **My order:** v1.5 first (no kernel change, most of the gain), then v2 (the most efficient). This is also SFT Q&A question 10.

Sources: HF Transformers `group_by_length` / LengthGroupedSampler · HF TRL `SFTTrainer` docs (packing strategies `bfd`, `bfd_split`, `wrapped`; `padding_free`) · simulation script `pack_sim.py` on my stage-0 data

**Step 6: Kernels that will be new when I build these (benchmark when built)**

**v1.5: length bucketing.**
* No new kernel.
* New GEMM shapes: M = 8·T, with T anywhere from 256 to 4096. The BluBLAS dispatch is tuned for M = 32,768, so each new shape must be checked against cuBLAS.
* Attention v62 needs T to be a multiple of 256 in the forward, and of 64 in the backward.
* The fused embedding kernel needs the real-N fix, because N changes every micro-batch.

**v2: packing several chats into each 4096 row.**
* Attention forward (v62) and backward (Vj1d) with a block-diagonal causal mask, so each chat sees only itself.
* A guard for fully-masked tiles (they give NaN today).
* RoPE positions restarting at 0 for each chat.
* The loader passing the chat boundaries.
* Correctness check: compare against PyTorch SDPA with an explicit mask. A mask bug gives no error, and the loss still goes down.
* Speed rivals:
  * **FlashAttention-3 `flash_attn_varlen_func`**: forward + backward, takes the chat boundaries as `cu_seqlens`. I checked its code in the hopper folder. FA3 reaches up to 840 TFLOP/s in BF16 on H100 (85% of peak), 1.5–2.0× FA2.
  * **FlashAttention-2 varlen.**
  * **PyTorch FlexAttention** document mask: 90% of FA2 forward and 85% backward (A100), and +71% sample-packing throughput in torchtune.
  * **NVIDIA Transformer Engine / cuDNN "THD" format**, used by NeMo.

**Logits only at trained positions (Q11).**
* A gather of the trained rows, then the lm_head GEMM with M = the number of trained tokens (for example 7,533 in one micro-batch), then a scatter back in the backward.
* Risk: BluBLAS silently returns wrong numbers when M or N is not a multiple of 64 with a transposed operand. I saw this on 09-26 in Muon's Newton–Schulz. So M must be padded to a multiple of 64, or a guard added.
* Saving: about 4.9% of a step's work today, but only about 1.5% after v2, because then only prompt rows are wasted.
* Rivals: Liger fused linear CE, Apple CCE.

**Long-context think SFT.**
* A chunked or fused linear + loss kernel, so the full logits are never stored. At T = 32,768, one sequence's logits take 3.3 GB in bf16.
* Rivals: Liger fused linear CE, Apple CCE.

**DFT / focal loss** (future): loss-kernel variants, compared for numbers against a PyTorch reference.

Sources: FlashAttention-3 (NeurIPS 2024, arXiv 2407.08608) · Dao-AILab/flash-attention (hopper `flash_attn_varlen_func`) · FlexAttention (PyTorch blog; arXiv 2412.05496) · NVIDIA NeMo sequence packing docs

**Step 7: What doesn't need new benchmarks**

* **RMSNorm, RoPE (v1), SwiGLU, the GEMMs at today's shapes, AdamW/Muon, the all-reduce:** same shapes and same kind of inputs as pretraining, which are already benchmarked.
* **The denominator:** no kernel. It's the CPU count from `valid_counts.bin` plus one MPI all-reduce of a single number. The library's GPU count kernel (`LossKernels.cu:104`) is not used by the trainer.

**Step 8: The rivals I compete against**

| What | Rivals |
|---|---|
| Loss kernel | Apple Cut Cross-Entropy, Liger (fused linear CE), PyTorch `F.cross_entropy` |
| Attention (v1, v1.5, and v2 packed) | FlashAttention-3 (incl. varlen), FlexAttention, PyTorch SDPA |
| Embedding backward | PyTorch's embedding backward |
| Whole SFT step | NVIDIA NeMo / Megatron + Transformer Engine, HF TRL (+ FlashAttention) |

Whole-step claims (theirs, not mine):
* NeMo sequence packing: "up to 10X performance improvement in terms of FLOPs, up to 6X … in terms of training time, and no impact on model convergence".
* HF + IBM packing with FlashAttention-2: "up to 2x improvement in training throughput".

PyTorch vs torchtitan:
* **torchtitan** is a separate project from the PyTorch team, installed on its own. It's a training platform built on top of PyTorch.
* Its loss calls PyTorch's `F.cross_entropy` with `reduction="sum"` and `ignore_index = −100`, then divides by the global trained-token count.
* So the kernel and `ignore_index` come from PyTorch. The "sum, then divide once by the whole step's token count" recipe comes from torchtitan's code, and that is the recipe I used in the SFT trainer.

Sources: NeMo packed sequence docs · HF blog "Improving Hugging Face Training Efficiency Through Packing with Flash Attention" · IBM paper (arXiv 2407.09105) · pytorch/torchtitan (`components/loss.py`)

**Step 9: How to benchmark fairly**

1. **Same shapes as my real run:**
   * 8 × 4096 = 32,768 rows;
   * vocabulary 50,304;
   * d_model 2,304, 26 layers;
   * head_dim 128, 18 query heads and 6 key/value heads.
2. **Same conditions:** bf16, the H200, free (unlocked) clocks, which is how production runs.
3. **Correctness before speed:** compare outputs and gradients against an fp64 reference first. A fast kernel that is wrong is useless.
4. **Timing:**
   * do warm-up runs first;
   * time many repetitions and report the median and the spread;
   * repeat the whole measurement at least twice.
5. **Memory:** record the peak memory of each kernel and of the whole step.
6. **Whole step:**
   * measure **useful tokens per second** (real non-pad tokens per second), because the logged MFU counts padding;
   * also measure step time, peak memory, and the final val loss, which must be the same.
7. **One nsys profile of a real SFT step on the H200**, to get measured kernel time shares instead of the estimates in Step 2.

**Step 10: My plan, in order**

1. **Loss kernel** vs PyTorch, Liger and Apple CCE, at 77% ignored rows: laptop GPU first, then H200.
2. **Embedding backward:**
   * port Kruthik's fused kernel with the real-N fix;
   * compare against the atomicAdd kernel and PyTorch for time, error and determinism.
3. **One nsys profile** of a real SFT step on the H200.
4. **v1.5:**
   * loader bucketing, the GEMM shape check, and the fused embedding with real N;
   * whole-step comparison against HF `group_by_length`.
5. **v2:**
   * masked attention forward and backward, RoPE restart, packing loader;
   * correctness against SDPA;
   * speed against FA3 varlen and FlexAttention;
   * whole-step comparison against NeMo and HF TRL packing.
6. **Logits only at trained positions (Q11)** after v2, with the BluBLAS M%64 guard.

Written for: your colleagues and sir, reading the Q7/Q8 section of the shared doc. This is the full kernel-benchmarks section in "I" voice, now with torchtitan added in Steps 8 and 10 and in the links.

**SFT – KERNEL BENCHMARKS —>**

**Step 1: What I have to decide**

The kernels used in pretraining are already benchmarked: the BluBLAS GEMMs, attention (forward v62 and backward Vj1d), RMSNorm, RoPE, SwiGLU, AdamW/Muon, and the gradient all-reduce. For SFT, only three groups of kernels need new benchmarks:
1. **Kernels I changed for SFT.**
2. **Kernels I didn't change, but which get different inputs in SFT.**
3. **Kernels that will be new** once I build the planned features (v1.5 bucketing, v2 packing, logits only at trained positions).

For each one I decide what to measure (speed, memory, correctness) and who to compare against.

**Step 2: Where the work goes in one SFT step today (v1, padding)**

This is my arithmetic from the model config (d_model 2304, 26 layers, ffn 6144, vocab 50,304) for one micro-batch of 8 × 4096 tokens. These are not measured kernel times.
* **Linear layers:** about 289 TFLOP, 80% of the work. About 70% of it is spent on padding rows, because the average chat in my data is 1,238 of 4,096 tokens.
* **Attention:** about 48 TFLOP, 13% of the work. Up to about 90% of it is spent on padding. The pads sit at the end of each row, where every position reads the most earlier positions.
* **lm_head (the logits):** about 23 TFLOP, 6% of the work. About 77% of it is spent on rows with no loss (prompt + padding).
* **In total, about 73% of each step's work goes to tokens that don't change the result.**
* The logged 53% MFU counts padding as useful work (`tokens = B·T·GA·W`, `bluscript_zero_ckpt.cpp:2666`). On real tokens it is about 14% (my estimate).

So for SFT speed, the biggest gain comes from removing padding (v1.5 / v2, Step 5), not from any single kernel. A one-step nsys profile on the H200 will replace these estimates with measured kernel times.

**Step 3: Kernels I changed for SFT (benchmark now)**

**Loss kernel** (`LossKernels.cu`). What changed:
* label 65535 is ignored: the forward skips the row (`:215`, `:350`), the backward writes a zero row (`:692`, `:777`), and the count skips it (`:110`);
* it can divide by the global trained-token count of the whole step;
* the loss value is always fp32;
* the bf16 vector path and the vocab%4 case are fixed.

It is tested correct on 136 cases.

What to measure:
* forward + backward time with 0%, 50%, 77% (the real share in my data) and 95% of rows ignored;
* peak memory;
* the numerical error against an fp64 reference.

One fact to keep in mind: the backward still writes a full row of 50,304 zeros for every ignored row. That is about 3.3 GB per micro-batch, or about 0.5 ms on the H200 out of a ~660 ms micro-step. So for this kernel, correctness and memory matter more than speed.

Rivals:
* **PyTorch `F.cross_entropy`** (fp32 and bf16): the baseline. Its `ignore_index` (default −100) "does not contribute to the input gradient", and the mean is taken over the non-ignored targets only.
* **Liger Kernel** (LinkedIn, Triton): about +20% throughput and −60% memory overall. Its fused linear cross-entropy (lm_head + loss in chunks) cuts loss memory more than 4× at a 128k vocabulary.
* **Apple Cut Cross-Entropy (CCE)**: from Apple researchers, written in Triton, needs an NVIDIA Ampere or newer GPU. It never stores the full logits. On Gemma 2 (2B), loss memory went from 24 GB to 1 MB and the classifier head from 28 GB to 1 GB, with no loss in speed (their claim).

Sources: PyTorch CrossEntropyLoss docs · Liger Kernel (arXiv 2410.10989) · Cut Your Losses (Apple, ICLR 2025, arXiv 2411.09009) · apple/ml-cross-entropy

**Step 4: Kernels I didn't change, but SFT gives them different inputs (measure now)**

**Embedding backward.** Checked in the code:
* My SFT runs use `BLU_ALL_BF16=1`, so the embedding table is bf16.
* The atomic-free "cooperative" kernel is fp32-only (`EmbeddingKernels.cu:415`). A bf16 table always falls back to the one-atomicAdd-per-element kernel (`:127-148`).
* The trainer passes `padding_idx = −1` (`bluscript_zero_ckpt.cpp:713`), so padding is not skipped.
* About 70% of every row is the pad id 50256. So in one micro-batch, about 22,900 pad positions × 2,304 columns ≈ **53 million atomic adds of 0.0 onto the same 2,304 memory addresses**, which all wait in line.
* For comparison, the most repeated pretraining token in my 10-01 test (`,`) appeared 1,290 times per micro-batch. The pad token appears about 18× more.

Precision:
* Adding 0.0 changes nothing, so the pads themselves don't hurt precision.
* But template tokens (`<`, `|`, `\n`, `user`, `ass`, `istant`) repeat in every chat, so the bf16 rounding problem is bigger in SFT.
* My 10-01 local test used real token ids and made-up gradients. On the most frequent tokens, the bf16 atomicAdd lost 4.2% (random-direction gradients) to 52–55% (aligned gradients), against about 3e-8 for an fp32 table.

Decision:
* Use **Kruthik's `EmbeddingBwdFused`** (BLUCCL branch) instead of the atomicAdd kernel. It sorts the token ids, adds each token's gradients in fp32, and rounds to bf16 once. No atomics, and the same result every run.
* Its file header (their numbers, not measured by me) gives the error against fp64: atomicAdd 1.83e-3 (different each run), cooperative 1.10e-3, fused 2.44e-4 (the same every run).
* **Required fix:** it ignores the real token count. It throws away `N` (`embedding_fused.cu:1300`) and always sorts the count fixed at install, B × T (`:1189`). That's correct while every micro-batch is 8 × 4096 (v1 and v2), and silently wrong when the count changes (v1.5, Step 5). The fix is to pass the real N into `run()` and size its buffer for the largest N.

What to measure:
* time and error with SFT-like ids (70% = 50256) and with pretraining ids;
* determinism: two runs must give identical results.

Rival: **PyTorch's embedding backward**. For large batches it sorts the indices and then sums each token's rows, the same idea as Kruthik's.

Sources: PyTorch embedding backward (commit #22016, "Optimization of the Embedding and Embedding-Bag CUDA Kernel") · work doc §36.2 · embedding_optimizer_zero_1_parallelism.md §6.2, §17

**Step 5: The three ways to put chats into rows: v1, v1.5 and v2**

How chats are put into the [8 × 4096] rows decides how much padding the GPU computes, and which kernels have to change.

**v1 (today): one chat per row, padded to 4096**

```
row 1: [chat A 1,200][pad ......................................... 2,896]
```

* Every pad position is fully computed: embedding lookup (id 50256), norms, Q/K/V, attention, MLP and its 50,304 logits. The kernels don't know which rows are pads, because no length or mask is passed.
* Causal attention lets a pad read everything before it, the whole chat included. So a pad near position 3,000 reads about 3,000 positions, while a chat token reads at most about 1,238.
* The result doesn't change:
  * a pad's label is 65535, so it has no loss;
  * nothing reads a pad, because pads come after the chat;
  * so its gradient is exactly 0, and it sends exactly 0 back to the chat.
* **Measured (my Q9 test):** I replaced the pads with random tokens, and also with tokens that appear in the chat (" France", "Paris", …). The weight gradients changed by **0.0**, bit-for-bit. The pad positions' own logits changed (by up to 0.36), but nothing uses them.
* So the pads' forward and backward work, and the memory for their activations, are all wasted: about 73% of each step's work (Step 2).

**The row length (T) and padding in each method**

| | Chats per row | Row length T | Padding | Attention change? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **v1** (today) | 1 | always 4096 | lots (~70%) | no |
| **v1.5** (bucketing) | 1 | **changes per micro-batch** (the longest chat in it, rounded up to 256) | some (~20%) | no |
| **v2** (packing) | many | **always 4096** | tiny (~0.4%) | **yes**: each chat may see only itself |

So the row length changes in **v1.5**, not in v2. The "variable size" I mentioned for v2 was a different style, "padding-free" (all chats in one flat stream with no rows). I don't need that. Packing into fixed 4096 rows is the right choice for me.

**About the padding-free style.** This is what HF TRL's `padding_free` and FlashAttention's varlen functions use: all chats of a micro-batch are joined into one flat stream, and only the chat start positions (`cu_seqlens`) are passed to attention. There are no rows at all. The number of tokens per micro-batch then changes every time, which breaks fixed-size kernels such as Kruthik's embedding kernel (Step 4). Fixed 4096 rows keep the same 8 × 4096 tokens every micro-batch.

**v1.5: still one chat per row, just shorter rows**

Sort the chats inside each step by length, put similar lengths in the same micro-batch, and pad only up to the longest one in that micro-batch:

```
v1 (today), every row padded to 4096:
row 1: [chat A 1,200][pad ......................................... 2,896]

v1.5, micro-batch of 8 similar chats, T = 1,280 (longest 1,250 → rounded up to 1,280):
row 1: [chat A 1,200][pad 80]
row 2: [chat B 1,250][pad 30]
row 3: [chat C 1,180][pad 100]
 ...
```

* Still one chat per row, padding at the end. Attention only looks back, so no attention change is needed, same as v1.
* Padding still exists, just much less: on my data, 79.8% of tokens are real vs 30.2% in v1.

Added details for v1.5:
* **Why sort only inside each step, not the whole dataset:** if the whole dataset were sorted, each step would hold only long chats or only short chats, and the order would no longer be random. So the realistic method is:
  1. shuffle;
  2. take one step's 64 chats;
  3. sort only those;
  4. cut them into 8 micro-batches of 8.

  HF Transformers' `group_by_length` does the same kind of thing: it groups similar lengths "while keeping a bit of randomness". Kathir's PyTorch script sorts inside each global batch too.
* **Why round up to 256:** the attention forward kernel (v62) needs T to be a multiple of 256 (the backward needs 64).
* **What changes for the kernels:**
  * the GEMMs get new shapes every micro-batch (M = 8·T), while the BluBLAS dispatch is tuned for M = 32,768;
  * the number of tokens per micro-batch changes, so Kruthik's fused embedding kernel needs the real-N fix.

**v2: several chats in one 4096 row**

```
row (T = 4096):
tokens:     [ chat A: 1,200 ][ chat B: 1,500 ][ chat C: 1,380 ][pad 16]
positions:   0 … 1,199        0 … 1,499        0 … 1,379        (RoPE restarts per chat)
labels:      A's own labels    B's own labels   C's own labels   65535
             (65535 on A's     (65535 on B's    (65535 on C's
              prompt)           prompt)          prompt)
```

The attention mask has to be **block-diagonal**: each chat sees only itself, and only backwards.

```
            A A A   B B B   C C C   pad
A           ■
A           ■ ■
A           ■ ■ ■
B                   ■
B                   ■ ■
B                   ■ ■ ■
C                           ■
C                           ■ ■
C                           ■ ■ ■
pad                                  ■   (its own block; label 65535, so no loss either way)
```

* Without this mask, chat B would read chat A. The loss would still go down and nothing would warn me.
* The skipped blocks are also why v2's attention is the cheapest: a chat of 1,500 tokens costs 1,500², not 4,096².

**"Must I fill exactly 4096?" No. A small leftover is padded**

Chats rarely add up to exactly 4096. The usual method is **best-fit decreasing**:
1. Sort the chats from longest to shortest.
2. Put each chat into the row where it fits best, with the least space left over.
3. If it fits nowhere, start a new row.
4. Fill whatever space is left at the end of each row with pad tokens (label 65535).

```
row 1: [ 2,000 ][ 1,500 ][ 580 ][pad 16]   = 4,096
row 2: [ 3,100 ][ 990 ][pad 6]             = 4,096
```

* **Measured on my 5,000 chats:** 1,517 rows, an average of **16 pad tokens per row**, 99.6% real.
* **Never split one chat across two rows.** The answer would lose its prompt, or the end token would land in another row. TRL has a split option (`bfd_split`), but it isn't for SFT.
* A chat longer than 4096 is dropped, same as today.
* The pad tail sits at the end of the row and only looks back, so it's harmless, same as in v1.

**Two small things that change with v2**

* **The number of chats per row varies** (here 1–5). So a "step" should be counted in tokens or chats, not rows. My loss already divides by the global trained-token count, so every token keeps the same weight.
* **Tokens per micro-batch stay 8 × 4096**, so Kruthik's fused embedding kernel (fixed N) still works with v2. With v1.5 it doesn't, until it takes the real count.

**Measured comparison on my real stage-0 data** (5,000 UltraChat chats; mean 1,238 tokens, median 1,154, longest 4,069). Work is my model's work per token plus attention, relative to v1:

| Method | Real tokens (not padding) | Total work vs v1 | Speed-up (upper bound) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **v1** (today) | 30.2% | 100% | ×1.00 |
| **v1.5** realistic (shuffle, sort each 64-chat step, pad to the longest ×256) | 79.8% | 35.2% | **×2.84** |
| v1.5 ideal (whole dataset sorted; not usable in practice) | 90.5% | 30.7% | ×3.26 |
| **v2** packing + block-diagonal mask | **99.6%** | **27.8%** | **×3.60** |
| v2 without the mask | 99.6% | 30.3% | ×3.30, and **wrong**: chats see each other |

* These are upper bounds. The optimizer step and the gradient all-reduce run once per step and don't shrink.
* **Which tokens-per-micro-batch each method gives, and whether Kruthik's fused embedding kernel works with it:**

| Method | Tokens per micro-batch | Fused kernel (fixed N = 32,768) |
|---|---|---|
| v1 | always 8 × 4096 | works |
| v1.5 | 8 × T, T changes | silently wrong until the real-N fix |
| v2 (fixed 4096 rows) | always 8 × 4096 | works |
| padding-free (flat stream) | changes | silently wrong until the real-N fix |

* **My order:** v1.5 first (no kernel change, most of the gain), then v2 (the most efficient). This is also SFT Q&A question 10.

Sources: HF Transformers `group_by_length` / LengthGroupedSampler · HF TRL `SFTTrainer` docs (packing strategies `bfd`, `bfd_split`, `wrapped`; `padding_free`) · simulation script `pack_sim.py` on my stage-0 data

**Step 6: Kernels that will be new when I build these (benchmark when built)**

**v1.5: length bucketing.**
* No new kernel.
* New GEMM shapes: M = 8·T, with T anywhere from 256 to 4096. The BluBLAS dispatch is tuned for M = 32,768, so each new shape must be checked against cuBLAS.
* Attention v62 needs T to be a multiple of 256 in the forward, and of 64 in the backward.
* The fused embedding kernel needs the real-N fix, because N changes every micro-batch.

**v2: packing several chats into each 4096 row.**
* Attention forward (v62) and backward (Vj1d) with a block-diagonal causal mask, so each chat sees only itself.
* A guard for fully-masked tiles (they give NaN today).
* RoPE positions restarting at 0 for each chat.
* The loader passing the chat boundaries.
* Correctness check: compare against PyTorch SDPA with an explicit mask. A mask bug gives no error, and the loss still goes down.
* Speed rivals:
  * **FlashAttention-3 `flash_attn_varlen_func`**: forward + backward, takes the chat boundaries as `cu_seqlens`. I checked its code in the hopper folder. FA3 reaches up to 840 TFLOP/s in BF16 on H100 (85% of peak), 1.5–2.0× FA2.
  * **FlashAttention-2 varlen.**
  * **PyTorch FlexAttention** document mask: 90% of FA2 forward and 85% backward (A100), and +71% sample-packing throughput in torchtune.
  * **NVIDIA Transformer Engine / cuDNN "THD" format**, used by NeMo.

**Logits only at trained positions (Q11).**
* A gather of the trained rows, then the lm_head GEMM with M = the number of trained tokens (for example 7,533 in one micro-batch), then a scatter back in the backward.
* Risk: BluBLAS silently returns wrong numbers when M or N is not a multiple of 64 with a transposed operand. I saw this on 09-26 in Muon's Newton–Schulz. So M must be padded to a multiple of 64, or a guard added.
* Saving: about 4.9% of a step's work today, but only about 1.5% after v2, because then only prompt rows are wasted.
* Rivals: Liger fused linear CE, Apple CCE.

**Long-context think SFT.**
* A chunked or fused linear + loss kernel, so the full logits are never stored. At T = 32,768, one sequence's logits take 3.3 GB in bf16.
* Rivals: Liger fused linear CE, Apple CCE.

**DFT / focal loss** (future): loss-kernel variants, compared for numbers against a PyTorch reference.

Sources: FlashAttention-3 (NeurIPS 2024, arXiv 2407.08608) · Dao-AILab/flash-attention (hopper `flash_attn_varlen_func`) · FlexAttention (PyTorch blog; arXiv 2412.05496) · NVIDIA NeMo sequence packing docs

**Step 7: What doesn't need new benchmarks**

* **RMSNorm, RoPE (v1), SwiGLU, the GEMMs at today's shapes, AdamW/Muon, the all-reduce:** same shapes and same kind of inputs as pretraining, which are already benchmarked.
* **The denominator:** no kernel. It's the CPU count from `valid_counts.bin` plus one MPI all-reduce of a single number. The library's GPU count kernel (`LossKernels.cu:104`) is not used by the trainer.

**Step 8: The rivals I compete against**

| What | Rivals |
|---|---|
| Loss kernel | Apple Cut Cross-Entropy, Liger (fused linear CE), PyTorch `F.cross_entropy` |
| Attention (v1, v1.5, and v2 packed) | FlashAttention-3 (incl. varlen), FlexAttention, PyTorch SDPA |
| Embedding backward | PyTorch's embedding backward |
| Whole SFT step | NVIDIA NeMo / Megatron + Transformer Engine, HF TRL (+ FlashAttention), **torchtitan** (PyTorch-native, SFT with chat datasets) |

Whole-step claims (theirs, not mine):
* NeMo sequence packing: "up to 10X performance improvement in terms of FLOPs, up to 6X … in terms of training time, and no impact on model convergence".
* HF + IBM packing with FlashAttention-2: "up to 2x improvement in training throughput".

PyTorch vs torchtitan:
* **torchtitan** is a separate project from the PyTorch team, installed on its own. It's a training platform built on top of PyTorch.
* Its loss calls PyTorch's `F.cross_entropy` with `reduction="sum"` and `ignore_index = −100`, then divides by the global trained-token count.
* So the kernel and `ignore_index` come from PyTorch. The "sum, then divide once by the whole step's token count" recipe comes from torchtitan's code, and that is the recipe I used in the SFT trainer.
* **torchtitan is a whole-step rival, not a kernel rival:**
  * its README lists "Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) with chat-formatted datasets";
  * its loss, attention and embedding are PyTorch's kernels, so my kernel comparisons against PyTorch already cover it at the kernel level;
  * as a whole SFT trainer, it's the PyTorch-native one to compare against (tokens/s, memory, final val loss);
  * its README doesn't mention packing or document masking, so I check its SFT code before comparing v2 against it.
* **torchtune** is no longer maintained ("torchtune development wound down in 2025"), so it isn't a rival target. Its FlexAttention packing number (+71%) is still a valid data point for FlexAttention.
* **torchforge**, PyTorch's newer post-training (RL) library, uses torchtitan for its distributed training.

Sources: NeMo packed sequence docs · HF blog "Improving Hugging Face Training Efficiency Through Packing with Flash Attention" · IBM paper (arXiv 2407.09105) · pytorch/torchtitan (README, `components/loss.py`) · pytorch/torchtune (maintenance notice) · torchforge (Thoughtworks Technology Radar)

**Step 9: How to benchmark fairly**

1. **Same shapes as my real run:**
   * 8 × 4096 = 32,768 rows;
   * vocabulary 50,304;
   * d_model 2,304, 26 layers;
   * head_dim 128, 18 query heads and 6 key/value heads.
2. **Same conditions:** bf16, the H200, free (unlocked) clocks, which is how production runs.
3. **Correctness before speed:** compare outputs and gradients against an fp64 reference first. A fast kernel that is wrong is useless.
4. **Timing:**
   * do warm-up runs first;
   * time many repetitions and report the median and the spread;
   * repeat the whole measurement at least twice.
5. **Memory:** record the peak memory of each kernel and of the whole step.
6. **Whole step:**
   * measure **useful tokens per second** (real non-pad tokens per second), because the logged MFU counts padding;
   * also measure step time, peak memory, and the final val loss, which must be the same.
7. **One nsys profile of a real SFT step on the H200**, to get measured kernel time shares instead of the estimates in Step 2.

**Step 10: My plan, in order**

1. **Loss kernel** vs PyTorch, Liger and Apple CCE, at 77% ignored rows: laptop GPU first, then H200.
2. **Embedding backward:**
   * port Kruthik's fused kernel with the real-N fix;
   * compare against the atomicAdd kernel and PyTorch for time, error and determinism.
3. **One nsys profile** of a real SFT step on the H200.
4. **v1.5:**
   * loader bucketing, the GEMM shape check, and the fused embedding with real N;
   * whole-step comparison against HF `group_by_length` and torchtitan's SFT.
5. **v2:**
   * masked attention forward and backward, RoPE restart, packing loader;
   * correctness against SDPA;
   * speed against FA3 varlen and FlexAttention;
   * whole-step comparison against NeMo, HF TRL packing, and torchtitan (if its SFT packs chats).
6. **Logits only at trained positions (Q11)** after v2, with the BluBLAS M%64 guard.

Written for: your colleagues and sir, reading the Q7/Q8 section of the shared doc. It's in the same format as the other two sections, in "I" voice.

**SFT – MODEL EVALUATION PLAN (Q7: benchmarks for the SFT model, Q8: checkpoints and overfitting) —>**

**Step 1: What I have to decide**

1. **Which benchmarks** measure what SFT is supposed to change, and which ones catch what SFT can break.
2. **How to run each benchmark** (prompt format, shots, decoding settings, answer extraction), so that scores are comparable between runs.
3. **How to compare the base model with the SFT model**, and different SFT runs and checkpoints with each other.
4. **How to know that a difference is real** and not noise, and how to see whether I'm overfitting.

**Step 2: Two ways a model can be scored**

| | Scoring by likelihood (no text generated) | Scoring by generation (the model writes an answer) |
|---|---|---|
| How it works | Each answer option is scored by the probability the model gives it; the highest-probability option counts as the model's choice | The model writes a full answer, then a program or a judge checks it |
| Examples | HellaSwag, ARC, MMLU (cloze form), TruthfulQA MC2 | IFEval, GSM8K, MATH, DROP, PopQA, HumanEval, AlpacaEval |
| Works for a base model? | Yes. This is how base models are scored | Only with few-shot examples in the prompt, and often badly |
| Measures | Mostly knowledge from pretraining | Answer format, following instructions, reasoning: the things SFT changes |

* **OLMo 3 uses two separate suites.**
  * **OlmoBaseEval** is for base models during pretraining. It is mainly likelihood-based (bits-per-byte), plus a main suite and a held-out suite.
  * The **post-training suite** is for SFT/DPO/RL models. It is fully generation-based.
* **The OLMES standard (Ai2)** says that for small base models, multiple-choice questions should be scored in **cloze form**: each full answer is scored by its probability, instead of asking the model for the letter A/B/C/D. The letter form stays near random until models are larger. OLMES runs both forms and reports the better one.

Sources: [OLMo 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13961) · [OLMES](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.08446)

**Step 3: How the top labs evaluate their SFT models**

**Tülu 3 (Ai2, 2024): three separate suites.**

The dev suite, used for every decision (Table 3):

| Benchmark | What it measures | Setup | Metric |
|---|---|---|---|
| MMLU | knowledge, 57 subjects | 0-shot, chain-of-thought | exact match |
| PopQA | rare facts | 15-shot | exact match |
| TruthfulQA | avoiding common false answers | 6-shot | MC2 |
| BigBench-Hard | multi-step reasoning | 3-shot, chain-of-thought | exact match |
| DROP | reading with arithmetic | 3-shot | F1 |
| MATH | competition math | 4-shot, chain-of-thought | "flex" exact match |
| GSM8K | grade-school math | 8-shot, chain-of-thought | exact match |
| HumanEval / HumanEval+ | writing Python | — | pass@10 |
| IFEval | following exact instructions | — | prompt-loose accuracy |
| AlpacaEval 2 | chat quality, judged by a model | — | length-controlled win rate |

* **Unseen suite** (never used for decisions): AGIEval English, MMLU-Pro, GPQA, DeepMind Mathematics, BigCodeBench, **IFEval-OOD** (new) and **HREF** (new). In their words: "we did not examine scores on our unseen set when developing our models, allowing us to observe how much we may have overfit."
* **Safety suite** (an average of six tests): XSTest, HarmBench, Do-Anything-Now, JailbreakTrigger, WildJailbreakTest and WildGuardTest. Together they check both refusing harmful requests and not refusing safe ones.

**OLMo 3 (Ai2, 2025): one generation-based suite, all zero-shot** (Table 16).

| Group | Benchmarks |
|---|---|
| Math | MATH, MATH-500, AIME 2024, AIME 2025, OMEGA |
| Reasoning | BigBench-Hard, ZebraLogic, AGIEval English |
| Code | HumanEval+, MBPP+, LiveCodeBench v3 |
| Instruction following | IFEval, IFBench |
| Knowledge / QA | MMLU, PopQA, GPQA |
| Chat | AlpacaEval 2 (length-controlled) |
| Tools (Instruct model) | SimpleQA, LitQA2, BFCL (function calling) |
| Safety | a separate safety average |

Settings:
* zero-shot for every benchmark;
* sampling temperature 0.6, top-p 0.95, up to 32,768 tokens;
* AIME is sampled 32 times and the code tasks 10 times, then averaged;
* thinking text (between `<think>` and `</think>`) is removed before scoring;
* every reported number is the **average of 3 runs**;
* evaluation cost **10–20% of their whole compute budget** while they developed the 7B recipe.

**What changed between them:** Tülu 3 (2024) mixed few-shot and zero-shot prompts. OLMo 3 (2025) uses **zero-shot for everything**, which is closer to how people actually use a chat model.

Sources: [Tülu 3, §7](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124) · [OLMo 3, §4.1 and Table 16](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13961)

**Step 4: What each stage changes, measured**

**Tülu 3 8B: SFT → DPO → final (RLVR):**

| | SFT | DPO | Final |
|---|---|---|---|
| Average | 60.6 | 64.7 | 65.1 |
| IFEval | 72.8 | 81.1 | 82.4 |
| AlpacaEval 2 | 12.4 | 33.5 | 34.5 |
| GSM8K | 76.2 | 84.3 | 87.6 |
| MATH | 31.5 | 42.0 | 43.7 |

**OLMo 3 Instruct 7B: SFT → DPO → final** (Table 26, average of 3 runs):

| | SFT | DPO | Final |
|---|---|---|---|
| MATH | 65.1 | 79.6 | 87.3 |
| AIME 2024 | 6.7 | 23.5 | 44.3 |
| BigBench-Hard | 51.0 | 69.3 | 71.2 |
| HumanEval+ | 69.8 | 72.9 | 77.2 |
| IFEval | 81.7 | 82.0 | 85.6 |
| IFBench | 27.4 | 29.3 | 32.3 |
| MMLU | 67.1 | 69.1 | 69.1 |
| PopQA | 16.5 | 20.7 | **14.1** |
| GPQA | 30.0 | 37.9 | 40.4 |
| AlpacaEval 2 LC | 21.8 | 43.3 | **40.9** |
| Safety | 89.5 | 89.9 | **87.6** |

**OLMo 3 Think 7B: combinations of stages after the same SFT** (Table 22, one run each):

| Pipeline | Average |
|---|---|
| SFT | 70.1 |
| SFT + DPO | 72.7 |
| SFT + RLVR | 71.9 |
| SFT + DPO + RLVR | **74.1** |

**At ~1B size, OLMo 2 1B: SFT → DPO → final:**
* average 36.9 → 40.6 → 42.7;
* GSM8K 52.1 → 59.0 → 68.3;
* IFEval 50.5 → 67.1 → 70.1;
* AlpacaEval 2 only 2.4 → 9.5 → 9.1.

**Close to my case: a colleague's result in this doc (DPO section).**
* 480M model, ~2,000 pretraining steps.
* TruthfulQA, PopQA and DROP improved in order base < SFT < DPO.
* MMLU, BBH, GSM8K, MATH and HumanEval/+ stayed at the floor at every stage.

**What these tables show:**
* **The ordering of the stages also matters.** OLMo 3 Instruct SFT started from the Think SFT model scored +3.3 on average (Table 29). The best pipeline in Table 22 is SFT, then DPO, then RL.
* **Some skills only move after SFT.**
  * AlpacaEval (chat quality, judged by a model) roughly doubles with DPO: 21.8 → 43.3 in OLMo 3, 12.4 → 33.5 in Tülu 3.
  * AIME jumps mostly with RL.
  * So a low AlpacaEval after SFT alone is normal, and it doesn't mean the SFT failed.
* **A later stage can lower some scores.** In OLMo 3 Instruct, PopQA, AlpacaEval and Safety are lower after RL than after DPO. So the stages must be compared per benchmark, not only by the average.
* **At small size, chat-judge scores barely move:** AlpacaEval stays under 10 at 1B. The floor is real.

Sources: [Tülu 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124) · [OLMo 3 (Tables 22, 24, 26, 29)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13961) · [OLMo 2 1B Instruct model card](https://huggingface.co/allenai/OLMo-2-0425-1B-Instruct)

**Step 5: Base vs SFT: measuring what SFT breaks (forgetting)**

* **"LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less"** measured forgetting with **HellaSwag, WinoGrande and ARC-Challenge**: the same likelihood tests, run before and after fine-tuning. Full fine-tuning forgot more than LoRA. In code training, full fine-tuning kept forgetting more as it saw more data.
* **Tülu 3:** TruthfulQA went **down** as more SFT data was added (Figure 4).
* **Ghosh et al. (ICML 2024):** full-parameter instruction tuning can degrade the knowledge the model had.
* **URIAL (ICLR 2024):** at most token positions, the base model and its SFT model pick the same token. SFT mostly changes style tokens. So knowledge tests should stay about the same after SFT, and a big drop is a warning.

**How I do this:**
1. Run the **base model and every SFT checkpoint** on the same likelihood tests in cloze form: HellaSwag, ARC, WinoGrande, MMLU.
2. If the scores stay about the same, SFT didn't hurt knowledge. A clear drop means forgetting. Then check the learning rate, the number of epochs and the data mix.

Sources: [LoRA Learns Less and Forgets Less](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.09673) · [A Closer Look at the Limitations of Instruction Tuning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.05119) · [URIAL](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.01552)

**Step 6: Choosing checkpoints, and seeing overfitting (Q8)**

**How the labs choose:**
* **OLMo 3:**
  * trains SFT for **2 epochs "to avoid overfitting"**;
  * sweeps the learning rate (4 values for the 32B model);
  * picks candidate checkpoints by the evaluation suite;
  * then tests each candidate with qualitative "vibe-test" questions;
  * the final Think SFT model is a **weighted merge of two checkpoints trained with different learning rates** (made with mergekit).
* **Tülu 3:**
  * trained the 8B SFT model with **5 random seeds**, which scored between **59.8 and 60.1** on average;
  * "the best random seed is comparable to the best model soup", so they used the best single run.
* **Model soups** (Wortsman et al., 2022): averaging the weights of several fine-tuned models often scores better than any single one.

**Signs of overfitting:**
1. **Validation loss goes back up while training loss keeps falling.** I already saw this in my Muon sweep: at LR 1.2e-4 the best val was 1.2747 at the end of epoch 1. In epoch 2 the train loss fell to 1.08 while val rose to 1.287.
2. **Dev scores go up but unseen scores don't.** That's overfitting to the dev benchmarks (see the dev/unseen section).
3. **Scores rise on one benchmark's style but not on a new version of it.** IFBench (Ai2, NeurIPS 2025) showed that most models "strongly overfit on a small set of verifiable constraints" from IFEval and don't generalize to its 58 new constraints. That's why IFEval-OOD and IFBench work as unseen tests.

Sources: [OLMo 3, §4.2.2](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13961) · [Tülu 3, Table 14](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124) · [Model soups](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.05482) · [IFBench](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.02833)

**Step 7: What changes a score besides the model itself**

1. **Prompt format and chat template.**
   * The SFT model must be evaluated with the same chat template it was trained with.
   * Tülu 3 compared chat templates on the same SFT data: averages from 51.6 to 53.0.
   * The lm-evaluation-harness authors ("Lessons from the Trenches", 2024) showed that scores are "highly sensitive to subtle prompt variations". They advise sharing the exact prompts and model outputs, and running significance tests.
2. **Few-shot vs zero-shot, and chain-of-thought or not.**
   * Tülu 3 tested several CoT prompts for MMLU and kept the one that helped the most subjects.
   * OLMo 3 uses zero-shot everywhere.
   * Changing either setting changes the score, so it must be fixed before comparing anything.
3. **Answer extraction.** Tülu 3: changing how the final answer is read out of the text ("flex" instead of the Minerva format) "can sometimes improve reported scores by up to 10 points".
4. **Decoding settings and randomness.** "A Sober Look at Progress in LM Reasoning" (2025) found that math benchmark scores are sensitive to:
   * decoding settings (temperature, top-p, maximum tokens);
   * random seeds;
   * prompt format;
   * even the GPU hardware and software stack (up to 8%).

   Small benchmarks are the worst: on AIME 2024 (30 questions), one question changes the score by 3.3 points.
5. **Run-to-run variation, measured by OLMo 3:**
   * They took the standard deviation across 3 runs of 14 models.
   * **High:** GPQA 1.48, AlpacaEval 1.24, IFEval 0.88.
   * **Stable:** BBH 0.39, AGIEval 0.43, HumanEval+ 0.46.
   * **Very stable:** MATH 0.25, MMLU 0.22, PopQA 0.16.
   * So they report the average of 3 runs, and they sample AIME 32 times.
6. **Benchmark size.** A small test is noisy in itself:
   * IFEval (541 prompts) is about ±2.1 points;
   * GSM8K (1,319 problems) is about ±1.4 points (one standard error at 50%).
7. **Signal vs noise.** Ai2's "Signal and Noise" (NeurIPS 2025): a benchmark is useful only if it separates better from worse models (signal) more than it changes randomly (noise).
   * They studied 30 benchmarks and 465 models (60M–32B).
   * Their fixes:
     * use metrics with less noise (likelihood or perplexity instead of accuracy, especially for small models);
     * drop noisy subtasks;
     * average over checkpoints.
   * OLMo 3 removed BoolQ for this reason: models "oscillate between predicting the majority and minority class".
8. **Judge-model benchmarks have their own biases.**
   * MT-Bench / LLM-as-a-judge (NeurIPS 2023): judges show **position, verbosity and self-enhancement bias**. GPT-4 as judge still agrees with humans over 80% of the time, the same rate at which humans agree with each other.
   * **AlpacaEval length-controlled** removes the preference for longer answers. Its correlation with human Chatbot Arena rankings rises from 0.94 to **0.98**.
   * **Arena-Hard** (500 hard prompts) separates models 3× better than MT-Bench, with 98.6% agreement with human rankings, at about $20 per model.
   * All of these need an external judge model: they cost money, and the model's answers leave the company.
9. **Contamination.** Tülu 3 checks every training prompt against every benchmark with 8-grams:
   * a training example is removed if more than 50% of a test question's tokens appear in matching 8-grams;
   * a whole dataset is removed or filtered if more than 2% of a benchmark's questions overlap with it.
10. **Model size and the floor.**
    * At ~1B, chat-judge scores stay under 10, and MATH and GSM8K need a strong base.
    * My base saw only 8.4B tokens (OLMo 2 1B saw ~4T). My colleague's 480M result already shows MMLU, GSM8K, MATH and HumanEval at the floor.
    * So I pick tests that can move at my size, and I keep the hard ones only as a floor check.

Sources: [Lessons from the Trenches (lm-eval)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14782) · [A Sober Look at Progress in LM Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07086) · [Signal and Noise (Ai2)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.13144) · [Judging LLM-as-a-Judge (MT-Bench)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685) · [Length-Controlled AlpacaEval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.04475) · [Arena-Hard / BenchBuilder](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11939) · [IFEval](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.07911) · [Tülu 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2411.15124) · [OLMo 3](https://arxiv.org/abs/2512.13961)

**Step 8: Tools that run these benchmarks**

* **lm-evaluation-harness** (EleutherAI): the most widely used. Supports likelihood and generation tasks.
* **OLMES** (Ai2): the standard behind the Tülu 3 and OLMo evaluations, with fixed prompts and few-shot examples, and cloze vs letter forms.
* **lighteval** (Hugging Face): used for the SmolLM2 evaluations.
* **AlpacaEval** (Stanford, tatsu-lab): for the length-controlled chat win rate.
* **What I need first:** my trainer can only score HellaSwag today. Generation-based tests need my SFT checkpoint converted to Hugging Face format, plus a generation loop. The DPO section of this doc says a colleague has already rebuilt Tülu 3's dev suite as an offline harness (10 benchmarks, no judge model), which I can reuse.

Sources: [lm-evaluation-harness](https://github.com/EleutherAI/lm-evaluation-harness) · [OLMES](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.08446) · [lighteval](https://github.com/huggingface/lighteval) · [AlpacaEval](https://github.com/tatsu-lab/alpaca_eval)

**Step 9: My evaluation plan for my SFT model**

1. **Dev list** (used for every decision):

   | Test | Why | How it's scored |
   |---|---|---|
   | Validation loss on answer tokens | fit to unseen chats from the same data | likelihood (running now) |
   | End-token rate | does the model stop after answering | generation |
   | IFEval (strict and loose) | following format instructions, the main SFT goal | generation |
   | TruthfulQA MC2 | avoiding false answers; moved with SFT at 480M | likelihood |
   | PopQA, DROP | facts and reading; moved with SFT at 480M | generation |
   | HellaSwag, ARC, WinoGrande (cloze) | **forgetting**: base vs SFT should stay about the same | likelihood |
   | GSM8K | floor check only | generation |

2. **Unseen list** (run once, on the final choice): IFBench or IFEval-OOD, MMLU-Pro (cloze), AGIEval English.
3. **Settings, fixed for every run:**
   * **SFT model:** zero-shot, inside my chat template (`tulu-plain-v1`).
   * **Base model:** OLMES few-shot.
   * one fixed decoding setting, one fixed max length, the same answer extraction everywhere.
4. **What I evaluate:** the base model, every saved SFT checkpoint, and the final model. For the noisy generation tests (IFEval), average 3 sampling runs.
5. **How I decide:**
   * look at each benchmark separately, not only the average;
   * treat a difference as real only if it's clearly bigger than the run-to-run spread and the benchmark's own noise;
   * choose the checkpoint on the dev list;
   * optionally merge the two best checkpoints (as OLMo 3 does);
   * check the final model once on the unseen list.
6. **Chat-quality judges** (AlpacaEval LC, Arena-Hard): later, and only if company policy allows sending outputs to an external judge. At my size the scores would be near the floor anyway.
7. **Dependency:** the HF export of my checkpoint plus generation. The likelihood tests and the validation loss can run before that.

Written for: your sir and colleagues. This continues your draft right after `and coming to today's work :`.

---first , q9 (how sft learns only from the answer tokens) , i measured it on a small model built like ours (4 layers , a tied embedding table of 50,304 rows , rmsnorm , causal attention , swiglu , fp64 on the laptop cpu) with one real chat tokenized by my own prepare_sft_data.py , only 3 of the 28 positions get a loss (the one before "paris" , "paris" and ".") and the logit gradient is non-zero only on those 3 rows , but in every layer below the top the prompt positions also get gradient , becoz the answer positions read their keys and values in attention , so the model learns to use the prompt but is never trained to predict it (in the last layer the prompt feeds only wk and wv) ,,, , the padding gets exactly 0 in every layer , and when i replaced the pads with random tokens , or even with tokens from the chat itself (" france" , "paris") , the weight gradients changed by 0.0 bit-for-bit ,,, , in a 60-step test the answer loss went 10.93 → 0.065 while the prompt loss stayed near 9 , and the true next prompt token was no more likely than any other chat token (9.00 vs 9.08) , i wrote all of it with diagrams , the measured tables , the exact lines in blutrain's loss kernels and trusted sources (nathan lambert's rlhf book , the hugging face trl docs , llama 2 , urial) in how_learning_happens_in_sft.md ,,, ,

---second , the kernel benchmarks (7a) , i checked in the code which kernels really change for sft , the loss kernel is the only one i changed (ignore 65535 , global denominator , fp32 loss) , and the embedding backward is unchanged but gets very different input , with blu_all_bf16=1 the table is bf16 , so it falls back to the one-atomicadd-per-element kernel (the atomic-free one is fp32 only) and padding is not skipped (padding_idx -1) , so in every micro-batch about 22,900 pad positions × 2,304 columns ≈ 53m atomic adds of 0.0 land on the same 2,304 addresses ,,, , so i decided to use kruthik's fused embedding backward instead (sort , add in fp32 , round once , no atomics) , after one fix : it ignores the real token count and always uses the b × t fixed at install (embedding_fused.cu:1300) ,,, , my arithmetic on the model config also shows that about 73% of each sft step's work goes to padding and prompt rows , and the logged 53% mfu counts padding as work (about 14% on real tokens) , so the biggest gain is removing padding , and i measured the three ways of putting chats into rows on my 5,000 stage-0 chats :

| method | real tokens (not padding) | total work vs v1 | speed-up (upper bound) |
|---|---|---|---|
| v1 , one chat per row padded to 4096 (today) | 30.2% | 100% | ×1.00 |
| v1.5 , length bucketing , one chat per shorter row | 79.8% | 35.2% | ×2.84 |
| v2 , packing several chats per 4096 row + block-diagonal mask | 99.6% | 27.8% | ×3.60 |

---so the order is v1.5 first (no kernel change) and then v2 (block-diagonal mask in the attention forward and backward , rope restarting per chat , and a packing loader) , and the rivals i compete with are apple cut cross-entropy , liger and pytorch for the loss kernel , flashattention-3 varlen , flexattention and sdpa for attention , pytorch for the embedding backward , and nvidia nemo / megatron , hf trl and torchtitan for the whole sft step ,,, ,

---third , benchmarks for sft data (7b) , i went through the papers on how labs decide their sft data , and every top lab does the same thing : train the model on each candidate with everything else fixed , then measure it on the same benchmarks (an ablation) ,,, , the first tülu paper trained on 12 instruction datasets and no single dataset was best on every benchmark , tülu 3 removed one category at a time (without math gsm8k fell 76.2 → 64.1 , without safety data the safety score fell 93.1 → 74.7) , olmo 3 added one category at a time and saw trade-offs (adding math raised math but dropped ifeval 61.7 → 54.0) , and openthoughts ran over 1,000 such experiments ,,, , the methods that score single examples without training (alpagasus , deita , ifd , less , long is more) looked good on small pools , but "rethinking data selection at scale" found that on a million examples almost none of them beat random selection and variety mattered more , so random and longest-answers must always be in my comparison , and the data has to be decontaminated against every benchmark (tülu 3's 8-gram rule) before any experiment ,,, ,

---fourth , benchmarks for the sft model and checkpoints (7c and 8) , tülu 3 uses three suites : a dev suite for every decision (mmlu , popqa , truthfulqa , bbh , drop , math , gsm8k , humaneval , ifeval , alpacaeval 2) , an unseen suite designed separately and never used for decisions (agieval , mmlu-pro , gpqa , ifeval-ood , href and others) , and a safety suite ,,, , the reason for two suites is information leakage : every choice made by the dev score (lr , data mix , checkpoint) partly picks whatever got lucky on those exact questions , so the dev score of the final model comes out too high , and only a suite that was never used for choosing , run once on the frozen model , gives an honest number ,,, , olmo 3 runs everything zero-shot (temperature 0.6 , top-p 0.95 , up to 32k tokens) and reports the average of 3 runs , becoz some benchmarks are noisy (std over 3 runs : gpqa 1.48 , alpacaeval 1.24 , ifeval 0.88) while others are stable (mmlu 0.22 , popqa 0.16) ,,, , their 7b instruct went sft → dpo → final on alpacaeval 21.8 → 43.3 → 40.9 and on ifeval 81.7 → 82.0 → 85.6 , so chat quality mostly comes after sft , and at ~1b size and on navin's 8.4b-token base many benchmarks sit at the floor (a colleague's 480m model moved only on truthfulqa , popqa and drop) , so i made a dev list that can move at my size , plus base-vs-sft likelihood tests (hellaswag , arc , winogrande) to catch forgetting ,,, ,

---first , the kernel benchmarks (7) , in sft only two kernels change compared to pretraining : the loss kernel (it now skips the prompt and padding positions and divides by the number of answer tokens in the whole step) , and the attention kernel once v2 is built (each chat inside a packed row must only look at itself) , every other kernel (matmuls , norms , rope , swiglu , optimizers , gpu communication) gets the same shapes as in pretraining and is already benchmarked ,,, , by my calculation on the model's sizes , about 73% of each sft step's compute today is spent on padding and prompt positions that add nothing to the result , and the 53% mfu in the logs counts that padding as useful work , so i measured three ways of putting chats into the 4096-token rows on my 5,000 stage-0 chats :

| method | real tokens (not padding) | total compute vs v1 | speed-up (upper bound) |
|---|---|---|---|
| v1 , one chat per row padded to 4096 (today) | 30.2% | 100% | ×1.00 |
| v1.5 , similar-length chats grouped , one chat per shorter row | 79.8% | 35.2% | ×2.84 |
| v2 , several chats packed into each 4096 row | 99.6% | 27.8% | ×3.60 |

---so v2 is the most efficient way , and i will compare my kernels with the best-known open ones : apple's cut cross-entropy , liger and pytorch for the loss kernel , flashattention-3 , pytorch flexattention and pytorch's standard attention for the attention kernel , and nvidia nemo , hugging face trl and pytorch's torchtitan for the whole sft training step , all on the same sizes , in bf16 , on the h200 , first checking that the results are correct and then measuring speed , memory , and real (non-padding) tokens per second ,,, ,

---second , benchmarks for sft data (7) , i read how the top labs decide which sft data to use , and they all do it the same way : take the same base model , train one copy on each candidate dataset with every other setting kept the same , then compare the copies on the same set of benchmarks , so the only reason for a score difference is the data ,,, , what their results show : no single dataset was best on every benchmark (the first tülu paper tried 12 datasets) , removing one kind of data removes that skill (in tülu 3 , taking out the math data dropped the math score from 76.2 to 64.1) , and adding one kind of data can lower another skill (in olmo 3 , adding math data lowered the instruction-following score from 61.7 to 54.0) , so a data mix is always a balance between skills ,,, , there are also cheaper methods that give every training example a quality score and keep only the best ones , without training a model for each choice , but a 2025 study showed that on large datasets (about a million examples) these methods did no better than picking examples at random , so whenever i try such a method , i will also compare it with a random pick of the same size ,,, , and before any experiment i will remove from the training data every example that is a near-copy of a benchmark question , otherwise the model just memorizes those answers and the scores are fake ,,, ,

---third , benchmarks for the sft model , checkpoints and overfitting (7 and 8) , the top labs keep two separate sets of benchmarks : a dev set used for every decision (which data , which learning rate , which checkpoint) , and an unseen set that is never used for decisions and is run only once on the final model ,,, , the reason is that every choice made by looking at the dev scores also picks up some luck on those exact questions , so the final model's dev score comes out higher than its real level , the unseen set gives the honest number , and if the unseen score is much lower than the dev score , my choices have overfitted the dev set ,,, , they also run each benchmark more than once and average the results , becoz some benchmarks change a lot from run to run and some barely change , and they train sft for only 2 epochs to avoid overfitting , picking the best checkpoint by the dev scores ,,, , for navin's base model (trained on 8.4b tokens) many hard benchmarks will stay near zero after sft , so my dev set uses tests that can actually move at this size , and i will also run the base model and every sft checkpoint on the same general-knowledge tests , so i can see if sft made the model forget anything ,,, ,

---so in short , all of q7 and q8 is researched with sources and written in the doc (the sft-data evaluation plan , the kernel benchmarks with v1 / v1.5 / v2 and the rivals , and the sft-model evaluation plan with dev and unseen sets) , and tomorrow i will start the kernel benchmarks with the loss kernel against pytorch , liger and apple's cut cross-entropy , and start on the variable-length attention (v2) path ,,, ,
