Yes. Before I write any kernel code, I'll study how the others built it. Here's the plan.

## Step 1: Study the existing implementations (reading their code, not just their docs)

**Attention kernels that support packed chats:**

| Library | What to study |
|---|---|
| **FlashAttention-2 / FA3 / FA4** (`flash_attn_varlen_func`) | how they take chat boundaries (`cu_seqlens`), how they skip tiles outside a chat, how the backward handles it, H100/H200 speed |
| **PyTorch FlexAttention** (document mask via `BlockMask`) | how the mask becomes "skip this tile / mask part of this tile / compute fully"; it's the cleanest model of tile skipping |
| **NVIDIA Transformer Engine / cuDNN** ("THD" format) | what NeMo/Megatron actually run in production for packed SFT |
| **xFormers** (`BlockDiagonalCausalMask`) | an older, simple reference |
| **PyTorch SDPA with an explicit mask** | the slow but exact reference for our correctness tests |

**Trainer and data side (packing + positions + loss):**

| Library | What to study |
|---|---|
| **NeMo / Megatron-Bridge** packed sequences | how they pack offline, `cu_seqlens` padding rules, context-parallel limits |
| **HF Transformers + TRL** (`DataCollatorWithFlattening`, `packing`, `padding_free`, `bfd`) | how position ids restart per chat and get turned into `cu_seqlens` |
| **torchtune** PackedDataset | greedy packing, document ids, positions; it's no longer maintained but still a clear reference |
| **torchtitan** | whether its SFT packs, and how its document mask is wired (I need to check this in its code) |
| **Axolotl** multipack, **OLMo-core** (OLMo 3 packs SFT at 32K) | packing algorithm and settings used at scale |

**For each one I'll write down:**
- the input format;
- how tiles are skipped vs partly masked;
- how the backward does it;
- how RoPE positions restart per chat;
- what happens to fully-masked tiles and the pad tail;
- size limits (e.g. multiples of 128);
- how they test correctness;
- their measured speed.

## Step 2: Compare with our kernels

Read our attention forward (v62) and backward (Vj1d) on H200, plus our RoPE and our loader, and mark exactly where chat boundaries have to enter:
- which loops skip tiles;
- where boundary tiles need a per-element mask;
- where the fully-masked-row guard goes (it gives NaN today).

## Step 3: Write the v2 design

From Steps 1 and 2, decide:
- the data format, for example the chat start offsets per row;
- the kernel changes;
- the RoPE change;
- the loader change (best-fit-decreasing packing);
- the tests: matching SDPA with an explicit mask in forward and backward, pad invariance, row isolation, and the same loss as v1 on the same chats;
- the benchmarks against FA3 varlen and FlexAttention.

## Step 4: Build it in this order

1. loader + positions;
2. RoPE;
3. attention forward;
4. attention backward;
5. trainer wiring;
6. tests;
7. benchmarks.

I've gone through all of them. Here is what they do, from their code (file:line where it matters).

## The two designs everyone uses

**Design A: "varlen". Each chat is treated as its own sequence.**
Used by FlashAttention-2/3, Transformer Engine (`thd` format), PyTorch `varlen_attn`, PyTorch's memory-efficient kernel, HF Transformers, Megatron, and torchtitan's varlen path.

- **Input:** all chats laid end to end in one buffer `[total_tokens, heads, 128]`, plus `cu_seqlens` = each chat's start offset, e.g. `[0, 1200, 2700, 4080]`.
- **FA2** (`csrc/flash_attn/src/block_info.h`, `flash_fwd_kernel.h`):
  - the grid is (query tiles of the **longest** chat) × (number of chats) × heads;
  - each block reads its chat's offset and length from `cu_seqlens`;
  - a tile past a short chat's end **exits immediately** (`flash_fwd_kernel.h:88`);
  - causal: each query tile loops only up to its own diagonal inside its chat (`:91-94`);
  - only the last 1–2 key tiles get a per-element mask (`:305`); everything else runs unmasked;
  - the end of a chat that isn't a multiple of the tile size is handled by bounds checks on loads and stores, not by a mask;
  - a tile with no keys writes 0 and LSE = ∞ instead of NaN (`:101-134`).
- **FA3 (Hopper)** (`hopper/seqlen.h`, `tile_scheduler.hpp`, `flash_prepare_scheduler.cu`): the same idea, plus:
  - a small **prepare kernel** counts each chat's tiles and can **sort chats longest-first** (`flash_prepare_scheduler.cu:165-203`), so the longest chats don't finish last;
  - a **persistent kernel** (grid = number of SMs) takes (chat, tile, head) jobs from a shared counter;
  - in the backward, each chat's start in the accumulation buffers is **padded up to a tile boundary** (`offset_q_padded`, `seqlen.h`), so tiles never mix two chats' results.
- **Result:** tiles that cross two chats **never exist**, so no block-diagonal mask is needed at all.

**Design B: one long row plus a block-sparse mask.**
Used by PyTorch FlexAttention and torchtitan's `block_causal` path.

- **Input:** the packed row as one sequence, plus a per-token **document id**.
- Before the kernel, a **block mask** lists, for each query tile, which key tiles to compute (`kv_num_blocks`, `kv_indices`). It marks them as:
  - **"full" tiles:** no mask needed;
  - **"partial" tiles:** apply the per-element "same chat and causal" check.
- The backward uses the same lists transposed (`q_num_blocks`, `q_indices`).
- Skipping the mask on full tiles is "about a 15% speedup" for causal (`flex_attention.py:504-509`).
- torchtitan has a fast special case for packed chats: `kv_idx >= start_of_my_chat` (`models/common/attention.py:490-530`). Because chats are contiguous, each query tile only needs a **lower bound** on its key range.
- Speed: 90% of FA2 forward and 85% backward (PyTorch blog, A100).

## What all the trainers agree on

| Topic | What they do |
|---|---|
| **Chat boundaries** | taken from positions that reset to 0 (HF `prepare_fa_kwargs_from_position_ids`, torchtitan `cumsum(positions == 0)`), or passed directly as `cu_seqlens` (Megatron `PackedSeqParams`, TE) |
| **RoPE** | positions **restart at 0 for every chat**: HF `position_ids`, torchtitan `positions` indexing the RoPE cache, Megatron applies RoPE per chat using `cu_seqlens` (`rope_utils.py:208`) |
| **Labels at a boundary** | HF's flattening collator puts −100 on the first token of each chat, so one chat's last token doesn't predict the next chat's first. **Our data already handles this**: labels are shifted inside each chat when preprocessing, so packing whole pre-shifted chats is already correct |
| **Packing** | TRL `bfd` = best-fit decreasing, keeps whole chats; `bfd_split` splits overflow and `wrapped` cuts mid-chat, so neither is for SFT |
| **The pad tail** | torchtitan treats padding as its own segments; TE allows gaps between chats (`cu_seqlens_padded`, `dot_product_attention.py:2021-2036`) |
| **Avoiding GPU→CPU syncs** | torchtitan builds fixed-size boundary metadata (`max_num_documents`); TE asks the loader to pass `max_seqlen` instead of computing it on the GPU |

## What this means for our kernel (preliminary)

Two ways to add v2 to our attention (v62 forward, Vj1d backward):

| | **A: varlen (FA style)** | **B: per-tile chat range (torchtitan / Flex style)** |
|---|---|---|
| What changes | the grid and indexing: chats become virtual batch items via `cu_seqlens` | keep the [8 × 4096] row grid; each query tile skips key tiles before its chat's start |
| Masking | only the diagonal and chat-end tiles (by length) | the diagonal, plus tiles where two chats meet |
| Work skipped | everything outside each chat | everything before the chat start; one partly wasted tile per boundary |
| Effort | larger: new grid, offsets in forward and backward, padded backward buffers | smaller: one lower bound per tile plus a chat-id check on boundary tiles |
| Proven by | FA2/FA3, TE, NeMo | FlexAttention, torchtitan |

## Causal mask: computed and masked, or skipped?

**Both happen, at different places. It depends on the tile:**

| Kind of tile | What optimized kernels do | Code |
|---|---|---|
| **Fully above the diagonal** (every key is after every query) | **never loaded, never computed**: the key loop stops at the diagonal | FA2 `flash_fwd_kernel.h:91-94`, FA2 backward `flash_bwd_kernel.h:318-320`, FA3 `block.h:23-33`, memory-efficient kernel `kernel_forward.h:282-290`, **ours** `GQA_fwd_sm90.cu:436` (`my_nkv`) and `:397-401` (it only loads `nkv = pair+1` key tiles) |
| **Crossing the diagonal** | **fully computed** (the tensor cores multiply the whole tile), then every score with key > query is set to **−∞** before softmax | FA2 `mask.h:96-100`, FA3 `mask.h:89-100`, **ours** `GQA_fwd_sm90.cu:479-498` (`if (gcol > grow) v = -INFINITY`, only when `diag`) |
| **Fully below the diagonal** | computed with no mask | the same kernels |

**Your colleague's description is how the naive path works.** PyTorch's math attention builds the full `L × S` lower-triangle mask (`attention.cpp:60-62`), computes the **whole** `Q·Kᵀ` (`:68`), then adds −∞ (`:71`). There, the upper triangle **is** computed and thrown away.

**Why −∞:** softmax uses `exp(score − max)`, and `exp(−∞) = 0`. So those keys get exactly zero weight, and they never become the row's maximum.

**Our kernel at T = 4096** (query tiles of 64, key tiles of 128), per sequence and head:
- the full grid is 64 × 32 = **2,048 tiles**;
- causal computes **1,056 (51.6%)**; the other 992 are skipped completely;
- 64 of the computed tiles cross the diagonal, and about half of each is masked: roughly 32 tiles' worth of wasted work, **~3% of what is computed**;
- the naive path would compute all 2,048, about **2× our work**.

## Are there really two options? Yes. Every library uses one of these two

| Design | Who | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| **A: each chat as its own sequence** (`cu_seqlens` offsets; tiles never cross chats) | FA2 | forward `block_info.h`, early exit `flash_fwd_kernel.h:88`; backward early exit `flash_bwd_kernel.h:101`; backward per-chat buffer offset `+128 × chat` (`:123`) |
| | FA3 | `seqlen.h` (`offset_q_padded`), chats sorted longest-first `flash_prepare_scheduler.cu:165-203`, persistent scheduler `tile_scheduler.hpp:493` |
| | PyTorch memory-efficient kernel (from xFormers) | per-chat `seqstart` offsets + early exit `kernel_forward.h:211-235` |
| | Transformer Engine | cuDNN with "ragged offsets" `fused_attn_f16_arbitrary_seqlen.cu:124-140`, or FlashAttention varlen (`backends.py`) |
| | PyTorch `varlen_attn` | calls FlashAttention or cuDNN (`varlen.py:53-84`) |
| **B: one long row + a block-sparse mask** | FlexAttention | the kernel runs two loops, "partial" blocks with the mask and "full" blocks without it, and only over the listed blocks (`flex_attention.py.jinja:129-180`; loop `common.py.jinja:30`) |
| | torchtitan | document mask built from positions that reset to 0, plus the packed fast path `kv_idx >= chat_start` (`attention.py:467-530`) |
| **Naive: a dense −∞ mask** | PyTorch math attention | `attention.cpp:60-71`. Only useful as the slow, exact **correctness reference** |

**No attention kernels of their own:**
- **HF Transformers** calls FlashAttention's `flash_attn_varlen_func` (`modeling_flash_attention_utils.py`).
- **Megatron** calls Transformer Engine (`extensions/transformer_engine.py:72`).
- **TRL** has no GPU kernels at all; it only packs data.
- **Liger** has neighborhood and multi-token attention ops, but nothing for packed causal training.

## What our v62 forward already does (facts that matter for choosing)

- It's a **persistent kernel**: 132 blocks, one per SM.
- Each work unit is (sequence, head, a **pair** of query tiles), with an early tile paired with a late one (`decode_u`, `:349-354`). This pairing balances the triangle's uneven work, and it assumes the plain causal triangle.
- Its stated limits: causal only, head_dim 128, **S a multiple of 256** (`:18`).
- So **Design B** fits its current shape: per query tile, add "first key tile = the start of my chat", plus a −∞ check for keys before the chat start on that first tile.
- **Design A** needs new work units (chat, tile, head) and handling for chat lengths that aren't multiples of 256.
- With packing, the work per query tile no longer follows the triangle, so the pairing would need re-balancing in **either** design.

Paper facts below come from my knowledge of each paper, with the arXiv ID so you can check. Re-checked today: the FlashAttention-2 causal quote (arXiv page), the DeepSeek-V4 model card, the MiniMax M2 post, and the code lines in your cloned repos.

## 0. The basic operation, and the 5 things a "type" can change

For each query position `i`:
1. Score every key `j`: `s_ij = score(q_i, k_j)`.
2. Turn the scores into weights that add up to 1: `w_ij = softmax_j(s_ij)`.
3. Output = `Σ_j w_ij · v_j`.

Every attention type below changes one or more of these:

| Axis | What changes | Examples |
|---|---|---|
| A. Score function | how `q` and `k` are compared | additive (Bahdanau), dot (Luong), scaled dot (Transformer) |
| B. Allowed pairs | which `(i, j)` pairs are scored | bidirectional, **causal**, sliding window, sparse, block-diagonal |
| C. K/V storage | how many K/V heads, or compressed K/V | MHA, MQA, GQA, MLA |
| D. Replace softmax | a running state instead of all past keys | linear attention, Mamba, DeltaNet |
| E. Computation only | same math, different GPU code | FlashAttention 1/2/3/4, our kernel |

## 1. Before Transformers: attention on top of RNNs

### 1.1 Bahdanau, additive attention (2014, arXiv 1409.0473)
- **Problem it solved:** the 2014 encoder-decoder RNNs squeezed the whole source sentence into one fixed vector, and translation quality fell on long sentences.
- **How it works:** the encoder (a bidirectional RNN) gives one vector `h_j` per source word. At decoder step `i`:
  - `e_ij = vᵀ · tanh(W·s_(i-1) + U·h_j)`, a small 1-layer network per pair;
  - `α_ij = softmax_j(e_ij)`;
  - context `c_i = Σ_j α_ij · h_j`.
- **Cost:** `m × n` pairs (target × source), and each pair runs a tanh layer.
- **Good:** no fixed-vector bottleneck, and the `α` matrix shows which source word each output used.
- **Bad:**
  - the decoder is an RNN, so step `i` must wait for step `i-1`: no parallelism across positions;
  - the per-pair tanh layer is not one big matrix multiply, so it's slow on GPUs.

### 1.2 Luong, multiplicative attention (2015, arXiv 1508.04025)
- **Scores:** `dot = sᵀh`, `general = sᵀ·W·h`, `concat` (Bahdanau-style).
- **Two modes:**
  - **global:** all source words;
  - **local:** only a window of `2D+1` words around a predicted position.
- **Good:** the dot score for all pairs is one matrix multiply, which is fast. The local mode scores fewer pairs.
- **Bad:** still RNN-sequential. Local mode needs a predicted position, and if that's wrong, it attends to the wrong place.

### 1.3 Soft vs hard attention (Xu et al. 2015, arXiv 1502.03044)
- **Soft:** a weighted average over all positions. It's differentiable and trains with normal backprop.
- **Hard:** picks one position by sampling. It's not differentiable, so it needs REINFORCE-style training (high variance).
- **Every LLM today uses soft attention.**

### 1.4 Self-attention inside RNN models (2016–17)
- Cheng 2016 (1601.06733), Parikh 2016 (1606.01933), Lin 2017 (1703.03130).
- A sequence attends to **itself**, not to another sequence. RNNs were still there.

---

## 2. Transformer, scaled dot-product attention (2017, arXiv 1706.03762)

**Formula:** `Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax(Q·Kᵀ / √d_k) · V`

- **Why dot and not additive** (paper): both have similar theoretical cost, but "dot-product attention is much faster and more space-efficient in practice, since it can be implemented using highly optimized matrix multiplication code".
- **Why divide by √d_k** (paper): for large `d_k`, dot products grow large, "pushing the softmax function into regions where it has extremely small gradients".
- **Multi-head (MHA):**
  - base model: 8 heads × 64 dims = 512;
  - each head has its own Q, K and V projections and can attend to different positions;
  - total cost is about the same as one 512-dim head.
- **Three uses in the paper:**
  1. encoder self-attention: every token sees every token (**bidirectional**);
  2. decoder **masked** self-attention: **causal** (section 12);
  3. encoder-decoder **cross-attention**: decoder queries, encoder keys and values.
- **No order by itself.** Without a mask, attention doesn't know token order, so position information must be added:
  - sinusoidal in the paper;
  - RoPE today (2104.09864), which our model uses;
  - ALiBi (2108.12409).

**Paper's Table 1, cost per layer:**

| Layer type | Compute | Sequential steps | Longest path between 2 tokens |
|---|---|---|---|
| Self-attention | O(n²·d) | O(1) | O(1) |
| Recurrent | O(n·d²) | O(n) | O(n) |
| Convolution | O(k·n·d²) | O(1) | O(log_k n) |
| Restricted self-attention (window r) | O(r·n·d) | O(1) | O(n/r) |

- **Good:**
  - fully parallel training;
  - any token reaches any other token in 1 step;
  - the paper notes self-attention is faster than recurrence when `n < d`.
- **Bad: n² cost.** For one head at n = 4096, d = 128:
  - the score matrix is 16,777,216 entries: 64 MiB in fp32, per head, per layer, per sequence;
  - forward compute is 2·n²·d for QKᵀ plus 2·n²·d for PV, about **8.6 GFLOP per head**;
  - doubling `n` gives 4× the compute.

**Everything after 2017 tries to fix the n² cost (sections 4–9 and 11) or to improve quality and stability (section 10).**

---

## 3. Which pairs are allowed by design: the model shapes

| Shape | Allowed pairs | Example models | Good | Bad |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bidirectional (encoder-only) | all `(i, j)` | BERT (1810.04805) | each token sees full context, best for classification and embeddings | can't generate text left to right |
| **Causal (decoder-only)** | `j ≤ i` | GPT-1 (2018) → all current LLMs, **ours** | trains on every position in one pass; KV cache works | early tokens never see later ones |
| Prefix-LM | bidirectional inside the prompt, causal on the output | T5 paper's prefix-LM (1910.10683), UniLM (1905.03197) | prompt tokens see the full prompt | the mask depends on the prompt length, so it's more complex |
| Encoder-decoder | encoder bidirectional + decoder causal + cross | original Transformer, T5, Whisper | strong for translation and speech | two stacks; cross-attention adds a cost |

---

## 4. Cheaper by scoring fewer pairs: fixed sparse patterns

| Type | Paper | Idea | Compute | Problem |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Sparse Transformer | Child 2019, 1904.10509 | strided and fixed patterns; each token sees about √n others | O(n·√n) | info between far tokens needs 2+ layers to travel |
| Reformer (LSH) | Kitaev 2020, 2001.04451 | hash Q/K into buckets; attend only within a bucket | O(n log n) | needs Q = K (shared), several hash rounds, overhead; similar tokens can land in different buckets |
| Longformer | Beltagy 2020, 2004.05150 | sliding window `w` + a few "global" tokens | O(n·w) | outside the window, only reachable through layers or global tokens |
| BigBird | Zaheer 2020, 2007.14062 | window + global + random links | O(n) | random pattern = irregular memory access on GPU |
| Sliding window (production) | Mistral 7B (2310.06825): window 4,096. Gemma 2: alternating local 4,096 / global. Gemma 3 (2503.19786): 5 local : 1 global, window 1,024. gpt-oss (2025): alternating full / window 128 | only the last `w` tokens | O(n·w) in the windowed layers | exact recall beyond `w` relies on the full layers |

- **Shared weakness:** a skipped pair is gone. Long Range Arena (2011.04006) tested these against full attention, and no efficient type won across all tasks.
- **What survived in production:** only the simplest, GPU-friendly form, a sliding window mixed with some full-attention layers.

---

## 5. Cheaper by replacing softmax: linear attention (2020)

### Linformer (2006.04768)
- Projects K and V along the **sequence** axis, from `n` rows to `k` rows. Cost is O(n·k).
- **Problem:** each projected row mixes **all** `n` positions, including future ones. So it **cannot be used directly for causal LMs**, and `n` is fixed at training.

### Linear Transformer (Katharopoulos 2020, 2006.16236)
- Replaces `exp(q·k)` with `φ(q)·φ(k)`. Then `(φ(Q)·φ(K)ᵀ)·V = φ(Q)·(φ(K)ᵀ·V)`. Computing the right side first gives a `d × d` matrix: cost **O(n·d²)**, with no n².
- **Causal form is an RNN:**
  - `S_t = S_(t-1) + φ(k_t)·v_tᵀ`
  - `o_t = φ(q_t)·S_t`
  - Memory at generation is fixed at `d × d` per head (16,384 values for d = 128), whatever the length.

### Performer (2009.14794)
- Random features that approximate the softmax kernel.

### Shared problem
- The whole past is squeezed into one `d × d` state, so it can't hold many separate facts exactly.
- Measured weakness on recall and copying:
  - Zoology (2312.04927): associative recall;
  - "Repeat After Me" (2402.01032): Transformers copy long strings, while state-based models fail beyond their state size.
- Quality is below softmax at the same size.

---

## 6. Modern linear / recurrent types (2023–25): gates and the delta rule

| Type | Paper | What it adds |
|---|---|---|
| RetNet | 2307.08621 | fixed decay `γ` on the state: old info fades |
| RWKV | 2305.13048 | an RNN with decays that trains in parallel |
| Mamba | 2312.00752 | **input-dependent** decay (selective state space) |
| Mamba-2 | 2405.21060 | shows the state space model = attention with a special causal mask built from decay products, so it runs on tensor cores |
| GLA | 2312.06635 | data-dependent gate on the linear-attention state |
| DeltaNet | 2102.11174; parallel form 2406.06484 | `S_t = S_(t-1) + β_t·(v_t − S_(t-1)·k_t)·k_tᵀ`: **overwrites** the old value stored for a similar key instead of only adding |
| Gated DeltaNet | 2412.06464 | gate + delta rule |
| Kimi Delta Attention | Kimi Linear, 2510.26692 | per-channel gate on Gated DeltaNet |

- **Good:** O(n) training (chunked), and fixed memory per token at generation, so there's **no growing KV cache**.
- **Bad:** the fixed-state recall limit is smaller than in 2020, but still there. That led to hybrids.

---

## 7. Hybrids: a few full-attention layers + many linear ones

| Model | Layer mix |
|---|---|
| Jamba (2403.19887) | 1 attention : 7 Mamba |
| MiniMax-01 (2501.08313) | 7 linear ("lightning") : 1 softmax |
| Qwen3-Next (Sep 2025) | 3 Gated DeltaNet : 1 gated softmax attention |
| Kimi Linear (Oct 2025) | 3 KDA : 1 MLA. Reports up to 75% less KV cache and up to 6× decode throughput at 1M context |
| MiniCPM-SALA (Feb 2026, [2602.11761](https://arxiv.org/html/2602.11761v1)) | sparse attention + linear attention at 1:3 |

**Counter-fact:** MiniMax went **back to full attention** for M2 (Oct 2025). Their post says hybrids matched full attention on small-scale leaderboards, but multi-hop reasoning weaknesses showed up at larger scale. It also says "efficient attention still has some way to go before it can definitively beat full attention". ([MiniMax post](https://www.minimax.io/news/why-did-m2-end-up-as-a-full-attention-model))

---

## 8. Smaller KV cache: same full attention, fewer or compressed K/V

**KV cache** = the K and V of all past tokens kept in memory during generation. Size per token = 2 × layers × KV heads × head_dim × bytes.

| Type | Paper | How | Example per token, bf16 | Problem |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| MHA | Transformer | every query head has its own K/V | Llama-3-8B shape with 32 KV heads: **512 KiB** | big cache |
| MQA | Shazeer 2019, 1911.02150 | 1 K/V head shared by all query heads | same shape, 1 KV head: **16 KiB** | quality drop; the GQA paper reports training instability |
| **GQA** | Ainslie 2023, 2305.13245 | query heads in groups, one K/V per group | Llama 3 8B, 8 KV heads: **128 KiB** (32 layers × 8 × 128 × 2 × 2 B) | small quality drop vs MHA. **Our model and kernel are GQA** |
| MLA | DeepSeek-V2, 2405.04434 | store one compressed vector (512) + a 64-dim RoPE key per layer; rebuild K/V by matrix multiply, or fold the matrices into Q at decode | DeepSeek-V3: 61 layers × 576 × 2 B = **~69 KiB** for a 671B model | RoPE breaks the folding trick, so a separate "decoupled RoPE" part was needed; complex kernels. V2 paper: −93.3% KV cache vs DeepSeek 67B, 5.76× max generation throughput |

---

## 9. Learned sparse attention (2025–26, current long-context SOTA)

The model **learns** which past tokens to score, instead of using a fixed pattern.

| Type | Source | How | Problem |
|---|---|---|---|
| NSA | DeepSeek, 2502.11089 | 3 branches per query: compressed block summaries, top-n blocks at full detail, sliding window; learned gates mix them; blocks are GPU-aligned | 3 branches = more kernels; selection overhead |
| MoBA | Moonshot, 2502.13189 | keys split into blocks; a gate picks the top-k blocks per query, plus its own block with a causal mask; deployed for Kimi long context | top-k choice is not differentiable |
| DSA | DeepSeek-V3.2-Exp, Sep 2025 | a small cheap "lightning indexer" (FP8, few heads) scores all past tokens; keep the **top 2,048**; run normal MLA only on those | the indexer is still O(n²), just cheap; it needs a warm-up stage that trains it to match the main attention |
| CSA + HCA | DeepSeek-V4, Apr 2026 | "Compressed Sparse Attention" + "Heavily Compressed Attention". Model card: at 1M context, **27% of single-token inference FLOPs and 10% of KV cache vs V3.2** ([card](https://huggingface.co/deepseek-ai/DeepSeek-V4-Pro)) | internals not read; I only have the model card |
| Inference-only drop | StreamingLLM (2309.17453): keep the first 4 tokens + a recent window. H2O (2306.14048): drop low-score cached tokens | no retraining | a dropped token is gone for good, so recall falls |

---

## 10. Changes inside softmax attention for stability and quality (used now)

All of these keep the O(n²) cost and work with FlashAttention-style kernels.

| Change | Used in | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| QK-norm | OLMo 2, Gemma 3, Qwen3 | normalize `q` and `k` before the dot product, so scores can't grow without limit and loss spikes drop |
| Logit soft-cap | Gemma 2 | `s → cap·tanh(s / cap)` |
| Learned sink logit | gpt-oss | an extra learned term per head in the softmax denominator, so a head can put weight on "nothing" |
| Gated attention | Qwen, 2505.06708; used in Qwen3-Next | a sigmoid gate on each head's output; removes the attention-sink effect |
| Differential attention | 2410.05258 | subtracts two softmax maps to cancel noise weights |

---

## 11. Same math, faster computation: exact kernels

| Kernel | Source | What it changes | Measured |
|---|---|---|---|
| Online softmax | 1805.02867 | softmax in one pass with a running max and running sum | needed by every kernel below |
| Chunked attention | Rabe & Staats 2021, 2112.05682 | process keys in chunks | memory O(√n) instead of O(n²) |
| FlashAttention | 2205.14135 | tiles in on-chip SRAM; the n×n matrix is **never written** to HBM; backward recomputes it | 3× GPT-2 (1K length); 15% on BERT-large |
| FlashAttention-2 | 2307.08691 | better work split, parallel over the sequence, **skips causal tiles** | 2× FA1, 50–73% of A100 peak |
| FlashAttention-3 | 2407.08608 | Hopper: TMA, wgmma, warp specialization, softmax overlapped with GEMM, FP8 | 740 TFLOPs/s FP16 (75% of H100), close to 1.2 PFLOPs/s FP8 |
| FlashAttention-4 | your clone, `README.md:80-82` | written in CuTeDSL for Hopper + Blackwell | — |
| **Our v62** | `GQA_fwd_sm90.cu` | same family as FA3: persistent, 1 producer + 2 consumer warpgroups | — |
| FlexAttention | 2412.05496 | write the mask as a Python function; the compiler makes a fused kernel that skips blocks | — |
| PagedAttention / Flash-Decoding | vLLM 2309.06180 / Dao et al. 2023 | KV cache in pages / split keys across SMs for 1-query decode | inference only |

- **Good:** exact. Only the order of floating-point additions changes.
- **Bad:** still O(n²) compute; very hardware-specific; complex code.

## 12. Causal: how it works now, in detail

### 12.1 The rule
Token `i` may use key `j` only when `j ≤ i`. For 5 tokens, where ✓ = scored and · = not allowed:

```
          key:  The  cat  sat  on   the
query The        ✓    ·    ·    ·    ·
query cat        ✓    ✓    ·    ·    ·
query sat        ✓    ✓    ✓    ·    ·
query on         ✓    ✓    ✓    ✓    ·
query the        ✓    ✓    ✓    ✓    ✓
```
15 of 25 pairs are allowed. In general it's `n(n+1)/2` of `n²`, about half.

### 12.2 Why it's needed
- Training predicts token `t+1` at every position `t`, all in **one** pass. The labels are the input shifted by one.
- If position "sat" could see "on", the answer would be in its input: loss goes near 0, and the model learns nothing it can use at generation time, when the next token doesn't exist yet.

### 12.3 How the 2017 paper defines it
Section 3.2.3: "masking out (setting to −∞) all values in the input of the softmax which correspond to illegal connections". **So your colleague describes the math definition correctly.** The question is what kernels actually do.

### 12.4 What kernels actually do: 3 kinds of tile
The kernel cuts the score matrix into tiles. For a 4 × 4 grid of tiles:
```
 D  -  -  -        - = fully above the diagonal → NEVER loaded, NEVER computed
 F  D  -  -        D = crosses the diagonal → fully computed, then the upper part set to −∞
 F  F  D  -        F = fully below → computed, no mask
 F  F  F  D
```

| Implementation | What it does | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Naive (PyTorch math path) | computes **all** of Q·Kᵀ, then adds −∞, so the upper half is computed and thrown away | `attention.cpp:60-71` |
| FA2 | skips "−" tiles; masks "D" | paper: skip blocks "(approximately half of the blocks for large sequence length)… around 1.7-1.8× speedup compared to attention without the causal mask"; mask applied "to 1 block" per row ([2307.08691](https://arxiv.org/html/2307.08691)); code `flash_fwd_kernel.h:91-94`, `mask.h:96-100` |
| FA3 | same | `block.h:23-33`, `mask.h:89-100` |
| **Ours v62** | same | loop limit `GQA_fwd_sm90.cu:436`, producer loads `pair+1` tiles `:397-401`, `-INFINITY` only on diagonal tiles `:479-498` |

**Answer:** in naive code your colleague is right: it is computed, then masked. In every fast kernel (FA2, FA3, FA4, xFormers, Flex, **ours**), about half the tiles are **never computed**. Only the thin diagonal band is computed and then masked.

### 12.5 Numbers for our kernel at T = 4096 (tile 64 × 128)
- Full grid: 64 × 32 = **2,048 tiles**.
- Computed: **1,056 (51.6%)**. Skipped: 992.
- Diagonal tiles: 64, about half masked, so about 32 tiles of wasted work: **~3%** of what we compute.

**Why the speedup is 1.7–1.8× and not 2×:**
- the diagonal tiles do extra masking work;
- rows have unequal work (12.6);
- fixed costs (launch, epilogue) don't shrink.

### 12.6 The cost causal adds: unequal work per row
Query tile 0 reads 1 key tile; the last query tile reads all of them. If SMs take tiles in order, some finish early and sit idle. How each kernel handles it:
- **FA2:** loops key tiles in **reverse**, so the masked tile comes first (`flash_fwd_kernel.h:138-140`).
- **FA3:** "longest-processing-time-first scheduling: the longest remaining tile is assigned to the first SM that's free" (`tile_scheduler.hpp:222-224`); it reverses the tile order at `:309-310`. The backward pass has its own LPT scheduler (`:368`).
- **Ours:** pairs an early tile with a late tile, so every work unit has equal size (`decode_u`).

### 12.7 Why −∞, and the NaN trap
- Softmax uses `exp(s − max)`, and `exp(−∞) = 0`, so masked keys get **exactly** 0 weight and can never be the row maximum.
- **Trap:** if a whole row is masked, then `max = −∞` and `−∞ − (−∞) = NaN`. FA guards against this (`softmax.h:73-76`: "If max is -inf, then all elements must have been -inf (possibly due to masking). We don't want (-inf - (-inf)) since that would give NaN.").
- In plain causal this never happens, because each row always sees itself.
- **In our v2 packing it can:** padding rows. So the guard matters for us.

### 12.8 Causal is what makes the KV cache possible
- With causal, a past token's K and V never change when new tokens arrive, so they are computed once and stored.
- **Prefill** (the prompt): causal attention over the prompt.
- **Decode** (1 new token): its query uses **all** cached keys, and **no mask is needed**, because every cached key is in the past.
- In a bidirectional model, a new token changes every old token's output, so everything would be recomputed each step.
- When `seqlen_q ≠ seqlen_k` (e.g., 2 new queries over 5 cached keys), FA2 since v2.1 aligns the mask to the **bottom-right** (`README.md:436-440`).

### 12.9 Causal in the other types
| Type | How causal is applied |
|---|---|
| Linear / Mamba / DeltaNet | no mask matrix: the running state contains only the past, so causal comes for free |
| Sliding window | a band `i−w ≤ j ≤ i`: skip tiles above the diagonal **and** tiles older than the window |
| NSA / MoBA / DSA | select only past blocks or tokens; the query's own block uses a normal causal mask |
| **Packing (our v2)** | block-diagonal causal, below |

Two chats A (3 tokens) and B (3 tokens) packed in one row:
```
      A1 A2 A3 B1 B2 B3
A1     ✓  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·
A2     ✓  ✓  ·  ·  ·  ·
A3     ✓  ✓  ✓  ·  ·  ·
B1     ·  ·  ·  ✓  ·  ·     ← B must not see A
B2     ·  ·  ·  ✓  ✓  ·
B3     ·  ·  ·  ✓  ✓  ✓
```

### 12.10 A side effect: causal carries position information
NoPE (2203.16634): causal LMs trained **without** any position encoding still learn positions, because token `i` sees exactly `i` keys. A bidirectional model with no position encoding can't do this.

### 12.11 The downsides of causal
- Early tokens' outputs never use later context. That's why embedding and classification models prefer bidirectional attention.
- Every query can see token 0, so many heads dump unused weight there: the "attention sink" that StreamingLLM keeps and gated attention removes.
- Unequal work per row needs a scheduler (12.6).

---

## 13. All types in one table

| Type | Pairs scored per layer | Generation memory per token | Exact softmax? | Causal OK? | Main weakness | Used now in |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Bahdanau / Luong | m·n | — (RNN) | yes | yes | RNN is sequential | none (historic) |
| Full MHA | n² (½ with causal) | K+V, all heads | yes | yes | n² cost, big cache | older LLMs |
| **GQA + causal** | n²/2 | K+V, fewer heads | yes | yes | n² cost | **ours**, Llama 3, Qwen, Mistral |
| MLA | n²/2 | 576 values per layer | yes | yes | complex RoPE handling | DeepSeek V2/V3, Kimi K2 |
| Sliding window | n·w | w tokens | yes, in the window | yes | nothing beyond w | Mistral, Gemma 2/3, gpt-oss (mixed with full) |
| Fixed sparse (BigBird etc.) | ~n·√n or n | — | yes, on chosen pairs | partly | irregular, slow on GPU | mostly dropped |
| Linformer | n·k | — | no | **no** | can't do causal | dropped |
| Linear / Performer | n·d² | d×d fixed | no | yes | weak recall | dropped alone |
| Mamba / GDN / KDA | n·d² | fixed state | no | yes | weaker recall, so mixed with full | Qwen3-Next, Kimi Linear, Jamba (hybrids) |
| Learned sparse (NSA / MoBA / DSA / CSA) | n·k (+ cheap indexer) | compressed / selected | yes, on the selected pairs | yes | selection cost, complex kernels | DeepSeek V3.2 / V4, Kimi |

**For us:** our model uses GQA + causal + RoPE with an exact FA3-style kernel. v2 doesn't change the attention type. It only changes the allowed-pairs pattern, from one causal triangle to block-diagonal causal (12.9).

## 1. What each library is

| Library | Made by | What it is | Built on | Own attention kernel? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **PyTorch** | Meta / PyTorch Foundation | **the base**: tensors, autograd, CUDA ops, distributed | itself | yes: math, FA2 (compiled from FlashAttention's code), memory-efficient (from xFormers), cuDNN, FlexAttention |
| **flash-attention** | Tri Dao's lab (Dao-AILab) | **a kernel library**, not a framework. FA2 in `csrc/`, FA3 in `hopper/`, FA4 in `flash_attn/cute/`, plus small extras (rotary, layer norm, cross-entropy) | PyTorch: it's a PyTorch C++/CUDA extension (`setup.py:821` requires torch; `flash_api.cpp:6` includes `torch/python.h`) | **yes, this is its whole purpose** |
| **Liger-Kernel** | LinkedIn | a kernel library (Triton): losses, norms, RoPE, SwiGLU | PyTorch + Triton | **no varlen attention** (0 files contain `cu_seqlens`) |
| **Transformer Engine (TE)** | NVIDIA | a library of fused layers + FP8/FP4 for PyTorch and JAX; has its own C++/CUDA core in `transformer_engine/common` | PyTorch (or JAX) | partly: its attention calls **cuDNN** (closed source) or **FlashAttention** |
| **Megatron-LM / Megatron-Core** | NVIDIA | **a training framework**: model parallelism (tensor, pipeline, context, expert), models, datasets, optimizers | **PyTorch** (`pyproject.toml`: `torch>=2.6.0`) | no. Packed attention goes through TE |
| **transformers** | Hugging Face | **a library of model definitions** (Llama, Qwen, …) + Trainer | PyTorch (`setup.py:177`) | no. It dispatches to eager / SDPA / FlashAttention / Flex (`modeling_utils.py:5120-5123`) |
| **TRL** | Hugging Face | "**Transformers Reinforcement Learning**" (`README.md:1`): SFT, DPO, GRPO trainers | transformers + accelerate + datasets (`pyproject.toml`) | no. Its only kernel is a loss (`trl_losses/logprob_entropy.py`) |
| **torchtitan** | PyTorch org (Meta) | "**A PyTorch native platform for training**" (README): a training framework using only PyTorch features | PyTorch | no. It calls PyTorch's varlen / Flex / SDPA |

**Your questions:**
- **Is flash-attention like Liger?** Yes, same kind of thing: a kernel library. Neither is a framework like PyTorch or Megatron.
- **Does Megatron have its own tensor class and autograd?** No. It uses `torch.Tensor`, PyTorch autograd (it writes custom `torch.autograd.Function` classes in 39 files) and `torch.distributed`. It adds parallelism, models and data on top.
- **Are TRL and Transformer Engine both Hugging Face?** No:
  - TRL = Hugging Face.
  - Transformer Engine = **NVIDIA**.
  - TRL is **not** part of TE, and TRL does **not** use TE: 0 TRL files mention `transformer_engine`. TRL uses HF **transformers**.
- **Is transformers the same as Transformer Engine?** No. They're different companies and different things: model definitions (HF) vs fused kernels and layers (NVIDIA).

## 2. Do we benchmark against all of them?

**No. Only the libraries that have real kernels.** HF transformers, TRL, Megatron and torchtitan call someone else's kernel, so benchmarking them against our kernel would only re-measure FA or cuDNN.

| Level | Who | What we measure |
|---|---|---|
| **Kernel** (after v2) | FA2 varlen, **FA3 varlen** (the best on H200), FA4, cuDNN via TE, FlexAttention | attention fwd+bwd time on the same packed rows |
| **Framework** (later, separate) | TRL, Megatron(+TE), torchtitan | whole SFT step: tokens/s and memory |

PyTorch's `varlen_attn` uses the **FA2 kernels** (section 5.4), so it's the same benchmark as FA2.

## 3. Is varlen a feature in the existing kernel, or a new attention?

**From the code: in every library it's the same attention kernel with extra handling, not a new algorithm.**
- **FA2:** same kernel function `compute_attn`. Varlen just picks the template with `Is_even_MN=false`, which turns on per-chat bounds (`flash_fwd_launch_template.h:65`, `flash_fwd_kernel.h:87`).
- **FA3:** same main loop with a compile-time flag `Varlen` (`mainloop_fwd_sm90_tma_gmma_ws.hpp:32, 48`), so it's compiled as separate copies of the same kernel.
- **FlexAttention:** same Triton kernel template. The mask is a function compiled into it.

**But the "extra handling" touches 7 places:**
1. input layout;
2. per-chat start offsets;
3. which tiles each query tile runs;
4. masking past the chat end;
5. output writes;
6. work scheduling;
7. the backward dQ buffer.

**For us, that means extending v62 forward + Vj1d backward, not writing a new attention.**

## 4. How varlen works: one example

3 chats packed in one row: A = 5 tokens, B = 3, C = 4. Total 12.

```
packed rows:  A0 A1 A2 A3 A4 B0 B1 B2 C0 C1 C2 C3
positions:     0  1  2  3  4  0  1  2  0  1  2  3   ← restart per chat (RoPE needs this)
cu_seqlens:   [0, 5, 8, 12]                         ← start of each chat + total
chat id:       0  0  0  0  0  1  1  1  2  2  2  2
```

Allowed pairs: same chat **and** key ≤ query.
```
      A0 A1 A2 A3 A4 B0 B1 B2 C0 C1 C2 C3
A0     ✓  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·
A1     ✓  ✓  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·
A2     ✓  ✓  ✓  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·
A3     ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·
A4     ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·
B0     ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ✓  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·
B1     ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ✓  ✓  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·
B2     ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ✓  ✓  ✓  ·  ·  ·  ·
C0     ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ✓  ·  ·  ·
C1     ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ✓  ✓  ·  ·
C2     ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ✓  ✓  ✓  ·
C3     ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ·  ✓  ✓  ✓  ✓
```
31 of 144 pairs are allowed. Plain causal over the 12 tokens would allow 78.

The two ways to compute this, using tile size 4 to keep the example small:

**Design A: each chat is its own small attention.**
```
chat A: q-tiles [A0..A3] [A4 + 3 empty rows]
chat B: q-tiles [B0..B2 + 1 empty row]
chat C: q-tiles [C0..C3]
```
- A tile never holds two chats.
- Waste: the partly empty tiles at each chat's end.

**Design B: one 12-token row + a block mask.** The tile grid is 3 × 3; each block is labelled:
```
             keys 0-3   keys 4-7   keys 8-11
rows 0-3      partial    SKIP       SKIP        (A0..A3)
rows 4-7      partial    partial    SKIP        (A4,B0,B1,B2: two chats in one tile)
rows 8-11     SKIP       SKIP       partial     (C0..C3)
```
- 4 of 9 blocks computed; plain causal would compute 6.
- Waste: "partial" blocks contain masked pairs.

## 5. How each library does it, from the code

### 5.1 FA2 (CUDA C++), design A
1. **API.** Python `flash_attn_varlen_func(q, k, v, cu_seqlens_q, cu_seqlens_k, max_seqlen_q, max_seqlen_k, causal)` (`flash_attn_interface.py:1391`) calls C++ `mha_varlen_fwd` (`flash_api.cpp:539`).
   - Layout is `total_tokens × heads × dim`, with **no batch dimension**.
   - `cu_seqlens` must be int32 (`:579`).
2. **Grid.** `dim3 grid(ceil(max_seqlen_q / BlockM), num_chats, heads)` (`flash_fwd_launch_template.h:63-64`). **Every chat gets as many thread blocks as the longest chat needs.**
3. **Each block finds its chat** through `BlockInfo` (`block_info.h`): start = `cu_seqlens[b]`, length = `cu_seqlens[b+1] − cu_seqlens[b]`, pointer = start × row stride.
4. **Early exit:** `if (m_block * kBlockM >= actual_seqlen_q) return;` (`flash_fwd_kernel.h:88`).
   - Example: chats of 3,000 + 1,096 tokens with BlockM = 128 → 24 blocks per chat per head. The second chat needs 9, so **15 blocks start and exit immediately**.
5. **Causal per chat:** the key-tile limit uses the chat's own length (`:91-94`).
6. **Chat end:**
   - rows past the end aren't loaded (`:277`, bound `actual_seqlen_k − n_block*kBlockN`);
   - their scores are set to −INFINITY (`mask.h:96-100`);
   - uneven lengths need one extra masked step (`:300-307`).
7. **Output and LSE** are written only for real rows (`:484, :499`).
8. **Backward:** dQ is summed in an fp32 buffer of size `total + 128 × num_chats`, so one chat's writes never touch the next chat (`flash_api.cpp:1145-1155`).

### 5.2 FA3 (Hopper, CUTLASS), design A. The most relevant for us: TMA + persistent, like v62
1. **Per-chat info:** `SeqlenInfoQK` (`seqlen.h`) holds the offset, the length, and `offset_q_padded = (cu[b] + b·BlockM)/BlockM·BlockM`, used for the LSE and dQ buffers.
2. **TMA:**
   - **one descriptor over the whole packed tensor**, batch index forced to 0 (`mainloop:657`);
   - the chat start is a **coordinate shift**: `domain_offset(make_coord(offset_q, 0), mQ)` (`:663-665`);
   - so a tile crossing the chat end **reads the next chat's rows**, and the mask gives them weight 0.
3. **Empty work:** if the key range is empty, the block returns **before loading K**. The code comment: "Loading K can cause illegal memory access" (`:612-617`).
4. **Mask:** column limit = min(causal limit, chat length) → −INFINITY (`mask.h:66-100`).
5. **Output: TMA store is switched off for varlen.**
   - `Use_TMA_O = … && !Varlen` (`epilogue_fwd.hpp:37`), with the comment "Don't use TMA in Varlen case since we don't want to overwrite the output of another sequence" (`:331`).
   - Same for dK/dV in the backward pass (`epilogue_bwd.hpp:31`).
6. **Scheduler (persistent):** `VarlenDynamicPersistentTileScheduler` (`tile_scheduler.hpp:493`).
   - One warp reads 31 chats' lengths, prefix-sums their tile counts, and turns a global tile number into (chat, tile, head) (`:600-680`).
   - Inside a chat, the longest tiles go first.
   - An optional prepare kernel **sorts chats longest first** (`flash_prepare_scheduler.cu:163-179`).
7. **Backward:** dQ is accumulated with `atomicAdd` into the fp32 buffer at `offset_q_padded` (`mainloop_bwd:621, :964`).

### 5.3 FA4 (CuTeDSL, Python), design A + block-sparse
- Same structure: `SeqlenInfo` / `SeqlenInfoQK` with offsets and padded offsets (`seqlen_info.py:18, 67`), a `cu_seqlens` API (`interface.py:682-813`), `prepare_scheduler.py`, `tile_scheduler.py`.
- It also has `block_sparsity.py`, which is what FlexAttention's FLASH backend uses (5.5).
- I read FA4 at the API level, not the kernel bodies.

### 5.4 PyTorch, design A
- **`varlen_attn`** (`torch/nn/attention/varlen.py:127`) calls `aten._flash_attention_forward` with `cu_seq` (`:75-84`).
  - A cuDNN path exists but is off: `_should_use_cudnn` returns `False` (`:21-23`).
  - The aten flash kernel **is FA2**, compiled from the `third_party/flash-attention` submodule (`caffe2/CMakeLists.txt:1076-1079`; `flash_api.cpp` includes `flash.h`).
- **Nested (jagged) tensors + SDPA** call the same flash or memory-efficient kernels, with the nested tensor's offsets used as `cu_seqlens` (`nested/_internal/sdpa.py:352, 793, 830`).
- **Memory-efficient kernel (from xFormers):** per-chat `seqstart` + early exit (`kernel_forward.h:211-235`).
- **SDPA with a dense mask tensor:** computes every tile and masks. No skipping.

### 5.5 FlexAttention (PyTorch, Triton), design B
1. You write `mask_mod(b, h, q_idx, kv_idx) → bool`.
2. **`create_block_mask`:**
   - evaluates it on **every** (q, kv) pair into a dense bool tensor (`create_mask`, `flex_attention.py:1093`);
   - cuts that into **128 × 128 blocks** (`:395`) and counts the trues per block (`_convert_mask_to_block_mask`, `:979-1030`): 0 = skip, all = **full**, in between = **partial**;
   - stores, per query block, a list of partial key blocks and a list of full key blocks. The backward lists are generated from these (`:495-515`).
3. **Kernel:** per query block, **two loops** (`flex_attention.py.jinja:129-180`):
   - partial blocks, with the mask applied (→ −inf);
   - full blocks, with **no mask** (the mask runs only `if not IS_FULL_BLOCKS`, `common.py.jinja:67-81`).
   - Skipped blocks are in neither list, so they're never touched.
4. Their docstring: splitting out the full blocks gives "about a 15% speedup" for causal (`:495-515`).
5. **BACKEND='FLASH':** the same block mask is passed to FA4 (`flash_attention.py.jinja` imports `flash_attn.cute.interface._flash_attn_fwd`).
6. **Cost:** the block mask must be **rebuilt for every new packing layout**, i.e., every micro-batch, and it builds a dense 4096 × 4096 bool tensor per row first.

### 5.6 Transformer Engine: a dispatcher plus closed cuDNN
1. **API:** `DotProductAttention(qkv_format="thd", attn_mask_type="padding_causal")` with `cu_seqlens_q/kv` and optional `cu_seqlens_*_padded` (`dot_product_attention.py:2015-2050`).
2. **Backend choice** (`utils.py`): "thd" is supported by Fused (cuDNN), FA2, FA3 and Unfused (`:942-949`). It has filters, for example a known cuDNN problem with deterministic thd backward on sm90 (`:1803-1824`).
3. **cuDNN path:**
   - builds a cuDNN graph where Q/K/V/O get `set_ragged_offset`, the chat start offsets (`fused_attn_f16_arbitrary_seqlen.cu:124-155`);
   - padding mask with per-chat lengths (`:213, :229`);
   - causal as a diagonal band with right bound 0 (`:183-186`).
   - **The kernel itself is closed.**
4. **FlashAttention path:** imports `flash_attn_varlen_func` from FA2, FA3 or FA4 (`backends.py:130, 191, 246-248`).
5. **`cu_seqlens_padded`:** chats can have padding between them in the buffer. `get_thd_padding_mask` marks those positions (`utils.py:1956`).

### 5.7 Megatron: data + RoPE, attention through TE
1. **Data** (`training/datasets/sft_dataset.py:120-200`):
   - appends chats **in order** (greedy, not best-fit);
   - positions restart per chat (`range(len(tokens))`);
   - pads **each chat** to a multiple of `padding_divisor`;
   - records `cu_seqlens`;
   - a chat that overflows the row is **truncated**, not dropped;
   - prompt tokens are masked out of the loss.
2. **Trainer:** builds `PackedSeqParams(qkv_format="thd", cu_seqlens…, max_seqlen)` (`pretrain_gpt.py:341-365`). `int(max_seqlen.item())` is one GPU→CPU sync per step.
3. **Attention:** passed to TE (`extensions/transformer_engine.py:2426-2445`). Megatron's own attention refuses packing: "Packed sequence is not supported by DotProductAttention. Please use TEDotProductAttention instead." (`core/transformer/dot_product_attention.py:161-164`).
4. **RoPE:** `_apply_rotary_pos_emb_thd` computes each token's position inside its chat from `cu_seqlens` using `searchsorted` (`rope_utils.py:208-275`).

### 5.8 HF transformers: detects packing, then calls FA or builds a mask
1. **Detection:** packed if the batch size is 1 and `position_ids` aren't one increasing run (`modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:558-572`).
2. **FlashAttention path:** `cu_seqlens` = the indices where `position_ids == 0`, plus the total length (`:480-517`), then `flash_varlen_fn(q, k, v, cu_seqlens…)` (`:843-847`).
3. **SDPA / eager / Flex path:**
   - a chat id per token, from jumps in the positions (`masking_utils.py:734-757`);
   - mask = same chat id AND causal (`:183-190`);
   - SDPA gets a **dense** mask tensor (`:522`); Flex gets a block mask.

### 5.9 TRL: packing only
1. **`_pack_bfd`** (`data_utils.py:739`): sorts lengths descending, then best-fit. On overflow: "truncate" (the default) or "split".
2. **Padding-free mode** turns on automatically with best-fit packing (`sft_trainer.py:1180`). The collator flattens the batch into **one row** with positions restarting per chat (`:528-552`) and no attention mask.
3. **Sets the label at each chat's first token to −100** (`:516`). HF shifts labels inside the loss, so otherwise a chat's first token would be predicted from the previous chat's last token. **Our labels are already shifted per chat**, so we don't need this.
4. **Warns** if attention isn't FlashAttention (`:1184-1200`). After this, transformers (5.8) calls FA varlen.

### 5.10 torchtitan: chooses PyTorch's varlen or Flex
- **Three attention options** (`models/common/attention.py`):
  - `VarlenInnerAttention` (`:132`) → PyTorch `varlen_attn` (`:39-41, :92`), which is the FA2 kernels;
  - `FlexInnerAttention` (`:228`) → compiled `flex_attention` + block mask;
  - SDPA (`:388`), no packing.
- **Masks from positions:** chat id = `cumsum(positions == 0) − 1` (`:467-488`). The fast causal mask only adds a lower bound, `kv_idx >= chat_start[chat_id[q_idx]]`; causal already gives the upper bound (`:490-530`).
- **Varlen metadata:** `cu_seqlens` from `positions == 0`. An optional fixed-size version (`max_num_documents`) works with CUDA graphs and avoids a GPU→CPU sync (`:598+`).

## 6. Summary

| Library | Kind | Packed attention through | Design | Real kernel |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| FlashAttention 2 / 3 / 4 | kernel library | itself | A (FA4 also block-sparse) | **own** |
| PyTorch `varlen_attn` / nested / memory-efficient | base | FA2 / xFormers kernels | A | own copies |
| FlexAttention | inside PyTorch | Triton template, or FA4 | **B** | **own** (generated) |
| Transformer Engine | layer library | cuDNN or FA | A | cuDNN (closed) |
| Megatron | framework | TE | A | none of its own |
| HF transformers | model library | FA, SDPA mask, or Flex | A or B | none |
| TRL | trainer | transformers | A | none |
| torchtitan | framework | PyTorch varlen or Flex | A or B | none |
| Liger | kernel library | — | — | no varlen attention |

## 7. What this means for our design (facts, not a decision yet)
- **Design A on a TMA kernel like ours:** FA3 shows what it costs:
  - per-chat coordinate offsets;
  - masking past the chat end;
  - **turning off TMA stores for the output**, so a tile doesn't overwrite the next chat;
  - a scheduler that maps tiles to chats.
- **Design B on our kernel:**
  - the row stays one 4096-token sequence, so output writes stay as they are;
  - the kernel needs a skip / full / partial decision per tile, plus the mask on partial tiles;
  - our v62 already skips tiles above the diagonal and masks the diagonal, so this extends what it does.

## 1. Does PyTorch have it?

**Yes, but not in all of its attention kernels.** PyTorch has 5 attention backends. From `native_functions.yaml`:

| PyTorch backend | Takes chat boundaries? | Evidence |
|---|---|---|
| Math (naive) | **no**. Only a full mask tensor, and it computes everything | `_scaled_dot_product_attention_math`, `:15125`: no `cu_seqlens` argument |
| Flash (a copy of FA2) | **yes** | `_flash_attention_forward(…, cum_seq_q, cum_seq_k, max_q, max_k…)`, `:15196` |
| Memory-efficient (from xFormers) | **yes** | `_efficient_attention_forward(…, cu_seqlens_q, cu_seqlens_k…)`, `:15209` |
| cuDNN | the op takes it (`:15221`), but `varlen_attn` has it **switched off** | `varlen.py:21-23` returns `False` |
| FlexAttention | **yes**, the other way: a block mask | section 5.5 of my last message |

**Note:** the normal `scaled_dot_product_attention` entry points (`:15134, :15172, :15184`) take **no** chat boundaries. To use them you must call `varlen_attn` or use nested tensors.

## 2. Is varlen a new type of attention?

**No.** The math is exactly the same: `softmax(Q·Kᵀ/√d)·V`, the same causal rule, the same GQA. The only new input is **where each chat starts and ends**. It's a **feature added to a kernel**, not a separate attention.

**Libraries added it kernel by kernel, and not to all of them:**

| Library | Kernels **with** the feature | Kernels **without** it, and what happens there |
|---|---|---|
| FA2 | forward, backward, the decode kernel. All the same code with a flag (`Is_even_MN=false`) | — |
| FA3 | forward, backward (compile-time flag `Varlen`) | — |
| FA4 | forward, backward | — |
| PyTorch | Flash, memory-efficient, Flex | Math: you pass a full mask, and everything is computed |
| Transformer Engine | cuDNN, FlashAttention | **Unfused:** converts packed back to padded (`ConvertTHDtoBSHD`, `backends.py:545-563`), then runs normal attention with a padding mask. The slow path just **undoes the packing** |
| Megatron | none of its own; uses TE | its own attention **refuses** packed input: "Packed sequence is not supported by DotProductAttention" (`dot_product_attention.py:161`) |
| HF transformers | none of its own; uses FA | eager / SDPA: builds a full mask (`masking_utils.py:522`) |

**The pattern in every library:**
1. **Fast kernels** get the feature.
2. **Slow or reference paths** use a full mask, or undo the packing.
3. **Paths without it refuse** packed input with an error.

## 3. So do we write a separate attention?

**No. We add the feature to the kernels our SFT run actually uses.** From our tree (`~/Downloads/BluTrain_sft`):

1. The trainer calls `autograd::scaled_dot_product_attention(q, k, v, Nq, Nkv, is_causal=true, FlashAttention)` (`bluscript_zero_ckpt.cpp:642-644`).
2. **Forward on H200:** Hopper + causal + shape check → **v62** (`GQA_fwd_generic.cu:333-335`).
3. **Backward on H200:** **Vj1d** by default; Vj1 and V44 can be picked by an environment variable (`GQA_bwd_generic.cu:126-130`).
4. **Other paths in our tree:**
   - generic WMMA kernels (other GPUs or shapes);
   - sm103 kernels (B300);
   - the math path (`sdpa_math`, which uses `fused_tril_softmax`, `AttentionOps.cpp:30-63`);
   - the fp32 memory-efficient paths.

**Minimum work: 2 kernels, v62 forward + Vj1d backward.** Every other path must either get the feature or **refuse packed input with an error**, like Megatron does. It must never silently ignore the chat boundaries: chats would see each other and no error would show.

## 4. What the feature changes inside a kernel

1. **Read the chat boundaries:** `cu_seqlens` (the start of each chat) or a chat id per token.
2. **Per query tile:** start the key loop at **its own chat's start**, not at 0. The causal end stays the same.
3. **Boundary tiles:** set to −∞ the keys that belong to another chat. The causal −∞ is already there.
4. **Backward:** the same rules, from the other side. For each key tile, run only the query tiles of the same chat.
5. **Design A only:** output writes must stop at the chat end (FA3 turned off TMA stores for this), plus a scheduler that maps tiles to chats.

**Outside the kernels:**
- **RoPE:** positions restart at 0 for each chat.
- **Loader:** packs the chats and passes the boundaries.

They are completely different concepts, but they are highly complementary and often used together in modern Large Language Models (like LLaMA 3, Mistral, etc.).

Here is the difference in simple terms:

1. Grouped Query Attention (GQA) = An Architectural Change
GQA changes the actual math and structure of the neural network to save memory during inference (generation).

The Problem: In standard Multi-Head Attention (MHA), every "Query" head has its own "Key" and "Value" head. When generating text, storing all those Keys and Values in memory (the KV Cache) takes up massive amounts of VRAM.
The GQA Solution: GQA groups multiple Query heads together and forces them to share a single Key and Value head. This drastically shrinks the size of the KV Cache, allowing you to generate text much faster and fit larger batch sizes on a single GPU, with almost no loss in model quality.
2. Flash Attention = A Hardware Optimization Algorithm
Flash Attention does not change the math or the architecture of the model. The output of Flash Attention is mathematically identical to standard attention.

The Problem: Calculating attention requires reading and writing huge matrices to the GPU's main memory (HBM), which is very slow. The GPU spends more time moving data around than doing actual math.
The Flash Attention Solution: It is a cleverly written CUDA algorithm that breaks the attention matrix into blocks ("tiling") and computes the attention entirely inside the GPU's ultra-fast, on-chip SRAM memory. This avoids the slow reads/writes to main memory, making the attention calculation significantly faster and using much less memory during training.
Summary: How they work together
GQA changes what the model is computing (sharing KV heads) to save memory during inference.
Flash Attention changes how the GPU computes it (memory tiling) to speed up both training and inference.
Modern models like Llama 3 use both: They have a GQA architecture, and under the hood, they use the Flash Attention algorithm to compute that GQA extremely fast.

You are asking all the right questions! You are seeing how the whole puzzle fits together. Let's break it down exactly as you asked.

1. What is Scaled Dot-Product Attention (SDPA)? Is it the core technique?
Yes, exactly. Scaled Dot-Product Attention is the fundamental math equation introduced in the original "Attention Is All You Need" paper.

The formula is: Attention(Q, K, V) = softmax((Q * K^T) / sqrt(d)) * V

You are 100% correct: MHA, MQA, and GQA are all just architectural wrappers around SDPA.

MHA means you run that SDPA equation, say, 32 times in parallel (32 heads), giving each head its own Q, K, and V.
GQA means you run that SDPA equation 32 times in parallel, but you force groups of Qs to share the same K and V in the equation.
(Fun fact: If you use PyTorch, the function torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention actually computes this, and it acts as a smart manager that automatically uses Flash Attention under the hood if your hardware supports it!)

2. What was the "inefficient one" that Flash Attention replaced?
The inefficient one is the "Standard" or "Naive" implementation.

Before Flash Attention, researchers just wrote out the SDPA math formula step-by-step in standard PyTorch or TensorFlow. The problem with doing it step-by-step is that GPUs have a memory bottleneck.

Naive way: Compute Q * K^T -> Save massive matrix to slow GPU memory (HBM).
Then load it back -> Calculate softmax -> Save massive matrix to slow GPU memory.
Then load it back -> Multiply by V -> Save final result.
Flash Attention's optimization: It realized the GPU was spending 90% of its time just moving data back and forth to slow memory. Flash Attention rewrote the operation in raw CUDA so that the GPU loads chunks of Q, K, and V into its ultra-fast internal cache (SRAM), does all the math at once (fused operation), and only writes the final answer back to slow memory.

3. Does Flash Attention have "rivals"?
Yes, it does! While Flash Attention (currently on version 3) is the king right now, it has a few rivals/alternatives in the hardware-optimization space:

xFormers (Memory Efficient Attention): Created by Meta (Facebook). It is a library that provides an alternative optimized attention implementation. Before Flash Attention 2 came out, xFormers was often considered its biggest rival and was sometimes faster depending on your exact GPU.
Triton Attention: OpenAI created a programming language called Triton (easier to write than CUDA). People write Flash Attention-like algorithms in Triton. It's often used as an alternative because it's easier to modify than the raw C++/CUDA of official Flash Attention.
PagedAttention (by vLLM): This isn't a direct rival to the math, but rather a rival optimization for inference. While Flash Attention makes the math fast, PagedAttention makes storing the KV Cache efficient (treating GPU memory like OS virtual memory to prevent fragmentation). Today, the best serving engines use Flash Attention and PagedAttention together.
To summarize your whole thought process:

SDPA is the core math equation.
MHA / GQA are the architectural designs of how you group the inputs to that math equation.
Standard Attention is the slow, naive way to compute it.
Flash Attention (or xFormers) is the hyper-optimized hardware algorithm to actually crunch the numbers on the GPU ,,, ,

## 1. PyTorch: flash vs memory-efficient. Is datatype the only difference?

**No.** They are two different kernels from two different code bases, with different rules. From `aten/.../cuda/sdp_utils.cpp` (your clone is from 2025-12-05):

| | **Flash** | **Memory-efficient** |
|---|---|---|
| Code | Tri Dao's FA2, compiled from `third_party/flash-attention` | Meta's xFormers kernel, built on CUTLASS (`mem_eff_attention/`) |
| Input dtypes | fp16, bf16 **only** (`:662-664`) | fp16, bf16, **fp32** (`:830-831`) |
| Attention mask | **not allowed**; only `is_causal` (`check_for_attn_mask`, `:777`) | **allowed** (any additive mask) |
| GQA (fewer K/V heads) | **yes** (`backend_supports_grouped_query_attention = true`, `:801`) | **no**: K, V and Q must have the same head count (`:871`, `sdp_utils_cpp.h:415-428`) |
| GPU | sm80 and newer (`:291`) | sm50 and newer (`:348`) |
| Head dim | up to 256 | any multiple of the alignment |
| Order PyTorch tries them | **1st** | **2nd** (`Context.h:457-462`) |

So dtype is **one** real difference. Masks, GQA, GPU support and head size also differ. For **GQA**, PyTorch's memory-efficient kernel doesn't run at all; it falls to the next backend.

**What they share:** both use the same idea:
- tiles;
- online softmax;
- the T×T matrix is never written to GPU memory;
- the result is exact.

"Memory-efficient attention" (Rabe & Staats 2021) and "FlashAttention" (Dao 2022) are two names for this same idea. In PyTorch, the two names point to two specific kernels.

## 2. Does flash compute everything in bf16? **No**

FA2's forward pass, step by step (`flash-attention/csrc/flash_attn/src`):

| Step | Precision | Code |
|---|---|---|
| Q, K, V inputs | bf16 | `kernel_traits.h:19` |
| S = Q·Kᵀ | bf16 × bf16, **fp32 accumulate** | MMA `SM80_16x8x16_F32BF16BF16F32_TN` (`kernel_traits.h:33`); `acc_s` is fp32 (`flash_fwd_kernel.h:310`) |
| softmax: max, exp, sum | **fp32** | `row_max`, `row_sum` are `float` (`softmax.h:131-132`); `exp2f` on floats (`:86-118`) |
| P for the second matmul | **rounded to bf16** | `convert_type<Element>(acc_s)` (`flash_fwd_kernel.h:354`) |
| O = P·V | **fp32 accumulate** | `acc_o` (`:194`) |
| LSE (saved for backward) | **fp32** | `ElementAccum = float` (`kernel_traits.h:26`) |
| Output O | bf16 | `convert_type<Element>(acc_o)` (`:443`) |

**So only the inputs, P, and the output are bf16. Softmax and all sums are fp32.**

## 3. Does memory-efficient compute everything in fp32? **No: it follows the input dtype**

- **bf16 inputs:** the same scheme as flash.
  - Accumulation is fp32 (`accum_t = float`, `kernel_forward.h:99`).
  - Softmax max and sum are fp32 (`:516, :643`).
  - P is stored as bf16 for the second matmul (`mma_from_smem.h:1526`: `scalar_t, // accum_t`).
- **fp32 inputs:** the matmuls use `OpMultiplyAddFastF32` (`gemm_kernel_utils.h:112-123`). In CUTLASS that means **3×TF32**: each fp32 number is split into a big and a small TF32 part, and three tensor-core multiplies are done (`cutlass/arch/mma.h:77-79`). The result is close to true fp32.

**So for bf16 inputs, flash and memory-efficient use the same precision scheme.** Their differences are the rules in section 1, speed, and code.

I checked both checkouts. `sft_research/BluTrain` and `BluTrain_sft` (branch `dist_side_merge`, TI `d96b991`) have **identical** attention code. SFT runs use `bluscript_zero_ckpt.cpp` (SFT mode, `:920`).

**Yes: GQA, bf16, our own FlashAttention-style kernels.**
- **Model:** 18 query heads, **6 KV heads**, group size 3, head_dim 128 (`bluscript_zero_ckpt.cpp:132-134`).
- **Call:** `scaled_dot_product_attention(q_bf, k_bf, v_bf, 18, 6, is_causal=true, FlashAttention)` (`:642-644`). This path **requires bf16** (`AttentionOps.cpp`, `sdpa_flash_attention_qkv`). On H200 it runs **v62 forward + Vj1d backward**.
- **Before attention:** QK-norm + RoPE run in **fp32** (`qk_dtype()` = Float32, `:198`; fused kernel `:612-618`). Then q and k are cast to bf16. v stays bf16 (`:640`).

**v62 forward** (`GQA_fwd_sm90.cu`):

| Step | Precision | Line |
|---|---|---|
| S = Q·Kᵀ | bf16 in, **fp32 accumulate** (`wgmma … f32.bf16.bf16`) | `:278` |
| softmax max / sum | **fp32** (`m0, m1, l0, l1`) | `:440` |
| exp | fp32, approximate exp2 (`ex2_approx`) | `:511`. FA2 does the same: built with `--use_fast_math` (`setup.py:366`) |
| P | **rounded to bf16** (`pack_bf16`) | `~:540` |

| Output | bf16 | `:605` |

**Vj1d backward** (`GQA_bwd_vj1d_sm90.cu`):
- `D = rowsum(dO·O)` in **fp32** (`:283`).
- Matmuls: bf16 in, fp32 accumulate.
- **dQ:** summed in an **fp32** buffer (TMA reduce-add, `:373`), then converted to bf16 (`:646`).
- **dK/dV:** each query head writes a bf16 partial, then the 3 heads of a group are summed in **fp32** and rounded to bf16 (`:395-413`). **FA2 does exactly the same for GQA:** per-head bf16 buffers (`dk_expanded`), then `at::sum_out` over the group (`flash_api.cpp:935-1004`).

## 5. Our "MemoryEfficient" path: what it really is

- `sdpa_memory_efficient` **requires fp32** (`AttentionOps.cpp:89-90`) and calls `mem_efficient_attn_forward_tc` (`AttentionForward.cu:1051`).
- Inputs and outputs are fp32. The matmuls run on tensor cores in **TF32**: the inputs are rounded with `round_tf32_wmma_frag`, then fp32 accumulate (`:727-733`).
- It handles **MHA only**: Q, K and V have the same head count.
- It is a real memory-efficient kernel: fused, online softmax, never stores T×T (`AttentionOps.cpp:115`).
- **Who uses it today:** only `Tensor-Implementations/gpt2_fmha.cpp:189, 210` and an old test (`dist/…/AC_DDP/script1.cpp:150`). **Not SFT, and not the current trainers.** All of those call FlashAttention + bf16:

  - `bluscript_zero.cpp:537`;
  - `bluscript_zero_ckpt.cpp:644`;
  - `train/production/bluscript.cpp:228, 276`.

| Question | Answer |
|---|---|
| Are we doing FlashAttention? | **Yes.** Our own FA3-style kernels (v62 + Vj1d), bf16, causal GQA 18/6. Not Tri Dao's library |

**For v2:** this changes nothing. The kernels that need varlen are still v62 + Vj1d, the bf16 GQA path. The old fp32 path isn't used by SFT.

| Dropout | not in this op | yes |
| Varlen (packing) | no | **yes** (`cu_seqlens_q/k`, `native_functions.yaml:15209`) |
| GQA | **no, MHA only** | **no, MHA only** (same head count required, `sdp_utils.cpp:871`) |

**Same:** the idea (tiled, online softmax, never stores T×T) and MHA-only. **Different:** everything else in the table.

## 2. Can FlashAttention do GQA?

**Yes.** Only PyTorch's memory-efficient kernel can't.

| Kernel | GQA? | Code |
|---|---|---|
| FA2 | **yes** | KV head = query head / ratio (`flash_fwd_kernel.h:155, 161`); check "Number of heads in key/value must divide number of heads in query" (`flash_api.cpp:418`) |
| PyTorch flash backend | **yes** | `backend_supports_grouped_query_attention = true` (`sdp_utils.cpp:801`) |
| PyTorch cuDNN backend | **yes** | `<true /*enable_gqa*/>` (`sdp_utils.cpp:742`) |
| PyTorch memory-efficient | **no** | `<false>` (`sdp_utils.cpp:871`) |
| **Our v62 / Vj1d** | **yes**: 18 query heads, 6 KV heads | `bluscript_zero_ckpt.cpp:132-134` |

## 3. Are our latest pretraining scripts using "FlashAttention-3 GQA"?

**Our own kernels, written in the FA3 style. Not Tri Dao's FA3 code.**
- v62's own header: "Persistent, warp-specialised FlashAttention-style kernel … FA3-style consumer ping-pong" (`GQA_fwd_sm90.cu:1-12`).
- **All current trainers call the same bf16 GQA FlashAttention API:**
  - `bluscript_single.cpp:272`;
  - `bluscript_zero.cpp:537`;
  - `bluscript_zero_ckpt.cpp:644` (SFT uses this one);
  - `train/production/bluscript.cpp:228, 276`.
- **On H200:**
  - forward = **v62** (`GQA_fwd_generic.cu:330-336`);
  - backward = **Vj1d** by default. `USE_FLASH=1` picks Vj1, `USE_DETERMINISTIC_DQ=1` picks V44 (`GQA_bwd_generic.cu:96-112, 126-130`).
- **B300** has separate sm103 kernels (e.g., v48 for head_dim 64). SFT doesn't use them.

## 4. Does PyTorch do the same as us?

**Same math, different kernels.** In your PyTorch clone (2025-12-05), on H100/H200, `F.scaled_dot_product_attention` tries backends in this order:

| Order | Backend | Condition |
|---|---|---|
| **1st** | **cuDNN** (NVIDIA, closed source) | cuDNN ≥ 9.9 and GPU is sm90 or sm100 (`sdp_utils.cpp:78-108`) |
| 2nd | flash = **FA2** (not FA3) | FA2 uses the older Ampere `mma.sync` instructions (`kernel_traits.h:33`), not Hopper's wgmma/TMA |
| 3rd | memory-efficient | no GQA |
| 4th | math | naive |

- **FA3 is not inside PyTorch.** FA4 can be switched on by hand: `activate_flash_attention_impl("FA4")`, sm90/sm100 only (`_fa4.py:105-106`; `_registry.py:17` lists only "FA4").
- **Our v62 was measured against PyTorch's cuDNN path.** Its header says: H200, B=8, Hq=12, Hkv=4, S=4096, causal bf16 → **0.7075 ms, 579 TFLOPS, ~1.6% faster than PyTorch SDPA's cuDNN path** (`GQA_fwd_sm90.cu:14-15`).
  - That's the header's claim; I didn't re-run it.
  - That run used 12/4 heads. Our SFT model is 18/6 (same group size, 3).

## 5. Forward vs backward: separate? Who are the rivals?

**PyTorch doesn't use cuDNN for backward only.** PyTorch picks one backend at forward time, and autograd calls **that same backend's** backward (`derivatives.yaml`):
- flash forward → flash backward (`:2886-2888`);
- cuDNN forward → cuDNN backward (`:2906-2908`);
- memory-efficient forward → memory-efficient backward (`:2882`).

**The backward is always a separate kernel, because the math is different:**
- **forward:** 2 matmuls, `S = Q·Kᵀ` and `O = P·V`;
- **backward:** recompute P from the saved LSE, then 5 matmuls: `Q·Kᵀ`, `dO·Vᵀ`, `Pᵀ·dO`, `dS·K`, `dSᵀ·Q`. That's about 2.5× the forward work.

Every library ships its own **pair**:

| Library | Forward + backward |
|---|---|
| **Ours** | v62 + Vj1d. Vj1d also runs helper kernels: rowsum, two greduce passes, dQ convert (`GQA_bwd_vj1d_sm90.cu:637-646`) |
| cuDNN | its own pair (PyTorch's default on H200) |
| FA2 / FA3 / FA4 | each its own pair |
| FlexAttention | Triton forward + backward templates |
| ThunderKittens | its own pair |

**Liger is not an attention rival.** It has no standard attention kernel; its ops are cross-entropy, fused linear cross-entropy, RMSNorm, RoPE, SwiGLU and so on. Liger is a rival for our **loss** kernel.

**ThunderKittens** (Stanford, ICLR 2025): a framework for writing kernels. It has H100 attention forward and backward for causal, non-causal and GQA, at head dim 64/128. **Their paper says:** forward about equal to FA3 (non-causal), backward faster than FA3 by over 40% at short sequences and about 10% at long ones. I haven't cloned it, so this isn't checked in code.

**So our attention rivals on H200, for both forward and backward:** cuDNN (PyTorch's default), FA3, FA4, FA2 (PyTorch's fallback), FlexAttention, ThunderKittens.

Sources:
- [ThunderKittens paper (arXiv 2410.20399)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.20399)
- [ThunderKittens HTML v1](https://arxiv.org/html/2410.20399v1)

Yes, H200 only, GPU 5. Nothing has been run yet. Here's the plan.

## What we measure
Our SFT loss kernels, **forward and backward**, run **alone** (no trainer), on **H200 GPU 5**, at the exact SFT micro-batch:
- **B=8 × T=4096 = 32,768 positions**, vocab **50,304**;
- **bf16 logits**, the same as our `BLU_ALL_BF16=1` runs;
- labels as uint16, where **65535 = masked** (prompt and pad);
- **v1 padding**: every row padded to 4096.

## Which code runs
The same library functions the trainer reaches through `autograd::sparse_cross_entropy_loss`:

| Pass | Kernel | What it does |
|---|---|---|
| Forward | `sparse_ce_forward_kernel_vec_save_stats` | one block per position. **Masked:** writes 3 numbers and exits. **Trained:** one pass over 50,304 logits (max, sum of exp, loss) and saves max and sum for the backward |
| | `sum_reduction_kernel` ×2 | adds the 32,768 losses and divides by the trained count |
| Backward | `sparseCENormalize_from_stats` | **Trained:** reads logits, writes (softmax − one-hot) ÷ count. **Masked:** writes 50,304 zeros |

## Test cases: real batches from our stage-0 labels.bin
Our labels.bin has 5,000 rows, which makes 625 micro-batches. Trained share per batch: min 8.9%, median 23.1%, mean 23.3%, max 38.9%.

| Case | Trained | Why |
|---|---|---|
| real_first | 18.65% | the first micro-batch of the run |
| real_min | 8.9% | fewest trained tokens |
| real_median | ~23.1% | the typical batch |
| real_max | 38.9% | most trained tokens |
| nomask | 100%, masking off | the pretraining path. Shows what masking saves |
| all_masked | 0% | the floor: backward only writes zeros |

## How we time it (two ways, same binary)
1. **Our timing (CUDA events):** per case, 5 warm-up rounds, then 50 forward calls and 50 backward calls, each timed alone. Reported as median / min / mean ms.
2. **nsys:** one case per run. The kernel summary gives each kernel's own time (forward kernel, the 2 reduction kernels, backward kernel). This checks our event timings and splits the forward into its 3 kernels.

## How we judge the numbers: bytes the GPU memory must move
- Logits = 32,768 × 50,304 × 2 B = **3.30 GB**.
- **Forward** reads only the trained positions: median batch ≈ 0.76 GB; nomask 3.30 GB.
- **Backward** reads the trained positions and writes the **whole** gradient, zeros included: (1 + trained share) × 3.30 GB. Median ≈ 4.06 GB; nomask 6.60 GB.
- H200 peak is 4.8 TB/s. So the best possible times are: median forward ≈ 0.16 ms, median backward ≈ 0.85 ms. We report how close we get, as GB/s and % of peak.

## Checks per case (so a fast number isn't a kernel that skipped work)
- The loss is finite, and exactly 0 for all_masked.
- The number of positions the forward actually computed equals the trained count.
- A masked position's gradient is all zero bits.
- A trained position's gradient sums to about 0 and is negative at its target.

## Stats for your colleague
- Per case: forward ms, backward ms, total, GB/s, % of peak.
- nsys per-kernel split.
- Cost per optimizer step: 8 micro-batches × (forward + backward), and its share of our ~5.3 s step.
- How much masking saves vs nomask.

**Not covered:** v2 packing, the logits matmul, and the trainer's extra work around the loss.

Yes. Since the trainer uses the save_stats path, we time **each kernel alone and the two together**. I added that to the draft, plus the no-stats path as a reference. It **compiles cleanly** (still scratchpad only, nothing run).

## The 5 timings, for each of the 6 cases

| Timing | What runs | Who uses it | Best possible on the median batch (at 4.8 TB/s) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **F** | forward save_stats alone | trainer, every training micro-batch | 0.16 ms (reads 0.76 GB) |
| **B** | backward with stats alone | trainer | 0.85 ms (4.06 GB) |
| **F+B** | the two back to back, **timed as one** | trainer, the real pair | 1.01 ms |
| **Fv** | forward **without** stats | validation (no gradient) | 0.16 ms |
| **Fv+Bo** | forward without stats + a backward that **re-reads the logits** to recompute max and sum | reference only | 1.17 ms (Bo moves (2×trained + 1) × 3.30 GB) |

- **F+B vs F and B alone:** shows the real cost of the pair, with no gap between the two.
- **F+B vs Fv+Bo:** shows what saving the stats buys. The backward skips one full read of the trained positions' logits.

## Extra check
On top of the earlier checks, the no-stats path must give **the same loss and the same gradient row** as the save_stats path. If the two disagree, the numbers don't count.

## nsys
Every pass has its own kernel names, so one nsys run per case splits them by itself:
- **F:** `sparse_ce_forward_kernel_vec_save_stats` + `sum_reduction_kernel`;
- **B:** `sparseCENormalize_from_stats`;
- **Fv:** `sparse_ce_forward_kernel_vec`;
- **Bo:** `sparseCEReduce_kernel_optimized` + `sparseCENormalize_kernel_optimized`.

Only `sum_reduction_kernel` is shared by F and Fv, and it's tiny.

## The table you'll get
Columns: case, trained %, F ms, B ms, F+B ms, Fv ms, Fv+Bo ms, GB/s and % of peak, PASS/FAIL. Plus the cost per optimizer step: 8 × F+B.

| Case | Trained | **F** fwd | **B** bwd | **F+B** pair | Fv (val) | Fv+Bo (no stats) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| real_min | 8.9% | 0.132 ms | 1.095 ms | **1.229 ms** | 0.130 | 1.379 |
| real_first | 18.7% | 0.234 | 1.443 | **1.676** | 0.231 | 1.994 |
