## What the numbers say
1. **Masking pays.** On the same batch, the time drops from nomask to real_first:
   - forward 1.025 → 0.234 ms (**4.4× less**);
   - backward 4.353 → 1.443 ms (**3.0×**);
   - pair 5.376 → 1.676 ms (**3.2×**).
2. **Saving the stats pays.** Pair vs the no-stats version:
   - median batch 1.878 vs 2.258 ms (**−17%**);
   - nomask 5.376 vs 6.884 ms (**−22%**).
   - Saving them costs almost nothing: F vs Fv is +1.3 µs (+0.5%).
3. **The backward is 85% of the pair** (1.600 of 1.878 ms, median batch). Most of it is **writing zeros** to the masked positions:
   - all_masked shows that zero-write alone takes 0.823 ms for 3.30 GB, at **83% of peak**, which is good.
   - For the median batch (77% masked), that's ≈ 0.63 ms of zeros. That leaves ≈ 0.97 ms for the trained positions, which move 1.53 GB, so only **~33% of peak**. This split is my estimate by subtraction.
   - nomask backward is also **31.6%**. So the trained-row part of the backward is the slow part. The cause isn't measured yet; ncu would tell us.
4. **Per optimizer step:** 8 micro-batches × 1.878 = **15.0 ms**. Against our ~5.3 s step (the 10-06 one-GPU run), that's **0.28%**. The loss kernel isn't a bottleneck for SFT step time.
5. **Correctness:**
   - Positions computed = trained count in every case.
   - Masked gradients are bit-zero.
   - The no-stats path gives the **identical** loss and gradient (max difference 0).
   - The loss matches theory: random logits uniform in [−4, 4) should give ln(50304) + ln((e⁴−e⁻⁴)/8) = **12.746**. We measured 12.740–12.750.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-09 19:56 IST]

## What "trained" means
Each micro-batch has 8 rows × 4096 = **32,768 positions**. Each position is one of three kinds:

| Kind | Label | Loss computed? | Share in our stage-0 data |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Answer token** (assistant) | the real next token | **yes → "trained"** | **23.3%** |
| Prompt token (user / system) | 65535 = masked | no | ~6.9% |
| Pad (after the chat ends, filling to 4096) | 65535 = masked | no | ~69.8% |

**"Trained" = the share of positions that are answer tokens.**
- Real tokens are 30.2% of positions (measured in Q10).
- Trained is 23.3%.
- So prompts are the 6.9% difference, and pads are the rest.
- **Most of the masked positions are pads, not prompts.**

## Can we control the %?
**Not in the kernel.** The kernel follows the labels: masked positions are skipped in the forward and get zeros in the backward. **The data and the batching method decide the %.**
- **Data:** longer answers or shorter chats change it.
- **Batching:** v1 pads every chat to 4096, which is where the 69.8% pads come from.

**In real training, every micro-batch has its own %.** Over our 625 micro-batches: min 8.9%, median 23.1%, mean 23.3%, max 38.9%.

**What we did in the benchmark:** we didn't pick a % ourselves. We took **4 real micro-batches** from labels.bin (the first, the lowest, the median and the highest), plus the two ends: 0% (all masked) and 100% (masking off). That covers the whole real range.

## How it goes in a real run
The time follows a **straight line** in the trained share. From our numbers:

**F+B ≈ 0.87 ms + 4.51 ms × trained share**

| Case | Trained | Line predicts | Measured |
|---|---|---|---|
| real_min | 8.9% | 1.27 ms | 1.23 |
| real_median | 23.1% | 1.91 ms | 1.88 |
| real_max | 38.9% | 2.62 ms | 2.59 |

- **0.87 ms** is the fixed part: mostly writing zeros for every position in the backward.
- **4.51 ms** is what a fully trained batch adds.
- **Over the whole run:** the mean of 23.3% gives ≈ **1.92 ms per micro-batch**, ≈ **15.3 ms per step** (8 micro-batches), and ≈ **1.2 s per epoch** (625 micro-batches).

## What would change the %
- **v2 packing** removes the pads. Each micro-batch then has ≈ 77% trained positions (23.3 ÷ 30.2), and there are only ≈ 190 micro-batches instead of 625 (1,517 packed rows ÷ 8).
  - From the line: 0.87 + 4.51 × 0.77 ≈ 4.3 ms each, so ≈ **0.8 s per epoch instead of 1.2 s**.
  - That's an estimate from the fit, not measured.
- **Q11** (compute logits only at trained positions) would take the masked positions out of the loss completely, the zero-writes included.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-09 20:00 IST]

You're right, I explained it badly. Here it is plainly.

## 1. We trained nothing
No model and no training run. We ran **only the loss kernel**, by itself, over and over, and timed it.

## 2. What the loss kernel needs as input
1. **Logits:** the model's scores. One row of 50,304 numbers for each position, and 8 × 4096 = 32,768 positions.
2. **Labels:** for each position, the correct next token, **or 65535, which means "skip this position"**. Prompt and pad positions are skipped.

## 3. Where we got them
- **Logits:** **random numbers**, made inside the test. No model is needed, because the kernel takes the same time whatever the values are.
- **Labels:** taken from our **real SFT label file**: `labels.bin` from our stage-0 data (5,000 UltraChat chats, each padded to 4096). We only read the labels from it.

## 4. Why the labels matter
The kernel **skips** every position labelled 65535. So the number of positions that are **not** skipped decides the time.

**"Trained %"** = in one batch of 8 rows, the share of positions that are **not** skipped (the answer tokens).
- Example: 7,577 of 32,768 positions = **23.1%**.

## 5. The 6 cases = which 8 rows we fed the kernel

| Case | Which rows | Trained % |
|---|---|---|
| real_first | rows 0–7 of the file: the first batch a training run sees | 18.7% |
| real_min | the 8 rows with the **fewest** answer tokens in the whole file | 8.9% |
| real_median | a **typical** batch: half the batches have fewer, half more | 23.1% |
| real_max | the 8 rows with the **most** answer tokens | 38.9% |
| nomask | rows 0–7 with skipping **turned off**: every position computed, like pretraining | 100% |
| all_masked | **every** position skipped: the smallest possible time | 0% |

## 6. The columns (time in ms for one batch of 8 × 4096)
- **F** = loss forward.
- **B** = loss backward.
- **F+B** = both together. **This is what one batch costs in training.**
- **Fv**, **Fv+Bo** = an older way of doing the same thing, only to compare.

## 7. The result in 3 lines
1. A typical SFT batch costs **1.9 ms** for loss forward + backward. One training step (8 batches) costs about **15 ms**, out of a ~5.3 s step. That's tiny.
2. Skipping the masked positions makes the loss **~3× faster** than computing every position (1.7 ms vs 5.4 ms on the same rows).
3. All correctness checks passed.

## A or B: what I said, and what I recommend
**It isn't "PyTorch vs B".** PyTorch has both: `varlen_attn` is **A** (it runs the FA2 kernels), and FlexAttention is **B**.

**In general, A is the standard.** FlashAttention and Transformer Engine use it. It works for any chat length and wastes slightly less work.

**For our kernels I recommend B.** I'll confirm it tomorrow after reading our backward kernel (Vj1d). Why B fits us:
1. **v2 keeps every row at 4096 tokens.** So v62 and Vj1d still see 4096-long rows, and all their current limits still hold.
2. **Output writes stay as they are.** With A, FA3 had to switch off its fast output stores so one chat's tile wouldn't overwrite the next chat. B doesn't have that problem.
3. **The change is small:**
   - forward: each query tile starts its key loop at the start of its own chat, and masks keys from an earlier chat;
   - backward: the same rule, from the other side.
4. **No NaN risk:** every token always sees at least itself.

**What B costs:**
- part of a key tile is wasted at each chat start, because tiles line up with the row, not the chat. A wastes part of a tile at each chat end instead. I'll measure the exact difference on our packed rows in Step 3;
- the work balance between tiles changes. That happens in A too.

My table was wrong. **PyTorch isn't "A" and torchtitan isn't "B". Both designs live inside PyTorch, and torchtitan uses both.**

## 1. PyTorch and torchtitan are not the same thing
- **PyTorch** = the library that has the kernels.
- **torchtitan** = a training framework from the PyTorch team, **built on PyTorch**. It has **no attention kernel of its own**; it calls PyTorch's.

## 2. PyTorch itself provides both designs

| Design | PyTorch function | Kernel it runs |
|---|---|---|
| **A** (chat start offsets, `cu_seqlens`) | `torch.nn.attention.varlen.varlen_attn` | FA2 kernels in our clone. The cuDNN path is switched off (`varlen.py:21-23, 75-84`) |
| **B** (one row + block mask) | `torch.nn.attention.flex_attention` + `create_block_mask` | a Triton kernel generated by PyTorch, or FA4 with `BACKEND="FLASH"` |

## 3. torchtitan uses both, chosen per model
`models/common/config_utils.py:96-115` maps a config string to an attention type:

| torchtitan setting | Design | What it calls |
|---|---|---|
| `"varlen"` | **A** | PyTorch `varlen_attn` (`attention.py:39-41, 132+`) |
| `"flex"` | **B** | PyTorch FlexAttention, Triton kernel |
| `"flex_flash"` | **B** | FlexAttention on FA4, Hopper/Blackwell only |
| `"sdpa"` | refused for language models | the code says plain SDPA "cannot consume per-document positions" |

**Model defaults in torchtitan:**
- varlen: Qwen3 8B, gpt-oss (debug);
- flex: DeepSeek-V3, Kimi, muse_glimmer.

**Why both exist (from the code):**
- **varlen (A)** only does causal or sliding-window attention.
- **flex (B)** takes any mask or score change. Kimi needs this: "Kimi QK clipping requires the FlexInnerAttention backend" (`kimi_k2_7/__init__.py:196-198`).

## 4. One more fact
torchtitan calls `varlen_attn(..., window_size=...)`, but our PyTorch clone (Dec 2025) has no `window_size` argument. So torchtitan needs a **newer PyTorch nightly**. Which kernel `varlen_attn` runs there can't be seen in our clone; in ours it's FA2.

## Conclusion
There's no contradiction:
- **Both designs are PyTorch features.**
- torchtitan is a user of PyTorch, and lets each model pick:
  - **A** for plain causal attention;
  - **B** when the model needs a custom mask.
- This doesn't change our choice. B still fits our kernels for the reasons in §39.8; we confirm it tomorrow after reading Vj1d.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-09 21:14 IST]
> tool `Bash`: Check Qwen3 8B backend and torchtitan's SFT/RL support
> tool `Bash`: Check torchtitan README and dataset for SFT vs pretraining use

**No, on both points.**

## 1. torchtitan is mainly for pretraining, not only post-training
- Its paper title (README line 196): **"TorchTitan: One-stop PyTorch native solution for production ready LLM pretraining"**.
- It also supports post-training:
  - **SFT:** README line 75 lists "Supervised Fine-Tuning (SFT) with chat-formatted datasets". The code is `ChatProcessor` in `hf_datasets/text_datasets.py:96`, which masks the labels outside the assistant's answer.
  - **RL:** the `torchtitan/rl` folder (TitanRL, added 2026-08).

## 2. It uses PyTorch's A path too, not only B
- `config_utils.py:108-109`: the setting `"varlen"` → `VarlenInnerAttention` → PyTorch's `varlen_attn`. That's **design A**.
- **Qwen3 8B in torchtitan uses A:** `attn_backend="varlen"` (`models/qwen3/config_registry.py:262`).
- **DeepSeek-V3, Kimi and muse_glimmer use B** (`"flex"`).

## 3. Why chat or document masking matters in pretraining too
torchtitan's own comment (`config_utils.py:89-91`): "Language models always use block_causal masking (the dataloaders always emit per-document positions)".

So torchtitan **packs several documents into one row in pretraining as well**, and each document only attends to itself. That's the same problem as our SFT packing. So torchtitan needs A or B in pretraining too, not just in SFT.

**Summary:**

| | torchtitan |
|---|---|
| Main purpose | pretraining (also SFT and RL) |
| Uses design A (PyTorch `varlen_attn`) | yes, e.g. Qwen3 8B |
| Uses design B (PyTorch FlexAttention) | yes, e.g. DeepSeek-V3, Kimi |
| Uses plain SDPA for language models | no: refused, because it can't separate documents |

|---|---|---|

so today ,

| design | how it works | who uses it |
|---|---|---|

**Into these two kernels: v62 forward and Vj1d backward.** It's a feature added to them, not a new attention. The math stays the same; the kernels only also need to know where each chat starts.

| Part | Changes for v2? | Why |
|---|---|---|

| Embedding, matmuls | no | they don't care about chat boundaries |
| Other attention paths: the Vj1 / V44 backward modes, the generic kernels, the B300 kernels | **must refuse packed input with an error** | so chats can never silently see each other |

## 1. Did we fix B?
**Not yet.** Yesterday I *leaned* to B. The final decision comes after reading Vj1d (Step 2). Today's numbers below support B.

## 2. Is B fast and efficient?
I measured this just now. I counted the attention tiles each design computes over our real stage-0 data (5,000 chats packed into 1,517 rows of 4096), using our kernels' real tile sizes: forward v62 = 64×128, backward Vj1d = 64×64. Counts are per head, for one epoch.

| Design | Forward tiles | vs today | Useful work in computed tiles | Backward tiles | vs today | Useful work |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **v1 today** (every chat padded to 4096) | 5,280,000 | 100% | 10.9% | 10,400,000 | 100% | 11.1% |
| **A** (each chat its own sequence) | 651,014 | **12.3%** | 88.7% | 1,251,206 | **12.0%** | 92.3% |
| **B** (packed rows + block mask) | 672,961 | **12.7%** | 85.8% | 1,269,440 | **12.2%** | 90.9% |

- **Both cut attention work to about 1/8 of today's.**
- **B does only +3.4% more tiles than A in the forward, and +1.5% in the backward.** The reason: tiles line up with the row, not with the chat, so the first key tile of each chat partly covers the previous chat, and those entries are masked.
- **These are work counts, not timings.** Real speed is known only after we build it.
  - B keeps v62's structure as it is: fast output writes, fixed 4096 rows, the same grid.
  - A needs per-chat scheduling, and FA3 had to switch off its fast output writes for it, which costs speed per tile.
  - Both lose v62's current work balance (its early-tile + late-tile pairing assumes the plain triangle), so that needs re-balancing either way.

## 3. Same precision? Correct?
**Same precision.** B changes no data type: bf16 inputs; fp32 softmax, sums and accumulators; bf16 P and output. It's the same as today and the same as A.

**Correct: yes, exactly.** Keys from another chat get −∞, and exp(−∞) = 0 exactly. So other chats contribute exactly nothing, not "almost nothing".

**Not bit-identical to A**, though. In B, a chat's keys are grouped into tiles differently, so the order of the running-softmax updates differs. Results then differ only in the last bf16 bits, the same kind of difference as between FA2, FA3 and cuDNN.

**One thing B must add, or it gives NaN.**
- v62 walks key tiles from the first one upward (`GQA_fwd_sm90.cu:472`) and updates the running max with `(m0 − nm0)` (`:510-511`).
- In B, rows of a later chat inside a shared query tile start with key tiles that are **fully masked** for them. That makes −∞ − (−∞) = **NaN**.
- Today this never happens, because tile 0 always holds key 0.
- The fix is a one-line guard (use 0 when the max is still −∞), the same as FA2 (`softmax.h:73-76`).
- The backward doesn't have this problem: it uses the saved LSE, which is always finite.

**How we'll prove it's correct:**
1. Compare against a PyTorch fp32 reference with an explicit chat mask.
2. Compare against running each chat alone through today's v62.
3. Change one chat's tokens: the other chats' outputs must stay **bit-for-bit** the same.

Almost. One correction: **64 examples is per optimizer step, not per micro-step.**

## The numbers
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| Examples (chats) | 5,000, the **same ones** in both epochs and in the **same order** (no reshuffle) |
| Epochs | 2, so 5,000 + 5,000 = 10,000 passes |
| **Micro-step** | **8 chats** (B = 8 rows of 4096) |
| **Optimizer step** | 8 micro-steps added together (gradient accumulation 8 on 1 GPU) = **64 chats** |
| Steps | 10,000 ÷ 64 = 156.25, so **156 steps** |
| Exactly trained | 156 × 64 = **9,984 passes**. The last 16 chats of epoch 2 were not reached |

## DCP means
**Distributed CheckPoint**, our checkpoint library (`dist/Distributed_Checkpointing`, `DistCheckpoint::save` in `DCP.h`).
- It saves the **weights + the optimizer state + the epoch, step and loss**, with checksums.
- **`metadata.bin`:** an index. For every tensor it records the name, shape, dtype, and where its bytes are.
- **`data_rank_N.bin`:** the bytes. One file per GPU. Our run used 1 GPU, so there's only `data_rank_0.bin`.

PyTorch has the same idea under the same name (`torch.distributed.checkpoint`). But PyTorch and Hugging Face **can't load our files directly**. That's why it needs the DCP → HF converter first.

Step 2 is done. **Conclusion: design B.** Here's what I read, and the numbers behind it.

## What our kernels do today (from the code)
| Kernel | How it works now | What matters for v2 |
|---|---|---|
| **v62 forward** (`GQA_fwd_sm90.cu`) | 132 persistent blocks. Each work unit = an early + a late pair of query tiles (`:348-354`). Both consumers walk key tiles from **0** up to the diagonal (`:398, :436, :472`) | the causal mask is applied only on the diagonal tile (`:479-498`). O and LSE are written with **plain stores** (`:605-609`). The running-max update has **no −∞ guard** (`:510-511`) |
| **Vj1d backward** (`GQA_bwd_vj1d_sm90.cu`) | one block per (64-key tile, query head, batch). It loops query tiles from the diagonal **to the end of the row** (`nIter = nQ − kt`, `:464`) | the mask is applied only on the diagonal (`:496-497`). P comes from the saved LSE, so it can't produce NaN. dK/dV are written as **whole 64-row tiles with TMA** (`:549-555`), dQ with a TMA add (`:517-531`) |
| **RoPE** (QK-norm + RoPE) | position = token index + `pos_offset` (forward `FusedRMSRoPE_fwd_sm90_kernel.cu:123, 187`, backward `…bwd_sm90_kernel.cu:93`, plus 2 fallback kernels) | needs **per-token positions** in both designs |
| **Loader** + prep script | one chat per 4096 row. Copies 8 rows per micro-batch (`SftDataLoader.h:52-79`) | needs packed rows + a positions file in both designs |

## What each design would cost in **our** kernels
| | **A** (each chat its own sequence) | **B** (packed row + block mask) |
|---|---|---|
| v62 forward | new work split per chat (today's pairing assumes one 4096 triangle); stop the output stores at each chat end | each pair's key walk **starts at its chat's tile instead of 0**; extra mask on those first tiles; a **−∞ guard** (one line) |
| Vj1d backward | **its dK/dV TMA stores write whole 64-row tiles**, so a tile at a chat end would overwrite the next chat. That needs padded buffers or a different store (the same problem FA3 had) | the query loop **stops at the chat end instead of the row end**; extra mask on the border tiles. Stores, dQ add and the greduce are **unchanged** |
| Shape rules | the "length % 256" rule and the scheduling must be redone | unchanged: rows stay 4096 |

## The numbers (real stage-0 data packed into 1,517 rows, per head, one epoch)
| | Forward | Backward |
|---|---|---|
| Today (v1) | 100% | 100% |
| A (tiles) | 12.3% | 12.0% |
| **B (tiles)** | 13.1% (v62's two consumers share their key walk) | **12.2%** |
| **B, forward time with v62's current scheduler** | **14.8% of today**. Only 85.9% of the SMs' time is used, because B's work per unit is uneven | — (hardware schedules the backward blocks) |
| **B, forward time with longest-work-first scheduling** | **12.9% of today** (98.4% balanced) | — |

- So B costs about **6% more forward tiles and 1.5% more backward tiles than A**, which is small next to the **~7–8× cut** from today.
- Two easy wins inside B:
  1. give each consumer its own start tile: 691,644 → 672,961 tiles;
  2. schedule the longest work first: 14.8% → 12.9%.

## Decision: **B**
1. Every change in our kernels is a loop bound, an extra mask condition, or a one-line guard. The stores, the TMA descriptors, the 4096 shape and the greduce all stay.
2. A would force a rework of Vj1d's whole-tile dK/dV stores.
3. The extra work of B over A is +1.5% (backward) to +6% (forward), against a 7–8× gain over today.

**Precision:** same data types. The results aren't bit-identical to today for chats that don't start on a 128 boundary; the difference is in the last bf16 bits only.

- **In total:** much faster, because packing removes about 87% of the tiles.
- **Unpacked runs (pretraining, today's v1):** no change at all, if the new code is a separate compile-time variant. FA3 does exactly this.

## Where a slowdown can come from (B inside our v62)
| Cause | Today | With B | Measured how | Fix |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **1. More tiles take the masked path**, which costs extra compare/select work per element | **6.1%** of computed tiles (only the diagonal tiles) | **29.9%** (diagonal 14.1% + chat-border 15.8%) | counted just now on our 1,517 packed rows | unmasked tiles keep today's fast path unchanged; only border tiles pay |
| **2. Work spread over the 132 SMs** (today's fixed rotation) | 97.0% balanced | **85.9%** balanced (worst batch 77.4%) | simulated with v62's real unit order | longest-work-first order: **98.4%** |
| **3. The −∞ guard** in the softmax update | none | 2 extra instructions per row per tile | code reading (`GQA_fwd_sm90.cu:510-511`) | none needed; tiny next to a tile's matrix work |
| **4. Compiler risk** | — | if the new loop bounds differ between threads around the tensor-core instructions, `ptxas` serializes the tensor pipe | v62's own comment (`:467-471`): this happened before (warning C7518) | keep each pair's start tile the same for the whole warpgroup (pair-shared start); check `ptxas` warnings and register spills after building |
| **5. Extra input**: each row's chat start | — | 2 ints per thread (forward), 64 ints per tile (backward) | code reading | negligible next to the 32 KB of Q/dO each backward tile loads |

## How big the total effect can be
- The cost of one masked tile isn't measured yet, so take an example: **suppose a masked tile costs 30% more** than an unmasked one.
  - Today: +30% × 6.1% = +1.8% average per tile.
  - B: +30% × 29.9% = +9.0% per tile.
  - So B runs about **7% slower per tile**.
- But B computes only **13% of today's tiles**. Forward attention time ≈ 14.8% × 1.09 / 1.02 ≈ **16% of today**, even with today's scheduler. That's still **~6× faster** overall.
- With longest-work-first scheduling, that improves to about **14%**.

**So the feature costs a few percent per tile, and packing saves about 85% of the work.**

## How we'll prove it after building (no guessing)
1. **Regression gate:** the edited kernel on **unpacked** input vs today's kernel, same inputs, paired runs. They must be **equal within noise**.
2. **Per-tile cost:** time on packed rows ÷ tile count, against today's time per tile. This measures causes 1–3 directly.
3. **`ptxas` check:** no new C7518 warning, no register spills.

The checking workflow is still running in the background. I'll report its verdicts when it finishes.

## Which is faster: A or B?
**A is a little faster.** In forward attention, B is about **8% slower than A** (range 6–10%). In backward attention, it's about **1.5–3% slower**.

**For the whole training step, the difference is about 0.4%.** After packing, attention is only about **5%** of all the training work; the matmuls are the rest. So 8% of 5% ≈ 0.4%.

## The numbers (all counted on our real stage-0 data)
| | Today (each chat padded to 4096) | A | B |
|---|---|---|---|
| Forward attention work | 100% | 12.3% | 13.1% |
| Backward attention work | 100% | 12.0% | 12.2% |
| Tiles that need the extra mask step | 6.1% | 15.2% | 29.9% |
| **Forward attention time** (estimate) | 100% | **~12.4%** | **~13.4%** |
| **Whole training step work** | 100% | **~28%** | **~28%** (+0.4%) |

Both A and B make the training step about **3.6× less work** than today.

## How much the new feature slows our kernel (B)
- **Per tile: about 3.5% slower** (range 2–7%).
- **Why:** a tile at a chat border needs an extra "mask" step. Today 6% of tiles need it; with B, 30% do.
- **What one mask step costs:** I haven't measured it on our kernel yet. FlexAttention's own code says masking costs them about **15%** per block, and I used that. 10–30% gives the 2–7% range.
- **One more slowdown, which we can remove:** today's kernel hands out work in a fixed rotation. With packed rows that wastes ~13% (SMs idle 14% instead of 3%). Handing out the longest jobs first fixes it: **98.4%** busy, slightly better than today's 97%.

## So why B?
- B costs only **~0.4% of the training step**.
- A would need big rewrites in our kernels: new work splitting, and a change to how the backward writes dK/dV, because a whole tile would overwrite the next chat.
- B is only small changes: where each loop starts and stops, one extra mask condition, and a one-line NaN guard.

All of these are estimates from counting. The real numbers come after building, by timing the new kernel against today's.

## Re-check result
**All 77 claims hold.** The new code reproduced every number **exactly**: tile counts, balance, data shares, packing.

Small corrections found:
1. PyTorch's naive causal path is at `attention.cpp:886-913`, not `:60-71`. What it does is the same: it builds the full mask with `ones({L,S}).tril()` (`:897-898`), computes the full `matmul` (`:905`), then adds −∞ (`:910`).
2. The Q10 packing script is **first-fit**, not best-fit. A true best-fit gives the identical result: 1,517 rows.
3. Line-number shifts only: FA3's `domain_offset` is at `:660/:662`. FA4's GPU check is "major 9 or 10" (`_fa4.py:105`).
4. The web facts (FA3 TFLOPs, ThunderKittens, DeepSeek-V4, MiniMax) were checked on 10-09. The web-fetch tool isn't available today, so I didn't re-fetch them. None of them affects A vs B.

**One new fact that matters for A.** In A, our backward writes dK/dV as **whole 64-row tiles** (`GQA_bwd_vj1d_sm90.cu:549-555`). At a chat end, that tile would overwrite the next chat's rows. The simple fix is to pad every chat to a multiple of 64. Counted on our data, that's **+155,665 tokens = +2.52%** (31 per chat). Those tokens go through **the whole model**, not just attention.

## Your questions, with proof

**1. Does A break the existing kernel or pretraining? Does A need a separate kernel?**
**No, and no.** FlashAttention itself adds A to the **same** kernel as a compile-time switch:
- **FA2:** without `cu_seqlens` it picks the old fast variant: `is_even_MN = params.cu_seqlens_q == nullptr && …` (`flash_fwd_launch_template.h:65`), which becomes `BlockInfo<Varlen=false>` (`block_info.h:17,19`).
- **FA3:** `Varlen` is a template parameter (`mainloop…:32,48`). The non-varlen kernel keeps its fast TMA output stores: `Use_TMA_O = … && !Varlen` (`epilogue_fwd.hpp:37`).
- **For us:** we'd add A as a switch in v62 and Vj1d. Pretraining would compile and run today's exact code.

**2. Does B need no modification?**
**Wrong. B also changes the kernel.** These lines change:
- v62's key loop start (`:396-398, :472`);
- the mask (`:479-498`);
- a NaN guard. It's needed, proven: today's code gives `m − nm = NaN` for a fully masked tile (`:509-512, :518`; checked: −∞ − (−∞) = NaN);
- Vj1d's loop end (`:464`) and its mask (`:259`).

B keeps old behaviour the same way A does: a compile-time switch.

**3. So what's really different?** How much changes inside the switch:

| Change in our kernels | A | B |
|---|---|---|
| Work split (v62 `decode_u :348-352`, Vj1d grid `:424`) | rewrite per chat | keep |
| Row addresses for loads (`:389, :397`) | per-chat offsets | keep |
| Output stores (O `:605-609`, dK/dV `:549-555`) | must stop at chat ends, or pad chats (+2.52% tokens) | keep |
| Loop start/end + mask + NaN guard | yes | yes |

**4. Which is faster? Proven parts:**

| | A | B |
|---|---|---|
| Attention work (counted tile by tile) | forward 651,014 / backward 1,251,206 | +3.4% / +1.5% (≈ **+0.1–0.15% of the whole step**) |
| Tiles needing the extra mask step (counted) | 15.2% | 29.9% |
| If A pads chats to 64 | **+2.52% tokens through the whole model** | — |

- **B vs A with padded chats: B wins.** About +0.15% vs +2.5% of the step.
- **B vs A with stop-at-chat-end stores** (the way FA3 does it): A could win by a few tenths of a percent, minus the cost of slower stores. **Only building it can prove that.**

## Step 1 (RoPE positions): done and proven

**What changed** (11 files in TI on the laptop, plus 1 new test):
- Our QK-norm + RoPE kernels, forward and backward, now take an **optional per-token position array `[B,T]`**, so each packed chat can restart at position 0.
- When no array is passed, nothing changes.
- I followed torchtitan's approach (`rope_cache[positions]`). Every change has a comment: what it was before, what it is now, and why.

**Proofs:**

| Check | Result |
|---|---|
| Pretraining path unchanged: machine code (SASS), old vs new | **13 of 13 kernels identical, instruction for instruction**, on the laptop (CUDA 13.0) and on the box's real build (CUDA 13.4, sm_90a) |
| Is that check able to see a difference? | yes: the positions-on versions differ (+16 to +40 instructions, plus the extra loads) |
| Correctness test, 37 cases | **37 of 37 pass** on the laptop RTX 3060, on H200 GPU 7 (Hopper kernel), and on H200 with the portable kernel forced |
| What the tests prove | with positions given, outputs match the old path bit for bit; packed chats match each chat run alone bit for bit (353 chats, one-token chats included); random positions match an fp64 reference; bad inputs are rejected |

**Two mistakes I made along the way, both in the test, not in the kernels:**
1. The `dgamma` limit was below the portable kernel's own atomicAdd noise. Proven by two identical runs differing by 4e-6.
2. The test guessed which kernel runs from the GPU type, which is wrong when the portable kernel is forced. It now asks the library.

Both are fixed, with the reason written in the test.

Step 2 research is done. Below is the test design. No files are written yet.

## 1. How the big libraries test varlen attention

| Library | Rule | Source |
|---|---|---|
| FlashAttention 3 | Our error ≤ **2×** the error of plain PyTorch bf16 math + 2× fp32 rounding. Applies to out, dQ, dK, dV | `hopper/test_flash_attn.py:535-536, 579, 655-660` |
| FlashAttention 2 | 2× for out, **3×** for dQ/dK/dV | `tests/test_flash_attn.py:1440, 1449-1451` |
| PyTorch varlen | Same 2× rule, but checked **per sequence** | `test/test_varlen_attention.py:508-516, 583-595` |
| TransformerEngine | Pad rows must come out **exactly 0** | `test_attention.py:327-336` |

- Nobody gates the attention LSE directly. The 1e-5 LSE check in FA3 (`:1216`) belongs to the split-combine test only.
- "Truth" in all of them is the same math in higher precision, run on the same bf16 inputs.

## 2. What we test

- **Today:** `gqa_flash_attn_forward_qkv` and `gqa_flash_attn_backward_qkv`. These are the exact production path: v62 forward and Vj1d backward on H200.
- **Steps 3–5:** B and A get added to the same harness, on the same cases.

## 3. Three references

1. **Truth:** fp64 math on the same bf16 inputs. It runs on the GPU, and is itself checked against a CPU fp64 version on small shapes.
2. **Noise floor:** plain PyTorch bf16 math, copied step by step from FA's `attention_ref(upcast=False)`. Every op output is rounded to bf16.
3. **Chat alone:** today's kernel on one chat by itself, padded after the chat, with dO = 0 on the padding. Because attention is causal, padding after the chat cannot change the chat's results.

## 4. Six checks

| # | Check | Pass rule |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Precision | Per chat, for O, dQ, dK, dV: error ≤ 2× noise-floor error + 2× fp32 rounding. I use 2× for gradients too, the stricter choice. LSE gets the same 2× rule; this one is our own addition |
| 2 | Matches chat alone | A: expect bit-exact for every chat (same tiles, same order). B: bit-exact only for chats that start on a tile edge (128 in forward, 64 in backward). Other B chats differ by rounding only, so they use rule 1. These are expectations; the run proves or disproves them |
| 3 | Isolation | Change one chat's Q/K/V/dO. All other chats' O, LSE, dK, dV must stay bit-identical. dQ uses atomic adds (`GQA_bwd_generic.cu:50-54`), so dQ is allowed only the measured run-to-run noise. The changed chat must change, so the check can't pass vacuously |
| 4 | Pads | Fill the outputs with NaN before every call. Production allocates them with `Tensor::empty` (`AttentionOps.cpp:403-404`, `AttentionBackward.cpp:233-235`), so unwritten rows would be garbage in training too. dQ/dK/dV at pad rows must be exactly 0 when dO at pads is 0, which is the real training case |
| 5 | Determinism | Two runs: O, LSE, dK, dV bit-identical; dQ within noise |
| 6 | No NaN/Inf | Anywhere in any output |

## 5. Data loads

| Case | What is in each row | Why |
|---|---|---|
| D0 | 1 chat = the whole row (T = 256 / 1024 / 4096) | Today's pretraining shape |
| D1 | 1 chat + pad tail | Today's v1 SFT |
| D2 | 2048 + 2048 | Equal split |
| D3 | 1000 + 3096 | Chat border inside a tile |
| D4 | 1 + 4095 and 4095 + 1 | One-token chats at both ends |
| D5 | 64 chats × 64, 32 chats × 128 | Many chats, on tile edges |
| D6 | 4096 chats of 1 token | Worst case: only the diagonal |
| D7 | Chat lengths 63, 65, 127, 129, 255, 257 | Just around tile sizes |
| D8 | Random lengths + pad tail of 0/1/16/63/64/65/255 | Pad handling |
| D9 | All-pad row | Empty-row safety |
| D10 | Real stage-0 packed rows: all 1,517, 1–12 chats each | Real data; the fp64 truth for all rows is about 1 minute on H200 |

- **Heads:** 18/6 (production, from `run.log`), 12/4 (trainer default), 8/8 (G=1), 32/8 (G=4). hd is 128 only, since that's all v62 and Vj1d support.
- **Batch sizes:** 1, 2, 8.

## 6. Timing

- Method: cudaEvent timing, 5 warm-up + 20 timed runs, median. Forward and backward timed separately, on free clocks (the production setting), GPU 7.
- Cases:
  - today's dense B=8 at T=4096, which is the v1 cost per micro-batch;

> tool `Bash`: Check how TRL packs SFT chats (bfd vs wrapped)

Yes, each 4096 row gets filled as full as possible, but **only with whole chats**. "As full as possible" means fewest pad tokens, not the most chats.

**Rules:**
1. **Whole chats only.** A chat never continues into the next row. A cut chat's second half would lose its prompt. All our chats already fit in 4096, because the prep dropped the 10 longer ones (`"too_long": 10` in `meta.json`).
2. **Method:** sort chats longest first, then put each one into a row that still has room. This is first-fit; best-fit gives the same 1,517 rows on our data. TRL does the same by default: `packing_strategy="bfd"`, described in its source as "Preserves sequence boundaries … Ideal for SFT" (`trl/data_utils.py:863-865`).
3. **Leftover space:** space at the end of a row that no remaining chat fits into becomes pad, with labels ignored as today.
4. **Shuffle:** after packing, shuffle the rows with a fixed seed, so training doesn't see rows in length order. TRL also shuffles after packing (`sft_trainer.py:1699-1700`).

**We don't fill the leftover with part of a chat.** That is TRL's `"wrapped"` / `"bfd_split"` style, which cuts chats; TRL says it "may break conversation structure in SFT datasets" (`data_utils.py:866-869`). It's the pretraining style. Keeping the ~16 pad tokens per row costs only 0.4%.

**Our stage-0 numbers:**

| | v1 (today) | v2 packed |
|---|---|---|
| Rows | 5,000 | 1,517 |
| Chats per row | 1 | 1–12 (avg 3.3) |
| Pad | 69.8% of positions | 16.3 tokens per row (0.4%) |
| Real tokens | 6,188,911 | 6,188,911 (no chat lost or cut) |

**How close to the best possible:** 6,188,911 tokens ÷ 4096 = 1,510.96, so at least 1,511 rows are needed. Packing gives 1,517 rows, only 6 above that minimum.

Both points checked against the real source code of TRL, HF transformers, Megatron-LM, torchtitan and PyTorch, and against our own run logs.

## Point 1: the label at the border between two chats

**Our way is safe by design, so no extra code is needed.** The big libraries do this in two different ways:

| Library | Order | How the border is handled | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| **torchtitan** | Shift inside each chat, then pack | No border label can exist | `text_datasets.py:221-224` |
| **Ours** | Same as torchtitan | Same | `prepare_sft_data.py:69-79` |
| HF transformers | Pack first; the shift happens later, inside the loss | Sets the first label of every chat to -100 | `data_collator.py:1451`, `loss_utils.py:63-64` |
| TRL | Pack first, shift later | Sets labels where `position_id == 0` to -100 | `sft_trainer.py:516` |
| Megatron-LM | Pack first, then `labels = pack_targets[1:]` | No explicit mask | `sft_dataset.py:188-189` |

- **Megatron's gap:** it is safe only because the next chat starts with a prompt token, and prompt labels are masked (`sft_tokenizer.py:205-206`). In its `"default"` prompt format nothing is masked (`:178-181`), so there it **does** train the last token of one chat to predict the next chat's first token.

**Example with our layout** (E = end token):
```
chat 1 ids = a b c E      chat 2 ids = x y z E
inputs     = a b c | x y z | pad ...
labels     = b c E | y z E | ign ...
```
- `c` predicts `E`, its own chat's end token. `x` is never a label for chat 1.
- HF needs 8 positions and a -100 for the same thing. We need 6.

**Proof when I write the prep:** every chat's slice of a packed row must match its v1 row bit for bit, inputs and labels. Total trained labels must stay 4,771,516. If anything differs, the script stops.

## Point 2: leftover rows

**Today our loader throws the leftover rows away. It is always the same rows, because it never changes the order between epochs** (`SftDataLoader.h:56, 109`). None of these libraries do that:

| Library | Leftover rows | New order every epoch? | Source |
|---|---|---|---|
| PyTorch `DistributedSampler` (default) | Kept: repeats the first rows to fill | Yes, seed + epoch | `distributed.py:111, 116-120` |
| HF Trainer / TRL (Accelerate) | Kept: the short last batch stays; multi-GPU repeats the first rows | Yes, `set_epoch` | `training_args.py:1302-1304`; Accelerate `even_batches=True`; `trainer.py:1837-1844` |
| Megatron default | Nothing dropped: the data cycles, batches run into the next pass | Not checked | `sft_dataset.py:121` |
| Megatron "cyclic" | Leftover dropped | Yes, so different rows are dropped each epoch | `data_samplers.py:362, 395` |
| torchtitan | Nothing dropped: endless stream | Yes | `loader.py:148-152` |
| **Ours** | **Dropped, same rows every epoch** | **No** | `SftDataLoader.h:56, 109` |

**What it costs us after packing** (simulated on the real stage-0 lengths):

| GPUs | Rows per round (B×W) | Rows dropped per epoch | Chats never trained (rows shuffled) | Chats never trained (rows not shuffled) |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 8 | 5 | ~16 (12–22) | 47 |
| 2 | 16 | 13 | ~43 (36–52) | 119 |
| 4 | 32 | 13 | ~43 | 119 |

- Without a shuffle it is worse, because first-fit puts the many short chats into the last rows (10–12 chats each). So the short chats would be the ones lost.

**This already happens in v1** (from the 10-07 run logs):
- With 2 and 4 GPUs, the same 8 train rows are dropped every epoch.
- Val with 1 or 2 GPUs scores 496 of 500 rows; with 4 GPUs it scores 480. So the 4-GPU val loss was measured on 16 fewer chats than the 1-GPU one, and the two are not exactly comparable.

**Options:**

| Option | Used by | Effect |
|---|---|---|
| Keep dropping (today) | Nobody | The same chats are never trained |
| Repeat the first rows to fill | PyTorch, Accelerate | A few rows trained twice per epoch |
| **Endless stream: the batch continues into the next epoch** | Megatron, torchtitan | Nothing dropped, nothing doubled, works for any B and W |
| Make the prep write a multiple of 8 rows | Nobody | Breaks as soon as the GPU count changes (16, 32, 64) |

**My recommendation:**
- **Train:** endless stream plus a new order each epoch (seed + epoch, like PyTorch). This is about 10 lines in `first_row()` in `SftDataLoader.h`. Resume stays exact, because the order is computed from the micro-batch counter and the seed.
- **Val:** score all rows, and fill the last batch with all-pad rows. Those rows have zero trained tokens, so they add nothing to the loss or the count. Then val always covers all 500 chats, for any GPU count.
- **Note:** this changes v1 too. For a fair v1-vs-v2 comparison, both should use the same loader rule.

**No.** A and B are not tied to FlashAttention v3 or to GQA. They are the two ways to tell **any** attention kernel where each chat starts and ends. GQA vs MHA is a different, independent question.

## Why they are independent

```
attention work = [batch] x [heads] x [query tokens] x [key tokens]

MHA / GQA / MQA -> the [heads] axis : which K/V head each query head reads
A / B           -> the [tokens] axis: which key tokens each query token may see
```
- MHA: every query head has its own K/V head.
- GQA: several query heads share one K/V head. For us that is 18/6, so 3 share.
- MQA: all query heads share one K/V head.
- Chat borders lie along the token axis, so they don't depend on how heads are grouped.

## Proof from the sources

| Library | A (offsets / cu_seqlens) | B (mask) | Head types |
|---|---|---|---|
| FlashAttention 2 | varlen | — | Its varlen test runs MHA, MQA and GQA (`tests/test_flash_attn.py:1139, 1187`) |
| FlashAttention 3 | varlen | — | Same (`hopper/test_flash_attn.py:355, 417`) |
| HF transformers | On FlashAttention backends: cu_seqlens built from positions (`modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:480`) | On SDPA / eager / Flex backends: a "same chat" mask (`masking_utils.py:183-191, 734`) | Same model code for every model, MHA or GQA |
| torchtitan | `VarlenInnerAttention` (`common/attention.py:132`) | `FlexInnerAttention` (`:228`) | Both just take an `enable_gqa` flag (`:197-199, :293`) |

- The transformers row is the clearest proof. The **same model** gets A or B depending on **which kernel runs it**, not on its head type.

## How A and B look for each type of attention

| Attention type | A | B |
|---|---|---|
| Tiled softmax kernels: FlashAttention 2/3, **our v62/Vj1d** | Per-chat offsets; never touches other chats | Block mask; skips fully masked tiles |
| Plain "math/eager" attention (full T×T scores in memory) | Run each chat separately | Full T×T mask; no work is skipped |
| Linear attention / state models, e.g. KDA in torchtitan | **Only A works**: the running state must be reset at each chat start | **Impossible**: there is no T×T score matrix to mask. torchtitan's KDA rejects anything but cu_seqlens (`kimi_k3/kda.py:254-260`) |

## What this means for us

- v62 and Vj1d are FlashAttention-style tiled kernels with GQA built in, using `G = Hq / Hkv`. MHA is just `G = 1` and MQA is `Hkv = 1`, in the same kernel. So A or B, once built, covers MHA, GQA and MQA together, with no separate work.
- I won't assume that part. The planned Step 2 harness tests 8/8 (MHA, G=1) and 32/8 (G=4) next to our 18/6 to prove it.
- If we ever add a linear-attention or state model, only A applies there.

## 1. Step 2 harness: what the sources add

Already in the design: the per-chat 2× precision rule, the chat-alone check, isolation, NaN-filled outputs, and the data loads D0–D10.

New from the research:

| # | New test | Source | Why it matters for us |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Repeat test**: 1000 runs, O/LSE/dK/dV bitwise equal; dQ within `2×((dq+0.3−0.3)−dq).max()` | FA2 `:2199-2240` (250 runs, batch 60), FA3 `:1133-1165` (1000 runs) | Catches race conditions. New scheduling code in v62 (B work order, A chat list) is exactly where races appear. Our old plan had only 2 runs |
| 2 | **Large inputs**: q×5, k×3, v×3 with chats of 1, 2, 5, 17, 128 tokens | FA2 `:2247-2295`. Their real bug was NaN in dQ from unmasked rows past the sequence end | Hits the v62 rescale with no −inf guard, and the tile-edge masks |
| 3 | **No-NaN test with tiny chats** (1, 2, 3 tokens next to long ones) | FA2 `:2355-2380` | The same NaN family, at chat borders |
| 4 | **Same chat at different offsets** in the row: 0, 1, 63, 64, 65, 127, 128, near the end | PyTorch `test_batch_invariance` `:1507-1630` | Results must not depend on where a chat sits. A: bitwise. B: bitwise on tile edges, otherwise the 2× rule |
| 5 | **Zero-length entries** in the chat list, e.g. `[0,3,5,9,9,9]` | torchtitan fixed-shape metadata (`test_varlen_attention.py:40-62`), FA3 `zero_lengths`, TE `:218-236` | If our chat list has a fixed size, empty entries must be skipped safely |
| 6 | **Pad segment** at the row end, and pads between chats | torchtitan `:64-78` (pads get their own segment), TE `pad_between_seqs` | Our prep only puts pads at the end. Pads between chats must either work or be rejected, never silently wrong |
| 7 | **Rows that see no keys** (A's pad rows): exact output 0, dQ/dK/dV 0, a fixed LSE value | Flex `:5440-5475` (out 0, LSE −inf). FA2 uses LSE +inf (`softmax.h:180`), FA3 −inf (`hopper/softmax.h:151`) | Libraries disagree, so we must pick one value and test it exactly |
| 8 | **Bad-input rejection**: chat list not increasing, sum > T, chat crossing a row, wrong dtype or device, hd ≠ 128, T not a multiple of 256 | PyTorch varlen rejection tests (`:904`, `:1084`, `:1218`, `:1233`), TE capacity test | The API must throw, not compute garbage. Same style as Step 1's T5 |
| 9 | **Head types**: MHA 8/8, GQA 18/6, 12/4, 32/8, **MQA 8/1** | FA2 `:1139`, FA3 `:355` run mha/mqa/gqa | Adds MQA, which was missing |
| 10 | **Paths without varlen support must refuse it**: Vj1 (`USE_FLASH=1`), v44 (`USE_DETERMINISTIC_DQ=1`), the generic path, B300 | Our dispatcher, `GQA_bwd_generic.cu:91-131` | Found today. If chat info reaches a kernel without the mask, it would silently compute plain causal attention across chats |
| 11 | **Tile-count check** (debug build): tiles the kernel processed = tiles the host model predicts | Our addition; no library does this | Numbers can't show extra work, because masked tiles add zeros. Only a count proves B skips exactly the right tiles |
| 12 | **FLOP formula as FA counts it**: causal = 2·Lq·(Lk/2)·(hd+hd_v) per head, summed per chat; backward = 2.5× forward | FA3 `benchmark_attn.py:62-73, 386-387` | Our TFLOPS become directly comparable with published FA numbers |

These belong to Step 7, not Step 2:
- **Whole-model check:** padded vs packed logits must match within bf16 eps (transformers `generation/test_utils.py:2269-2397`).
- **Data checks**, like torchtitan's `test_chat_dataset.py`: labels shifted by one, positions reset, whole chats kept, same data after resume.

## 2. Step 7 plan (prep, loader, trainer)

1. **Prep:** pack whole chats first-fit; write inputs, labels, positions, chat lengths, `valid_counts` and meta to a new folder.
   - **Proof:** every chat's slice must match its v1 row bit for bit, and the total must stay 4,771,516 trained labels.
2. **Loader:** read the new files, check them on the host, and apply the leftover-row rule we pick below.
3. **Trainer:** pass positions to `fused_rms_rope` and the chat list to attention. Packing on `FUSED_RMS_ROPE=0` gets refused, or that path gets positions too.
4. **Tests:** the data checks, the whole-model check, and the strongest one: **val loss on v1 rows vs packed rows with the same weights must match** within noise.
5. **Real run:** packed SFT vs v1, same epochs, comparing loss curves, tokens/s and wall-clock time.

## 3. Leftover rows: how each library does it

| | Last short batch | Several GPUs, uneven split | New order each epoch | Optimizer step crosses an epoch? | Eval |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| **PyTorch** | Kept (`drop_last=False`) | Repeats the first rows (`distributed.py:116-120`) | Yes, seed+epoch (`:111`); `RandomSampler` new seed each epoch (`sampler.py:160-165`) | — | — |
| **HF Trainer / TRL** | Kept (`dataloader_drop_last=False`, `training_args.py:1302`) | Accelerate loops back to the start (`data_loader.py:110-136`) | Yes, random sampler by default | **No**: the last step of an epoch uses fewer micro-batches, scaled by token count (`trainer.py:1847-1862`) | Duplicates removed (`gather_for_metrics`, `accelerator.py:3108-3110`) |
| **Megatron SFT** (default) | Never: data cycles, run is driven by step count (`sft_dataset.py:78-79, 121`) | — | **No**: file order (`numpy.arange`, `blended_megatron_dataset_builder.py:485`) | Yes | — |
| **Megatron "cyclic"** | Dropped each epoch (`data_samplers.py:362, 378`) | — | Yes, seed = epoch (`:395`), so different rows are dropped each time | — | — |
| **torchtitan** | Never: endless stream (`loader.py:148-152`) | Refuses to run without repeat, so no rank runs out early (`:98-109`) | Yes, seed+epoch (`dataset.py:150-170`) | Yes | — |
| **Ours** | **Dropped** (`SftDataLoader.h:56`) | Dropped | **No: same order, so the same rows are dropped every epoch** (`:109`) | Yes (`bluscript_zero_ckpt.cpp:960`) | 4 val rows (1 GPU) or 20 (4 GPUs) never scored |

**What this shows:**
- **Nobody permanently skips the same rows.** Each library either keeps them (PyTorch, HF, Megatron default, torchtitan) or drops a different random set each epoch (Megatron "cyclic").
- **Our trainer is driven by step count, like Megatron and torchtitan.** `max_steps` comes from the epoch count, and steps already cross epochs (`:960`). So torchtitan's model fits us with the least change. HF's model, where epochs are separate and the last step is smaller, would need changes in the trainer and the LR schedule.
- **For eval, everyone scores each sample exactly once.**

**My conclusion:**
- **Train:** endless stream plus a new order each epoch (seed+epoch), as torchtitan does. That means:
  - nothing is dropped and nothing is doubled within an epoch, for any GPU count;
  - resume stays exact, because the order is computed from the counter and the seed;
  - the change is inside `first_row()`.
  - Add a switch to keep the old fixed order, so the 10-07 runs can be reproduced.
- **Val:** score all rows exactly once; the last batch is filled with all-pad rows, which have zero trained tokens.

2. Do you agree with the leftover-row conclusion?

Your colleague is right that cuDNN is the main bar on H200. The source code proves it, though cuDNN is not the "parent" of FlashAttention.

## Is cuDNN the "parent" everyone uses?

- **Not the parent.** cuDNN is NVIDIA's own closed-source library. FlashAttention is a separate open-source project; FA3 was written with NVIDIA engineers, but it is not cuDNN.
- **But it is the default on Hopper in NVIDIA's stack.** TransformerEngine runs its "FusedAttention" on cuDNN (`fused_attn_f16_arbitrary_seqlen.cu` uses `cudnn_frontend`). When both cuDNN and FlashAttention can run, TE turns FlashAttention off on Hopper: "Disabling FlashAttention to give FusedAttention preference on Hopper+ for performance reasons" (`dot_product_attention/utils.py:1922-1928`). Megatron-LM builds its layers on TE (`gpt_layer_specs.py:48-51`). So Megatron and NeMo users on H100/H200 run cuDNN attention.
- **In the PyTorch / HF world**, FA2/FA3 and PyTorch's own backends are the common choice. So cuDNN is the primary bar, and FA3 is second.

| | **Varlen.** cuDNN supports packed sequences with GQA, through TE's THD format and PyTorch's `varlen_attn` cuDNN backend. So cuDNN is the bar for design A too |

### CLAUDE [2026-10-10 16:17 IST]

Right, they are separate. The G-series tests only our kernels; the B-series compares us with the other libraries. They will share the same input files, so both see the exact same data.

| | **G-series** (`test_varlen_attention.cu`) | **B-series** (benchmark track) |
|---|---|---|
| Tests | Only **our** kernels (v62/Vj1d now, A/B later) | **All libraries**: ours, cuDNN, FA3, FA4, FA2, Flex, SDPA |
| Purpose | Correctness gate: must pass before any kernel change is accepted | Measurement: who is faster, more accurate, lighter on memory |
| Language | C++/CUDA, links only our `libtensor` | Python (those libraries live in PyTorch), plus nsys / ncu / power / memory scripts |
| Runs where | Anywhere via `make run-cuda` | Only on the box, in a Python env with torch, FA3 and FA4 |
| Timing | G7 times our kernels only | Same method for every library |

**Why I keep them apart:**
- **No new dependency in TI.** Calling cuDNN, FA3 or Flex from the G harness would mean linking PyTorch into our tests, and TI doesn't depend on torch today.
- **Different jobs.** G must give a clean pass/fail for our kernels every time we change them. B is a measuring campaign that needs installs, builds, and nsys/ncu wrapped around each library separately.

**How they connect (planned, not built yet):**
- **Shared input files.** I'll add an export mode to the G harness: one environment variable makes it write the exact Q/K/V/dO bytes, the chat lists and the fp64 truth for chosen cases.
- **Same correctness rule.** The B-series script loads those files, runs every library on them, and checks each result against the same truth with the same 2× rule. So every library is judged on identical bytes.
- **Same timing method.** CUDA events, same warm-up and repeats, and FA's FLOP formula on both sides.

The quick run is done. **138 of 142 checks pass.** The 4 failures all come from one gap in our pass rule, not from a kernel bug. Here's the evidence.

## Quick-run results (H200 GPU 7, log on laptop, md5 verified)

| Group | Result |
|---|---|
| G1 reference self-test (on H200 too) | ✅ 20/20. fp64 truth agrees to 1.9e-16; bf16 floor is bitwise identical |
| G2 dense rows | ✅ all pass, and no unwritten or non-finite output anywhere |
| G3 v1 SFT rows | ✅ the chat rows of today's v1 computation **are** per-chat attention |
| G4 repeat | ✅ O, LSE, dK, dV bitwise identical across 50 runs (8×4096) and 20 runs (60×1024). dQ varies by at most 9.8e-4 against an allowed 1.6e-2, as documented for its atomics |
| G5 large inputs | ✅ worst ratio 0.13 even under the strict 2× rule |
| G6 chat alone | ✅ every chat of D2, D3, D5, D7, D8 and 31 real chats passes. **The 4 failures are here**, all 1-token chats |
| G6c filler check | ✅ chat alone at T=4096 vs at the short length: 0 differing bits for O, LSE, dK, dV |
| D10 data | ✅ 5000 chats / 6,188,911 tokens / 1517 rows, exactly as `pack_sim.py` |

## The 4 failures: 1-token chats (D4, D6), dQ and dK only

- **Exact answer:** a 1-token chat only sees itself, so P = 1 and dS = P·(dP − D) = 0. dQ and dK are **exactly 0**. Both references give exactly 0.
- **Kernel answer:** 4.5e-7 to 1.3e-6. It works out dS from two sums of the **same** 128 products, computed in two different kernels and so added in different orders:
  - D comes from the separate `compute_drowsum_v22` kernel (`GQA_bwd_vj1d_sm90.cu:283-306`);
  - dP comes from the wgmma;
  - dS = P·(dP − D) (`:333-334`), with P re-made from LSE through `ex2.approx` (`:246-256`).
  
  Different summation orders round differently in fp32, so dP − D is a rounding leftover instead of 0.
- **Proof it's only rounding:** O for these chats has **error 0**, so the kernel reads the exact value. A leftover of ~1 fp32 rounding step of dP (values up to ~30) gives dS ≈ 2e-6, and dQ = scale·k·dS ≈ 0.088 × 2 × 2e-6 ≈ 4e-7. That matches the observed 4.5e-7 to 1.3e-6.
- **Why the rule fails it:** our allowance is 2 × (floor error) + 2 × (rounding of the truth). When the truth is exactly 0, both terms are 0, so any nonzero value fails. FA's rule has the same blind spot.

## Fix I propose (only where the exact answer is 0)

- **Where:** only 1-token chats, only dQ and dK, and only after confirming the truth there really is exactly 0. Everything else keeps the 2× rule unchanged.
- **Bound:** a worst-case fp32 rounding bound for dot products (any summation order). I use u = 2⁻²³, which also covers truncating tensor-core sums:
  - dQ allowance = scale·|k|·2γ₁₂₈·Σ|dO·v|, plus bf16 rounding;
  - dK allowance = the same, summed over the 3 query heads of the group;
  - γ₁₂₈ = 128·u/(1 − 128·u) ≈ 1.5e-5.
- **Size:** this comes to ~7e-4 to 9e-4, about **700× above** the observed values.
- **Still catches real bugs:** a real masking bug, a 1-token chat seeing its neighbour, gives dQ ~0.1, still **100× above** the allowance.

## Also worth watching

- **dV near the edge:** at 18/6, T=4096, dV's worst ratio is **0.946**. That passes, but the kernel's error is 1.9× the floor's. The full run may push it over. If it does, I'll analyse it rather than loosen the rule. FA2 itself allows 3× for gradients; FA3 and PyTorch allow 2×.
- **Speed (G7, first measurement of our SFT shape):**

  | Shape | Forward | Backward |
  |---|---|---|
  | 18/6 | 1.14 ms (543 TF/s) | 4.26 ms (363 TF/s) |
  | 12/4 | 0.729 ms (566 TF/s) | 2.732 ms (377 TF/s) |

  The 12/4 run is 1.0–1.5% faster than your colleague's 0.7403 / 2.760 ms. That's a different session, same direction.

### USER [2026-10-10 16:46 IST]

g6 is training run oer whar ?

### CLAUDE [2026-10-10 16:46 IST]

No, G6 is not a training run. Nothing trains: there is no model, no weights, no loss and no optimizer. **It only tests the attention kernel by itself.**

What G6 does, step by step:

1. **Build the rows.** It takes a packed layout: synthetic ones (D2–D9), or the real stage-0 packing (D10). From the real data it uses **only the chat lengths**, the 5,000 numbers, so the rows look like our real SFT batches. The token text isn't used.
2. **Fill in random inputs.** Q, K, V and dO get fixed-seed random bf16 values.
3. **Compute the correct answers.** The reference gives each chat's correct O, LSE, dQ, dK and dV: the fp64 truth plus the bf16 noise floor.
4. **Run each chat alone.** Each chat is copied into its own row, at position 0, with random filler after it. Today's v62 forward and Vj1d backward run on it **once**.
5. **Compare.** The kernel's outputs for that chat must match the correct answers under the 2× rule (1-token chats use the derived bound).
6. **G6c.** The same chat is run alone again at T=4096 and must be bitwise identical, which proves the filler can't change the result.

**Why it matters:** this proves our per-chat reference matches today's kernel for **every chat length in our real data**. In Steps 3–5, design B and design A will be checked against this same reference. If they ever disagree, the bug is in the new kernel code, not in the reference.

The only "real data" in G6 is the length list; the actual training run comes in Step 7.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-10 16:47 IST]

No. **A and B are not implemented yet**; they are Steps 3–5. The only change in our library so far is Step 1, RoPE per-token positions. What runs now is **Step 2: building and proving the test bench before any kernel changes.**

**What we're testing today:**
1. **The test harness itself.** G1 checks the reference math, GPU against CPU, plus the deliberately broken version that must fail.
2. **Today's existing kernels, v62 and Vj1d.** They do plain causal attention, so we only give them cases where plain causal **already is** the correct answer:
   - one chat per row (G2, G3);
   - each chat run **alone** in its own row (G6).

**Why test before implementing:**
- When we write B and A, we need a checker we already trust. If the checker could be wrong, a failure would leave us unsure whether the new kernel or the checker is at fault.
- So we prove the checker on kernels that are known to be correct: they're in production and were already benchmarked against cuDNN.
- G6 also produces exactly the answer packed attention must give: each chat computed as if alone.
- After this, in Steps 3–5:
  - packed rows go through the **new** B (then A) kernels;
  - the result is compared with the **same** proven reference;
  - any failure then means a bug in the new kernel code, nothing else.

**What waits for A/B:** the "PENDING" list in the harness summary:
- packed rows through B and A;
- isolation between chats;
- the same chat at different offsets;
- zero-length entries and pad segments;
- empty rows;
- bad-input rejection;
- tile counts.

These run the moment B and A exist.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-10 16:49 IST]

It's the optimized FlashAttention way, not naive. **Tiles entirely above the diagonal are never loaded or computed.** Only the one tile per row block that straddles the diagonal is computed in full and then has its "future" entries set to −∞.

**Forward (v62, `GQA_fwd_sm90.cu`):**
- **Skips future tiles.** The loader fetches only the key tiles a query tile can see (`nkv = pair+1`, `:396-398`). Each consumer stops at the tile holding its own last row (`my_nkv = (q_tile·64 + 63)/128 + 1`, `:436`). Everything to the right is never touched.
- **Masks only the diagonal tile.** `diag = (n·128 + 127 >= q_tile·64)` (`:479`). Only that tile runs `if (gcol > grow) v = -INFINITY` (`:497-498`). Fully visible tiles take the no-mask path (`:481-490`).
- **Never stores the T×T matrix.** It's an online softmax per tile with rescaling (`:510-532`).

```
one 64-row query tile, keys in tiles of 128 (T = 4096):

keys →   [tile 0][tile 1] ... [diag tile][  skipped  ...  skipped  ]
          full    full          masked     never loaded / computed
                               (−∞ only here)
```

**How much is wasted, for T=4096 per head:**
- **Computed:** 1056 tiles of 64×128 = 8.65M scores.
- **Needed (causal):** 4096×4097/2 = 8.39M.
- **Waste:** about **3%**, all from the masked part of the diagonal tiles.
- **For comparison:** naive attention would compute all 16.8M and mask half, about 2× the work.

**Backward (Vj1d):** same idea. Each key tile only loops over query tiles at or after itself (`nIter = nQ − kt`, `GQA_bwd_vj1d_sm90.cu:464`), and only the diagonal tile is masked.

**Why "plain causal" still matters for packing:** "plain causal" describes **what** is masked: the whole row is one sequence, and v62 doesn't know where chats start. On a packed row it would let chat 2 see chat 1. Design B adds exactly that knowledge, with the same tile skipping: skip tiles that are fully outside a token's own chat, and mask only the tiles at chat borders.

One thing not to confuse: the **reference** inside the test harness *is* the naive way. It computes the full matrix per chat in fp64 and masks. That's deliberate: it's a slow, simple checker, not a production kernel.

- **G6 real data (D10): all 5,000 chats pass for O, LSE, dK and dV.** The data matches `pack_sim.py`.
- **No unwritten or non-finite output anywhere.**
- **dV is the closest to the limit:** worst ratio 0.956. It passes.

## The one failure

- **Which chat:** dQ for **row 1022, chat at offset 2552, length 1276**. Its ratio is **1.156**: kernel error 2.87e-2 against a floor of 1.24e-2, so 2.3× where the rule allows 2×.
- **It's an outlier.** The next-worst dQ in the whole run is 0.812.
- **What it is not:**
  - Not a masking problem: a leak would be 10–100× the floor, and every other tensor of this chat passes.
  - Not a NaN.
  - Not a short or edge-length chat.

**Suspected cause (not proven yet):**
- Vj1d computes D = rowsum(dO ∘ O) from the **bf16-rounded** O (`GQA_bwd_vj1d_sm90.cu:283-306`). FlashAttention computes D the same way.
- The PyTorch-style floor uses a self-consistent row sum instead.
- The rounding error of D hits every key of a row in the same direction, so it adds a row-wide error of exactly −scale·ΔD·(attention-weighted average of K) to dQ.
- If that is the cause, the extra error is a property of the FlashAttention algorithm itself, not a bug in our kernel.

**Diagnostic, built into the harness:**
- It runs only that chat's batch, with the same seeds as the full run.
- **Repeat test:** 50 re-runs, to see whether it fails every time or only sometimes. dQ uses atomics, so each run can differ slightly.
- **Worst element:** location, kernel / truth / floor values, and the error in bf16 ulps.
- **Mechanism test:** at the worst row, the measured error vector against the predicted −scale·ΔD·v vector (cosine, fitted ΔD vs predicted ΔD, and what's left after removing it).
- **Percentiles:** I also added p50/p90/p99/max of the ratio to every check, so we see how close typical chats are to the limit.

**What each outcome means:**
- **Cosine ≈ 1 and fitted ΔD ≈ predicted:** the extra error is this known algorithm term. Then we decide the rule with evidence: either add this term to the floor, or use FA2's 3× for gradients. **I have not changed the rule.**
- **Neither:** a real Vj1d issue to dig into before any Step 3 work.

**Needs your OK for two runs on GPU 7:**
1. The diagnostic on that one batch, ~2 min.
2. D10 only, all 5,000 chats, for the percentiles, ~8 min.

Running now: the D10 pass over all 5,000 chats, about 8 min. Its log comes back to the laptop automatically.

## The failure is a real precision weakness in today's Vj1d, not a test problem

- **What Vj1d does:** it computes dS = P·(dP − D) using P **rounded to bf16**. It re-reads P from shared memory, where P sits as bf16 for the dV product (`fuse_dS_ldstsm`, `GQA_bwd_vj1d_sm90.cu:311-341`).
- **Why that's wrong:** bf16 P no longer sums to 1; on this row it sums to **1.00195** (1 + 2⁻⁹). D comes from O, which matches the exact P. So the dS values of a row no longer cancel, and the leftover × K lands straight in dQ.
- **Where it shows:** worst on rows with **few keys**, meaning the first tokens of a chat, combined with a large dP − D. That's why it hit one chat's 2nd token and nothing in the dense tests.
- **FA3 avoids this:** it computes dS from the **fp32** P (`mainloop_bwd_sm90_tma_gmma_ws.hpp:893`) and rounds P only for the dV product (`:897-898`). With that arithmetic, the same row lands at 1.09× the floor, a clean pass.
- **The proof:** modelling Vj1d's arithmetic reproduces the kernel's dQ on that row **exactly**.

**What this means:**
- **The rule stays at 2×.** It caught a genuine gap vs FA3, so loosening it would hide a real issue.
- **It's pre-existing.** It's in today's shipped kernel and has nothing to do with our changes.
- **Size:** at most ~2 bf16 ulps on a few dQ elements at chat starts. Packing adds more chat starts (3.3 per row), so slightly more such rows. The training effect is likely negligible, but it is a measurable precision gap vs FA3.

**Fix:** compute dS from fp32 P, the way FA3 does. Three ways, each with a possible speed cost, so it must be measured:
1. Keep P in fp32 registers until dS is done.
2. Recompute P in fp32 inside the dS step.
3. Keep an fp32 copy of P in shared memory.

My suggestion: make this fix in Vj1d **before** Step 4 (B's backward), as its own measured change. That keeps B's backward starting from a kernel that matches FA3's precision. OK?

### CLAUDE [2026-10-10 17:12 IST]

No, it's not wrong. It's **correct, but slightly less precise than FA3 in one rare spot.** Those are different things:

| | A real bug (not the case) | What we found |
|---|---|---|
| What it would look like | Wrong gradients by large amounts: a masking leak, a missing term, NaN | dQ off by **~2 bf16 steps** at a few elements; worst one 3.703 vs exact 3.674 (0.8%) |
| How often | Everywhere, or in a pattern | **1 chat out of 5,000**: one element on a chat's 2nd token |
| Our checks | Masking, isolation and finite-output checks would fail | All of those pass; dK, dV, O and LSE pass for all 5,000 chats |

- **What it is:** a rounding choice. Vj1d reuses the bf16 copy of P, already sitting in shared memory, when it computes dS. That's probably a deliberate speed/register saving. It costs a little precision, which shows up only on rows with very few keys and a large dP − D.
- **FA3's choice:** it uses the fp32 P there and stays within our strict 2× rule on that same row.
- **Why nobody saw it before:** dense tests never hit it (worst dQ ratio 0.53), and the cuDNN comparisons measured speed, not this precision corner.

So the gradients are correct, just a little less precise than FA3 at chat-start rows. Fixing it would bring Vj1d up to FA3-level precision. Whether that's worth any speed cost is the decision we make after this run.

I checked each library's backward source code. They are **not** all the same:

| Library | P used in dS | Source |
|---|---|---|
| **FlashAttention 2** (and PyTorch's flash backend, which compiles FA2's code via `#include <flash.h>`, `flash_api.cpp:41`) | **fp32** ✅ | `flash_bwd_kernel.h:591`; the bf16 copy is only for dV (`:547-555`) |
| **FlashAttention 3** | **fp32** ✅ | `mainloop_bwd_sm90_tma_gmma_ws.hpp:893`; bf16 only afterwards (`:897-898`) |
| **FlashAttention 4** (Hopper) | **fp32** ✅ | `flash_bwd_sm90.py:1569`; separate bf16 copy for dV (`:1555`) |
| **PyTorch Flex** | **fp32** ✅ | `flex_backwards.py.jinja:528, 541` and `:757, 775` |
| **PyTorch memory-efficient** (xformers / cutlass) | **bf16, same as our Vj1d** | P is stored in shared memory as `scalar_t` (`kernel_backward.h:341-351`) and read back for dS: `(accum - di) * attn` (`:1959-1960`) |
| PyTorch math (plain eager) | bf16 P, but the row term is computed from that same bf16 P | That's our noise floor. Being self-consistent, it never shows this problem |
| **cuDNN** | **unknown, closed source** | Can only be measured |
| **Ours (Vj1d)** | **bf16** | `GQA_bwd_vj1d_sm90.cu:311-341` |

**What this tells us:**
- **All four FlashAttention-family kernels avoid the issue.** FA2, FA3, FA4 and Flex keep P in fp32 for dS.
- **A mainstream kernel makes our same trade-off.** PyTorch's memory-efficient backend also uses bf16 P, so this is a known speed/precision choice, not something unusual.
- **cuDNN, the main bar, can't be read.** In the B-series I'll export the exact failing chat (row 1022) and run every library on the same bytes, cuDNN included. Then we'll see directly whether cuDNN shows the same dQ error or matches FA3.

## Step 3 plan: design B forward, as a compile-time variant of v62

The reference is FlexAttention, which I just checked in its source:
- It keeps **full** blocks (no mask) and **partial** blocks (masked) in separate lists. Other blocks are never loaded (`flex_attention.py.jinja:141-189`).
- It guards rows that haven't seen any key yet: `masked_out_rows = (m_ij == -inf)` → use 0 as the max (`common.py.jinja:115-123`).

**Changes:**
1. **Chat info.** A per-token `seg_start[B·T]` (int32): where each token's chat starts within its row. The pad tail counts as its own segment. That's one load per row, with no searching. It's the same idea as Flex's per-token document id, and costs 128 KB per batch.
2. **Where the key loop starts.** Today it starts at tile 0 (`:398`, `:472`). Now it starts at the tile holding the pair's first chat start, so earlier tiles are never loaded.
3. **The mask.** Today only the diagonal tile is masked (`:479-499`). The rule now is: a key is visible only if `seg_start(i) ≤ j ≤ i`. It applies only on tiles that contain a chat border or the diagonal; full tiles skip it, like Flex.
4. **The NaN guard,** done the way Flex does it. Today's `cc0 = ex2(m0 − nm0)` (`:510-512`) gives NaN when a row's first tile is fully masked.
5. **Keep it simple first.** Both consumers of a pair walk the pair's whole tile range. Fully masked tiles add exact zeros thanks to the guard. Per-consumer skipping (~2.8% fewer tiles) and LPT ordering (est. 86% → 98% balance) come later, as measured follow-ups.
6. **API.** `gqa_flash_attn_forward_qkv` gets an optional `seg_start`. Passing none means today's path, unchanged. Paths without support (Vj1, v44, generic, B300) must refuse it.

**Proofs (quick runs, ≤ 2 min each):**
- **SASS:** the dense instantiation must be **identical** to today's v62, as in Step 1.
- **G-series on packed rows, forward only:** O and LSE per chat against the same reference. The backward comes in Step 4.
- **Isolation:** change one chat, and every other chat stays bitwise identical.
- **Edge cases:** offsets, zero-length entries, pad segments.
- **Quick timing:** B forward vs dense v62 on packed rows.

**Order:** API and plumbing → kernel variant → tests → SASS proof → timing.

OK to start with this plan?

I reviewed every changed line. Checklist:

| Concern | Why it's safe |
|---|---|
| **Deadlock** (the 2 consumers and the producer must run the same number of tiles) | All three compute `n0` from the **same** element, `seg_start[pair's first row]`. Producer `nkv`, consumer `my_nkv` and `nkv_shared` all equal `pair + 1 − n0` |
| **No needed key skipped** | `n0` = tile of the pair's first row's chat start, which is the smallest chat start of all its rows (`seg_start` never decreases within a row) |
| **Unmasked tiles are truly fully visible** | A tile is unmasked only if it's not diagonal (all keys before the q-tile, so causal holds) **and** its first key is ≥ `smax`, the largest chat start in the q-tile. Then every key lies in `[chat start, row]`, which is exactly the row's own chat |
| **Masked element rule** | Masked if `key > row` or `key < row's chat start`, so a key is visible only if `chat start ≤ key ≤ row` |
| **NaN guard** | While a row has seen nothing, its max is −∞. Then `um = 0`, so `cc = ex2(−∞) = 0` and `p = 0`, and l and O stay exactly 0. Once a key is visible, the arithmetic is the same as the dense kernel |
| **Every row ends with l > 0** | Each row always sees itself, and its own key's tile is always in `[n0, pair]` |
| **Dense path unchanged** | SASS identical: 2304 / 2304 instructions |
| **API safety** | `seg_start` on any non-v62 path throws, so it is never silently ignored |

The fix trial is clean. Here is the race, in plain terms.

**What the race is (today's default backward, Vj1d; Vj1 has the same code):**
- Each CTA owns one key tile and loops over query tiles.
- For each query tile, threads 0–63 copy that tile's 64 LSE values from global memory into shared memory (`sLSE`). Then all 128 threads (4 warps) read `sLSE` to compute P = exp(S − LSE).
- **Query tiles 2, 3, …:** a `__syncthreads()` sits between that write and the read, so it's correct.
- **The first query tile has no barrier.** Between the write (`issue(0)`) and the first read, the only wait is the TMA wait for Q/dO. Only thread 0 arrives on that barrier, so it does not make the other 63 threads' writes visible to the other warps.
- **Proof in the machine code:** the write is at `0x1010`, the first read at `0x1ee0`, and there is no `BAR.SYNC` between them. v44 does this correctly: `producer_sync` plus a `d_ready` barrier.

**If it ever goes wrong:** some warps read stale shared memory as LSE. P for that tile is wrong, so dK, dV and dQ are silently wrong, with no error.

**Why it hasn't happened:** the read comes after a 32 KB Q/dO load plus 8 tensor-core steps, which take longer than the 256-byte LSE load. That is timing, not a guarantee. Our 1000× repeat test stayed bit-identical.

**The fix:** one `__syncthreads()` after the first tile's load. It runs once per CTA, not per tile. The trial build I just made:
- adds exactly 1 `BAR.SYNC`;
- the compiler moved 4 register-zeroing instructions around it;
- everything else is the same; only branch addresses shift by one instruction;
- registers stay at 218 and shared memory is unchanged.

It should cost about nothing, because the threads wait for the Q/dO load right after anyway. The packed kernel already has it.

**My recommendation: fix it,** because it's a silent-corruption risk in the default training backward. To apply it, after G9 full finishes:
1. Change Vj1d and Vj1.
2. SASS proof on the laptop and on the box.
3. Re-run the dense G tests plus a before/after timing on GPU 7 (~10–25 min, estimated). I'll ask before that run.

**Now:** G9 full has been running since 19:39 on GPU 7; I'll be notified when it ends (estimate around 20:00). Shall I prepare the race fix on the laptop meanwhile? It's a few lines plus a SASS check, cheap on quota.

Verified: FA2 `flash_bwd_kernel.h:411` sets `lse = row < actual_seqlen_q - m_block*kBlockM ? gLSE(row) : INFINITY`, and the comment at 413 reads "We want LSE = inf if the row is OOB". So it's a proven pattern I can reuse.

The reading is done. Here is the design for **Step 5 (A = per-chat offsets)** in our kernels, for your OK before I code. Design B is unchanged.

**Core idea:** same packed buffers `[B, H, T, D]` as B, so A vs B is apples to apples. Only the metadata differs: B passes `seg_start` per token, A passes a list of chats `(row b, start t0, length L)`. Every tile starts at its chat's start, so there are no border tiles shared by two chats.

**Forward (v62, variant A)**
- **Work list.** Built on the host per batch: one unit per (chat, query head, pair of query tiles), longest first (LPT). The 132 persistent CTAs walk this list. FA3 uses the same LPT ordering, with an atomic counter (`tile_scheduler.hpp:493-700`); I'll start with a static walk and measure.
- **Tiles.** Q tiles load at `t0 + pair*128` and K/V at `t0 + n*128`. The diagonal mask is relative to the chat start, so it's identical to dense causal with S = L.
- **Rows past the chat end** in the last tile are computed but not stored: one `if (row < L)` on the existing O/LSE stores. FA3 does the same in varlen mode (`epilogue_fwd.hpp:303, 331, 358`).
- **Keys past the chat end** come after every row of the chat, so the causal mask already hides them. No new mask is needed.

**Backward (Vj1d, variant A)**
- **Grid.** One CTA per (chat, key tile) per query head, from a host-built tile list.
- **Rows past the chat end:** LSE = +∞ and D = 0, which gives P = 0 and dS = 0 with no new mask code. This is FA2's trick, `flash_bwd_kernel.h:411-413`.
- **dQ:** the TMA reduce-add stays as is; rows past the end add exact zeros.
- **dK/dV:** full tiles keep the TMA store. Only a chat's last, partial key tile uses a row-checked store, so it never overwrites the next chat's partial. FA3 stores all varlen dK/dV this way (`epilogue_bwd.hpp:31, 263-268`).

|---|---|---|
| Wasted work | border tiles shared by 2 chats | one partial tail tile per chat |
| Forward balance | row pairs, irregular; my suspect for the 102.5% | per-chat units, longest first |
| Many tiny chats (e.g. 1-token) | share tiles, cheap | each gets its own tile, costlier |
