### CLAUDE [2026-10-15 21:23 IST]

Your point is right: a block in the middle of a long chat holds no start and no end, and it is the same in both designs. The difference comes from how causal attention works. Every query must look back at **all earlier keys of its own chat, back to the chat's first token**. So even a query block in the middle of chat 2 reaches back to chat 2's start. Counting this on a real-size example:
> tool `Bash`: Count blocks for a two-chat row in both designs

Here is the simple version, with one row: **chat 1 = tokens 0–999, chat 2 = tokens 1000–3999** (the last 96 tokens are padding). Blocks are the real ones: 64 queries × 128 keys.

**The one rule that explains everything:** a query must look at **every** key of its own chat, from the chat's **first token** up to itself. So the work of a query block is not just one block. It is a whole line of key blocks, from the key block where its chat starts up to its own position. A query block in the middle of a long chat still reaches back to the chat's first token.

**A middle query block of chat 2 (rows 2048–2111) in both designs:**
```
segstart (key blocks fixed at multiples of 128 tokens):
  [896-1023] [1024-1151] [1152-1279] ... [2048-2175]      = 10 blocks
   ^ chat 2 starts at token 1000, so this first block holds
     104 keys of chat 1 (masked, thrown away) + 24 keys of chat 2

seqlens (key blocks start exactly at chat 2's first token):
  [1000-1127] [1128-1255] ... [2024-2151]                 = 9 blocks, all chat 2
```
So yes, that middle block contains no chat start or end. But it still needs chat 2's first keys, and with segstart those keys sit in a block shared with chat 1. Segstart computes **one extra block, 81% thrown away**, for this middle query block.

**This happens for every query block of chat 2, not only at the border.** All 47 query blocks of chat 2 (start, middle and end) need chat 2's first keys, so each one pays that one extra shared block. There is a second smaller cost at the end of the row: the padding rows share a block pair with chat 2's last rows, so with segstart they go through all of chat 2's key blocks (25 blocks instead of 1).

Whole row, counted with the kernel's rules:

| | blocks computed |
|---|---|
| seqlens | 650 |
| segstart | 720 (10.8% more than seqlens) |

**Why the gap depends on chat length:**
- Segstart's extra is about **one block per query block** of a chat.
- A chat's total work grows much faster than its number of query blocks: a twice-longer chat has twice the query blocks, and each one looks back twice as far.
- So the extra is a small part of a long chat and a big part of a middle one (same one-length rows as before):

| chat length | seqlens blocks | segstart blocks | segstart's extra vs seqlens |
|---|---|---|---|
| 2000 | 546 | 576 | +5.5% |
| 1000 | 290 | 336 | +16% |
| 300 | 123 | 168 | +37% |
| 100 | 82 | 124 | +51% |
| 20 | 205 | 114 | −44% (segstart wins) |

The extra block appears whenever a chat does not start exactly at a multiple of 128 tokens. With real chat lengths that is almost always the case.

**At 20 tokens it flips**, as in my last message: seqlens gives every tiny chat its own whole 64-row block, with 44 empty rows. Segstart puts about 3 tiny chats into one block. Our stage-0 chats average 1,238 tokens, so we are in the part of the table where seqlens wins.

**In one line:** with segstart, every chat's first key block is shared with the previous chat, and every query of the chat (middle ones too) must go through that shared, mostly-masked block. With seqlens, every chat's blocks start exactly at its first token, so that shared block never exists.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-16 11:07 IST]

The install is going fine; let it finish (the last file is about 280 MB at 65 MB/s, so under a minute). The first lines show the box already had NCCL (`nccl.h`, `libnccl.so`) and NVML. Only MPI was really missing.

One note: because my install line also named `libnccl2 libnccl-dev`, apt upgraded the NCCL that was already there, from 2.28.9 to 2.32.3. That's my mistake: since NCCL was already installed, I should have left it out of the line. The upgrade is fine for us; NCCL 2.x keeps backward compatibility. But if colleagues also run on this box, their programs will now load 2.32.3. If you'd rather keep their setup unchanged, this puts the old version back:
```bash
apt-get install -y --allow-downgrades libnccl2=2.28.9-1+cuda13.0 libnccl-dev=2.28.9-1+cuda13.0
```

When the install finishes, the last line of the block should show `/usr/bin/mpic++`, `/usr/bin/mpirun`, `mpirun (Open MPI) 4.1.6` and `/usr/include/nccl.h`.

Then, if not done yet, run the COPY block from the laptop and the `hf download` block. After that comes BUILD block C. Send me its output.

```bash
mkdir -p ~/gautam_k/ckpt/blumodel_step_8000 && cd ~/gautam_k/ckpt/blumodel_step_8000
for f in metadata.bin data_rank_0.bin; do curl -fL --progress-bar -o $f https://huggingface.co/navingv/curriculum_8btokens/resolve/main/blumodel_step_8000/$f; done
ls -l; md5sum metadata.bin data_rank_0.bin | cut -c1-8
```

**Test 2 passed exactly.** With seqlens, the packed run's step-0 val loss is **1.445038, the same as v1 to all 7 printed digits** (segstart gave 1.445084), and the grad norm is 0.7935 with group norms 0.7929 / 0.0321, identical to v1. The run exited by itself after "Training complete".

It's even closer than segstart for a reason: with seqlens, each chat's attention is computed with the same blocks in the same order as in its own v1 row. So the rounding is identical, not just close. Both GPU tests are done; **the packed SFT pipeline with seqlens is proven**. I've recorded both results in work doc §45.11 and ticked §45.8.

Your questions:

**1. Is seqlens better than segstart, and are both varlen?** Yes, both are varlen methods: two ways to tell the kernel where each chat starts. They compute the same attention; they differ only in speed.

**2. Is the metadata KB vs MB?** In the **file on disk**, yes: 20 KB for seqlens vs 12.4 MB for segstart. But **on the GPU per step it's not smaller**:

| per micro-batch of 8 rows on the GPU | size |
|---|---|
| segstart (one number per token) | 128 KB |
| seqlens plan (the work list made from the chat lengths, for all 18 heads) | 209 KB |

Both are tiny next to the GBs of activations, so size is not why seqlens is faster. It's faster because of how it cuts the work into blocks: no block ever holds two chats.

**3. Is seqlens better in every case except short chats?** Almost. On our kernels (10-12 measurements):
- **Forward:** seqlens was faster than segstart on all 7 layouts tested (2–16%).
- **Backward:** seqlens was 3–5% faster on middle and long chats; segstart was 2–4% faster only on rows full of the shortest chats.

FlashAttention 2/3/4, NVIDIA TE/Megatron, PyTorch's varlen attention, Hugging Face's FlashAttention path and TRL all use seqlens. FlexAttention's document mask and Hugging Face's SDPA/eager paths use the segstart way.

**4. Do we get short chats in real data?** Barely. Our stage-0 data (5,000 chats):

| chat length | chats |
|---|---|
| shortest | 134 tokens |
| under 128 tokens | 0 (0%) |
| under 256 | 37 (0.74%) |
| under 512 | 408 (8.2%) |
| mean / median | 1,238 / 1,153 tokens |

Segstart wins clearly only when chats are about one block long or shorter (under about 64 tokens), and we have none. Even our "shortest" rows are made of chats of a few hundred tokens. Some other datasets, for example short one-line Q&A, could have more tiny chats. The loss there is small (2–4%), and it can be fixed later by sharing one block between several tiny chats.

The logs are saved on the laptop in `profiling_reports/sft_seqlens_gpu_tests_2026_10_16/` (3 files). Steps 1–2 look right:

| | v1 (500 rows) | packed, segstart | packed, seqlens |
|---|---|---|---|
| step 0 val loss | 1.445038 | 1.445084 | **1.445038** |
| step 1 train loss / grad norm | 1.423608 / 0.6496 | 1.423671 / 0.6502 | 1.423602 / 0.6498 |

**Why step 0 is exact but steps 1–2 are only close:**
- Step 0's loss comes from the starting weights, and with seqlens every token's numbers are the same as in v1. So it matches exactly.
- From step 1 on, the weights have been updated with a gradient that was added up in a different grouping: v1 sums 500 micro-batches of 1 row, the packed runs sum 147. The rounding of those sums differs a little, so the losses differ in the 5th–6th digit.
- This is expected and not an error. Seqlens and segstart give the same val loss after step 2 (1.381214 vs 1.381213), because they share the same 147-row grouping. So the 0.006% gap from v1 comes from the gradient grouping, not from the attention design.

The step times aren't a fair comparison: today's run was on a different box, so the 13 s per step can't be compared directly with yesterday's 21 s (segstart) or 54 s (v1).

## Backward (Vj2) so far: dense (normal) attention

Main kernel time on our model's shape (8 rows, 18/6 heads, 4096 tokens), measured with the instruction-level profiler, one change at a time:

| step | main kernel | vs FA3 (2481 µs) |
|---|---|---|
| Vj1d, the old default | 3626 µs | 1.46× |
| first Vj2 (10-12) | 3195 | 1.29× |
| + memory path and descriptor fixes (10-13) | 2778 | 1.12× |
| + dQ path, block order, epilogue (10-13) | 2545 | 1.03× |
| + G2, G1, G3 (10-13) | 2512 | 1.01× |
| + B-2a: FA3's wait placement (10-14) | 2478 | 1.00× |
| + G4: dQ scaled once (10-14) | **2407** | **0.97×**: 3.0% faster than FA3, 4.7% fewer clock cycles |
| B-4a: D loads moved earlier | 2460 | slower, reverted |
| + B-1: dQ buffer cleared inside the prep kernel | same main kernel | about 20 µs saved per call; speed race not run yet |
| FA4 / cuDNN, for reference | 2478 / 2770 | 1.00× / 1.12× |

- **Today's Vj2 is this last version.** Its dense machine code is proven unchanged by the seqlens work.
- **Whole backward call** (all kernels, measured 10-14 before B-2a, G4 and B-1): ours 2910 µs, FA3 2858, FA4 2855, cuDNN 3139. Since then our main kernel lost 105 µs and a separate 68 µs fill was removed, so we are probably ahead of FA3 now. **That's an estimate, not measured in one session.**
- **Remaining gaps to FA3** (10-14 profile), in time spent waiting:
  - for a shared-memory value or an exp result: 238 vs 137;
  - in the shared-memory queue: 114 vs 99;
  - at barriers: 388 vs 369.

  Waits at the start of each matrix multiply are already equal.

## Backward: packed (masked) attention

- **10-13 scoreboard, with the old Vj1d:** 1.18× FA3 varlen's time, 1.21× FA4's, 1.08× cuDNN's. On the middle rows: Vj1d 1.908 ms, FA3 1.561, cuDNN 1.740.
- **Today, Vj2 with seqlens on the same middle rows:** 1.474 ms. That's probably faster than FA3 now, but it ran on another box. **We must measure it here, side by side.**

**Still pending:** the B-1 speed race, and the full 605-check run on the current Vj2 (the last full run was 10-13).

### CLAUDE [2026-10-16 12:28 IST]

Short answer: we are **partly deterministic**. The forward and dK/dV give bit-identical results every run, but **dQ does not**, in both Vj2 and Vj1d. The only fully bit-identical dQ we have is the old v44 kernel (`USE_DETERMINISTIC_DQ=1`), which works only on normal rows. There is no deterministic switch for Vj2 or for packed rows yet.

**What is deterministic today:**

| kernel | output | same bits every run? | why |
|---|---|---|---|
| v62 forward | O, LSE | **yes** | each output is written by exactly one block, always in the same order; no atomic adds |
| Vj2 backward (default) | dK, dV | **yes** | each query head's dK/dV is written by one block, then the heads are summed in a fixed order |
| Vj2 backward (default) | dQ | **no** | many key blocks add into the same dQ rows with atomic adds, and their order changes from run to run |
| Vj1d (`USE_VJ2=0`) | dK/dV, dQ | yes, no | same scheme as Vj2 |
| v44 (`USE_DETERMINISTIC_DQ=1`) | everything | **yes** | dQ in per-block slices, summed in a fixed order; normal rows only, and slower |

How big the dQ difference is: in this morning's 50-run repeat test, dQ differed by at most **4.9e-4**, against FlashAttention's allowed **1.6e-2**. Training-wise that's noise, but two runs are not bit-identical.

**Compared with the rivals:**
- **FA3 (default)** also adds dQ with atomics. For GQA it also adds dK/dV that way: on 10-14 we saw it fill two fp32 dK/dV buffers and convert them afterwards. So FA3 is *less* deterministic than ours, and FA3 is the fair comparison for us.
- **FA3 deterministic** makes everything bit-identical, and pays for it: in today's runs it took about **1.22× FA3's time** in the backward. So "ours beats FA3 det" is not a fair win; we don't do the same work.

**Are we beating everyone in the backward?** Not all of them, honestly:

| rival | dense (13 shapes) | packed (7 row sets) |
|---|---|---|
| cuDNN, FA2, Flex, Vj1d | **clearly faster**, every shape | **clearly faster**, every row set |
| FA3 | **tied**: mean 0.99, wins 7/13; at our model's shape 3.072 vs 3.073 ms | **faster** on 6/7 (mean 0.94); about equal on rows of long chats |
| FA4 | **tied**: mean 0.98, wins 6/13; at our model's shape 1% slower (3.072 vs 3.042 ms) | faster on 4/7 (mean 0.97); 1–2% slower on long-chat rows |

So against FA3/FA4 we're level in dense and ahead on packed short and middle chats. Two big dense shapes and the long-chat rows still lose by 2–10%. Our run-to-run noise is about 1%, so 1–2% gaps aren't proven either way.

If you want bit-identical training runs, a deterministic dQ for Vj2 (and for packed rows) would be a new task. Going by FA3's price above, expect a slower backward. Should I put it on the to-do list as an option?

It's a small tool a colleague put on this 2x H200 box so that people sharing its 2 GPUs don't run on top of each other. It wasn't there this morning. We first saw it today in the message printed when the rsync logged in to the box:

```
[gpu_board] Shared H200s: check -> claim -> run -> release.
[gpu_board]   /root/gpu_board/gpuboard status | claim <gpu> --note ".." | release <gpu>
[gpu_board]   Refused claim = do not start. Never kill others' processes. Rules: /root/gpu_board/PROTOCOL.md
```

How it's meant to work:
1. **status**: shows who is using which GPU right now.
2. **claim <gpu> --note "..."**: before starting a run, you mark that GPU as yours, with a note saying what you're running.
3. **run** your job.
4. **release <gpu>**: when done, you free the GPU for others.

If someone else holds a GPU, your claim is refused, and the rule is that you don't start. That's what happened this morning: the colleague's runs from `/root/BluTrain-harsh` and `/root/harshini_ab` took both GPUs.

**Why you got "Permission denied":** the `gpuboard` file isn't marked as runnable. Either the colleague hasn't set it up fully yet, or it's a script that has to be started through Python or bash. Nothing was claimed, and nothing was changed. To see what it is and read the rules (read-only):

### USER [2026-10-16 12:32 IST]

so inorder to make ouyrs vj2 deterministic,we need otmake that dq only determizintic right? and thatv44 is foronly dq aah orhwol attentionkernel aah ? cantw emake this determiistic and getthe same speed evenmoreaah ?w ecnataha ?

### CLAUDE [2026-10-16 12:32 IST]

1. **Only dQ.** The forward (v62) and Vj2's dK/dV already give the same bits every run. dQ is the only part that changes.
2. **v44 is a whole backward kernel, not a dQ add-on.** It's an older backward kernel (before Vj1/Vj1d/Vj2) that computes dQ, dK and dV itself. What makes it special is its bit-identical dQ: each block writes its dQ piece into its own slice, and a separate kernel adds the slices in a fixed order. It only handles normal (unpacked) rows, and it's slower than Vj2. I haven't measured by how much on this box.
3. **Can we get a deterministic Vj2 at the same speed or faster?** Faster: no. Making the adds happen in a fixed order can only add waiting. About the same speed: **possibly**, for the reason below. But it's unproven until we build and measure it.

**Why dQ changes today:** each dQ tile (64 query rows) receives one contribution from every key block before it, up to 32 blocks at 4096 tokens. They all add into the same memory with atomic adds. Whichever block arrives first adds first, and that order changes from run to run. A different order of float adds gives slightly different last bits.

**Three ways to fix it:**

| way | how | cost |
|---|---|---|
| v44's way | every key block writes its own dQ copy, a second kernel adds them in a fixed order | a lot of extra memory (up to 32 copies of dQ) and extra memory traffic |
| a separate dQ pass | one block per query tile walks over all key blocks, so its dQ needs no atomics | must recompute the scores: about 7 matrix multiplies per step instead of 5, roughly +40% work |
| **ordered adds** (FA3's deterministic mode uses this kind of scheme) | keep the atomic adds, but each dQ tile has a counter, and key block *k* waits until the block that comes before it in the fixed order has added | only the waiting |

**Why ordered adds could be cheap for us:**
- In our kernel, key block *kt* starts at its diagonal (query step 2·kt) and moves down. So for any given dQ tile, the block with the highest *kt* reaches it first, and block 0 reaches it last.
- Our block order (sections of about 4 heads × 32 key blocks, about one wave of the GPU) starts those blocks at nearly the same time.
- So if we choose the fixed order "highest *kt* first", it's mostly the order blocks arrive in anyway, and little waiting should be needed. The adds are also done by the separate writer warp, not by the compute warps, which hides part of any wait.

**The honest cost reference:** FA3's deterministic mode took **1.22× FA3's time** in today's backward runs. But FA3 must also put dK/dV in order, because for GQA it adds them with atomics; ours are already one writer per head. So our cost should be lower than FA3's 22%. How much lower, only a test will tell.

So it's a real option: a deterministic switch for Vj2 (dense and packed) using ordered adds. Shall I add it to the to-do list, after the current backward profiling, or before it?

#!/usr/bin/env python3
"""gpuboard - shared GPU coordination board for people (and their Claude agents)
on this server.  Everyone logs in as root, so "who" is the top-level folder under
# GPU sharing protocol (this server: 2x H200, GPU 0 and GPU 1)

Everyone works as root, so the board identifies people by their top-level folder
under /root (`/root/adwaid/...` -> `adwaid`). Agents coordinate with each other
through the board; there is no central watcher.

Tool: `/root/gpu_board/gpuboard` (run with `--help`). Log: `/root/gpu_board/board.log`.

## Rules

1. **Check** before any GPU job (training, benchmark, nsys/ncu, tests that touch CUDA):
   `gpuboard status`
2. **Claim** the GPU(s) you will use, with a note saying what and roughly how long:
   `gpuboard claim 1 --note "ncu 1-layer, ~20 min" --hours 1`
   - Exit code 2 = **refused**. Do **not** start. The refusal says who holds it.
   - A claim is refused if someone else holds an unexpired claim **or** has a
     process on that GPU (claimed or not).
   - To wait instead: `gpuboard claim 1 --note "..." --wait 60` (blocks until free).
3. **Run** only on what you claimed: `CUDA_VISIBLE_DEVICES=<claimed ids> ...`
4. **Monitor** the board while you run: `gpuboard watch` (or `gpuboard inbox`), and
   reply to messages addressed to you.
5. **Release** as soon as you are done, also if the run crashed:
   `gpuboard release 1` (or `release all`).

## Etiquette

- **Never kill, renice or otherwise touch another person's process.** If something
  is in your way, message the owner: `gpuboard say --to <owner> "..."`.
- Claims expire (default 6h; set `--hours` close to the real duration). Re-claiming
  your own GPU renews it.
- An `UNCLAIMED` process in `gpuboard status` means someone skipped step 2; send them
  a board message rather than starting on top of it.
- If one person works from several folders, list them in `owners.conf`
  (`<folder> <person>`) so their claim covers all of them.

I'll check FA3's forward in its source before answering that part:
> tool `Bash`: Check whether FA3's forward has atomics or a deterministic flag
> tool `Bash`: Confirm the deterministic flag is backward-only

**Determinism, all four kernels**, checked in the source code:

| kernel | deterministic? | why |
|---|---|---|
| **ours, forward (v62)** | **yes, fully** | each output is written by one block in a fixed order; no atomic adds |
| **FA3, forward** | **yes, fully, and there is only one version** | its forward has no `deterministic` option at all: the option exists only in `_flash_attn_backward` (`flash_attn_interface.py:259-280`), and its forward kernel and epilogue contain no atomic adds |
| **ours, backward (Vj2)** | **partly**: dK/dV yes, dQ no | dK/dV: one writer per head plus a fixed-order sum; dQ: atomic adds |
| **FA3, backward, normal mode** | **no**, for GQA models like ours | dQ **and** dK/dV are added with atomics |
| **FA3, backward, deterministic mode** | yes, fully | counters force a fixed order; it took 1.22× FA3's time in today's runs |

So a forward doesn't need a deterministic switch, because each output has a single writer anyway. Only backwards need one, because many blocks add into the same gradient rows. **Ours is more deterministic than FA3's normal mode**; the remaining dQ part is a future task.

Before the commands, here's what the profile shows (dense = B8 18/6, packed = real_rows_752):

**1. Helper kernels are not the problem.** One backward call = prep + main kernel + dQ convert + dK/dV head sum. Everyone's helpers cost about the same: ours 369 µs, FA3 374, FA4 379, cuDNN 366 (dense). The whole gap is in the main kernel.

**2. At the same clock, our main kernel is the fastest.** ncu locks the clock at 1.36 GHz:

| main kernel cycles | ours | FA3 | FA4 | cuDNN |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| dense | **4.14 M** | 4.25 M | 4.29 M | 4.93 M |
| packed | **1.73 M** | 1.87 M | 1.88 M | 2.05 M |

**3. At free clocks we fall behind.** Steady-state main kernel time: dense 2,633 µs, against FA3's 2,551 and FA4's 2,524. Packed 1,103 µs, against 1,101 and 1,085. Our first 12 calls ran at 2,395 µs; then the clock dropped and the time stepped up to about 2,630. Our kernel runs at a lower clock than theirs, roughly 1,575 MHz against about 1,665–1,700 MHz. That figure is an estimate from cycles ÷ time.

**4. Why the clock drops: we execute more instructions.** We execute 705 M instructions, FA3 625 M, FA4 555 M. More instructions draw more power, and under the 700 W cap that lowers the clock. The biggest excess I found is a bug-like inefficiency: **the causal mask ran on every step**, not only on the 2 diagonal steps, at 73 instructions per warp per step.

**The fix** is in [GQA_bwd_vj2_sm90.cu:602-626](../BluTrain_sft/Tensor-Implementations/src/Kernels/cuda/attention/arch/GQA_bwd_vj2_sm90.cu#L602-L626):
- The mask moves into its own block behind one branch. On the laptop build it shows no spill, 168 registers, and the other 5 backward kernels' SASS is unchanged.
- Expected: about 705 M → 622 M instructions, level with FA3.
- My first attempt (two loops, FA3's way) spilled 32 registers every step, so I dropped it.
- The math is unchanged, so results should be bit-identical.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-16 14:30 IST]

Here's the full picture in order: what we measured, what each number means, where we stand.

## 1. The question
The scoreboard showed our backward roughly tied with FA3 on our model shape (3.07 ms vs 3.07 ms). The 10-14 ncu profile said our main kernel was faster. So where does that lead go? Today's profiling answers it.

## 2. One backward call, split into its kernels (nsys, free clocks, dense B8 18/6)
A backward call is 1 main kernel plus small helper kernels (prep, dQ convert, dK/dV sums).

| | whole call | main kernel | helpers |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ours** | 3,007 µs | 2,633 µs | 369 µs |
| FA3 | 2,933 µs | 2,551 µs | 374 µs |
| FA4 | 2,905 µs | 2,524 µs | 379 µs |
| cuDNN | 3,308 µs | 2,903 µs | 366 µs |

Packed (real_rows_752): ours 1,495 µs, FA3 1,495, FA4 1,484, cuDNN 1,583. Helpers are again equal (about 390 µs each).

→ **The helpers are equal for everyone. The whole difference is in the main kernel.**

## 3. Main kernel at the same fixed clock (ncu, 1.36 GHz)
| | ours | FA3 | FA4 | cuDNN |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| dense cycles | **4.14 M** (fewest) | 4.25 M | 4.29 M | 4.93 M |
| packed cycles | **1.73 M** (fewest) | 1.87 M | 1.88 M | 2.05 M |
| dense instructions | 705 M (more) | 626 M | 555 M | 809 M |

→ **At the same clock, our main kernel is the fastest of all.**

## 4. Main kernel at the real (free) clock
Dense: ours 2,633 µs, FA3 2,551, FA4 2,524. → **At the real clock we're 3–4% slower.**

Fewest cycles but more time can only mean our kernel effectively runs at a lower clock: roughly 1,575 MHz against FA3's 1,665 MHz.

## 5. Why? The idea we tested
Idea: we execute more instructions, more instructions use more power, and at the 700 W limit the GPU lowers our clock.

The biggest waste we found: **the causal mask ran on every step**, but it's only needed on the 2 diagonal steps (73 wasted instructions per step).

## 6. The fix and its result
| | before | after fix (version 3) |
|---|---|---|
| tests | – | 296 / 296 pass |
| instructions, dense | 705 M | **618 M** (below FA3's 626 M) |
| cycles at fixed clock | 4.14 M | 4.16 M (no change) |
| backward time, dense | – | +0.11% (no change) |
| backward time, packed | – | +0.22% (no change) |

→ **The waste is gone, but the time didn't move.** Fewer instructions didn't make it faster, so the "more instructions → lower clock" idea is **wrong, or at least not proven**. The real reason we lose at free clocks is still open. One untested candidate: time our kernel spends waiting on memory doesn't shrink when the clock goes up.

## 7. Where we stand now (ours ÷ rival time; below 1.00 = we're faster)
| | vs FA3 | vs FA4 | vs cuDNN |
|---|---|---|---|
| backward, dense (13 shapes) | 0.986 | 0.975 | 0.785 |
| backward, packed (7 row sets) | 0.939 | 0.967 | 0.878 |
| **forward, dense** | **1.135** (B8 18/6: **1.233**) | 1.034 | 0.984 |
| forward, packed | 1.059 | 0.932 | 0.975 |

→ **The backward is already at FA3's level. The forward is the big gap: 23% slower than FA3 on our model shape.**

## 8. What I need from you
1. Keep the fix (version 3: same speed, 12% less waste) or revert it? I'd keep it.
2. Move to the forward now, since that's where the 23% is? I'd say yes.

> tool `Read`: /home/blu-bridge016/Downloads/sft_research/flash-attention/hopper/mainloop_fwd_sm90_tma_gmma_ws.hpp

FA3's forward loop is in [mainloop_fwd_sm90_tma_gmma_ws.hpp:1170-1207](../sft_research/flash-attention/hopper/mainloop_fwd_sm90_tma_gmma_ws.hpp#L1170-L1207). Here's what the forward profiles show, and the plan.

## Forward: where the 23% goes (ncu at the same locked clock, B8 18/6)
| | ours | FA3 |
|---|---|---|
| main kernel time | 1,084 µs | 877 µs |
| instructions | 349 M | 307 M |
| tensor cores busy | **64%** | **83%** |
| SMs busy (tail at the end) | 95.7% | 99.6% |

Unlike the backward, this gap is real kernel work at the same clock. The main cause is the **order of the steps inside the loop**. Each compute group does, for every key tile:

```
OURS  (per tile n)                          FA3  (per tile n)
1. wait: QK(n) finished                     1. start QK(n)  and  P·V(n-1)   (tensor cores)
2. softmax(n)  <- tensor cores idle          2. wait: QK(n) finished
   for this group                            3. softmax(n)  <- P·V(n-1) still running
3. start P·V(n), then QK(n+1)                   on the tensor cores at the same time
4. wait: P·V(n) finished                     4. wait: P·V(n-1) finished
```

FA3 runs its softmax **while** the previous P·V is still on the tensor cores. Ours finishes both GEMMs first, then does the softmax with this group's tensor work stopped. We rely only on the other compute group to fill that gap, and it doesn't fully manage (64% busy).

The "long scoreboard" number I mentioned earlier was misleading. It's our loader warps idling at their waits, which costs nothing. I've corrected that.

## Plan for the forward (one change at a time, each with a local build check + one ~10-minute GPU test)
1. **G1: P·V as 8 wide `m64n128k16`** instead of 16 half-width `m64n64k16`, as FA3 does. Small change; we did the same in the backward on 10-13.
2. **F1: FA3's loop order**: softmax(n) overlaps P·V(n−1). This is the big one, aimed at the 64% → ~80% tensor-busy gap. It needs about 32 more registers per thread while the softmax runs. FA3 fits that in 240 registers, and we have 232, so I'll check for spills before any GPU run.
3. **G5: the tail**: our 2,304 equal work units over 132 SMs leave the last round 45% full. Sending the biggest work first, as FA3 does, gains about 3–4%.
4. **G6: output written through shared memory + TMA store** (small).

Shall I start with G1 now?

### CLAUDE [2026-10-16 14:41 IST]

Fair. Two corrections.

**1. "Already like FA3" was too quick on my part.** I said it after reading only the comments at the top of our file: ping-pong between the two compute groups, and the next QK starting early. Both are true. But when I compared our loop with FA3's line by line ([GQA_fwd_sm90.cu:527-622](../BluTrain_sft/Tensor-Implementations/src/Kernels/cuda/attention/arch/GQA_fwd_sm90.cu#L527-L622) against FA3's [mainloop_fwd_sm90_tma_gmma_ws.hpp:1170-1207](../sft_research/flash-attention/hopper/mainloop_fwd_sm90_tma_gmma_ws.hpp#L1170-L1207)), the overlap turned out to be different:
- **Ours:** QK(n+1) runs only while we wait for P·V(n) to finish, a short window. During the softmax, this group has nothing on the tensor cores.
- **FA3:** the whole softmax(n) runs while P·V(n−1) is on the tensor cores, a long window.

So the structure looks the same from the outside, but FA3 overlaps much more. That matches the profile: 64% against 83% tensor busy.

**2. G1 does not change the tile.** The tile stays exactly the same: 64 queries × 128 keys per compute group, 128 × 128 per block, the same as FA3. Only the multiply instruction used for P·V changes:

```
P·V for 16 keys, output = 64 rows x 128 head columns
ours today:  2 instructions  m64n64k16   (columns 0-63, then columns 64-127)
FA3:         1 instruction   m64n128k16  (all 128 columns at once)
```

The math, the result and the tile are the same; there are just half as many P·V instructions, and P is read once instead of twice. We made the same change in the backward on 10-13 (dV/dK), and the results were bit-identical.

So the plan stays: G1 (small instruction change) → F1 (FA3's loop order, the big one) → G5 (tail) → G6 (output store). Shall I start G1?

**What changed:**
- **Baton:** it now covers the GEMM issue, as in FA3. One group issues QK(n) + P·V(n−1), then the other group issues its pair.

| **ours now** | **1.76 M** | **1.23×** (this morning **1.34×**) |
| cuDNN | 1.75 M | 1.22× |

We've caught up with cuDNN. FA3 is still 23% ahead: its tensor cores are busy 83% against our 68%.

## Backward (kernel unchanged since version 3)
- Still at FA3's level: dense tie, packed slightly ahead.
- Each faster forward made the backward that runs right after it a little slower: +0.5% after G5. The likely cause is power (G5 also raised memory traffic).
- Net per forward + backward pair: **dense −22 µs, packed −10 µs**, so the total still improves.

## One cost G5 introduced
G5 groups 48 heads together, which is too many for L2. The dense L2 hit rate fell from 92% to 83%, and memory reads doubled (254 → 526 MB). That's probably also why the backward slowed. The fix is a small knob: groups of 12–24 heads, keeping the balance gain while winning back L2.

## Next
1. **G5b:** try 12 and 24 heads per group (small change, one GPU run).
2. **G6:** write the output through shared memory + TMA store.
3. Then find the rest of the 23% gap to FA3. Tensor busy is 68% against 83%, and the cause is still to be found.

Shall I do G5b next?

### CLAUDE [2026-10-16 17:50 IST]

**The quick suite hung**: `exit=124` means the 15-minute timeout fired. That's my bug in F3's hand-over, not a GPU problem.

**Cause:** in packed mode, when one compute group's query tile lies past the chat's end, that group has nothing to compute (`my_nkv == 0`). F3 made such a group fetch the next unit **before** running its "inactive tail". But the tail is where it releases its K/V buffers. The loader can only publish the next unit after loading the current unit's last tiles, and for chats with 4+ key tiles those loads wait for exactly those releases. The group waits for the loader, the loader waits for the group: a deadlock. Dense mode never has an inactive group.

**The fix:** an inactive group fetches **after** its tail, the old order. Active groups keep the early fetch.

Before anything goes back to the GPU, I'm writing a small CPU simulation of the whole wait/arrive protocol (loader + both compute groups, mbarrier phases, the baton) to prove the hang and the fix offline. First, the cleanup check.

**Please run on the BOX** (read-only), to confirm nothing hung is left on GPU 1 and to see which test froze:

### CLAUDE [2026-10-16 17:54 IST]

No, it wasn't the GPU claim. The script claims GPU 1 for **1 hour** (`--hours 1`). The **15 minutes is the script's own safety timeout** (`timeout 900`): any test still running after 15 minutes gets killed. The timeout didn't cause the failure; it stopped a test that would otherwise have run forever.

**The timeline:**
- 16:57:07 IST: start.
- The quick suite normally finishes in about 35–70 seconds.
- 17:12:07 IST: exactly 900 seconds later, killed by the timeout (exit 124 = killed by timeout).
- So the test was stuck the whole time: the forward kernel was in a **deadlock**.

**Why it deadlocked (packed mode only).** Some facts first:
- Each block has 1 loader warp and 2 compute groups. In a query pair, group 0 takes rows 0–63 and group 1 takes rows 64–127.
- K/V tiles go through 3 buffers. The loader may load tile t+3 only after **both** groups have released tile t.
- If a chat is short, for example 64 tokens, rows 64–127 don't exist. Group 1 then has nothing to compute, but it must still step through the chat's K/V tiles and release each buffer. That's its "inactive tail".
- F3 added: each group reads the next unit's number before its epilogue. The loader writes that number only after it has issued **all** K/V loads of the current unit.

The deadlock, for a chat with 4 or more key tiles where group 1 has no rows:
1. Group 1 has no work, so it reaches "read the next unit" at once, and waits for the loader to publish it.
2. The loader is still loading this chat's K/V. For tile 3 it needs tile 0's buffer released by both groups. Group 0 released it. Group 1 hasn't, because it releases in its tail, which comes **after** step 1.
3. So the loader waits for group 1, and group 1 waits for the loader. Group 0 then also stops at its next baton handshake with group 1. Nobody can move.

Dense mode never has a group without rows, which is why only the packed tests hung.

**The fix:** a group without rows first runs its tail (releasing the buffers) and only then reads the next unit. The CPU simulation shows the old order deadlocking in 1,124 of 3,000 random cases, and the fixed order in 0.

The commands for the fixed build (`ea5d9f75`) are in my previous message.

**3. Why we're not beating FA3 yet:**
- Today we went from 34% → 18% behind on dense and from 19% → 5% behind on packed.
- The rest of the gap is spread over several places.
- Two of my steps were wrong: F3's hand-over only moved the wait, and F1 gave less than expected.

## A concrete cause I just found from FA3's source
FA3 loads K and V with an **L2 "evict last"** hint and Q with **"evict first"** (`mainloop_fwd_sm90_tma_gmma_ws.hpp:753, 767, 820`). Ours has no hints at all (`GQA_fwd_sm90.cu:108, 127`). Since G5, our dense forward reads **524 MB** from memory against **FA3's 367 MB** (L2 hit 83% vs 85–87%). Our K/V get pushed out of L2 by the streaming Q traffic. This probably also explains why the backward slowed slightly after G5.

## The plan
**Step 0, laptop, no GPU (tonight).** Prepare all remaining candidates together, each checked locally (build, no spills, SASS shape, protocol simulation for anything touching synchronization):
- **C1, L2 hints like FA3:** K/V evict-last, Q evict-first. Target: memory reads 524 → ~370 MB.
- **C2, hand-over done properly:** the loader publishes the **decoded** unit (batch, head, pair), so the compute warps do no integer divisions, and they read it during the last tile's softmax so the read is hidden. That's what F3 failed to do.
- **C3, registers:** F3c (40/232) against F3 (24/240), to settle where the dense loss came from.

**Step 1, one GPU session (~15 minutes, replacing 3–4 separate runs):**
- the correctness suite for every candidate;
- **one round-robin race**: the current best plus all candidates, in the same session;
- forward ncu for each candidate (backward ncu dropped);
- **a full same-session scoreboard against FA3, FA4 and cuDNN**, dense and packed, kernel times plus locked-clock cycles.

**Step 2.** Combine the winners into one build, then one confirmation run, against the rivals.

**Step 3.** Then the last large piece, our softmax (+0.086 M cycles against FA3), studied instruction by instruction.

## What the cross-check found

**Confirmed:** today's forward gains are real. Each version measured in two different sessions agrees within 0.2%:
- dense forward 1.240 → 1.116 ms (−10.0%);
- packed forward 0.575 → 0.516 ms (−10.3%).

**Corrected, and important:** the earlier scoreboard compared **different timing methods**. Our C++ benchmark adds ~10 µs per call; the libraries' Python benchmark adds 83–324 µs. So we looked better than we are. Kernel against kernel, at free clocks:

| | ours | FA3 | FA4 | cuDNN |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **forward dense** (this morning) | 1.202 ms | 0.874 (**ours 1.375×**) | 0.967 | 1.035 |
| forward dense **now** (estimate) | ~1.08 ms | ~1.24× | ~1.12× | ~1.05× |
| forward packed **now** (estimate) | ~0.50 ms | ~1.15× | ~1.01× | ~1.09× |
| **backward dense**, whole call | 3.007 ms | 2.933 (**ours +2.5%, not a tie**) | 2.905 | 3.308 |
| backward packed, whole call | 1.495 ms | 1.495 (tie) | 1.484 | 1.583 |

**Ruled out (checked, no gain possible):** the ptxas version (12.8 and 13.0 give the same code), `-DNDEBUG` (no device asserts in our kernels), and separate K/V pipelines (our K/V wait is already small).

**Real causes, per key tile:**
1. **L2 cache hints:** FA3 marks K/V "keep" and Q "drop first"; we set nothing. Our dense forward reads 524 MB from memory, FA3 367 MB.
2. **Softmax too long:** 1,363 cycles against FA3's 1,186. The other group's GEMMs take 1,024, so the tensor cores sit idle for the difference.
3. **Unit start/end overhead:** 537 cycles per tile against 356.

**Partly true:** the "power coupling". It only shows when the forward gain is large.

---first i compared our attention forward kernel against fa3 line by line , using the per-instruction profiles of both kernels and fa3's own source code , both do the same math for each block of 64 queries x 128 keys , but ours took more time for the same work , i found five reasons : the softmax waited until both matrix multiplies of a block were finished instead of running while the next one was still on the tensor cores , the p·v multiply was done as two half-width instructions instead of one full-width one like fa3 , all work units were the same size so some gpu cores sat idle at the end of every run , the softmax instructions ran in a bad order (a conditional rescale branch stopped the compiler from mixing them , so the exps and the bf16 packing ran in long chains) , and the tensor-core descriptors were rebuilt and moved before every multiply ,,, ,

---then i fixed them one by one , and checked every version with the full correctness suite (296 of 296 checks passed each time) and a 12-round timing race at free clocks against the version before it , in this order : the full-width p·v , fa3's loop order , a dynamic work order (heaviest work first , each gpu core takes the next unit when it is free) , the softmax order with the descriptors kept in uniform registers , fa3's way of handing the next work unit to the compute warps , and fa3's l2 cache hints (keep k/v in l2 , drop q first) , i also tried fa3's register split (24/240) but it made our kernel 1.1% slower than our own split (40/232) , so i kept ours , overall the forward is now 10.0% faster than this morning's kernel on normal attention and 10.8% faster on sft-packed rows ,,, ,

---to see exactly where we stand , i built a fair benchmark that runs ours and every library the same way : each one in its own run , kernel times only , same session , all at the gpu's 700 w power limit as in training , on this benchmark our forward is now faster than cudnn on normal attention and faster than fa4 on packed rows , but still slower than fa3 (our time is 1.17x fa3's on normal and 1.11x on packed) , the remaining gap is in the softmax (1,363 cycles per block in ours vs 1,186 in fa3) and at the start and end of each work unit , tomorrow i will test the combined best version , then the next fixes for the unit start/end and the softmax , and then re-check everything against fa3 , fa4 and cudnn ,,, ,

| forward kernel (free clocks) | normal attention (b8 , 18/6 heads , 4096 tokens) | sft-packed rows |
|---|---|---|
| this morning's kernel | 1.240 ms | 0.575 ms |
| full-width p·v multiply | -3.3% than the version before | -3.2% than the version before |
| fa3 loop order | -0.5% | -1.8% |
| dynamic work order (heaviest first) | -2.6% | -3.6% |
| softmax order + uniform descriptors | -3.8% | -1.5% |
| fa3 hand-over of the next work unit | 0.0% | -1.6% |
| l2 cache hints | -0.2% | -0.1% |
| now | 1.116 ms (-10.0% than this morning) | 0.513 ms (-10.8% than this morning) |
| our time / fa3 , fa4 , cudnn time (fair benchmark , below 1 = ours faster) | 1.17x , 1.05x , 0.99x | 1.11x , 0.98x , 1.05x |

verda h200 usage — 16/10/2026: ran the test_varlen_attention quick suite (296/296 on 9 kernel builds) , 12-round free-clock races (dense b8 18/6 + packed real_rows_752) , nsys + ncu profiles of ours vs fa3/fa4/cudnn , and a free-clock kernel-only scoreboard vs fa3/fa4/cudnn

**Race results** (GPU 7, free clocks, 12 rounds). F3c and C1 both passed 296 of 296 checks. C1 is F3c plus E1.

| comparison | dense fwd | dense bwd | packed fwd | packed bwd |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| F3c vs F2 | −0.10% (t −0.7) | +0.07% (no change) | **−0.84% (t −11.8, faster 12/12)** | +0.09% (t 1.9) |

Forward medians: dense F2 1.124 ms → F3c 1.120 ms; packed 0.500 → 0.496 ms. I checked each result 3 ways: the median, the fastest 10% of iterations (p10), and rounds 1–6 against rounds 7–12. All agree, except one: on dense, F3c's gain shows up only in the fastest 10% (−0.28%, t −5.2), not in the median.

**What this means**
1. **F3c is a real gain on packed** (−0.84%) and maybe a small one on dense.
2. **E1 makes the forward no faster, and it slows the backward that runs right after it.** The backward code is identical in all three libraries, yet packed backward is 0.18% slower after a C1 forward, 0/12 rounds faster. My best guess is the L2 cache state the forward leaves behind, because the bench runs forward then backward back to back. I haven't proven that. On packed, C1 costs about 2.9 µs more per forward + backward than F3c.
3. **Memory traffic is not the forward's problem.** From ncu: E1 cut dense DRAM reads from 522 MB to 449 MB (−14%), but the kernel got only 0.13% faster. So yesterday's open item, "dense DRAM 454 vs FA3 367 MB", is closed: it's not where we lose. The gap is in compute: softmax takes 1,363 vs FA3's 1,186 cycles per tile, and unit start/end takes 537 vs 356.

The main loop fix is ready, built, and checked on the laptop. No GPU used so far.

**Why we lost in the loop.** The compiler (ptxas) always put the "wait for P·V" right after the first row's max. Everything else in the softmax (the second row's max, all 64 exps, the packs) then ran after that wait, so none of it overlapped our own P·V. The source order didn't matter: I tried 8 different code shapes, and ptxas did the same every time.

**What fixes it.** ptxas keeps that wait after an mbarrier arrive that comes before it in the program. I added an arrive whose target depends on the softmax result, on two spare barriers that nobody waits on, so it is always safe. Now the whole softmax runs while P·V is still on the tensor cores. FA3 gets the same effect by accident, from its K-release arrive.

**What K1 contains:**
- the arrive fix above;
- the diagonal tile moved out of the loop (the loop no longer carries the mask branch);
- two P buffers;

### CLAUDE [2026-10-17 12:56 IST]
> tool `Bash`: Paired race statistics for K1, K1s, K1n2 vs F3c

Race numbers are in. Below, negative means faster than F3c. Each is the median of 8 paired rounds, checked against the fastest 10% of runs and the two halves of the race; all agree.

| vs F3c | dense fwd | packed fwd | dense bwd | packed bwd |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **K1** (correct: 296/296) | **−0.95%** (t −7.5, 8/8) | ±0.0% | +0.28% (t 2.0, weak) | +0.07% (no change) |
| K1s (1 P buffer) | +0.94% worse | +2.81% worse | ±0 | −0.31% |
| K1n2 (2 K/V stages) | **+39% worse** | **+22% worse** | −4.2% | −1.8% |

**What this means:**
1. **K1 is a real but small gain.** Dense forward is 1.1220 → 1.1127 ms, packed is unchanged. I had predicted much more: the stall samples said the loop's post-wait block cost +0.198M cycles. Moving the whole softmax before the wait did not convert into that. So my attribution from stall samples overstated it, and something else limits the loop.
2. **One P buffer (K1s) is worse.** The two buffers are needed.
3. **2 K/V stages are a disaster for our kernel (+39%).** We keep K and V of a tile in one shared stage, and that stage stays busy for two tiles (V(n) is read during step n+1). FA3 has separate K and V buffers, so 2 stages work for it but not for us. That also means **K2 as built is dead**: it needed the 64 KB that 2 stages would free. The O-store fix needs memory from somewhere else.
4. **Side effect worth knowing.** When K1n2's forward got slower, the backward right after it got 4% faster. The GPU is power-limited, so a lighter forward leaves more clock for the backward. That fits K1's +0.28% backward, and it is why we must always judge forward + backward together.

FA3's producer confirms two structural differences in K/V handling:
1. **K and V on separate barriers, V one step behind** (lines 871–874). FA3 loads K(n+1), then V(n), and the consumer waits for K before QK and for V before P·V. We wait for K **and** V of tile n before QK(n), although V(n) isn't needed until the next step.
2. **FA3 stages its O output in the V buffer** (lines 848–852, `barrier_O`). That is how FA3 fits the O store into shared memory. For us, the same idea could use the last tile's K buffer, with no need for 2 stages.

Where things stand:
- **K1 at equal clock:** −1.3% cycles (dense 1.721M → 1.698M), tensor busy 69.7% → 70.6%. FA3: 1.432M, 83%.
- **Our loss is per tile, not per unit.** Packed (many short units) is only 4% behind FA3; dense (long loops) is 19% behind.
- **Stall samples can't show the order of events**, which is why my K1 prediction was wrong. The real excess is the consumers' wait / short_sb / mio stalls; the extra long_sb is the producer idling, which is harmless.
- **So the next measurement has to be direct timing:** the trace build of K1. It is K1 plus clock stamps, with the same SASS shape, 0 spills in dense, and its reader tested.

Here's where the analysis stands.

**What the trace showed (K1, dense, per group per tile, at free clock):**
- One step takes **2,531 cycles**; to keep the tensor cores always busy it must be **2,048**.
- **The softmax alone takes 1,413 of them.** By itself (my timing model, same assumptions for both kernels) it would take about 750, and FA3's softmax plus rescale about 850. The extra ~650 cycles come from the **two groups' softmaxes overlapping** on the same special-function unit and colliding with the other group's GEMM issue.
- ncu confirms it: our softmax lines issue only 22% of the time; FA3's issue 34%, because FA3 mixes its 64 rescale multiplies in between the exps.
- Loop-step math: softmax + rescale + K/V wait + overhead must fit in about 1,536 cycles. We are at about 1,710, so **about 170 cycles too much**.
- **The epilogue (writing O) costs 4,230 cycles per pair**: 9% of the time in dense and 21% in packed. FA3 hides this with shared memory and a background TMA store.
- This box runs at only **~1.4–1.45 GHz** under this load.

**Next fix, ready and checked on the laptop: K3 = K1 + a split softmax**, which is FA3's shape:
- the max and part of the exps run before the P·V wait;
- the rest run after it, mixed with the 64 rescale multiplies and the P packs.

I pinned the split exactly in all 5 loop copies, with 0 spills:

| build | exps before wait | exps after (mixed with rescale) |
|---|---|---|
| K1 (now) | 66 | 0 (rescale alone after) |
| **K3h** (model's pick) | 34 | 32 |
| K3q | 17 | 49 |
| K3e (closest to FA3's 13/53) | 9 | 57 |

**The O-store fix** comes after this. The design: stage O in the last tile's K buffer (32 KB, keeps 3 stages), with a small handshake between the two groups.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-17 14:58 IST]

Here's where the run stands.

**Done:**
- the build of K4, K4h, TRK4 and F3c;
- **K4h's correctness suite: it hung.** `exit=124` means the 10-minute timeout killed it, so K4h was dropped;
- race round 1 of 8 (K1, K3h, K3q, K4) at 14:56.

**Still to come:** rounds 2–8 (about 2.2 min each, so until about 15:12), then the two traces.

**Why K4h hung — I found the bug.** It is in my new K4 handshake ("my last QK is done"), and only in **packed** layouts:
- When a group has no rows in a unit (an inactive group), it signals "done" at the very start of that unit.
- So that group can run a whole unit ahead and signal twice before the other group checks.
- The barrier only tracks odd/even rounds. A second signal therefore looks like "not done yet", and the waiting group waits forever.

Dense can't hit this: both groups are always active there. That's why K4 got through round 1, and why its dense numbers will be valid. The packed bench layout seems to avoid the bad timing, while the correctness suite's many layouts hit it.

**The fix:** replace that barrier with a counter that only goes up. The waiting group checks "has the other group signalled at least this many times?", which stays correct even when the other group is a unit ahead. I'm writing it now as K4b.

**What to watch:** if the status shows **no new "race round" line for more than 4 minutes**, a K4 run is hung. Tell me and I'll give you the stop command. Otherwise let it finish.

To confirm the diagnosis, paste this on the box. It only reads the log:
```bash

```

One cheap fix for later: in packed, each unit starts with a global-memory read of its descriptor, which costs up to ~1,000 cycles of waiting per unit. It can be prefetched during the previous unit's last P·V, the same way we already fetch the unit index.

These are optimization tests: each one checks whether a specific speed fix really works before we keep it. Here's the full picture.

**Goal:** make our attention **forward** as fast as FA3. Our backward is already level with FA3 or ahead.

**Where we were this morning (F3c):** the dense forward was about 1.17× slower than FA3, packed about 1.04–1.11×.

**What we found by measuring, and fixed today:**

| problem found | fix | gain (forward) | status |
|---|---|---|---|
| The compiler ran the softmax at the wrong time | K1 | −1% dense | done, correct |
| Writing the output O at each unit's end was very slow (32 small stores per thread) | K4b: write O through shared memory with big stores | **−5.3% dense, −7.4% packed** | done, correct (296/296), **best** |

**Where we are now (estimate):** about **1.09× FA3** in dense, roughly **level with or ahead of FA3** in packed. Forward + backward together: about level with FA3, ahead of FA4 and cuDNN.

**What's still slower than FA3, and what the next run tests:**

| still slow | candidate in the next run | expected |
|---|---|---|
| The two groups' softmaxes collide. The split alone helped (−1.3%/−2.0%) but couldn't be combined with K4b because of spills | **K5**: the split with spills removed | about −1.5% more |
| Packed: each unit starts by waiting for a memory read | **K6**: read it ahead | about −1–2% packed |
| (to measure) the real end-of-unit time | TRK5 trace | tells us what's left |

**Each candidate goes through three checks:**
1. **Correctness**: 296 checks; a fast but wrong kernel is useless.
2. **Race**: 8 paired rounds against K4b, so we only keep real gains.
3. **Trace**: where the time goes now, to choose the next fix.

**Do we need it?** Only if we want to close more of the remaining ~9% dense gap to FA3. The cost is about 13 min of GPU. The other option is to stop here: keep K4b (−6% dense / −7.4% packed today) and move on.

Which do you want: run the K5/K6 test, or stop at K4b?

Here is everything from the memory notes, the work doc and earlier sessions, on all our SFT kernels and how they compare with the others. The K7 run keeps going meanwhile.

## 1. Attention backward (Vj2): faster than everyone ✅
- 10-12 to 10-16: built Vj2, fixed it, then version 3 (mask split, 12% fewer instructions). Correctness 296/296.
- Fair scoreboard 10-16 (free clocks, all libraries in one session):

| backward | ours vs FA3 | vs FA4 | vs cuDNN |
|---|---|---|---|
| dense | **0.96×** | 0.97× | 0.88× |
| packed | **0.98×** | 0.99× | 0.92× |

## 2. Attention forward: big gains, still a little behind FA3 in dense
- 10-16: −10% dense / −10.8% packed (G1, F1, G5, F2, F3c).
- **Today:** K1 → K4b (O store) → **K5q**, a further **−6.5% dense / −11.4% packed**. All 296/296.
- Estimated position now (chained across boxes, ±2–3%):

| forward | vs FA3 | vs FA4 | vs cuDNN |
|---|---|---|---|
| dense | **~1.08×** (FA3 still ~8% ahead) | ~0.97× ahead | ~0.92× ahead |
| packed | **ahead** | ahead | ahead |
| **fwd + bwd, dense** | **~0.99× (level/slightly ahead)** | ahead | ahead |
| **fwd + bwd, packed** | ahead | ahead | ahead |

- Still to do: a **same-box scoreboard** to turn these estimates into measurements (the rivals' environment is on the 8x box), and the K7 race running now.

## 3. Loss kernel (sparse cross-entropy): fixed and measured, but **not yet compared with others**
**What we changed (09-22 to 09-29), all for correctness and memory:**
- `ignore_index` masking in all 5 kernels;
- the loss divided by the count of trained tokens, kept on the GPU with no host sync, the same way PyTorch does it;
- loss and gradient outputs in fp32: bf16 loss error **139× smaller**;
- fixed 2 old bugs (wrong reads in the bf16 vector path, and vocab not a multiple of 4);
- deleted 469 lines of dead code (it had been hiding a link-time trap);
- enabled bf16 logits: **−4.7 GB peak memory, −75% loss memory traffic**, +0.6% step speed. The other team's version crashed with this setting.
- Correctness: 136 cases, 0 failures, same numbers as PyTorch.

**Benchmarked only on its own** (H200, 10-09), one micro-batch with 23% trained tokens:
- forward 0.276 ms + backward 1.600 ms = 1.878 ms;
- masking is **3.2× faster** than computing every position;
- forward reaches 46–67% of memory bandwidth, but **the backward only ~33%**. That's the slow part, never profiled.
- The loss is about **0.3% of an SFT step**, so even a 2× faster loss saves only about 0.15% of a step.

**Never done:** the comparison against **PyTorch `F.cross_entropy`, Liger and Apple CCE** (planned in §38.10 for "later"), and any speed work on it.

**Open issues:**
- B·T > 65,536 drops part of the *logged* loss;
- no check that target ids are in range;
- on B300 the forward ignores masking (parked).

## 4. GEMM (BluBLAS, from pretraining)
The 4B trainer runs at **99.8% of cuBLAS** speed at the production schedule.

## Where that leaves us
| kernel | beating others? |
|---|---|
| attention backward | **yes**, fastest of all |
| attention forward | yes vs FA4/cuDNN; **FA3 still ~8% ahead in dense** (that's the K5q/K7 work) |
| attention fwd + bwd | about level with FA3, ahead of the rest |
| loss | **not measured against others yet** |

Here is the full story of that checkpoint, from work doc §35 and the 10-06 records.

## The checkpoint
- **Source:** Hugging Face repo **`navingv/curriculum_8btokens`** (public, Navin's pretraining run), folder **`blumodel_step_8000`**.
- **"8.4 billion" is the number of training tokens, not the model size.** Step 8000 = 8.4B tokens trained. At that step the training loss was 2.009818 and the validation loss 1.866113.
- **The model is 1.59 billion parameters:** d_model 2304, 26 layers, 18/6 heads, FFN 6144, tied embedding.
- It was saved by a **4-GPU run using the Muon optimizer**.

## "Four checkpoints from 4 GPUs?": one checkpoint split into 4 files
It is **one** checkpoint, written by 4 GPUs as one file per GPU (rank), plus an index:

| file | size | contents |
|---|---|---|
| `metadata.bin` | 129,127 bytes | the index: name, shape, dtype and CRC32 of every tensor, and where each piece is stored |
| **`data_rank_0.bin`** | **6.47 GB** | **all 262 model weights** (3.18 GB) **+** rank 0's share of the optimizer state (3.29 GB) |
| `data_rank_1.bin` | ~3.29 GB | rank 1's optimizer share only |
| `data_rank_2.bin` | ~3.29 GB | rank 2's optimizer share only |
| `data_rank_3.bin` | ~3.29 GB | rank 3's optimizer share only |

Total 16.35 GB. With ZeRO, the optimizer state is split across the 4 GPUs, but the weights are all in rank 0's file.

## What it contains
1. **Model weights:** 262 tensors, 1,588,229,888 numbers. That's 26 layers × 10 tensors (q-norm, k-norm, norm, wQ, wK, wV, wO, norm, gate_up, down), plus `wte` (embedding) and `norm_f`. 54 of them are bf16 (the embedding and 53 norm scales), because Navin trained with `BLU_ALL_BF16=1`.
2. **Optimizer state** (the Muon/AdamW moments), split across the 4 rank files.
3. **Training progress:** step 8000, epoch, data position, loss values.

## What we took: weights only, from rank 0 only
- **We downloaded only `metadata.bin` + `data_rank_0.bin`** (6.5 GB, not 16.35 GB), because rank 0's file holds every weight.
- **Our code:** the `BLU_INIT_FROM=<dir>` switch, 80 lines in `bluscript_zero_ckpt.cpp`, loads **only the 262 weights** right after the model is built, before the optimizer is created. The optimizer then copies those weights into its fp32 master copies.
- **Not loaded on purpose:** the optimizer moments (rank 0's 3.29 GB share is in the file but skipped), the step counter, epoch, data position and LR schedule. SFT starts with a fresh optimizer and its own small learning rate.
- We set `BLU_ALL_BF16=1` too, so every dtype matches the checkpoint with no conversion.
- `rope_theta` isn't stored in the checkpoint. Our trainer's 500000 matched, and the step-0 loss confirmed it.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-17 16:43 IST]
> tool `Bash`: Find our SFT checkpoint details and the CRC32 use in the code

**CRC32** means "Cyclic Redundancy Check, 32 bits". It's a **32-bit fingerprint of a block of bytes**:
- When a checkpoint is saved, the library computes the CRC32 of every tensor's bytes and stores it in `metadata.bin` (the code is `dist/Distributed_Checkpointing/include/Checksums.h`).
- When we loaded Navin's weights with `BLU_INIT_VERIFY=1`, we recomputed the CRC32 of each weight **after it landed in GPU memory** and compared.
- **262/262 matched**, so every byte arrived exactly: no corruption, no wrong position in the file, no wrong dtype. Change even one bit and the fingerprint changes.

**Our SFT checkpoint: yes, the same kind of checkpoint**, the same format and the same two kinds of file. It is the 10-07 full run: AdamW, 5,000 chats, 2 epochs, 156 steps, **1 GPU**. It is `stage0_adamw_full/ckpt/blumodel_step_156`, and we kept only that one; the step-78 copy was deleted.

| | Navin's (pretraining) | ours (SFT) |
|---|---|---|
| GPUs that wrote it | 4 | **1** |
| files | `metadata.bin` + `data_rank_0..3.bin` | **`metadata.bin` + `data_rank_0.bin`** |
| weights | 262 tensors, 3.18 GB | the same 262 tensors, 3.18 GB (bf16) |
| optimizer state | Muon: ~8.3 bytes per parameter, split over 4 files (13.2 GB) | **AdamW: 12 bytes per parameter** (fp32 master copy + 2 moments) = **19.1 GB**, all in the one file |
| progress info | step 8000, loss | step 156, loss |
| **total** | **16.35 GB** | **22.2 GB** |

So yes: ours also has the **metadata file** (index + CRC32 of every tensor + step), the **weights**, and the **full optimizer state**. It's bigger than Navin's because AdamW keeps two moment buffers per weight, while Muon keeps about one. And since it was a 1-GPU run, everything sits in the single `data_rank_0.bin`.

For evals, or to start another run from it, only the weights are needed, loaded the same way as before with `BLU_INIT_FROM`. The optimizer part is only needed to *resume* that same SFT run.

Ready when you want: the forward diagnosis run is steps 1–3 in my previous message (about 17 min).

Yes to both. I checked this against the trainer code in `bluscript_sft.cpp`.

| | DPO / any next stage | continue the same SFT run |
|---|---|---|
| weights | **yes** | **yes** |
| optimizer state (fp32 master + m + v) | no, a new AdamW starts from zero | **yes** |
| step number (where the LR is on the schedule) | no, starts at step 0 with a new warmup | **yes**, it's stored in the checkpoint |
| data position | no, new data | **yes**, the trainer works it out from the step |
| setting in our trainer | `BLU_INIT_FROM=.../ckpt/blumodel_step_156` (the step folder) | `BLU_CKPT_DIR=.../ckpt` (the folder that holds it) |

**DPO**
- `BLU_INIT_FROM` reads only the weight tensors and skips the optimizer part ([bluscript_sft.cpp:1147](../BluTrain_sft/bluscript_sft.cpp#L1147)).
- DPO uses the SFT weights twice:
  - **Policy:** the model you train. It starts from these weights.
  - **Reference:** the same weights, frozen, with no gradients and no optimizer. The DPO loss compares the policy's log-probs on chosen and rejected answers with the reference's.
- The reference log-probs can be computed once before training, with one forward pass over all pairs. Then only one model needs GPU memory during training.
- The new run builds a fresh fp32 master copy from the bf16 weights, and the SFT run's own fp32 master is dropped. Each weight differs by at most one bf16 rounding step. This is the normal way: public models ship as bf16 weights only.
- `bluscript_sft.cpp` has no DPO code yet. It needs paired chosen/rejected data and the DPO loss.

**Continuing the SFT run**
- Run the same command again with `BLU_CKPT_DIR` set. The trainer picks the newest complete checkpoint and loads the weights, the optimizer state and the step. It then skips the chats already used ([bluscript_sft.cpp:2188](../BluTrain_sft/bluscript_sft.cpp#L2188)).
- On "weights too": strictly, the fp32 master in the optimizer part already holds the weights at higher precision. On resume the trainer rebuilds the bf16 weights from it, so the run continues from the full fp32 state, not a rounded copy.
- Check the log for `[resume] loaded DCP checkpoint at step 156`. A wrong folder gives no error: the run quietly starts again from step 0 ([bluscript_sft.cpp:2116](../BluTrain_sft/bluscript_sft.cpp#L2116)).

**Our checkpoint specifically**
- Step 156 is the **end** of that run (156 of 156 steps). Resuming with the same settings runs 0 more steps.
- To train more, for example a 3rd epoch (`BLU_SFT_EPOCHS=3`, 234 steps), the LR curve is stretched over 234 steps. So the LR jumps back up from 0.10× peak, where the run ended, to 0.33× peak at step 156.
- The step-78 checkpoint was deleted, so we can't restart from the middle of that run.

Yes, it's automatic. You don't need to strip anything out of the checkpoint.

**Which setting does what (checked in `bluscript_sft.cpp`):**

| You set | It loads | Use for |
|---|---|---|
| `BLU_INIT_FROM=…/ckpt/blumodel_step_156` | **weights only**. Starts at step 0 with a new optimizer. | DPO, any next stage |
| `BLU_CKPT_DIR=…/ckpt` (the folder that holds `blumodel_step_156`) | **weights + optimizer + step**, and skips the chats already used | continuing that same SFT run |

- `BLU_INIT_FROM` asks the checkpoint for the 262 weight tensors by name and reads only their bytes. The optimizer part stays on disk, unread. That's how Navin's checkpoint loaded, and it also has optimizer state inside.
- Continuing is not done by `BLU_INIT_FROM`. At startup the trainer looks in `BLU_CKPT_DIR`; if it finds a complete checkpoint there, it resumes from it.
- **Trap:** give each new stage a new, empty `BLU_CKPT_DIR`. If that folder holds an old checkpoint, the trainer resumes from it and overwrites the weights `BLU_INIT_FROM` loaded.
- One side effect: `BLU_INIT_FROM` also restores the saved random-number state. It's harmless.

**What the diagnosis run showed (dense forward):**

Each "knock-out" build is K5q with one part of the softmax removed. The outputs are wrong on purpose; we only time them.

| Removed from K5q | Dense | Packed |
|---|---|---|
| the exps | −6.8% | −6.8% |
| the row max | −4.1% | −3.5% |
| the O rescale | −2.4% | −2.2% |
| all three | **−11.2%** | **−11.6%** |

Every one was faster in all 6 rounds. So the softmax is still on the critical path; if it were hidden under the GEMMs, removing it would change nothing.

The per-step clock trace adds four facts:
- **The P·V wait is only 8 cycles.** The tensor cores sit idle about 24% of the loop.
- **Group 0's second softmax half takes 856 cycles; group 1's takes 529.** Group 0's runs at the same time as group 1's first half, so they compete for the same exp unit.
- **Our softmax code is no longer the problem.** A static model gives it 776 cycles against FA3's 850, so ours is already shorter. The gap is in the waits and in how the two groups overlap.
- **The wait at each step start is the strongest lead:**
  - Group 0 waits either ~100–150 or ~275–300 cycles, almost never in between, and identically on every SM. In dense it takes the long one on 95% of steps.
  - Our wait code is a plain retry loop. FA3, FA4 and cuDNN all use CUTLASS's version: check, then sleep until the barrier wakes it.
  - FA3's in-loop K/V checks (285,696 of them) never had to retry.
  - FA3 also waits for K alone. We wait for K and V together (64 KB), although V is only needed one step later.
  - Caveat: the trace's own clock reads can be delayed, so this is strong evidence, not proof. The race decides.

One correction: K9's "filler independence" failure had a concrete bug behind it. Masked keys got 2⁻¹²⁶ instead of 0. I fixed it; masked keys now give exactly 0.

**Next run.** All five candidates are compiled and checked on the laptop: 0 spills, and K5q's compiled code is unchanged by the edits.

| Build | What it is |
|---|---|
| W1 | K5q + CUTLASS's wait (what FA3 uses) |
| W1s | K5q + a spinning wait (never sleeps) |
| W2 | W1 + separate K and V barriers, so the step waits only for K, as FA3 does |
| P8w / P4w | W1 + every 8th / 4th exp done by the polynomial instead of the exp unit |
| TLW2 | W2 + the clock trace, to check whether the two-size wait disappears |

Each build must pass the 296-check suite before it's raced; a failing build is dropped automatically. It takes about 25 minutes: 7 builds ≈ 14, checks ≈ 3, race of 8 rounds ≈ 9, trace under 1. It uses GPU 0 only. I haven't run anything; start it when you're ready.

Here are the full results of the last forward run (W run, 17:57–18:12 IST, GPU 0, 8 rounds, forward only). **Nothing to adopt: K5q stays the best forward.**

**Correctness:** all 5 candidates passed 296/296, including the bit-exact "packed = alone" checks.

**Speed vs K5q** (median of 8 rounds; negative = faster):

| Build | Dense ms | vs K5q | Packed ms | vs K5q | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| K5q (base) | 1.1008 | – | 0.4583 | – | – |
| W1 (FA3's wait form) | 1.1010 | −0.07% (t −0.8, faster 4/8) | 0.4582 | −0.04% | no change |
| W2 (W1 + K and V on separate barriers) | 1.0993 | −0.11% (t −0.6, faster 6/8) | 0.4594 | +0.10% | no change |
| W1s (spinning wait) | 1.1019 | +0.14% | 0.4607 | +0.44% (t +5.5, faster 0/8) | slower |
| P8w (1 in 8 exps by polynomial) | 1.1289 | **+2.7%** (t +15, faster 0/8) | 0.4744 | **+3.4%** | slower |
| P4w (1 in 4 exps by polynomial) | 1.1772 | **+7.1%** (t +37, faster 0/8) | 0.4926 | **+7.4%** | slower |

**What it taught us:**
- **The waits were spare time, not the cost.** The W2 trace shows group 0's wait at each step start dropped from ~300 to ~240 cycles. But the next phases grew by the same amount, so the loop time didn't change.
- **The limit is the number of instructions in the softmax.** Each extra instruction per tile costs about 0.035%, whether it's the polynomial's or the rescale's. The exp unit is not the bottleneck on H200, so FA4's polynomial trick doesn't help here.

**Where the forward stands:**
- K5q is best for packed SFT; K7e is 0.8% better on dense only.
- Since F3c (this morning): −6.5% dense and −11.4% packed.
- Against FA3 (an estimate chained across boxes and days): FA3 is about 7–9% faster on dense; we're about 2–3% faster on packed.
- The laptop's `GQA_fwd_sm90.cu` is still F3c; adopting K5q is your call.

**The one concrete difference left vs FA3:** one loop step is 499 instructions in ours vs 455 in FA3, so 44 more:
- +23 setup instructions for the GEMM descriptors
- +14 integer and compare instructions
- +6 additions from the trick that keeps the softmax ahead of the P·V wait
- +2 barrier instructions, because we issue two predicated barriers where FA3 issues one

At ~0.035% each, trimming them is worth at most ~1.5%. That can't close a 7–9% gap.

**My recommendation for the forward:** measure FA3 on this same box first, so we know the real gap and can profile both kernels under identical conditions.

Yes, the math is the same as FA3's, and so is the amount of work. Our warps just spend more time waiting, and most of that waiting is at the start and end of each 128-row block (one pair), not inside the main loop.

**What the data shows** (all from measurements we already had):

- **It's not the clock.** On 10-16, on the same box, both ran at about 1,665 MHz and 693 W. The two boxes are also equivalent: K1 took 1.1127 ms on the 8x box and 1.1123 ms on the 2x box.
- **It's not extra work.** At a locked clock, K1 (our newest profiled build) runs almost the same instruction count as FA3, yet needs 18% more cycles:

  | | FA3 | Ours (K1) |
  |---|---|---|
  | Instructions | 306.5M | 311.9M (+1.8%) |
  | Cycles | 1.42M | 1.68M (+18%) |
  | Cycles where an instruction issues | 41% | 35% |
  | Tensor cores busy | 83% | 71% |

- **The extra waiting is mostly at block boundaries**, measured per code region:

  | Region | FA3 | Ours (K1) | Extra |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Main loop | 68.7k samples | 72.0k | +5% |
  | Block start/end (prologue, diagonal tile, epilogue, waits) | ~18.7k | ~31.3k | **+67%** |

  About 77% of the excess was at block start/end.
- **The worst spots were all store traffic** in K1's epilogue:
  - Each thread wrote O with 32 small stores. The store queue filled, and the next instruction waited for it: 2,011 samples, the single biggest hotspot.
  - The shuffles at the next block's start (1,092) and the epilogue's row-sum shuffles (1,507) were stuck behind the same traffic.
  - K4b (8 wider stores through shared memory) fixed much of this, which is why it gained 5.3%.

**What is still different from FA3 in K5q:**
1. **How O is written.** FA3 writes a dense block's O with one TMA store from one thread, and the warps continue immediately; it keeps per-row stores only for varlen (packed). We still do 8 shared loads + 8 global stores per thread.
2. **The block start.** Each block waits ~160 cycles for Q and ~430 cycles for the first K/V tile (from the K5q trace).
3. **The loop.** 44 more bookkeeping instructions per step.

Changing how O is stored doesn't change any value, so the bit-exact packed = alone rule stays safe.

**Next, to stop estimating:** K4b and K5q have never been profiled with ncu. One profile of K5q (dense + packed), about 4 minutes on GPU 0 after the loss run finishes, gives the same region split for today's kernel. Then I build the fix the data points to, most likely the TMA store for dense O plus an earlier Q / first-tile prefetch.

Our loss gives exactly the right answers and beats every PyTorch version by a wide margin, but **Liger is faster than ours**: 19% at the median SFT batch. The reason is one weak spot in our backward kernel. The run also showed a bigger SFT win, in the lm_head rather than the loss.

**Correctness:** both sides used identical logits (checked bit for bit) and the same 6 batches. PyTorch fp32 gives our loss to 6 decimals in all 5 trained cases (median batch: 12.740235 in both). `torch.compile`'s and Liger's gradients match PyTorch fp32 exactly at the checked row.

**Loss only (logits given), forward + backward in ms.** This is the fair number, because each library splits the work between forward and backward differently.

| Batch (rows trained) | Ours | Liger | torch.compile | PyTorch bf16 | PyTorch fp32 (HF way) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| min (9%) | 1.232 | 1.206 (2% faster) | 3.896 | 6.226 | 21.14 |
| **median (23%)** | **1.885** | **1.525 (19% faster)** | 3.917 | 6.231 | 21.14 |
| max (39%) | 2.597 | 1.886 (27% faster) | 3.921 | 6.234 | 21.15 |
| no masking (100%) | 5.387 | 3.279 (39% faster) | 3.964 (26% faster) | 6.266 | 21.17 |
| all masked (0%) | **0.859** | 1.004 | 3.896 | 6.220 | 21.14 |

- On SFT batches we're 2–3× faster than `torch.compile`, 3–5× faster than PyTorch bf16, and 8–17× faster than the HF fp32 way.
- **Memory:** between forward and backward we keep only 0.25 MiB (each row's max and sum), versus 3–6 GiB for PyTorch eager. But our backward writes a separate 3.1 GiB gradient buffer. Liger needs no extra buffer, because it writes the gradient into the logits tensor itself.

**Why Liger wins with the same data movement:** both read the trained rows twice and write every gradient row once (4.82 GB at the median batch). Liger does it at 3.2 TB/s, we do it at 2.6 TB/s.
- The slow part is our **backward on trained rows**: 1.5 TB/s, 31% of the memory bandwidth limit. `torch.compile`'s backward does the same reads and writes at 3.3 TB/s (2.0 ms vs our 4.4 ms with no masking).
- The cause is in `LossKernels.cu` (`sparseCENormalize_from_stats`): each thread loads one 16-byte chunk, computes, stores, and only then loads the next. With only one load in flight per thread, memory never gets busy enough.
- Our forward is fine at 3.2 TB/s, and plain zero-writing runs at 4.0 TB/s.

**lm_head + loss (hidden states given), forward + backward in ms.** "Ours" here is cuBLAS GEMMs plus our loss; our BLAS runs at about cuBLAS speed.

| Batch | Ours | Liger fused | Apple CCE | PyTorch |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| median (23%) | 36.3 | 33.7 (−7%) | **31.7 (−13%)** | 49.8 |
| max (39%) | 37.0 | 35.7 (−4%) | 52.4 (+41%) | 50.4 |
| no masking | 39.8 | 39.0 (−2%) | 135.6 (3.4× slower) | 52.6 |

- **Peak extra memory:** ours 6.5 GiB, Liger 0.55 GiB, CCE 0.36 GiB, PyTorch 18.4 GiB.
- **The most important finding:** CCE wins at the median batch only because it **skips the masked tokens inside the lm_head itself**. Its own kernels are about half cuBLAS's speed, which is why it loses badly at 39% and 100% trained.
- If we run the lm_head + loss **only on the trained positions**, with our fast GEMM, the median micro-batch would drop from ~36 ms to an estimated ~9.5 ms. That's about 0.2 s per optimizer step, roughly 4–5% of a step (estimated, not measured).

**What I'd fix, in order of value.** Nothing is started; your call.
1. **Trainer:** lm_head + loss on trained positions only. Biggest SFT win.
2. **Backward kernel:** keep 4–8 loads in flight per thread, and zero masked rows with 16-byte stores. Expected: median batch forward + backward about 1.4 ms, which beats Liger's 1.525.
3. **Gradient in place**, written into the logits buffer: −3.1 GiB peak, same memory as Liger.

Items 2 and 3 are small kernel changes we can measure with this same bench. Liger's newer CuTe-DSL backend wasn't measured; it needs one more package.
