I've fixed my earlier claim in both the work doc (§45.63) and memory.

**1. There's no difference between ours and hers.** In our compiled bf16 loss backward, 20 of the 21 conversion instructions convert **two** values each. The one single conversion is the leftover tail element. The compiler pairs our one-at-a-time calls automatically, because in our 16-byte store two results always sit side by side. So we and she get the **same instruction** (`F2FP.BF16.F32.PACK_AB` with two sources).

**2. Is 2 the maximum?** Yes, on H100/H200. The fp32→bf16 conversion instruction writes one 32-bit register, which holds exactly 2 bf16 values. 8 values need 4 instructions, in our kernel and in hers. Don't mix this up with memory: loads and stores move 8 values at once (16 bytes), and that part is separate. The other direction, bf16→fp32, is one bit shift per value in both kernels.

**3. Which one does `Types.h` use?** The scalar one: `__float2bfloat16_rn`, one value per call, because a `bfloat16_t` holds one value. It costs nothing extra, since the compiler merges neighbouring calls into the paired instruction.

**4. Do the loss kernels use our conversion kernel?** No. They convert in registers: `bfloat16_t` → `Types.h` → the hardware instruction, as you said.

**5. Future task #1 is a different kernel.** It's the trainer's separate cast kernel, `convert_type_kernel`, used by `to_dtype`/`as_type` and the optimizer for whole tensors:

| | H200 today (`convert_type_kernel`) | B300 vec8 kernel |
|---|---|---|
| work per thread | **1 element** (2–4 byte accesses) | **8 elements** (2 × `float4` in, 16 bytes out) |
| conversion | 1 value per instruction | 2 per instruction (`__float22bfloat162_rn`) |
| result | 35–40% of memory bandwidth | fast |

Its slowness comes from **memory access**, not from the conversion instruction. Enabling vec8 for H200 is the task, after measuring how much of the step casts still take.

**So:** her DPO kernel needs no change. Moving our loss kernels to `CudaNativeType` later would change only how the code is written, not the instructions it runs.

**The cast kernel is the real place to gain.** Each thread there converts **one** element. It writes CUDA's intrinsics by hand (`__float2bfloat16`, `__bfloat162float`) for bf16/fp16 inputs, and uses our type otherwise. With one value per thread there's nothing to pair, and each thread also moves only 2–4 bytes, which is why it reaches only 35–40% of memory bandwidth. The fix is the vec8 design: 8 values per thread, 16-byte accesses, paired conversions.

**"SFT kernels" = the three kernels we modified; no new kernels:**
1. **Loss:** masking, the 1/N denominator, plus our optimizations.
2. **Attention:** packed rows (per-chat plan) in QPU forward and Vj2 backward.

Everything else in an SFT step is the unchanged pretraining kernels.

**Schedule on one GPU (about 1 hour from when you're back):**

| Time | GPU | In parallel (CPU) |
|---|---|---|

| T+46 → 55 | **A5 RoPE:** with vs without positions (= feature overhead) vs PyTorch, torch.compile, Liger | |
| T+55 → 60 | pull everything, build the tables | |

**Results** (time; less is better):

| kernel | result |
|---|---|
| loss fwd+bwd | fastest in all 6 cases. Liger takes 1.29–1.39× our time, torch.compile 1.5–4.9×, PyTorch 2.4–7.9×. Bit-identical to the old kernel, at 0.49–0.91 of its time |
| lm_head + loss | **behind:** CCE is 9% and Liger FLCE 5% faster on the median SFT batch. Our lm_head computes logits for the 77% masked tokens too |
| attention, dense | forward ties with FA3 (+0.6%). fwd+bwd: 1.8% / 3.0% / 12.7% less time than FA3 / FA4 / cuDNN |
| attention, packed | fwd+bwd: 6.5% / 7.7% / 11.9% less time. FlexAttention takes 1.6–1.8× our time |
| RMSNorm + RoPE | 26% / 34% less time than torch.compile (fwd / bwd). The positions feature costs +0.7% / +2.5% |
| full SFT run | packing gives the same val drop (0.1629 vs 0.1625) in 5.1 min instead of 17.0 min |

Three things the report states openly:
- **Small val gap between the runs:** the 0.003 gap comes from the loader dropping different leftover rows from the two val sets, not from training.
- **Memory:** the lower memory of the packed run comes mostly from its smaller micro-batch (4 rows vs 8).
- **The 7-layout attention sweep is biased:** it favours the other libraries because our process ran at a 17% lower clock there. That's why the report quotes the one-library-per-process scoreboard.

**Email text, ready to paste:**

> Hi Kathirvel, here are the SFT kernel stats against the other libraries, all measured today on one H200 with the current SFT code. Full tables are in the attached doc.
> - Loss (fwd+bwd): fastest in all cases. Liger takes 1.29-1.39x our time, torch.compile 1.5-4.9x, PyTorch 2.4-7.9x.
> - Attention (fwd+bwd): dense takes 1.8% / 3.0% / 12.7% less time than FlashAttention 3 / FlashAttention 4 / cuDNN. Packed rows take 6.5% / 7.7% / 11.9% less. The dense forward alone is a tie with FA3.
> - QK RMSNorm + RoPE: 26% (fwd) and 34% (bwd) less time than torch.compile. Liger takes 3.4-3.7x our time.
> - Padding vs packing, full SFT run on 5,000 chats: the same loss curve in 5.1 min instead of 17.0 min.
> - Still behind: lm_head + loss on SFT batches, where Apple CCE is 9% faster because it skips masked tokens. My next step is to run the lm_head only on the trained tokens.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-21 19:19 IST]

**Not one chat per row in both.** The padded run is the same run as before (not rerun). Only the new packed run is built differently: it uses the same chats in every step as the padded run.

| | padded run (from before) | new packed run (running now) |
|---|---|---|
| chats per row | 1, rest is pad | 1 to 6 (2.3 on average) |
| chats per step | 64 | **the same 64 chats as padded step s** |
| rows per step | 64 | 28 |
| rows per micro-batch × micro-batches | 8 × 8 | 4 × 7 |
| steps | 156 | 156 |
| trained tokens per step | 49,618–74,892 | **identical to padded, every step** |
| learning rate per step | same schedule | same schedule |
| val set | 496 chats, 1 per row | **the same 496 chats, 1 per row** |

**How a step is built:**
1. Take the 64 chats that padded step s used.
2. Pack them into 28 rows of 4,096 tokens: the longest chat goes first, and each chat goes into the row with the most free space. That way every row gets at least one chat, because the loader refuses empty rows.
3. Each chat attends only to itself, and its positions restart at 0.

```
padded step s:  row 1 [chat A ....pad....]      packed step s:  row 1 [chat A | chat F | pad]
                row 2 [chat B ...pad.....]                      row 2 [chat B | chat G | chat K | pad]
                ...  64 rows                                     ...  28 rows, the same 64 chats
```

**Why 28 rows:** the longest steps need up to 27 rows for their 64 chats. 28 is the next multiple of 4 (4 rows per micro-batch).

**Steps are based on chats, not tokens:** always the same 64 chats per step as padding. So the token count per step also comes out identical.

**Difference from the first packed run:** that run took 20 rows per step from a file packed and shuffled over the whole dataset. So each of its steps had 54–78 different chats. This run fixes exactly that.

**Cost:** the rows are only 69% full, compared with 99.6% in the first packed run. So this run is slower than the first packed run (2.2 s per step against 1.6 s). It is only for proving that the numbers match, not for speed.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-21 19:35 IST]

**The val-set gap was my mistake.** For the packed run I picked 4 rows per micro-batch, because 20 rows per step has to divide by it. The loader uses the same micro-batch size for val, and it drops the last incomplete micro-batch:

- **Padded val:** 500 rows ÷ 8 = 62 micro-batches, so 4 chats were dropped.
- **Packed val:** 147 rows ÷ 4 = 36 micro-batches, so 3 rows (10 chats) were dropped.

I didn't check that before the run, so the two runs measured slightly different val chats. The right setup was the same val rows in both runs, which is what I did in test 2. That's why the gap disappeared there.

**Why packing's line in graph (c) comes down sooner although both do 156 steps:**

The x-axis of (c) is minutes, not steps. Per step both runs learn exactly the same: graph (b), which uses steps (epochs), shows the lines on top of each other. (c) only shows that a packed step takes less time, because it computes fewer tokens for the same chats:

| | padding | packing (test 2) |
|---|---|---|
| chats per step | 64 | the same 64 |
| rows per step | 64 | 28 |
| token positions computed per step (rows × 4,096) | 262,144 | 114,688 (0.44×) |
| share of those that are real chat tokens | ~30% (the rest is pad) | 69% |
| step time | 5.01 s | 2.18 s (0.44×) |

The GPU computes every position of every row, pad included: all the matmuls, the attention and the lm_head. Padding spends about 70% of each step on pad tokens. Packing puts the same chats into fewer rows, so each step does 0.44× the work and takes 0.44× the time. The same val loss at step k is therefore reached after fewer minutes. Learning per step is the same; only the time per step is shorter. (In test 1 the rows were 99.6% full, so a step took only 1.63 s.)

- **5.2 (c) and 5.5 (c):** why packing's line comes down sooner over time. It is less compute per step for the same chats, not faster learning.

I checked the time numbers against the logs. Validation took about 4 minutes in both test 2 runs, because both used the same 496 rows. So the whole gap in (c) comes from the training steps: 156 × 5.01 s = 13.0 min for padding against 156 × 2.18 s = 5.7 min for packing.

## How to read these tables

- **Micro-batch:** one call of the kernel = 8 rows × 4,096 tokens = 32,768 token positions.
- **Trained tokens:** in supervised fine-tuning (SFT), the loss is computed only on the assistant's answer tokens. Prompt tokens and padding tokens are masked, which means the loss skips them.
- **The six loss cases (table 1 and 2):**

| case name | what it is | trained tokens of 32,768 |
|---|---|---|
| fewest trained | the real micro-batch from the stage-0 data with the fewest answer tokens | 2,920 (8.9%) |
| first | the first micro-batch of the stage-0 data | 6,112 (18.7%) |
| median | the typical micro-batch: the middle one when all micro-batches are sorted by trained tokens | 7,577 (23.1%) |
| most trained | the real micro-batch with the most answer tokens | 12,729 (38.8%) |
| no masking | every token is trained; this is what pretraining does | 32,768 (100%) |
| all masked | no token is trained; the lowest possible cost | 0 (0%) |

- **Ratio:** other library's time ÷ BluTrain's time. **Above 1.00 means BluTrain is faster.** For example, 1.30× means the other library takes 1.30 times as long as BluTrain.
- **bf16:** 16-bit floating point (bfloat16). **fp32:** 32-bit floating point.

## 0. Setup (applies to every table)

| | |
|---|---|
| **GPU** | 1× NVIDIA H200 with 141 GB memory, 700 W power limit, clocks not locked (the same as in training) |
| **Software** | CUDA 13.2, NVIDIA driver 580.178.04, PyTorch 2.14.1 (built for CUDA 13.0), Triton 3.8.0 |
| **Other libraries compared** | FlashAttention 3 version 3.0.0 (Hopper build), FlashAttention 4 version 4.0.0b34, NVIDIA cuDNN 9.24 (called through PyTorch), Liger Kernel 0.8.5, Apple Cut Cross-Entropy 25.1.1, PyTorch torch.compile, plain PyTorch (eager mode) |
| **Model** | 1.6 billion parameters: 8 rows × 4,096 tokens per micro-batch, 18 query heads and 6 key/value heads, head dimension 128, vocabulary 50,304 tokens, bf16 |
| **Data** | real stage-0 SFT data from UltraChat: 5,000 chats, either padded (one chat per row, 5,000 rows) or packed (several chats per row, 1,517 rows) |
| **Timing method** | median of 30 to 2,000 calls, after at least 4 seconds of warm-up; the same inputs for every library. For attention: kernel time from the NVIDIA Nsight Systems profiler, each library in its own process, run in the order BluTrain, FlashAttention 3, FlashAttention 4, cuDNN and then in reverse, twice |
| **Date** | all measured fresh on 21 October 2026 with the current SFT branch code |

## 1. Loss: sparse cross-entropy, forward + backward

| | |
|---|---|
| **BluTrain kernel** | the SFT loss: skips masked prompt and padding tokens, one shared denominator (the trained-token count) for the whole optimizer step, 16-byte memory loads, gradient written over the logits (no second buffer) |
| **Shape** | logits of 32,768 tokens × 50,304 vocabulary entries in bf16; targets as 16-bit integers |
| **Other libraries** | Liger cross-entropy; torch.compile of the fp32 loss; plain PyTorch on bf16 logits; plain PyTorch on fp32 logits (what Hugging Face Transformers does) |
| **Measured** | forward + backward together (Liger computes its gradient inside its forward, so only the sum is a fair comparison) |

| case (trained tokens) | BluTrain time | Liger | torch.compile | PyTorch bf16 | PyTorch fp32 (Hugging Face way) |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| fewest trained (8.9%) | **1.003 ms** | 1.30× | 3.86× | 6.21× | 21.1× |
| first (18.7%) | **1.173 ms** | 1.30× | 3.30× | 5.31× | 18.0× |
| median (23.1%) | **1.255 ms** | 1.29× | 3.09× | 4.96× | 16.8× |
| most trained (38.8%) | **1.530 ms** | 1.29× | 2.55× | 4.08× | 13.8× |
| no masking (100%, pretraining) | **2.603 ms** | 1.38× | 1.51× | 2.41× | 8.14× |
| all masked (0%) | **0.789 ms** | 1.39× | 4.91× | 7.89× | 26.8× |
| extra memory used | **0.2 MiB** | 0.3 MiB | 3,144 MiB | 9,432 MiB | 18,864 MiB |

**Result:** BluTrain is the fastest in all 6 cases. Its loss value equals PyTorch fp32 within 0.000001, and all 6 gradient checks pass.

## 2. Output layer + loss together (compared with fused libraries)

| | |
|---|---|
| **Measured** | the output layer (language-model head: hidden states of 32,768 tokens × 2,304 times a 2,304 × 50,304 weight matrix) plus the loss, forward + backward |
| **BluTrain** | the matrix multiplications (cuBLAS in this test; BluBLAS in training, which runs at the same speed) plus the BluTrain loss |
| **Other libraries** | plain PyTorch; Liger Fused Linear Cross-Entropy (it fuses the output layer and the loss); Apple Cut Cross-Entropy (it never stores the full logits), in its default mode and its exact mode |

| case (trained tokens) | BluTrain time | PyTorch | Liger Fused Linear Cross-Entropy | Apple Cut Cross-Entropy | Apple Cut Cross-Entropy, exact |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| median (23.1%) | 34.93 ms | 1.40× | 0.95× | 0.91× | 0.90× |
| most trained (38.8%) | 35.20 ms | 1.41× | 0.98× | 1.50× | 1.47× |
| no masking (100%) | **36.28 ms** | 1.44× | 1.07× | 3.73× | 3.67× |
| peak memory | 3,144 MiB (keeps the bf16 logits for the backward) | 18,864 MiB | 563 MiB | 367 MiB | |

**Result:** on the typical SFT micro-batch (median), Apple Cut Cross-Entropy is 9% faster and Liger Fused Linear Cross-Entropy 5% faster. The reason: the BluTrain output layer also computes logits for the 77% of tokens that are masked. With every token trained, BluTrain is the fastest. **Next step:** run the output layer only on the trained tokens.

## 3. Attention, dense (pretraining, and SFT with padding)

| | |
|---|---|
| **BluTrain kernel** | causal grouped-query attention: our forward kernel (version "QPU") and backward kernel (version "Vj2") |
| **Shape** | 8 rows × 4,096 tokens, 18 query heads and 6 key/value heads, head dimension 128, bf16, causal (each token sees only earlier tokens) |
| **Other libraries** | FlashAttention 3 (its default backward), FlashAttention 4, NVIDIA cuDNN |
| **Method** | kernel time from NVIDIA Nsight Systems, one library per process, at least 4 seconds of work per run, alternating order twice, only the steady part after the first 2 seconds |

| pass | BluTrain time | FlashAttention 3 | FlashAttention 4 | cuDNN |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| forward | 0.983 ms | 0.977 ms (0.99×) | 1.071 ms (1.09×) | 1.188 ms (1.21×) |
| backward | **3.190 ms** | 3.271 ms (1.03×) | 3.230 ms (1.01×) | 3.593 ms (1.13×) |
| forward + backward | **4.173 ms** | 4.248 ms (1.02×) | 4.301 ms (1.03×) | 4.781 ms (1.15×) |

**Result:** the forward is a tie with FlashAttention 3 (BluTrain takes 0.6% longer). Everywhere else BluTrain is faster. The same test on 19 October on the 8-GPU machine gave the same result.

## 6. Query/key RMS normalization + rotary position embedding (fused)

| | |
|---|---|
| **BluTrain kernel** | one fused kernel that does the RMS normalization (with its learned scale) and the rotary position embedding for the queries and the keys, one pass forward and one pass backward |
| **Shape** | queries [8, 18, 4096, 128] and keys [8, 6, 4096, 128] in fp32; rotary base 10,000; normalization epsilon 0.000001; positions of 8 real packed rows (29 chats, every chat restarts at position 0) |

| pass | BluTrain time | torch.compile | Liger | plain PyTorch |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| forward | **0.210 ms** | 0.285 ms (1.36×) | 0.780 ms (3.71×) | 2.483 ms (11.8×) |

## 7. What the SFT features cost, against the BluTrain pretraining kernels

| feature | cost |
|---|---|
| per-chat positions in the rotary embedding (packed vs no positions) | forward +0.7%, backward +2.5%; with positions 0, 1, 2, … the output is bit-identical to the version without positions |
| packed attention on rows with one full 4,096-token chat (nothing to save) | forward +1.5%, backward 0% compared with the dense kernel |
| dense attention | the same code as pretraining, so no SFT cost |
| loss | the same kernel for pretraining and SFT |

| against the older pretraining kernels (same machine, same day) | new time ÷ old time |
|---|---|
| attention, dense | forward 0.84, backward 0.71, forward + backward 0.74 |
| loss on the six SFT cases | forward + backward 0.49 to 0.91; gradients bit-identical |
| loss with the gradient written in place (what training uses) | within 1.7% of the separate-buffer version; gradients bit-identical |

## 8. Padding vs packing for the same chats (kernel level)

**How it is computed:** padded time = number of chats × the dense kernel's time for one 4,096-token row (one chat per row, the rest is padding). Packed time = the BluTrain packed kernel on the 8 packed rows that hold those chats. Attention forward + backward:

| rows | chats | padded | packed | packed ÷ padded |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| real rows 0–7 (the longest chats) | 15 | 7.69 ms | 3.86 ms | 0.50 |
| real rows 752–759 (middle) | 24 | 12.57 ms | 2.01 ms | 0.16 |
| real rows 1504–1511 (the shortest chats) | 72 | 36.95 ms | 1.29 ms | 0.035 |
| chats of 512 tokens | 64 | 32.83 ms | 1.23 ms | 0.038 |
| chats of 1,024 tokens | 32 | 16.58 ms | 1.64 ms | 0.099 |
| chats of 2,048 tokens | 16 | 8.35 ms | 2.49 ms | 0.30 |
| chats of 4,096 tokens (nothing to save) | 8 | 4.19 ms | 4.21 ms | 1.00 |

**Result:** on real rows, attention needs 2 to 28 times less time when packed. The loss for one full pass over the data takes 0.78 s padded and 0.42 s packed.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-21 21:23 IST]

**Short answer:**

- **Loss change:** needed for any SFT, padded or packed.
- **Per-chat attention (varlen):** needed only when you pack.
- **RoPE position restart:** **not strictly needed** once attention is per chat. Without it the training math is the same and only the rounding changes. I kept it because it makes a packed chat give exactly the same numbers as the chat alone, it matches inference, and it costs almost nothing.

## 1. Why the RoPE restart is not strictly needed

RoPE rotates q and k by an angle that grows with the position. When attention multiplies q of token i with k of token j, the rotations cancel except for the **difference i − j**. So the attention score depends only on how far apart the two tokens are, not on where the chat starts.

```
packed row:  [ chat A: positions 0..1199 | chat B: positions 1200..1999 | pad ]

chat B, token 1210 looks at token 1205:
  without restart:  positions 1210 and 1205  -> distance 5
  with restart:     positions   10 and    5  -> distance 5      (same score)
```

Per-chat attention already stops chat B from seeing chat A. Every score inside chat B then uses the same distances with or without the restart, so the result is the same in exact math.

**What changes without the restart:** only rounding. The rotated q and k are computed in fp32 at different angles and then rounded to bf16. The numbers then differ in the last bits, not in any systematic way.

**Why I still restart the positions:**
1. **Exact equality:** a packed chat gives bit-for-bit the same q, k, attention and loss as the same chat alone. That is what let us test packing exactly. The attention tests require "packed == alone, bit for bit", and test 2 matched padding to 6 digits at step 0. Without the restart, only "close" could be checked, not "equal".
2. **Training matches inference:** at inference a chat always starts at position 0.
3. **It is the standard way:** Hugging Face's packing collator (DataCollatorWithFlattening) and torchtitan also restart the positions for every chat.
4. **It costs almost nothing:** +0.7% forward and +2.5% backward on a kernel that is a very small part of the step.

## 2. What matters a lot: per-chat attention when packing

Without it, in a packed row chat B's tokens also attend to all of chat A's tokens (they are earlier in the row, so the causal mask allows it):

```
without per-chat attention:   chat B sees  [ chat A ......... | chat B so far ]   <- wrong
with per-chat attention:      chat B sees  [                  | chat B so far ]   <- same as alone
```

- The model then trains with an unrelated conversation in its context. At inference that context never exists, so training and use don't match.
- **Restart without per-chat attention is even worse.** Chat B would see chat A at nonsense distances, for example token 5 of B looking at token 1100 of A with a negative distance.

So for packing, per-chat attention is **required**. The RoPE restart on top is optional for correctness, and I keep it for the reasons above.

## 3. The loss changes are needed for any SFT

| loss change | what goes wrong without it |
|---|---|
| mask prompt and pad tokens | the model also trains to write the user's prompt and to output pad tokens. In padded rows about 70% of positions are pad. |
| one denominator per optimizer step (all trained tokens of the step) | with a mean per micro-batch, a token's weight depends on how many trained tokens share its micro-batch. Tokens of short answers get much more weight than tokens of long answers. |
| 16-byte loads, gradient written in place | not needed for correctness, only speed (loss about 1.5–2× faster) and memory (one 3 GiB buffer less) |

## 4. All the cases in one table

| setup | per-chat attention | RoPE restart | loss masking + one denominator | result |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| padded SFT (1 chat per row) | not needed: pads come after the chat, and causal attention never looks forward | not needed: the chat starts at 0 anyway | **needed** | correct |
| packed, neither attention nor restart | ✗ | ✗ | needed | chats see earlier chats in the row; training ≠ inference |
| packed, restart only | ✗ | ✓ | needed | chats still see each other, at wrong distances; worse |
| packed, per-chat attention only | ✓ | ✗ | needed | same math as padded; differs only in rounding |
| **packed, both (what BluTrain has)** | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | bit-identical to each chat alone; test 2 matched padding step by step |

For our SFT pipeline: with padding, only the loss change is needed. With packing, the loss change and per-chat attention are needed. The RoPE restart is the small extra that makes packing exactly equal to padding, instead of equal up to rounding.

Subject : improving the fwd gqa

After yesterday's grid reordering and uniform fixes, the baseline kernel was taking ~1.70M cycles with tensor cores 69.7% busy. looked into NCU to check where the time is still being lost, ~24% of all warp stalls were spent waiting on matrix multiply instructions (wgmma.wait_group), and consumer warps were executing the entire Softmax while tensor cores sat completely idle.

Implemented a loop rotation, an order fence, and a split Softmax which cut runtime by 7.4% in cycles (1,704,528 -> 1,578,448), pushed tensor core busy up to 77.6%, and kept identical numerical parity across all shapes. B4 also dropped from ~870k to 809k cycles.

Softmax running with tensor cores idle: The original loop waited for all matrix multiplies (DEPBAR 0x0) before starting Softmax. During that entire Softmax period, the warpgroup had no tensor instructions in flight, leaving tensor cores underutilized.
So for this, I pipelined P x V into the next iteration to issue QK(n) and PV(n−1) together. Alone, this only gave −1.1% because ptxas hoisted the wait.


When i rotated the loop to issue QK(n) and PV(n−1) together, ptxas moved the PV wait right behind the QK wait (before all 66 exponential operations) to reuse registers. This wiped out any actual overlap and serialized the kernel again.
So added an mbarrier arrive right before the PV wait that depends on the running row sum of Softmax, plus a dummy zero subtraction on the output because ptxas cannot reorder past the mbarrier, the wait is forced to stay after Softmax

Post-wait critical path stall: Even after forcing Softmax ahead of the PV wait, each iteration was still slower than expected. So split Softmax directly across the PV wait and solved this

**My recommendation for your 1.5B model: the Tülu 3 SFT mix**, specifically the variant AllenAI used for its own 1B model: `allenai/tulu-3-sft-olmo-2-mixture-0225`, 866,138 chats. OLMo 3's SFT data is built for long reasoning (up to 32K tokens) and only used on 7B and 32B, so it doesn't fit our 4,096-token model.

## The facts, from the official sources

| | Tülu 3 SFT mix | Tülu 3 mix, OLMo 2 variant (0225) | OLMo 3 Dolci Think SFT | OLMo 3 Dolci Instruct SFT |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| chats | **939,344** | **866,138** | **2,268,178** | **2,152,112** |
| used on | Llama 3.1 **8B, 70B, 405B** base | **OLMo 2 1B** and OLMo 2 32B | Olmo 3 **7B and 32B** Think | Olmo 3 **7B** Instruct |
| total tokens trained | not stated in the paper | not stated | **45.4B** (7B), 45.2B (32B) | **3.4B** |
| max sequence length | **4,096** | (1B model's context: 4,096) | **32,768** | **32,768** |
| epochs / learning rate | 2 epochs; LR 5e-6 (8B), 2e-6 (70B); batch 128; warm-up 3% | not listed on the card | 2 epochs; LR 5e-5 (7B) | 2 epochs; LR 8e-5 (7B) |
| content | chat, knowledge, math, reasoning, code, safety, multilingual, precise instruction following | the same, with a filtered math part (kept only answers that won a 5-way majority vote) and with date-cutoff instructions removed | the same domains, but **every answer has a long thinking trace**; completions generated "up to 32K tokens" | built on the OLMo 2 Instruct (Tülu 3-based) mix, plus new chat, logic, verifiable reasoning, **tool-use / function-calling** trajectories |
| source | Tülu 3 paper, Table 7 (counts), Table 1 (models), §4.3 and Table 11 (settings) | Hugging Face dataset card and OLMo-2-0425-1B-SFT card | OLMo 3 paper, Appendix A.6.1, Table 47, §4.2; dataset card | OLMo 3 paper, §5.2, Table 47; dataset card |

So your numbers are right: Tülu 3 is about 1 million chats (939k), and OLMo 3's "2.3 million" is the **Think** SFT set (2.27M). The Instruct set is a separate 2.15M.

## Why Tülu 3 (OLMo 2 variant) fits our model

1. **AllenAI already ran exactly this at our size.** OLMo 2 1B was fine-tuned on this mix, and its published scores give us a reference:

   | OLMo 2 1B | average | GSM8K | IFEval | MATH | MMLU |
   |---|---|---|---|---|---|
   | after SFT | 36.9 | 52.1 | 50.5 | 13.2 | 36.4 |
   | after DPO | 40.6 | 59.0 | 67.1 | 14.1 | 39.9 |
   | final (after RL) | 42.7 | 68.3 | 70.1 | 20.7 | 40.0 |

2. **It fits our context length.** Tülu 3 trained with a 4,096-token maximum, the same as our model (T 4,096). OLMo 3 Think trains at 32,768 tokens with traces up to 32K tokens, so most of it would be cut or dropped.
3. **Size and cost:** OLMo 3 Think is 45.4B tokens of SFT, about 2× the whole 23B tokens our base model was pretrained on.
4. **It matches our pipeline:** our chat template is already the Tülu 3 one (decided 15 Oct), and our packed pipeline handles 4,096-token rows.
5. **The DPO team gets a matching next step:** AllenAI's `olmo-2-0425-1b-preference-mix` has 378,301 preference pairs, and its card lists the OLMo 2 1B DPO model as trained on it. That gives a complete published 1B recipe: Tülu 3 SFT, then this DPO data.

## One thing to tell the DPO team plainly

Our base model saw **23B** pretraining tokens. OLMo 2 1B saw about **4 trillion** (+50B in midtraining), about 175× more. SmolLM2 1.7B saw 11 trillion. SFT mostly teaches format and instruction following; it can't add knowledge the base model never learned. So our scores will be well below OLMo 2 1B's table above, with the same data. Their experiments should compare against our own SFT checkpoint, not against OLMo 2 1B's numbers.

## What I'd do next (only after your OK)

1. Download `tulu-3-sft-olmo-2-mixture-0225`, run it through our `prepare_sft_data.py` (our tokenizer and template, prompt masking, packing), and count:
   - the real token total;
   - how many chats are longer than 4,096 tokens.
2. From the token count, give you the exact run time (CPU only; no GPU needed).
3. Short learning-rate sweep on a subset (both Tülu 3 and OLMo 3 picked their learning rate by a sweep), then the full 2-epoch run on the 23B-token checkpoint.

Then the RoPE explanation, as planned.

Why I still restart the positions:

Exact equality: a packed chat gives bit-for-bit the same q, k, attention and loss as the same chat alone. That is what let us test packing exactly. The attention tests require "packed == alone, bit for bit", and test 2 matched padding to 6 digits at step 0. Without the restart, only "close" could be checked, not "equal".
Training matches inference: at inference a chat always starts at position 0.
It is the standard way: Hugging Face's packing collator (DataCollatorWithFlattening) and torchtitan also restart the positions for every chat.
It costs almost nothing: +0.7% forward and +2.5% backward on a kernel that is a very small part of the step.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-22 12:32 IST]

The download worked: 866,138 chats, 19 sources. The multilingual part is `tulu_v3.9_aya_100k` with **99,989 chats**. Before answering the tokenizer question, I'm checking OLMo 2's tokenizer in its official paper rather than from memory:
> tool `WebFetch`: https://arxiv.org/html/2501.00656
> tool `Bash`: Count GPT-2 tokens for the same sentence in three languages
> tool `Bash`: Install tiktoken in scratch and count tokens per language

## Short answers

1. **We must keep our own GPT-2 tokenizer (tiktoken).** A model can only use the tokenizer it was pretrained with.
2. **The Tülu data works with it**, because the dataset is plain text and we tokenize it ourselves.
3. **The only real cost is non-English text** (the Aya part), which takes many more tokens. That's why I suggest dropping it.

## 1. What tokenizers they used

| model | tokenizer | vocabulary |
|---|---|---|
| Tülu 3 (fine-tuned Llama 3.1 8B / 70B / 405B) | Llama 3's tokenizer | 128K |
| OLMo 2 (including the 1B) | built from **cl100k**, the GPT-3.5 / GPT-4 tokenizer (OLMo 2 paper, §2.2) | ~100K |
| **our 1.5B model** | **GPT-2 tokenizer (tiktoken "gpt2")** | 50,257 (our embedding table has 50,304 rows) |

## 2. Why we can't switch to their tokenizer

During pretraining, our model learned:
- one row of numbers for each **GPT-2 token id**, in its input embedding table;
- one output score for each GPT-2 token id, in its last layer.

Each token id stands for a fixed piece of text. In GPT-2, id 1000 is one piece of text; in cl100k, id 1000 is a different piece. With another tokenizer, the model would get ids whose meaning it never learned, and ids above 50,303 don't exist in our model at all.

So **SFT must use the same tokenizer as pretraining**. Changing the tokenizer means pretraining again. Their tokenizer doesn't matter for us: the Tülu dataset stores the chats as **text** (the `messages` field), not as token ids, and our prep script turns that text into GPT-2 tokens.

## 3. Is GPT-2's tokenizer enough for this data?

Yes. It works on raw bytes, so it can encode **any text in any language**; nothing becomes "unknown", and decoding gives back exactly the same text. The cost is the number of tokens. I measured our tokenizer on the laptop, with the same question in each language:

| text | characters | GPT-2 tokens |
|---|---|---|
| English: "How do I make a cup of tea?" | 27 | **9** |
| the same question in Hindi | 25 | **37** (4.1× English) |
| the same question in Chinese | 8 | **17** (1.9× English) |
| Python code with 4-space indentation | 40 | 22 |

The Hindi sentence decoded back exactly (checked). English, math and code are fine.

## 4. Why drop Aya (99,989 multilingual chats)

1. **Our model doesn't know those languages.** It was pretrained on 23B tokens of English. SFT teaches how to answer, on top of what the model already knows; 100,000 chats can't teach a new language.
2. **They cost much more for the same content:** about 2 to 4× more tokens per sentence (table above). So they'd take a large share of the training time, and many of them would pass 4,096 tokens and be dropped anyway.
3. **Why OLMo 2 kept them:** its tokenizer handles other languages much better, and its 4 trillion pretraining tokens include more of them.

Dropping Aya leaves **766,149 chats**. It's your choice. The prep step prints, for each source, how many chats were kept and how many were too long, so either way we'll see the real numbers.

## 5. What the 2,000-chat validation set is

- **Validation chats are never trained on.** Every 10 steps the trainer computes the loss on them.
  - If the training loss falls and the validation loss also falls, the model is learning things that carry over to new chats.
  - If the training loss falls but the validation loss rises, the model is memorizing its training chats (overfitting), and we should stop.
- **UltraChat came with its own test split, which is why we had 500 validation chats before.** The Tülu mix has only one split, so we have to take some chats out ourselves: 2,000 random ones (0.25% of the mix), removed from training.
- **Why 2,000:** that's about a million tokens, enough for a steady loss number, and each check still takes only seconds.
- **It doesn't depend on the tokenizer.**

### CLAUDE [2026-10-22 12:53 IST]

Checking Kruthik's bf16 kernel source, so I tell you exactly how it computes rather than guess:
> tool `Bash`: Read the bf16 kernel's header and compute types

Short answer: **both kernels compute in fp32.** The difference is only what they read and write in memory. We changed the fp32-in/fp32-out one because our SFT branch has only that one; Kruthik's bf16 kernel was added to BLUCCL after our SFT branch split off. **We can use Kruthik's kernel in SFT too,** after we add the same positions change to it.

## The two kernels

| | our SFT branch: `fused_rms_rope` | Kruthik's: `fused_rms_rope_bf16` (BLUCCL only) |
|---|---|---|
| reads | **fp32** q, k in head-major layout `[B, H, T, hd]` | **bf16** q, k straight from the projection, token-major `[B, T, H, hd]` |
| math (RMS norm + rotation) | **fp32** | **fp32** (it converts each bf16 value to fp32 in registers) |
| writes | fp32 | **bf16**, head-major |
| has per-chat positions (packing) | **yes**, our 10 Oct change | **no** |
| who uses it | our SFT trainer | the BLUCCL production pretraining trainer, by default (`BLU_QKROPE_FP32=1` switches back to the fp32 one) |

Kruthik's own comment at the top of his file says the same: *"reads Q/K in the projection's token-major [B,T,H,hd] layout and writes head-major bf16, **with the fp32 math and reduction order of the sm90 kernels**."* It loads bf16 values and turns them into fp32 (`__bfloat1622float2`), computes `rsqrtf` and the rotation in fp32, and rounds to bf16 only when storing. So his kernel is not "computing in bf16". It does the same fp32 math with half the memory traffic.

**One correction to what you remembered:** our SFT trainer uses the fp32 kernel, but the BLUCCL **pretraining** trainer uses Kruthik's bf16 kernel by default. That includes the hand-over branch `dist_side_gautam_lottn`, which is built on BLUCCL.

## Why his kernel is faster

Our SFT trainer has to do 3 extra copies around the fp32 kernel (`bluscript_sft.cpp` lines 640–644, then 651–652):

```
q, k (bf16, [B,T,H,hd])
  -> transpose + copy to [B,H,T,hd]   (copy 1, bf16)
  -> widen to fp32                     (copy 2, twice the bytes)
  -> fp32 kernel (reads and writes fp32)
  -> narrow back to bf16               (copy 3)
```

Kruthik's kernel does all of that in **one pass**: it reads bf16 in the projection's layout and writes bf16 in attention's layout. Fewer passes over memory make it faster, but I haven't measured the gain for our SFT step. The RoPE part is a small share of the step, so I'd expect a few percent, and we should measure before claiming a number.

## Why we didn't change the bf16 one

- **Timing:** our SFT branch split off on 25 Sep (`dist_side_merge` `ad10e7d`). Kruthik added his kernel to BLUCCL on 1 Oct (commit `a60099b`). Our positions change was on 10 Oct, on the SFT branch, where only the fp32 kernel existed.
- **Effect on the result:** none on correctness. Same fp32 math and same single rounding to bf16 at the end, so the values should match.

## Can we use Kruthik's kernel in SFT?

Yes, in 3 steps:
1. **Bring his kernel into the SFT branch** from BLUCCL.
2. **Add the positions change to it.** It picks the cos/sin row in 3 places: lines 108 and 160 (forward) and line 232 (backward) of `FusedRMSRoPE_bf16.cu`. Each becomes `positions[b*T + t]` behind the same `HAS_POS` switch, plus passing `positions` through his API.
3. **Test it** (packed chat == chat alone, bit for bit, like our 37-case test), then switch the SFT trainer to `fused_rms_rope_bf16`.

**My suggestion:** run today's Tülu SFT with the tested fp32 path, and do the bf16 + positions port afterwards as a separate task. It changes speed, not results. That port also gives the production branch per-chat positions, if they ever pack in pretraining.

```
OUR SFT PATH (fp32 kernel)
q, k from the projection: bf16 [B,T,H,hd]
  1. transpose copy          -> bf16 [B,H,T,hd]
  2. widen copy bf16 -> fp32  -> fp32 [B,H,T,hd]      exact: no information added or lost
  3. fused kernel: reads fp32, math in fp32, writes fp32
  4. narrow copy fp32 -> bf16 -> bf16 [B,H,T,hd]      <- the only rounding
  5. attention reads bf16

KRUTHIK'S PATH (bf16 kernel)
q, k from the projection: bf16 [B,T,H,hd]
  1. fused kernel: reads bf16 (turns each value into fp32 in registers), math in fp32,
     rounds to bf16 when writing                      <- the only rounding
     -> bf16 [B,H,T,hd]
  2. attention reads bf16
```

- **Step 2 of our path adds nothing.** A bf16 value turned into fp32 is the same number, so the kernel gets the same inputs either way.
- **The math is fp32 in both.** Kruthik's file says it keeps "the fp32 math and reduction order of the sm90 kernels".
- **Both round to bf16 exactly once, with the same rule** (round to nearest even). Ours does it in step 4, his does it inside the kernel.
- **So the bf16 values that reach attention should be bit-identical.** The fp32 write in step 3 and the read-back in step 4 are pure extra memory traffic.

## The backward is the same story

- **Ours:** the gradient from attention arrives in bf16, is widened to fp32, goes through the fp32 backward kernel, and is narrowed back to bf16.
- **Kruthik's backward:** it reads the bf16 gradient and the bf16 q, k, does fp32 math inside, and writes bf16 gradients. (Its declaration takes `bfloat16_t*` for the incoming gradient, q, k and the outgoing gradients.)
- **Result:** the same single rounding at the end.

## So his is faster and uses less memory, with the same results

| | our fp32 path | Kruthik's bf16 path |
|---|---|---|
| separate copies around the kernel | 3 (transpose, widen, narrow), and the backward has its own | 0 |
| bytes the kernel reads and writes | fp32 (4 bytes per value) | bf16 (2 bytes per value) |
| q, k kept for the backward | the **fp32** copies | **bf16** |
| final values | bf16, rounded once | the same |

The memory part is real. The backward of our fused op needs its inputs, which are the fp32 copies of q and k. At our SFT size (4 rows of 4,096 tokens, 18 + 6 heads of 128), that's about **200 MB per layer**, so about **5.2 GB over the 26 layers**. In bf16 it would be about half.

**Why our path is like that:** the fp32 kernel came first, and Kruthik's bf16 kernel is the newer, better version. Our SFT branch split off before his kernel existed (it reached BLUCCL on 1 Oct), and on 10 Oct I added positions to the only kernel the SFT branch had.

**What I'd do:** run today's Tülu SFT on the tested fp32 path. Then, as a separate task:

2. add per-chat positions to it (3 lines plus passing the parameter through);
3. check bit-identical output against the fp32 path;
4. switch the SFT trainer to it.

The speed and memory gain are then something to measure, not guess.

## Your questions

**1. Does pretraining get any overhead? No.**
- The kernel has a compile-time switch, `HAS_POS`. Pretraining passes no positions, so the launcher picks the `HAS_POS=false` version.
- I compared the compiled GPU code: **9 of 9 kernels are instruction-for-instruction identical** to Kruthik's original. So pretraining runs his exact old machine code.
- The only new work is one `if (positions == nullptr)` on the CPU per launch.
- The positions version is really different code (8 to 32 more instructions in the binary), so the comparison is not empty.

**2. In SFT, how much does it cost?** One extra 4-byte read per token per head. The real time is measured by check 4 of the test below, so I'm not giving a number yet.

**3. How is it switched on today? Automatically, by the data. There is no switch.**
- [SftDataLoader.h:67-73](../BluTrain_sft/sft/SftDataLoader.h#L67-L73): the data counts as packed when `seq_lengths.bin` and `seq_offsets.bin` exist. Our Tülu data has them.
- [bluscript_sft.cpp:125](../BluTrain_sft/bluscript_sft.cpp#L125): `if (!l.packed()) return PackedRows{};`, so with no packed data there are no positions and no per-chat attention.
- [bluscript_sft.cpp:649](../BluTrain_sft/bluscript_sft.cpp#L649): the positions go into RoPE.
- With one chat per row, positions would be 0..T−1 anyway, so the result is the same as with no positions.

**4. Can we turn it off for SFT? Yes, about 5 lines (an env variable). I don't recommend it, and I haven't added one.**
- With per-chat attention still on, turning it off doesn't change the math. Chat 2 would get positions like 1000..3499 instead of 0..2499. RoPE depends only on the distance i−j inside a chat, and shifting every position by the same amount keeps i−j.
- What changes is the bf16 rounding. The packed result would also no longer match the same chat run alone bit for bit. The saving is one 4-byte read, so there is nothing to gain.

## How the other libraries do it (from their source, in `~/Downloads/sft_research`)

| Library | SFT packing: positions restart per chat? | Can you turn it off? | Proof |
|---|---|---|---|
| **TRL** (478624d) | Yes, built from `seq_lengths`; example output `[[0,1,2,0,1]]` | **No** for chat-aware packing: `padding_free` is forced on | `sft_trainer.py:1180`, `:487-489`, `:528-552`, `:465` |
| **HF transformers** (4cc2aa8) | Yes: `DataCollatorWithFlattening` restarts at 0 for every sequence | It is a switch (`return_position_ids`), **on by default**. Its FlashAttention path finds chat starts from the restarts, so turning it off breaks per-chat attention | `data_collator.py:1377-1378, 1409, 1456`; `modeling_flash_attention_utils.py:558-571` |
| **Megatron-LM** (8b2f660) | Yes, **hard-coded**: `pack_positions.extend(range(len(tokens_list)))` | **No.** It even asserts that the generic flag is off, because SFT does its own restart | `training/datasets/sft_dataset.py:149-150` |
| **Megatron-LM pretraining** | Only with the flag `--reset-position-ids` | **Off by default**, like our pretraining | `arguments.py:3488-3489`, `gpt_dataset.py:848-868` |
| **torchtitan** (1e4d33d) | Yes: packing builds `np.arange(...)` per document | RoPE reads `rope_cache[:num_tokens]` without positions and `rope_cache[positions]` with them, the same design as ours | `components/data/packing.py:167`, `models/common/rope.py:382-385` |

In short, everyone restarts positions automatically for chat packing. Megatron and TRL don't let you turn it off. Pretraining doesn't restart by default. Our setup matches this.

## Your questions, from the code

**1. The trainer does not pass `HAS_POS`. It passes the positions tensor, or nothing.**
- The launcher checks that pointer. If it is null, it runs the `HAS_POS=false` kernel; if not, the `HAS_POS=true` one.
- In SFT it turns on by itself when the data is packed. Packed means the folder has `seq_lengths.bin` + `seq_offsets.bin` ([SftDataLoader.h:67-73](../BluTrain_sft/sft/SftDataLoader.h#L67-L73)). Our Tülu data has them.

**2. The attention does not read positions. The trainer gives it a separate "chat plan".**
- The loader reads `seq_lengths.bin` and builds two things for every micro-batch:
  - the positions, for RoPE;
  - the chat list (row, start, length).
- The trainer turns the chat list into a plan with `gqa_chat_plan_make` ([bluscript_sft.cpp:125-131](../BluTrain_sft/bluscript_sft.cpp#L125-L131)). It passes the plan to attention as `g_packed.chats` ([:677-678](../BluTrain_sft/bluscript_sft.cpp#L677-L678)).
- With no plan, attention runs the plain causal kernel, unchanged. The default is `chats = nullptr` in `AttentionOps.h:133`.

**3. Loss: what changed, and the pretraining default.** The function is `sparse_cross_entropy_loss(logits, target, ignore_index, denom)`. Its defaults are `-1, nullptr` (`LossOps.h:48-50`).

| | Pretraining (default) | SFT |
|---|---|---|
| ignore index | `-1`. Token ids are 0..50303, never −1, so nothing is ignored | `65535`. Labels are uint16, which can't hold −1, and 65535 is outside the vocabulary |
| denominator | `nullptr`: each micro-batch's loss is divided by its own B×T tokens | the whole step's trained-token count. It is summed over this rank's GRAD_ACCUM micro-batches, then summed over all ranks with MPI_Allreduce ([:2399-2406](../BluTrain_sft/bluscript_sft.cpp#L2399-L2406)) |
| backward seed | `1/GRAD_ACCUM`: turns the micro-batch losses into their mean | `W` (number of ranks). The micro-batches just add up, and `W` cancels the ZeRO ÷W average ([:1995-2001](../BluTrain_sft/bluscript_sft.cpp#L1995-L2001)) |

Why the denominator changed. In pretraining, every micro-batch has exactly B×T trained tokens. In SFT the counts differ, for example 1,000 in one micro-batch and 9,000 in the next:
- **Mean of the two means:** each token of the first gets weight 1/2,000, each token of the second 1/18,000. The first micro-batch's tokens count 9× more.
- **Global count:** every token gets 1/10,000, equal weight.
- torchtitan does the same: `loss = loss / global_valid_tokens`, cited in `LossOps.h:36`.

**4. So what changes from the pretraining script to the SFT script, kernel-wise?** The whole difference between `bluscript_zero_ckpt.cpp` and `bluscript_sft.cpp` is **61 lines**.

| Piece | Pretraining | SFT | Turned on by |
|---|---|---|---|
| Data | token shards | `SftDataLoader` (inputs, labels, valid_counts, seq_lengths) | `BLU_SFT_DATA=<dir>` ([:975-976](../BluTrain_sft/bluscript_sft.cpp#L975-L976)) |
| Loss kernel | `-1, nullptr` | `65535, &sft_denom` ([:2417-2419](../BluTrain_sft/bluscript_sft.cpp#L2417-L2419)) | `BLU_SFT_DATA` |
| Backward seed | `1/GRAD_ACCUM` | `W` | `BLU_SFT_DATA` |
| RoPE kernel | no positions | `g_packed.positions` ([:649](../BluTrain_sft/bluscript_sft.cpp#L649)) | packed data |
| Attention kernel | no plan → plain causal | `g_packed.chats` ([:677-678](../BluTrain_sft/bluscript_sft.cpp#L677-L678)) | packed data |

The first three rows are already in the pretraining file too (SFT v1, one chat per row): `bluscript_zero_ckpt.cpp:939, 1963, 2361, 2369`. `bluscript_sft.cpp` adds only the packed rows' parts:
- positions into RoPE;
- the chat plan into attention;
- `BLU_SFT_B` (rows per micro-batch);
- building `g_packed` every micro-batch;
- freeing it at exit.

Stage C changes only the RoPE row. The SFT trainer will call Kruthik's bf16 `fused_rms_rope_bf16(..., g_packed.positions)` instead of the fp32 path.

## Your question: yes, kernel-wise only attention, RoPE and the loss change

An op needs a change for packed SFT only if it mixes tokens with each other, uses a token's position, or uses the labels. Every op in our model, from the trainer code:

| Op | Mixes tokens? | Uses position? | Uses labels? | Change? |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Embedding lookup (`wte`) | no | no (there is no learned position table) | no | no |
| RMSNorm (pre-attention, pre-MLP, final) | no | no | no | no |
| Linear layers / GEMMs (qkv, out, gate_up, down, lm_head): each output row comes from its own input row | no | no | no | no |
| QK-RMSNorm | no | no | no | no |
| SwiGLU, residual add, casts, reshape/transpose | no | no | no | no |
| **RoPE** | no | **yes** | no | **positions** |
| **Attention** | **yes** | no | no | **chat plan** |
| **Loss** | no | no | **yes** | **ignore 65535 + global count** |

- Dropout is 0 (`dropout_p=0.0f`, [bluscript_sft.cpp:677](../BluTrain_sft/bluscript_sft.cpp#L677)).
- The pad tail adds exactly zero gradient. Its labels are all 65535, and it attends only to itself.

Non-kernel things that also differ in our SFT:
- the data loader;
- the backward seed (`W` instead of `1/GRAD_ACCUM`);
- the `BLU_SFT_*` settings (LR, epochs, warmup, B, validation interval);
- `BLU_INIT_FROM` (start from the pretrained checkpoint).

It covers:

## Did we test the positions cost before?

Yes, but on a different kernel.
- **Yesterday's +0.7% forward / +2.5% backward** was **our fp32 kernel** (`sft_kernel_benchmarks.md` section 2).
- **Today's +28 to +36%** is **Kruthik's bf16 kernel**. It only got positions this morning, so this was its first timing.

Why his kernel pays more (my reading of its code; the test timed forward and backward together, so the split isn't measured):
- With positions, the cos/sin read has to wait for the position read first. Without positions, both reads can be in flight together.
- His backward runs one warp per block, and each warp walks 128 tokens one after another, so that wait repeats every token.
- His kernel moves half the bytes of the fp32 one. The same wait is then a bigger share of a shorter time.

## Should we keep the restart? Yes. Decided now, not later

| | per 20-row step | over the 5.2 h run |
|---|---|---|
| Switching fp32 → bf16 with positions (Stage C) | **saves 56 ms (3.4%)** | saves ~11 min |
| The positions' own cost | +11 ms (0.7%) | ~2 min |

1. **Keep it and run now.** We are still 3.4% faster than the fp32 path SFT runs today. The restart costs about 2 minutes of a 5-hour run.
2. **Don't drop it.** It would save about 2 minutes. We would lose the bit-exact "packed == alone" property that all our packed tests rely on, and we would differ from every library.
3. **Make it cheaper later.** For example, read the next token's position early, only in the positions code, so pretraining stays SASS-identical. That could bring the cost toward the fp32 kernel's +2%. It's about an hour of work. Do it after the run or in a separate folder: rebuilding `libtensor.so` while a run uses it can crash the run.

**What theta is and where it lives.** RoPE turns q and k by an angle before attention. For position p and pair i of the 128 head dimensions, the angle is

  angle = p × theta^(−2i/128)

so `rope_theta` sets how fast that angle grows with position, for each pair. It is one number in the `ModelConfig` block at the top of the training script:
- ours: [bluscript_sft.cpp:166](../BluTrain_sft/bluscript_sft.cpp#L166) `int rope_theta = 500000;`
- production: `bluscript_zero_ckpt.cpp:146` `int rope_theta = 10000;`

The trainer builds the cos/sin table from it once at startup (`build_rope_cache`). It is not a weight, so it isn't saved in the checkpoint. That's why we have to ask, or measure it the way we just did.

In his run log, the line looks like `rope_theta      : 10000`, next to `n_layers : 28` and `context_length : 4096`. If his says 10000, it matches our measurement and we run with it.

**"interleaved" says which dimensions RoPE rotates together.** RoPE splits each q/k head vector (128 numbers) into 64 pairs and turns each pair (a, b) by its own angle:

  (a, b) → (a·cos − b·sin, a·sin + b·cos), with angle = position × theta^(−2i/128) for pair i

The two conventions pick the pairs differently. Example with a head of 8 numbers x0..x7:

```
NeoX (half-split)      pairs: (x0,x4) (x1,x5) (x2,x6) (x3,x7)    -> pair i = (x[i], x[i+64]) at head dim 128
GPT-J (interleaved)    pairs: (x0,x1) (x2,x3) (x4,x5) (x6,x7)    -> pair i = (x[2i], x[2i+1])
```

- The angles are the same in both; only which two numbers form a pair differs.
- **NeoX** is the GPT-NeoX / Llama / Hugging Face convention. **Interleaved** is the original RoFormer / GPT-J one.
- The model learns during pretraining which numbers rotate together, so SFT must use the same convention.
- Navin's log: `rope_theta : 50000 (interleaved=NeoX)`. Ours: `rope_interleaved = false` ([bluscript_sft.cpp:175](../BluTrain_sft/bluscript_sft.cpp#L175)). The trainer passes `/*interleaved=*/false`, and the kernel launcher then picks `IS_NEOX=true` (`if (!interleaved) { DISPATCH_F(true, …) }`). **They match.** It is not a weight either, so like theta it has to match by config.

## 3. Your two questions

**SFT: is the per-chat position restart mandatory? No.**
- What is mandatory for packing is **per-chat attention**. Without it, chats read each other.
- With per-chat attention, restarting positions changes only bf16 rounding, because RoPE depends only on the distance between two tokens.
- We keep it because it is bit-exact with each chat run alone, it is standard practice, and it costs only about 0.7%.

**Inference: it depends on how requests are batched.**

| How inference runs | What it needs |
|---|---|
| one chat per sequence (one request, or rows that all start at 0) | nothing new: positions are 0, 1, 2, … = t. For decoding with a KV cache, the existing `pos_offset` (one number) gives the new token's position |
| a batch of chats with different lengths (left-padded prompts, or decoding where every row is at a different length) | **per-row positions**, so each chat starts at 0. Hugging Face does exactly this: `position_ids = attention_mask.cumsum(-1) - 1` (`generation/utils.py:898-900`). The attention just uses the padding mask |
| packed serving (all requests' tokens in one flat row, for throughput) | **both** of our SFT pieces: per-token positions + per-chat (varlen) attention |

So for inference it is a choice that depends on the batching. In every case each chat should start at position 0, the way SFT trained it. I checked this in HF's code only, not in vLLM or SGLang.

## 4. RoPE bf16 work: the benchmark is ready

[bench_rope_bf16.cu](profiling_reports/rope_bf16_port_2026_10_22/bench_rope_bf16.cu) fixes what was missing yesterday:
- it times **each kernel on its own**: forward, backward, and the dgamma reduce;
- kernel only, no op-layer allocations;
- with and without positions, at B=4 and 8;
- after a 2 s warm-up, alternating rounds, reporting medians;
- it prints the bandwidth each kernel achieves as a percentage of the H200 peak.

It compiles the kernel file directly, so it **needs no `libtensor` build and can't touch the run**. On the laptop GPU it builds, and the sanity check passes (identity positions = no positions, bit for bit). Laptop timings don't count.

Two things already visible in the code:
- **The dgamma reduce runs as a single block of 128 threads, on 1 of the H200's 132 SMs.** It costs pretraining as much as SFT.
- The forward reads a 512-byte cos/sin row for every (token, head) pair, 24 times per token. That's twice the bytes of the q/k data itself, served from cache.

The H200 numbers will show which of these matter.

No, it doesn't touch the GPU at all. Here is everything it does, once every 5 minutes:

| Command | Uses | Cost |
|---|---|---|
| `grep` / `awk` over `run.log` | CPU, reading a file | the log grows to about 3–4 MB by the end; reading it takes ~10 ms |
| `pgrep` (is the trainer process alive?) | CPU, the process list | about 1 ms |
| `df` (free disk) | CPU | about 1 ms |
| `echo` one line into `monitor.txt` | disk | one line |

In between, it sleeps for 300 seconds and does nothing. There is no `nvidia-smi`, no CUDA and no GPU memory, so it is fully independent of the training process. It only reads files the run writes. About 20 ms of CPU every 5 minutes can't slow a run that keeps the GPU busy.

The only thing in this setup that talks to the GPU is the `nvidia-smi ... -l 30` inside the run script itself, which writes `gpu.csv`. It is a read-only query of the GPU's counters (memory, power, clock, temperature) every 30 seconds. It doesn't run any kernel or take any GPU memory. We used the same logging in the 10-21 runs.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-22 16:13 IST]

The run looks good. Validation loss is dropping fast: **1.1757 (step 0) → 1.0489 (step 200) → 0.9928 (step 400)**, with no ALERT lines. Step time is a steady ~1.9 s and the ETA is about **22:01 IST**, counting step time only.

## What the 898,276 tokens are

They are the **answer tokens** of the 2,000 validation chats: the positions where the model is trained to predict the next token. Prompt tokens are not included.

A simplified example chat (real chats use our template; the idea is the same):
```
position   0           1     2     3     4              5     6        7         8
token      <|user|>    \n    Hi    \n    <|assistant|>  \n    Hello    " there"  <end>
                       '-------- prompt (user turn) --------'  '------- answer -------'
```
The model reads token t and must predict token t+1. `labels.bin` stores, for every position, the token to predict, **but only when that next token belongs to the answer**. Otherwise it stores 65535, meaning "no loss here":
```
position   0      1      2      3      4      5        6         7
input      <|user|> \n   Hi     \n     <|assistant|> \n  Hello    " there"
label      65535  65535  65535  65535  65535  Hello    " there"  <end>
                                              '---- trained: 3 tokens ----'
```
- Positions 0–4 predict prompt text, which the model shouldn't learn to write, so their label is 65535 and they get no loss.
- Positions 5–7 predict the answer, including the end token, so the model learns to stop. That's **3 trained tokens** for this chat.

`prepare_sft_data.py` counts these per row and stores the count in `valid_counts.bin`.

**For the whole val set:**
- 2,000 chats → 320 packed rows × 4,096 positions = **1,310,720 positions**;
- of those, **898,276 have a real label (answer tokens)**, 68.5%;
- the rest are prompt tokens plus the empty tail at the end of each row, all labelled 65535.

The val loss is the cross-entropy summed over those 898,276 positions, divided by 898,276. The val set never changes, so this count is the same in every `[val]` line, and each val loss is measured on exactly the same tokens.

The training data has the same share (68.6% of its positions are answer tokens). That's the "trained" number in each step line: about 57k of the 81,920 positions in a step.

Let me look at what the trainer actually prints for these two, rather than guess.
> tool `Bash`: Find where nsrej and nsratio are computed
> tool `Bash`: Read the nsrej and nsratio definitions

Both are health checks for **Muon's Newton–Schulz step**, printed by the trainer ([bluscript_sft.cpp:2769-2780](../BluTrain_sft/bluscript_sft.cpp#L2769-L2780)). Definitions are in `dist/zero/include/ShardedMuon.h:340-356, 652-662`.

**What Newton–Schulz does.** For each weight matrix, Muon takes the gradient (with momentum) G and runs 5 Newton–Schulz iterations. These turn G into a matrix O with the **same directions as G, but every singular value ≈ 1**. The weight update is lr × O. Muon does this so every direction moves by a similar amount, instead of a few large gradient directions dominating.

**`nsrej 0/0`, rejected updates: this step / whole run.**
- In bf16, Newton–Schulz can blow up for a badly conditioned gradient, producing values that aren't finite or are larger than 1000.
- A guard checks every result. If it trips, that matrix is **left unchanged for that step** rather than corrupted, and the count goes up.
- The first number counts this step, the second the whole run.
- The code comment: a handful over a long run is expected; **a steady stream means the gradients are pathological**.
- Your run: `0/0`, nothing rejected.

**`nsratio 1.02`, how big the largest update was compared with the ideal.**
- If all singular values of O are exactly 1, its size is ‖O‖ = √min(rows, cols).
- `nsratio` = the largest ‖O‖ / √min(rows, cols) over all matrices this step. **About 1.0 is healthy.**
- Example: `wK` is 2304 × 768, so ideally ‖O‖ = √768 ≈ 27.7, and its ratio is ‖O‖ / 27.7.
- Why it's printed: the guard only catches entries above 1000. An update can be several times too big and still be applied. This number is the only place that would show it.
- Your run: **1.021–1.025**, so the updates are the size Muon intends.

**What to watch:** `nsrej` staying `0/0` (or rising only rarely), and `nsratio` staying near 1. A value that stays well above 1, say over 1.5, would be the warning sign. Both look healthy now.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-22 16:19 IST]

The validation wasn't late. It's just the order in which the watchdog reports.

The watchdog wakes up every 5 minutes, and each time it writes:
1. first, the **current** step line;
2. then any **new** `[val]` lines that appeared in `run.log` since its last check.

So:
- **16:11:28 check:** the run was at step 567. The step-600 validation hadn't happened yet.
- **Between 16:11:28 and 16:16:28:** the run went from step 567 to 720. It passed step 600 at about **16:12:30** (33 steps × 1.9 s after 16:11:28), ran the validation right then, and carried on.
- **16:16:28 check:** the watchdog printed the current step (720) first, then the new val line it found (step 600).

The val loss in that line is the model's at step 600. Only the report comes at the next 5-minute check, up to 5 minutes later.

The val trend so far is clean and still falling: **1.1757 → 1.0489 → 0.9928 → 0.9692** (steps 0 / 200 / 400 / 600). The first checkpoint is at step 1000, about **16:28 IST**. After that, `ls ~/gautam_k/runs/tulu3_sft_1022/checkpoints` should show a `step_1000`-style folder.

| Signal | What it shows | What it can't show |
|---|---|---|

| **dev suite benchmarks** | the skills (IFEval, GSM8K, …), and forgetting: HellaSwag / ARC / WinoGrande, base vs SFT | an unbiased final number |
| **unseen suite** | the honest final score | — (run once) |

### CLAUDE [2026-10-22 16:28 IST]

No, memorizing does not lower the val loss. The **val chats are not in the training data**:
- The 2,000 val chats were cut out before training (`--skip-kept 2000`).
- We checked that val and train don't overlap.

The model never trains on them, so memorizing training chats can't help it answer them.

**What memorizing does, in terms of the loss.** Cross-entropy at each answer position is −log(probability the model gives the correct next token).
- In epoch 2, the model sees every training chat a second time. If it memorizes, it pushes the probability of the **exact wording of those training answers** towards 1. → **train loss falls fast.**
- Probability is limited: raising some tokens' probability lowers others'. On a new chat, the model then confidently expects the phrasing it memorized, and the val answer's actual next token often gets a lower probability. → **val loss rises.**
- Small example: training answer `The capital of France is Paris.`; val answer to a similar question: `Paris is the capital of France.` A memorizing model gives `The` a high probability as the first token, but the val answer starts with `Paris`, so that position's loss goes up.

We have seen this ourselves: in the 10-07 sweep, Muon 1.2e-4 reached train loss **1.08** in epoch 2 while val rose from **1.2747** (step 80, end of epoch 1) to **1.2820** (end). So the overfitting sign is **train down, val up**.

**If val stays flat or keeps falling:**

| Question | Answered by |
|---|---|
| Does the model generalize to new chats of this kind? | **val loss** (it does, if val falls) |
| Did epoch 2 make the model *better at skills* than epoch 1? | the **dev suite**: run its benchmarks on **both** checkpoints (end of epoch 1, end of epoch 2) and compare |
| How good is the model we finally pick, honestly? | the **unseen suite**, **once**, on the chosen checkpoint only |

The unseen suite is **not** for choosing between epoch 1 and epoch 2. Once we use it to pick, our choice is fitted to it too, and it is no longer an honest number; it becomes a second dev suite. The order is:
1. val loss → is it overfitting?
2. dev suite → which checkpoint is better?
3. unseen suite → the final honest score of the winner.

That's also why the step-6000 checkpoint (end of epoch 1) needs saving between about 19:05 and 20:05 IST: step 2 needs both checkpoints. Send me the `ls` / `du` output after 16:28, when the first checkpoint exists.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-22 16:33 IST]

Let me confirm one fact in the code first: that validation never changes the weights.
> tool `Bash`: Check that the validation pass has no backward or update

Here it is step by step.

## 1. Validation every 200 steps does not teach the model anything

A **training step** does three things:
1. **forward**: the model reads the chats and gives a probability for every next token;
2. **backward**: it computes how each weight should change to make the correct tokens more likely;
3. **optimizer step**: it changes the weights.

Only step 3 changes the model. A model "learns" or "memorizes" a chat **only** if that chat goes through steps 2 and 3.

The **validation** at every 200th step does **only step 1**. The code ([bluscript_sft.cpp:2305-2329](../BluTrain_sft/bluscript_sft.cpp#L2305-L2329)):
```
if (sft && step % val_freq == 0 ...) {
    autograd::NoGradGuard no_grad;        // no gradients are recorded
    ... logits = model.forward(b.input);  // forward only
    ... loss summed over the 898,276 answer tokens -> printed as val_loss
}                                          // no backward, no optimizer step
```
So the weights are exactly the same before and after a validation. We can run it 58 times or 5,000 times, and the model never learns or remembers anything from those 2,000 chats. The model doesn't "see" them in the training sense, because they never change a weight.

## 2. Is the 200-step val loss the "dev suite"?

It is **one item** of the dev suite we listed on 10-08 ("answer val loss").
- **During the run we don't tweak anything based on it**, correct. We only watch it.
- It acts as "dev" only when we **make a decision** with it. At the end, "keep the epoch-1 checkpoint or the epoch-2 one?" is such a decision. That's fine; that is what a dev measure is for.

## 3. How overfitting is detected

You need **two losses on the same model at the same steps**:

| | computed on | what it measures |
|---|---|---|
| **train loss** | the chats the model is **trained on** at that step | how well it fits its training data |
| **val loss** | 2,000 chats the model **never trains on** | how well it does on **new** chats of the same kind |

Then you watch both over the steps:
- **Learning (generalizing):** both go down. What the model learns from the training chats also helps on new chats.
- **Overfitting:** the train loss keeps going down, but the val loss **stops going down and starts going up**. The model is getting better only on its own training chats (it fits their exact wording) and worse on new chats.

A real example from our own sweep on 10-07 (5,000 chats, 2 epochs, epoch 2 started after step 80):

| Run | val at step 80 (end of epoch 1) | val at the end (epoch 2) | train, epoch 2 | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Muon 5e-5 | 1.2920 | **1.2843** (went down) | 1.208 | learned more in epoch 2 |
| Muon 1.2e-4 | **1.2747** | 1.2820 (went **up**) | **1.084** (very low) | **overfitted in epoch 2** |

In the 1.2e-4 run, train dropped to 1.08 while val went up. That pattern is the signal.

## 4. What we'll do with this run

1. At the end, plot **train loss** (smoothed over ~100 steps, because each step has different chats and jumps between 1.0 and 1.3) and **val loss** against the step. Mark where epoch 2 starts (step ~5,795).
2. The train loss will drop a little at step ~5,795, because epoch 2 repeats the same chats. That is expected.
3. Look at the **val loss after step 5,795**:
   - still falling or flat → no overfitting, epoch 2 is fine;
   - rising → overfitting; the end-of-epoch-1 checkpoint (step 6000, which we save aside) is the better model.

**So overfitting is detected with train loss + val loss.** We're already collecting both, so nothing extra is needed.

The benchmarks answer different questions:
- **Dev suite:** after training, did the model get better at **skills** (following instructions, math), and did it **forget** base knowledge? That can happen even when val looks fine.
- **Unseen suite:** once, at the end, the honest score of the model we pick.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-22 16:43 IST]

Two parts of that are mixed up. The words "dev" and "unseen" are not about **what the model has seen**. **The model never trains on either suite.** They are about **what we look at when we make choices.**

## The four kinds of data

| Data | Does the model train on it? | Do **we** use its scores to make choices? | What it tells us |
|---|---|---|---|
| **training chats** (741,413) | **yes** | — | train loss |
| **val set** (2,000 held-out chats) | no | yes | with train loss: is the model overfitting its training chats? |
| **dev suite** (IFEval, GSM8K, HellaSwag, …) | **no** | **yes**: we use it to pick the checkpoint, LR, data | which choice gives the best skills |
| **unseen suite** (IFBench, MMLU-Pro, AGIEval) | **no** | **no**: we don't look at it until the very end, then run it **once** | the honest final score |

So:
- **Dev suite ≠ chats the model trained on.** It is benchmark questions the model never trained on. We call it "dev" because **we** use its scores while developing: we try options and keep the one that scores best on it.
- **Unseen suite ≠ "used to pick epoch 1 or epoch 2".** If we picked the checkpoint with it, we'd be using it to make a choice, and it would turn into a second dev suite. "Unseen" means **unseen by our decisions**: kept hidden until the choice is made, then run once.

**Picking epoch 1 vs epoch 2 = val loss + dev suite. Then the unseen suite, once, on the winner.**

## What "good on dev, worse on unseen" means

The model never trained on the dev questions, so it is **not** memorization of those questions. It means **our choices were tuned to the dev suite**:
- **Luck:** when we try many options and keep the best dev score, we also keep whichever option got lucky on those exact questions. From our 10-08 notes: the best of 10 equally good options looks about +3 points better on IFEval than it really is.
- **Benchmark-specific skill:** the model got good at the kind of task in the dev suite but not the general skill. From our 10-08 notes: models tuned on IFEval's constraints fail many of IFBench's 58 new ones.

## Three kinds of "too much", and how each is detected

| Problem | How to see it |
|---|---|
| **1. The model memorized its training chats** (overfitting to training data) | **train loss down + val loss up**. This is the main overfitting check, and the only one that needs no benchmark |
| **2. Our choices were tuned to the dev suite** | dev score clearly higher than the unseen score |
| **3. SFT made the model forget base knowledge** | base benchmarks (HellaSwag, ARC, WinoGrande) lower after SFT than before |

One more detail about the train loss, because it explains "seen":
- **In epoch 1**, each chat's loss is computed **before** the model trains on it (forward first, then the update). So the epoch-1 train loss is on chats the model has **not yet seen**, and it behaves almost like a val loss.
- **In epoch 2**, the same chats come again, now **already trained on once**. So the train loss drops at step ~5,795, and from then on the **gap between train and val** shows how much the model fits its own chats rather than new ones.
- A small gap with val still falling is fine. A growing gap with **val rising** is overfitting.

You're right. That middle row was too soft, and I'll correct it in the doc. Here is the precise picture.

## Train loss going down, val loss flat: what it really means

- **Val flat** = on **new** chats the model is no longer getting better (and not worse either).
- **Train still going down** = the model keeps getting better on **its own training chats only**.

That extra train drop doesn't carry over to new chats, so it is **fitting the training chats themselves: memorization starting**. The gap between train and val grows. It isn't harmful yet, because val hasn't got worse, but it is **no new general learning**. It is the **start of overfitting**, the point where more steps stop helping.

## Does a falling train loss guarantee anything?

**On its own, no.** It only says the model fits the chats it trains on better. The one exception is **epoch 1**:
- Each batch's loss is computed **before** the model trains on that batch.
- So in epoch 1 every train-loss value is measured on chats the model has **not seen yet**, and it behaves like a val loss. A falling epoch-1 train loss is real learning.
- **In epoch 2** the chats were already trained on once. A falling train loss there can be memorization. Only the val loss can tell.

## What gives the guarantee

| Question | What answers it |
|---|---|
| Is it learning things that carry over to new chats of this kind? | **val loss going down** (and train loss in epoch 1) |
| Is it memorizing? | **train going down while val is flat or rising**: the train–val gap grows |
| Did it gain a **skill** (following instructions, stopping correctly, math)? | **dev suite benchmarks** |

One honest limit of the val loss:
- It is the average over all 898,276 answer tokens.
- A narrow skill, like ending the answer at the right place or following a format, touches only a few of those tokens, so it can change while the average hardly moves.
- So "val flat" means "no more **general** improvement on Tülu-style answers". It does not prove that **no** skill changed. That is why we check the dev suite benchmarks on both checkpoints before choosing.

**Corrected table:**

| Train loss | Val loss | Meaning |
|---|---|---|
| down | down | **real learning**: it carries over to new chats |
| down | flat | **no more gain on new chats**; the extra train drop is fitting the training chats (**memorization starting**). Not harmful yet; more steps add nothing general. The dev suite decides whether a narrow skill still improved |
| down | up | **overfitting**: memorization now makes new chats worse |
| flat | flat | nothing more to learn at this learning rate |

You're right, and I've corrected the doc: the table in section 5 is now split by epoch, and a new **section 5.2** explains each case. In short:

**1. Epoch 1: train down, val flat → not memorization.** Every epoch-1 train value is measured on chats the model hasn't trained on yet, so a falling train loss there is real learning. Flat val means the gain is on things the 2,000 val chats barely contain, or it's too small or noisy to show on val. The dev suite checks that at the end.

**2. Epoch 2: train down, val flat → most likely memorization starting, but not proven.** The train gains are now on chats already trained on once.
- It's **proven only if val then goes up**.
- Val doesn't have to rise. Near the end, the cosine schedule drops the learning rate to 5e-6, so the updates get small and val can just stay flat.
- If val **goes down** again instead, epoch 2 was still real learning. Memorization never makes val go down.

**3. Epoch 1: train down, val UP → something is wrong.** Three possible causes:
1. **Duplicates in the training data.** Your guess is right: the "new" chats are really repeats, so the model memorizes even in epoch 1. **That is overfitting inside epoch 1.** Check it by counting duplicate and near-duplicate chats.
2. **Train and val are different kinds of data.** Not overfitting, just a mismatch. Unlikely for us: the chats are shuffled before val is cut (`prepare_sft_data.py:244`), and the rows are shuffled too (`:290`).
3. **Learning rate too high.** The updates damage what the model knew, usually together with grad-norm spikes.

**A direct memorization measure (added to the doc).** Both epochs read the rows in the same order (`SftDataLoader.h:24`), so step s of epoch 2 trains on almost the same rows as step s of epoch 1. Epoch 2 is shifted by one micro-batch, so 4 of the 5 micro-batches line up.
- The **drop in train loss on the same rows** from epoch 1 to epoch 2, **minus the val drop** over the same time, is how much the model improved on those exact chats beyond new ones. That extra part is memorization, measured directly.
- We can compute it from `run.log` after the run, using 100-step averages.

**Step 6000 vs 5000, and the exact step 5795:**
- You're right that **6000 is the better choice**:
  - at step 5000, 795 steps of epoch 1 (about 15,900 rows, 13.7% of the data) are **not yet trained even once**;
  - at step 6000, only 205 steps (about 4,100 rows, 3.5%) have been **trained twice**.
- **An exact step-5795 checkpoint isn't possible in this run.** The trainer saves only when `(step + 1)` is a multiple of `BLU_CKPT_FREQ`, or at the last step, and a running process can't change that.
- The only way would be to stop the run and resume from `blumodel_step_5000` with a save frequency that lands on 5796 (for example 966, since 966 × 6 = 5796). That costs about 6 minutes plus restart risk. Resuming is also not bit-exact (on 10-07: step exact, later steps within ~2e-4). 205 repeated steps is too small to be worth that. **We take 6000.**
