The sanity check passed: identity positions give the same bits as no positions. The totals agree with the stage-B op-level test (+92.7 µs here vs +86.8 µs there).

**Findings:**

1. **Forward: fine as it is.** Positions cost only +3.5%.
2. **The whole positions cost is in the backward kernel (+69–75%).** This matches the code reading from earlier:
   - each block is a single warp that walks its 128 tokens one after another;
   - with positions, every iteration must first load the position before it can load that token's cos/sin row, so one extra memory wait per token, 128 times in a row.
   - Not profiler-proven yet. An `ncu` run would show it as "long scoreboard" stalls.

   **Fix:** load the warp's positions ahead, 32 at once (one per lane), and hand each iteration its position from a register with a warp shuffle. This goes only in the `HAS_POS=true` code, so pretraining's code stays SASS-identical.
3. **New finding: the dgamma reduce is as slow as the forward kernel** (58 µs vs 78 µs at B=4; 23% of the whole no-positions time).
   - It runs as one block on 1 of the 132 SMs, each thread adding 2,304 rows one by one.
   - It costs **pretraining the same**.
   - **Fix that keeps the result bit-identical:** keep the exact same addition order per column, but issue the loads ahead (unroll), spread the 128 columns over 4 blocks (4 SMs), and do q and k in one launch instead of two.

**What it's worth:** RoPE is about 2.6% of an SFT step today (350 µs × 28 layers × 5 micro-batches ≈ 49 ms of ~1.88 s). Both fixes could bring 350 → roughly 215 µs (my estimate). That saves about 1% of the step, roughly 3–4 minutes per 6-hour run. The reduce fix alone saves pretraining about 0.3%. A real gain, but small.

## 1. One kernel for all architectures?

| Kernel | Per-architecture versions? | Proof |
|---|---|---|
| **fused RMSNorm + RoPE, bf16** (Kruthik's; now our SFT default and the production pretraining default) | **No: one generic kernel for every GPU** (H200, B300, others) | `norm/FusedRMSRoPE_bf16.cu` has no architecture check at all |
| fused RMSNorm + RoPE, fp32 (the old path, now the `BLU_QKROPE_FP32=1` fallback) | yes: H200-specific kernels + a portable one | `norm/arch/FusedRMSRoPE_{fwd,bwd}_sm90*.cu` |
| **loss (cross-entropy)** | **Not only one:** generic for H200 and others, **plus a B300-only forward** | `loss/arch/CrossEntropyKernels_sm103.cu`, routed at `LossKernels.cu:1093-1100` |
| attention | per architecture (as you said) | — |

The loss is **not** one-for-all. On B300 its forward goes to an sm103 kernel that, per the TODO in the code (`LossKernels.cu:1096`), **does not support `ignore_index` yet**. So SFT on B300 would currently get the loss forward wrong; it's already on our future list. For RoPE, any optimization we make applies to every GPU at once.

## 2. Is the overhead only from the SFT feature? No: two separate problems

| | Where | Who pays |
|---|---|---|
| **A. the positions cost** | **backward kernel only**: 121 → 211 µs (+75%) at B=4; the forward is only +3.5% | SFT only |
| **B. inefficiencies already in Kruthik's kernel** | forward and backward reach only **53–56% of the H200's memory bandwidth**; the **dgamma reduce** takes 58 µs (B=4) on **1 of the 132 SMs** | **pretraining and SFT alike** |

**What the dgamma reduce is.** It **is** part of fused RMSNorm + RoPE: the backward of the RMSNorm's scale weights (`q_gamma`, `k_gamma`, 128 numbers each).
- Every (token, head) adds a contribution to those 128 numbers.
- To keep the result deterministic (the same bits every run, unlike atomics), the backward kernel writes **partial sums**: one row of 128 per (batch, head, token-chunk). That's B×18×32 rows for q, 2,304 at B=4.
- A second kernel, the reduce, adds the rows up **in a fixed order** (`FusedRMSRoPE_bf16.cu:282-299`). That fixed order is why our dgamma is bit-identical to the fp32 path.
- But it runs as **one block of 128 threads**: each thread adds 2,304 numbers one after another, on a single SM.

**Is the pretraining kernel fully optimized? No.** A memory-bound kernel like this one can reach roughly 85–90% of the 4.8 TB/s peak. From the measured bytes, my rough floor estimate at B=4 is:

| | now | estimated floor |
|---|---|---|
| forward | 78 µs | ~48 µs |
| backward | 121 µs | ~73 µs |
| reduce | 58 µs | ~3 µs |
| **pretraining total** | **258 µs** | **~125 µs (~2× headroom)** |
| **SFT total** | **350 µs** | **~125 µs (~2.8× headroom)** |

These floors are estimates, not promises.

## 3. Did we benchmark it against other libraries? No, never for this bf16 kernel

Yesterday's comparison (`sft_kernel_benchmarks.md` §2: vs torch.compile, Liger, PyTorch eager) used **our fp32 kernel with fp32 inputs**, not Kruthik's bf16 kernel. The bf16 kernel, which production pretraining also uses, has **never been compared with any rival**, in either the pretraining or the SFT case.

**What this means:**

- Each in **both cases**: pretraining (no positions) and SFT (packed positions). Same shapes, same GPU, alternated rounds, outputs checked against an fp64 reference.

## How each one does it, compared with Kruthik's kernel

**Forward (RMSNorm + RoPE on q and k):**

| | Work unit | cos/sin | How loads are issued | Proof |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Ours (Kruthik)** | 1 warp per (token, **one** head), 4 tokens per warp | fp32 table, 512 B per position, **read again for each of the 24 heads** | plain 8-byte loads per lane | `FusedRMSRoPE_bf16.cu:49-135` |
| vLLM basic, TensorRT-LLM, SGLang | 1 warp per (token, one head), the same as ours | table (bf16 or fp32, templated) | plain loads | `fused_qknorm_rope_kernel.cu:140-170, 241` (TRT-LLM and SGLang have the same signature and comments) |
| **vLLM advanced** | 1 warp per (token, **several heads**) | loaded **once per token** into shared memory, reused across heads | **`cp.async`** (many loads in flight) + **PDL** | `:320-437, 690-760` |
| Unsloth fused | 1 program per (token, up to 8 heads) | loaded once per token, half-width, caller's dtype | Triton | `qk_norm_rope.py:103-112, 245-249` |
| Liger RoPE | 1 program per token, **all** heads | once per token | Triton | `ops/rope.py:35-53` |
| TransformerEngine RoPE | 1 block per token, all heads | **computed** with `sincosf` from fp32 angles into shared memory, once per token | CUDA | `fused_rope.cu:50, 105` |

Everyone except vLLM's basic kernel (and its TensorRT-LLM / SGLang copies) **loads cos/sin once per token** and shares it across heads. Ours loads it 24 times per token.

**Backward, and dgamma (all of these are deterministic):**

| | Backward work split | dgamma | Proof |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Ours** | **1 warp per block**, each warp walks **128 tokens in a row**, **2-byte scalar loads and stores**, no loads issued ahead | 2,304 partial rows (B=4), then a **1-block reduce on 1 SM** | `:191-299` |
| Liger RMSNorm | one program per SM (persistent), whole rows | 132 partial rows + a full-GPU PyTorch `sum` | `ops/rms_norm.py:529-548` |
| FlashAttention RMSNorm | 8 programs per SM | 1,056 partial rows + PyTorch `sum` | `layer_norm.py:779-789` |
| TransformerEngine RMSNorm | per-block partials | a separate parallel **finalize** kernel | `rmsnorm_bwd_kernels.cuh:186-223` |
| Quack RMSNorm | persistent, one block per SM | per-block partials + its own final reduce | `rmsnorm.py:669-696, 1156`; `rms_final_reduce.py` |
| Unsloth fused | per (token, head block) | **none** (norm weights frozen; with trainable ones it falls back to separate kernels) | `qk_norm_rope.py:416-438` |

**Nobody else fuses QK-norm + RoPE with the dgamma backward**, so ours is the only complete fused training kernel. But **each of its parts is built less efficiently than the rivals' equivalents.**

## Where ours falls behind, by expected size

These are expectations from reading the code. The profiler must confirm each one before I change anything.

1. **Backward (121 µs; 211 µs with positions):** a single warp walks 128 tokens one after another and waits for its loads every time. It uses 2-byte loads where the forward uses 8-byte ones, and nothing is loaded ahead. That fits the 53% bandwidth, and the +90 µs from the extra position wait.
2. **dgamma reduce (58 µs):** 1 SM, where every rival uses a full-GPU reduction.
3. **Forward (78 µs, 54% of bandwidth):** cos/sin read once per head instead of once per token; small loads; no async copies. vLLM's advanced kernel fixes all three.

**One design point to keep:** our fp32 cos/sin table is exact, and TE also stays fp32 (it computes `sincosf`). Using a bf16 table, as some inference kernels allow, would change the numbers. I'd keep fp32 and just stop reading it 24 times.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-22 20:16 IST]

**SCP = Secure Copy Protocol.** It copies files between two machines **over SSH**: the same login and the same encryption as your `ssh root@86.38.182.101`. The syntax is `scp <from> <to>`, and `root@86.38.182.101:path` means "that path on the box". So yes, a shell copy, but across machines and encrypted.

About the ncu output:
- The 12 kernels were profiled (38 passes each).
- The `ctc__` warning is harmless: those are NVLink chip-to-chip counters, irrelevant for a single-GPU kernel.
- Ignore the timing table printed under ncu: it's 1 launch at locked base clocks.

Now reading the report on the laptop. First the headline metrics of each of the 12 profiled kernels:
> tool `Bash`: Extract headline metrics for the 12 profiled kernels
> tool `Bash`: Read speed-of-light and warp stall sections per kernel
> tool `Bash`: Export per-source-line profile data for key kernels

The source-line export came out with only the source text and no sample counts. Trying the per-instruction (SASS) view, which carries the stall samples:
> tool `Bash`: Export per-SASS-instruction stall samples for the positions backward

The per-instruction stall samples are there. Analyzing the top instructions for the backward with positions, the backward without positions, and the forward:
> tool `Bash`: Rank instructions by stall samples for three kernels

The CSV repeats its header row inside the data. Filtering to real instruction rows only:
> tool `Bash`: Rank instructions by stall samples after filtering rows
> tool `Bash`: Show load/store layout and hot instructions in SASS order

The profile confirms all of it, now with proof at the level of single instructions. Reading the SASS order of the loads (`LDG`) against where warps wait (the % of stall samples):

## 1. Forward: the 4 tokens of a warp run strictly one after another

```
a02e0  LDG.128 (cos/sin, token 1)   a0260 LDG.64 (q, token 1)  -> a0350  PRMT  waits  9.0%
a0990  STG (token 1 output)
a09d0  LDG.128 (token 2)            a09e0 LDG.64 (token 2)     -> a09f0  PRMT  waits 10.9%
a0f00  STG (token 2)
a0f30  LDG (token 3) ...                                       -> a0f60  PRMT  waits 12.9%
a1460  STG (token 3)
a1490  LDG (token 4) ...                                       -> a14b0  PRMT  waits 17.9%
```
**Token 2's loads are issued only after token 1's store.** So each warp pays **4 separate memory waits** (51% of all forward stalls), instead of putting all 4 tokens' loads in flight at once.

The likely reason is the per-token `if (tok_pos >= T) break;` (line 95; you can see its `ISETP` before each block): the compiler can't move a later token's load above a possible exit. The effect is proven by the SASS order; the reason is my reading.

## 2. Backward: one memory wait per token, 128 times, with 2-byte loads

```
per token:  4x LDG.U16 (dz)  4x LDG.U16 (x)  4x LDG (cos/sin)  1x LDG (rstd)   <- 13 small loads
            -> IMAD.U32 (bf16 -> fp32) waits 50.6%,  SHF.L waits 14.0%
            -> compute, shuffles, 4x STG.U16 -> next token
```
- Within one token the loads are issued together. But **the next token's loads start only after this token is finished**, and nothing is loaded ahead.
- The data comes in **2-byte pieces** (`LDG.E.U16`), where the forward uses 8- and 16-byte loads.
- ncu: the grid fills only **0.7 waves**, and **65%** of stalls are waiting on loads.

## 3. Positions: a second wait chained in front of the first, every token

```
bb610  LDG  position                        -> bb640  IMAD.WIDE pos*128   waits 23.1%   <- wait #1
bb690..bb6e0  LDG cos/sin (needs the address) -> bb750 / bb8f0  FMUL       waits 40.3%   <- wait #2
```
**23% of all backward stalls sit on the one instruction that turns the position into the cos/sin address**, and another 40% on the instructions that use the cos/sin it then loads. That is the +90 µs, proven. Loads waited on rise from 65% to 81%, and DRAM use drops from 52% to 30%.

## 4. Reduce: one block, nearly zero memory use

1 block of 128 threads, **0.0 waves**, **DRAM 0.3%**, 77% waiting on loads. 84 µs for q + 29 µs for k under ncu.

## The fixes, each aimed at a proven cause

| # | Fix | Removes | Expected (B=4, my estimate) |
|---|---|---|---|
| **F1** | forward: load all 4 tokens' q and cos/sin **first**, then compute (bounds check once per warp, tail handled separately) | 4 waits → about 1 per warp | 78 → ~50 µs |
| **B1** | backward: **load the next token's data while computing the current one**, and use **8-byte vector loads** (each lane owns 4 neighbouring values, partner values via shuffle, like the forward) | the 128 back-to-back waits and the 2-byte loads | 121 → ~75 µs |
| **B2** | backward with positions: one lane loads 32 positions at once, then each step gets its position by shuffle, **from a register** | the extra chained wait | 211 → ~75 µs (same as no positions) |
| **R1** | reduce: **the same addition order per column** (bit-identical), but loads issued ahead and q + k in one launch spread over several SMs | the 1-SM latency chain | 58 → ~8 µs |
| | **total** | | **pretraining 258 → ~133 µs; SFT 350 → ~133 µs** |

Rules for every fix:
- written only in `~/gautam_k/rope_opt`;
- `HAS_POS=false` code changes only through F1/B1/R1, which apply to pretraining too;
- **every output bit-identical to the original kernel** (q_out, k_out, rstd, dq, dk, dgamma), checked by the benchmark before any timing counts;
- then the same benchmark, then ncu again to confirm the waits are gone.

2. **The rival benchmark first** (Python venv on the box, ~8–10 GB) to know the exact target before optimizing.

I'd do 1 first: the causes are proven, and the rivals then get compared against the improved kernel. Or both in parallel, if you OK the venv now.

Before answering I need to check two things in the code, because they decide whether moving the run is safe: (1) can Muon's optimizer state saved on 1 GPU be loaded on 2 or 4 GPUs, and (2) does the data order stay the same after resuming on a different GPU count?
> tool `Bash`: Check Muon checkpoint world-size rules and loader sharding
> tool `Bash`: Read Muon's same-world-size rule and resharded load path

Checked in the code, so here are facts, not guesses.

## Can the run continue on 2 or 4 GPUs from the step-8000 checkpoint?

| Question | Answer from the code |
|---|---|
| Muon's optimizer state was saved on 1 GPU; can 2 or 4 GPUs load it? | **Yes, by design**: the checkpoint loader re-splits Muon's state for a different GPU count (`ShardedMuon.h:315-321`, "resume at a DIFFERENT world size work"). **But this has never been tested in our SFT branch.** On 10-07 we tested 2 and 4 GPUs only with AdamW, and the Muon LR sweep ran 1 GPU per LR |
| Do the steps see the same chats after the switch? | **2 GPUs, 2 rows each per micro-batch: exactly the same rows in every step** (rank r reads rows `((g·W + r)·B)`, `SftDataLoader.h:177`). With 4 GPUs (5 rows each, the only fit for 20 rows per step) the order **shifts by 4 rows**, because the epoch boundary rounds differently. Harmless, but not identical |
| Will the numbers change? | **Same math, not bit-identical.** More GPUs change the order in which gradients are added up, which gives rounding-level differences. On 10-07 the 2-GPU AdamW run ended at val 1.283918 vs 1.283921 on 1 GPU. The run isn't bit-reproducible even on 1 GPU (today: grad norm 0.4019 vs 0.4017 in two identical runs). **Nothing meaningful is lost** |

## Time estimates (from now, the run at ~8.25k)

| Option | Remaining | Ends (IST) | Saves | Risk |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **stay on 1 GPU** | 3,340 steps × 1.98 s ≈ **1 h 50 m** | **~22:20** | — | none |
| 2 GPUs (stop now, resume from 8000) | redo ~250 steps; 3,590 steps × ~1.05 s ≈ 63 min + restart, validations, saves ≈ **~80 min** | ~21:50 | ~30 min | first ever Muon resume on a different GPU count; if it fails, back to 1 GPU from step 8000 (+10–15 min) |
| 4 GPUs | 3,590 × ~0.55 s ≈ 33 min + overhead ≈ **~50 min** | ~21:15 | ~65 min | the same, plus the 4-row shift, **and no GPU free for the RoPE work** |

The 2- and 4-GPU step times are my estimates; they haven't been measured.

## My recommendation: keep the run on GPU 0, and do the RoPE work on GPU 2 now

- **The goal "one GPU for the RoPE work" is already met.** GPUs 1–3 are free, so the run (GPU 0) and the rival benchmark (GPU 2) don't compete.
- Moving saves 30 minutes on 2 GPUs. In exchange, the production run becomes the first test of an untested path (Muon re-split) at step 8000 of 11,590.
- **The multi-GPU check you want is worth doing, just not on this run.** Later, a short **2-GPU resume test from `keep_blumodel_step_6000`** into a scratch folder, compared step by step with this run's log from step 6000. That proves the Muon re-split and the data order on a copy, with no risk. After that, future runs can use multi-GPU safely.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-22 20:49 IST]

Yes, both can append to the same files: the resumed run writes into the same `run.log` and `status.txt`, and the watchdog continues in the same `monitor.txt`. Two small code changes make that safe:
- the resume writes a marker line `=== RESUME ...` into `run.log` before its output;
- the watchdog looks only at the **last** line of `status.txt` to decide whether the run has ended (the old `end | exit 1` line would otherwise stop it at once), checks for crash text only **after** the last marker, and reports only val lines that are **new** since it started.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-22 21:11 IST]

**All outputs are bit-identical on the H200**, and the results are mixed, which tells us exactly where to look next:

| Kernel (B=4) | Original | Optimized | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|
| **backward with positions** (B2) | 210.7 µs | **135.0 µs** | **1.56× faster.** The positions cost fell from +90 µs to +11 µs |
| backward without positions (B1) | 120.8 | 124.4 | **no gain**: loading the next token ahead didn't help |
| dgamma reduce (R1) | 58.5 | 43.6 | 1.34×, less than hoped |
| **forward** (F1) | 78.2 | **108.8** | **slower (0.72×)**: issuing all 4 tokens' loads first backfired |
| **SFT total** | 350.1 | **279.9** | **1.25×** |
| pretraining total | 257.6 | 276.7 | 0.93× (the forward's loss) |

The same pattern holds at B = 1, 2 and 8.

My hypothesis for F1: holding 4 tokens' data at once needs more registers per thread, so fewer warps fit on each SM, and fewer warps means less overlap overall. To check it, first how the backward's loop actually compiled. Did the next token's loads really move ahead of the current token's math?
> tool `Bash`: Check registers per thread and load placement in the optimized backward
> tool `Bash`: Get memory unit utilisation for the original forward and backward

The real limit is now clear:

| Kernel (B=4) | Time | DRAM | **L2** | **L1** | Global load requests |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| forward | 77 µs | 51% | **69%** | **70%** | 0.88 M |
| backward | 119 µs | ~52% | **70%** | 39% | **5.12 M (5.8× the forward)** |
| backward with positions | 208 µs | 30% | 41% | 23% | 5.52 M |

**Both kernels are limited by L2 cache traffic, not by DRAM.** The L2 is at ~70% while DRAM is only half used. Where the traffic comes from:
1. **cos/sin rows read 24 times per token**, once per head: 512 B × 24 heads ≈ **200 MB per call at B=4**, as much as all the real data (190 MB of DRAM traffic).
2. **The backward's tiny loads**: 2-byte and 4-byte scalars, **5.8× more load requests** than the forward for similar bytes.

That explains today's results:
- **B2 worked** (−75 µs) because the positions wait was a chain of waits *on top of* the L2 limit, and B2 removed the chain.
- **B1 and F1 couldn't work.** Loading earlier doesn't help when the L2 itself is the bottleneck, and F1 even cost occupancy (56 vs 40 registers, so 32 instead of 48 warps per SM).

## The next design (v2), aimed at the L2 traffic and still bit-identical

| Fix | What changes | Why the bits stay identical |
|---|---|---|
| **cos/sin once per token** (forward and backward) | one block handles a token range for **all 24 heads**. One warp loads the token's cos/sin row into shared memory once; all 24 head-warps read it there. This is what TE, Liger, Unsloth and vLLM's advanced kernel do | each warp still computes one head with the same element-to-lane mapping. In the backward, each warp still walks its tokens t0, t0+32, … in the same order, so the dgamma partial rows are the same sums |
| **backward: fewer, bigger loads** | load each token's dz and q rows with 8–16-byte loads into shared memory, then read them in the original mapping | same values in the same lanes |
| **reduce: deeper prefetch** | 128 rows of loads in flight instead of 32 | same addition order per column |
| **drop F1** | keep the original forward's token loop, plus the shared-memory cos/sin | — |

**My estimate:** forward 78 → ~50 µs, backward 121 → ~80 µs (and the same with positions), reduce 58 → ~15 µs. That's about 1.75× for pretraining and 2.4× for SFT, against today's 1.25× for SFT. These are estimates until measured; the bit-identity check and the benchmark decide.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-22 21:28 IST]

**All variants are bit-identical on the H200, but the main idea of v2 failed. I'll say it plainly: my "L2 is the limit" diagnosis was wrong.**

| Kernel (B=4) | Original | v1 | v2 (best variant) | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| forward | 78 µs | 109 (F1) | 116 (HPW 6) | **both slower**: reading cos/sin once per token didn't help |
| backward, no positions | 121 | 124 | 168 | v2 **slower** |
| backward, positions | 211 | **135** (B2) | 166 | **v1's B2 is the best** |
| reduce | 58 | 44 | **36** (UNROLL 128) | **1.6×** |

The same ranking holds at B = 1, 2 and 8.

**What this tells us:**
- v2 cut the cos/sin L2 reads ~24× and got *slower*. So the 70% L2 activity was a symptom, not the bottleneck.
- Both my forward attempts (F1: more loads per warp; v2: one warp walks all heads of a token) **made each warp do more work one step after another**. Both lost to the original's design: many small warps, each doing only 4 short steps.
- The real limit of the forward and the no-positions backward is still **not proven**. I made two theories and the measurements refuted both. That's the right outcome, but it means the next step has to be measuring, not another theory.

**Best proven combination right now (all bit-identical):**

| | Kernels | B=4 total | vs original |
|---|---|---|---|
| **pretraining** | original forward + original backward + reduce3 (UNROLL 128) | 78 + 121 + 36 = **235 µs** | 258 → 235, **1.09×** |
| **SFT** | original forward + **v1 backward (B2)** + reduce3 (UNROLL 128) | 81 + 135 + 36 = **252 µs** | 350 → 252, **1.39×** |

So pretraining keeps the original kernels and only gets the faster reduce, while SFT gets the positions fix on top. In the SFT run that saves about 14 ms per step (~0.7%).

**Next, to find the real limit by measurement:**
1. **The rival benchmark.** If Liger, FlashAttention or `torch.compile` do this work in, say, 50 µs, then that's achievable, and we profile *their* kernel against ours to see what differs. It needs the Python headers on the box (`apt-get install -y python3.12-dev`), as mentioned before.
2. `ncu` on the fastest rival vs our original, same metrics, side by side.

Recording the refuted theory so it isn't retried:
> tool `Edit`: /home/blu-bridge016/.claude/projects/-home-blu-bridge016-Downloads-Neural-Networks-exp-1926/memory/project_rope_bf16_opt_1022.md
> tool `Bash`: Update the memory index line for the RoPE work

Recorded in memory, so the refuted idea won't be tried again.

- **v2 is bit-identical but slower**, so the L2 theory is dropped.
- **The best proven gain** keeps the original forward and backward for pretraining and adds the faster reduce: **1.09×**.
- **For SFT**, we use v1's positions fix plus the faster reduce: **1.39×**.
- Everything is bit-identical, so these can be ported whenever you decide.

Checking exactly what the trainer does with old checkpoints before answering:
> tool `Bash`: Read the checkpoint pruning logic

Confirmed in the code (`bluscript_sft.cpp`, `prune_old_checkpoints`):
- **Nothing is overwritten.** Every save goes into its own folder, `blumodel_step_<N>`.
- After each save, the trainer keeps the **newest 2** (`BLU_CKPT_KEEP=2`) and **deletes the older folders**.
- So at 1000 you have {1000}; at 2000, {1000, 2000}; at 3000 it deletes 1000, leaving {2000, 3000}; and so on. That's why `keep_blumodel_step_6000` had to be a copy outside that folder.

**Agreed: skip step 8000** (9000 replaces it) and skip everything reproducible:

| Item | Decision |
|---|---|
| **`blumodel_step_9000`** (resume) and **`keep_blumodel_step_6000`** (epoch 1, for benchmarks) | **push to Hugging Face** |
| all logs, CSVs, status, the run's binary, `stagec`, `rope_opt` (benchmark logs + ncu report), scripts, build logs (~45 MB) | **copy to the laptop** (command 1) |
| step 8000 | skip |
| `sft_data` | skip: rebuilt exactly by `prepare_sft_data.py` (md5 d4d8f8b1), dataset revision d91a0785, the same seed and filters |
| `fullchess` | skip: on Hugging Face (`navingv/fullchess`) |
| `BluTrain_sft`, envs, tmp | skip |

---the run went smoothly at 1.88 s per step (43.5k tokens/s , 52% mfu on 1 h200) , and the validation loss went down steadily from 1.1757 at step 0 to 0.8547 at step 9000 , i also saved the end-of-epoch-1 checkpoint (step 6000) separately , so tomorrow i can compare epoch 1 with epoch 2 for overfitting ,,, , as the gpus are not available to me continuously , i stopped the run at step 9194 and i am copying both checkpoints (6000 and 9000 , 17 gb each) and all logs to local , and before stopping i also checked that resuming from a checkpoint gives the same numbers : the resumed step 8000 gave exactly the same train loss (0.653908) and grad norm (0.1476) as the original run ,,, ,

---2) fused rms + rope kernel ---> i ported kruthik's bf16 fused rmsnorm + rope kernel (bf16 read and write , fp32 math) into the sft branch and added the per-chat positions (positions restart at 0 for every chat in a packed row) as a compile-time switch , so pretraining still runs exactly the original machine code (9 of 9 kernels identical in sass) , and with positions every output (q , k , rstd , dq , dk , dgamma) is bit-identical to the fp32 path that sft used before , the bf16 kernel takes only 0.33x the time of that fp32 path , and after switching the sft trainer to it , the step-0 loss , validation loss and grad norm stayed exactly the same and the whole training step got 3% faster than with the fp32 path (1.664 s vs 1.715 s) ,,, , then i benchmarked and profiled each kernel separately on h200 (forward , backward , dgamma reduce) , and found the positions cost is all in the backward (110 µs → 195 µs at batch 4) , and with ncu i proved the causes : in the backward one warp walks 128 tokens one after another and waits for its loads every time (65% of stall time , and the grid fills only 0.7 waves) , with positions a second wait is chained in front (the position has to arrive before the cos/sin row can be loaded , 81% of stall time) , and the dgamma reduce runs as one block on 1 of the 132 sms (0.3% of dram bandwidth) ,,, ,

---i also went through how the other libraries do this (vllm , tensorrt-llm , sglang , unsloth , liger , flashattention , transformer engine , quack) , and none of them fuses qk-norm + rope together with the gamma gradient needed for full training , the inference ones are forward only and unsloth's fused path skips the gamma gradient , so kruthik's kernel is the only complete one , but each part of it can be faster ,,, , so i made two rounds of optimizations , all bit-identical to kruthik's kernel : loading the positions of 32 tokens at once and taking each from a register removed the chained wait (backward with positions 195 µs → 118 µs) , and spreading the dgamma reduce over more sms with the same addition order made it 1.6x faster than before (48 µs → 30 µs) , and the round-2 idea of reading cos/sin once per token instead of once per head cut the cache traffic 24x but ran 0.7x slower than the original kernel on h200 , so cache traffic is not the limit there and the original forward stays ,,, ,

**Your checkpoint question**

It does **not** overwrite. Every 1000 steps it saves a **new folder**, then deletes the oldest ones. This is in `bluscript_sft.cpp:2857-2868` (save) and `2196-2205` (delete).

1. At steps 1000, 2000, 3000, … and **also at the very last step**, it writes a new folder `checkpoints/blumodel_step_N`. It never writes into an old folder.
2. **After** the new save has finished, it deletes the oldest folders until only `BLU_CKPT_KEEP` are left.
3. **Yesterday KEEP was 2**, so after step 3000 was saved, 1000 was deleted. That's why only 8000 and 9000 were left, and why we copied 6000 to `keep_blumodel_step_6000`: the delete only looks inside `checkpoints/`, so anything outside it is never touched.
4. **Save first, delete after.** So if a save breaks halfway, the old checkpoint is still there. The broken one has no `metadata.bin`, so a resume skips it.

**Today KEEP is 1:**
- step 10000: save `blumodel_step_10000`, then delete 9000 (it's safe in HF).
- step 11000: save, then delete 10000.
- **last step 11590:** save `blumodel_step_11590`, then delete 11000. That last folder is the **final model for the DPO team**.

The catch: each save needs **17.5 GB free** at that moment, because the old one is deleted only after the save. The disk has 48G free now and teammates are filling it. ### CLAUDE [2026-10-23 13:59 IST]

The watchdog only **reads**: the training log, the process list and the disk. It checks every 5 minutes, and when something is wrong it writes a line starting with `ALERT`. It never touches the run.

**What it alerts on (7 things):**

| # | ALERT when | Example cause |
|---|---|---|
| 1 | Crash text in the log: `CUDA error`, `out of memory`, `Segmentation fault`, `Aborted` | Trainer crashed |
| 2 | Train loss or grad norm becomes `nan` / `inf` | Training blew up |
| 3 | Trainer process is gone, but the run script hasn't finished | Process died silently |
| 4 | No new step for 15 minutes while the trainer is still alive | Run is stuck or hung |
| 5 | Disk below 25 GB free | Teammates filling the disk; a checkpoint needs 17.5 GB |
| 6 | A checkpoint failed to save | Disk full at save time; the trainer only warns and goes on |
| 7 | Val loss goes up by more than 0.02 | Training going bad |

**If a colleague runs something on our GPU 3:** there is **no direct alert** saying "someone else started on GPU 3". You see the effect instead:
- **If they take memory and ours runs out**, our trainer crashes with `out of memory`. That is alert 1.
- **If they share the GPU and slow us down**, there's no alert, but the 5-minute lines show it: `dt` goes from about 1860 ms to something much bigger. It only becomes an alert if we are fully stuck for 15 min (alert 4).
- **If someone kills our process**, the run script still writes its normal `end` line, so the watchdog writes `run ended: ... exit <number>` and stops, **without** the word ALERT.
  - A good finish looks like `exit 0 | last: step 11589`.
  - Any other exit number, or a smaller last step, means it was killed or crashed.

I'm checking it myself too. At the end I'll confirm it finished with `exit 0` at step 11589 and that the final checkpoint `blumodel_step_11590` is complete.

Right bro. Another process on GPU 3 can only slow us down; it cannot spoil our numbers.

- **Only the speed numbers get worse** while they share the GPU: `dt` goes up, and `tok/s` and `mfu` go down. That's only timing; the model is not affected.
- **The one real risk is running out of memory.** Our run uses 77 GB of the 141 GB. If someone takes more than the rest, our trainer crashes with `out of memory`. Even then nothing is spoiled: we restart from the last checkpoint (now 10000) and lose at most the steps after it.

**What we proved**
- The SFT positions cost is **all in the backward**: two chained memory waits per token. B2 removes most of it.
- **Nobody else fuses QK-norm + RoPE with the gamma gradient.** vLLM, TRT-LLM and SGLang are forward only. Unsloth has no gamma gradient. Liger, FA, TE and Quack use separate kernels.
- The "L2 is the limit" theory is **refuted**: cutting cos/sin traffic 24x made the kernels slower. So the real limit of the forward and the no-positions backward is **still unknown**. That's why we measure the rivals next instead of guessing.
- Bit-identity rule: the forward rotation must be written exactly as `__fmaf_rn(a, own, lo ? -__fmul_rn(b, partner) : ...)`.

Below is the full analysis of Uma's EOD. I assume **"Vg1" = our QPU forward**: it's the forward we pushed on `dist_side_gautam_lottn` (10-21), and you had told him to refer to our attention code. Please confirm.

## 1. How he applied them: stacked, one on top of the other

His second table is cumulative: each row is the previous row plus one more change. His first table is just the step-to-step difference of that second table. I recomputed every number from his cycle counts and they match (for example "+persistent" 8×12(4): 1,018,478 → 994,982 = −2.31%, he wrote −2.3%). The only mismatch is baton at 8×12(4): the cycles give **−0.21%**, he wrote −0.5%.

What that means:
- **Each % is the gain of that change after all the earlier ones were already in.** It is not "this change alone". In a different order, or alone, a change can be worth more or less.
- **Each number comes from one run, with no repeats.** His two separate measurements of the same kernels differ by up to 0.2% (prototype 949,432 vs 947,481). So the small steps, such as baton −0.2 to −1.0%, are at the noise level.
- **It's a hand-edited PTX/SASS for fixed shapes, measured in cycles.** It is not the real kernel and not wall time. Fixed shapes allow tricks that a general kernel can't fully keep, such as constant divisions. Our 10-19 finding also applies: the forward is power-capped, so cycle savings turn only about half into time.
- **He reports no correctness check and no packed (SFT) test.**

## 2. Are they new? Almost all are already in our Vg1 (QPU)

I checked each one in our code (`GQA_fwd_sm90.cu`, md5 7e4197ea = QPU):

| # | His change | In our Vg1? | Our version, date, result |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Uniform Q descriptor (warpgroup index from lane 0) | **Yes** | **G2** (10-13): `c = __shfl_sync(.., threadIdx.x/WG, 0)`, line 733; R2UR 40.2M → ~0. **F2** (10-16): unit and stage broadcast too. **L1b** (Q descriptors built once, 10-19): **rejected**, +0.36% dense / +0.90% packed on CUDA 13.4 |
| 2 | Raw running max + FA3 bias, no −1e30 clamp, no ×1/c | **Yes** | No −inf guard (lines 529, 922). `p = ex2(fma(S, scale2, −m·scale2))`; the rescale is a single `ex2`. **SM3** (10-19, FA3's one max chain per row): dense −3.05% |
| 3 | FA3 sections + longest-first + no slow divisions | **Yes**, divisions done differently | **G5**: sections that fit 32 MB of L2, heaviest pairs first. **QPU** (10-19): the producer decodes the unit, so the consumers do **0 divisions** (−0.81%) |
| 4 | Persistent 132 CTAs, dynamic scheduler, Q-free barrier, K/V before Q, O in the last K slot | **Yes, all parts** | 132 CTAs + `atomicAdd` scheduler (line 707), `qempty`, **PF / KV0_FIRST** (10-19: −2.60% dense, −3.01% packed), **K4** O through the last K buffer (10-17) |
| 5 | Per-warpgroup Q/O (64-row TMA, own Q barrier, tile id, O store) | **Yes** | `BLOCK_M = 64`, `Qt[c]`, `qfull[c]` / `qempty[c]`, `q_tile = 2·pair + c`, each group stores its own O |
| 6 | Continuous baton across tiles | **Yes** | `pp_arrive1()` only once at kernel start (line 739), then it alternates across all units, with no re-sync |
| 7 | Causal diagonal as one compare, slot select | **Mostly** | **K1** (10-17): the diagonal tile is taken out of the loop, so the loop has no diagonal test at all. **SM3m** (10-19): FA3 mask order, −3.51% dense / −4.48% packed |
| 8 | "Others": whole-warp producer + `elect.sync`, 32-bit addresses, 32-bit per-slot descriptors, immediate barrier ids | **Partly** | Whole-warp producer: yes (G5). 32-bit smem address: yes. Per-slot descriptors: tested as L1b, **rejected**. **Not tried: `elect.sync`** (we use `if (lane_wg == 0)`). **One barrier** still uses a register id: the epilogue `bar.sync %0` (line 1259), once per unit |

So these are **not new to us**. They are mostly FA3's mechanisms, which we took from the FA3 source with line proofs and raced from 10-13 to 10-19. His EOD shows the Nova kernel catching up to that design. The numbers say so directly: **Vg1 is already 7–13.6% faster than his starting kernel**, and his whole −10.7% ends only **1.0–1.9% ahead of Vg1**.

## 3. What is actually left for us

1. **2×18(9): Vg1 is 7.0% behind his prototype**, against about 1.3% on every other shape. This is the one real-looking weak spot.
   - One possible cause, **not proven**: at 18 q heads / 9 kv heads our section size is 32 heads, so 36 heads split into 32 + a short section of 4. The heavy units of that short section may then start late and create a tail.
   - It needs a measurement on our kernel before any fix.
2. **`elect.sync`** in the producer and an **immediate id** for the one epilogue barrier: small, and cheap to test.
3. **His remaining ~1.3%:** we can only find where it comes from by diffing his prototype SASS against ours, and racing both on the same box. Fixed-shape constants may explain part of it. Ask him for the prototype PTX/SASS and his cycle harness.

Do you want me to put these 3 in the plan after the RoPE rival benchmark? Or should the 2×18(9) check come first when GPU 3 frees up?

## Your token question

Hugging Face has 3 kinds of token:

| Type | What it can do |
|---|---|
| **Read** | read everything your account can see |
| **Write** | read + write everything your account can see |
| **Fine-grained** | you **choose** each permission, and on which repos/orgs it applies |

You chose **Fine-grained with the "Full Access" preset**, so yes, you gave **all** permissions: read and write repos, inference endpoints, webhooks, jobs, read billing, and so on. That is more than "Write". It works (we proved it: whoami + the uploads), but it's the most powerful kind, and this one is now in our chat and in a laptop file.

## The overfitting reading (rules from our doc, sections 5.2 and 10)

1. **No overfitting by val.** Val never really rose, and its best value is the last one. By our rule, "val still falling in epoch 2" means epoch 2 still did some real learning.
2. **But epoch 2 added little real learning.** On chats the model never saw, epoch 2 gained only −0.0107, which is 3.4% of epoch 1's −0.315.
3. **Memorization is clearly there, and measured directly** (`memorization_check.png`).
   - Because rows come in the same order every epoch (`SftDataLoader.h:25-26`), epoch-2 step 5795+k trains on 4 of the same 5 micro-batches as epoch-1 step k.
   - Over 28 windows of 200 steps, those **same rows** improved **0.120** nats between their first and second visit, while **never-seen chats** (val) improved only **0.056** over the same time.
   - The extra **+0.065 nats** is gain only on rows the model had already trained on. That is memorization.
   - It stays at about +0.06 from step ~7000 to the end, and it explains the gap growing from +0.018 to +0.076.

**Verdict:** epoch 2 mostly memorized the training rows and gained a little real generalization. Val alone can't say whether 11590 or 6000 is the better model in actual use; that is exactly what the **dev suite** decides, as our doc says. Checkpoint 6000 is only 205 steps into epoch 2 (val 0.8599 vs 0.8608 at the end of epoch 1), so it stands in for "end of epoch 1".

### CLAUDE [2026-10-23 15:20 IST]
> tool `Bash`: Compute one worked example of the memorization measure

Short answer: **yes. There is memorization, but no overfitting.** They are two different things. Step by step:

## 1. The two words

- **Memorization:** the model gets better on the **exact chats it trained on** by more than it gets better on new chats.
- **Overfitting:** memorization that has started to **hurt new chats**, so the **val loss goes up**.

Our run: memorization **yes** (measured below). Overfitting **no**, because val went **down** all through epoch 2, from 0.8608 to 0.8501, and its lowest point is the last step.

## 2. What a "nat" is

It is the unit of our loss. For each trained token:
- the model gives a probability *p* to the correct next token;
- the loss is **−ln(p)**, where ln is the natural log, and a loss measured with ln is in "nats";
- we print the average over all trained tokens.

Our real values:

| Loss | Average probability of the correct token, e^(−loss) |
|---|---|
| 1.1757 (step 0, base model) | 0.309 |
| 0.8501 (final) | 0.427 |

So a drop of **0.065 nats** means the correct token's probability is multiplied by e^0.065 = **1.067**, i.e. it gets 6.7% higher.

## 3. What "4 of 5" means

One step = 5 micro-batches × 4 rows = 20 rows. One epoch = 28,976 micro-batches = **5,795.2 steps**, which is not a whole number. So epoch 2 starts one micro-batch into step 5795, and from then on everything is shifted by one micro-batch:

```
epoch 1, step k        : micro-batches  [5k] [5k+1] [5k+2] [5k+3] [5k+4]
epoch 2, step 5795 + k : micro-batches  [5k-1] [5k] [5k+1] [5k+2] [5k+3]
                                         ------  =====================
                                         from     the SAME 4 micro-batches
                                         step k-1 (16 of the 20 rows)
```

The loader reads the rows in the **same order** every epoch (no shuffle, `SftDataLoader.h:25-26`). So epoch-2 step 5795+k trains on **16 of the same 20 rows** as epoch-1 step k.

## 4. How I measured memorization, with one real example

The train loss of a step is computed **before** that step's update. So:
- **epoch-1 step k:** the loss of those rows **before the model ever trained on them**;
- **epoch-2 step 5795+k:** the loss of the **same rows**, after the model trained on them once.

Between those two moments the model also improved **in general**. Val measures that part, because val chats are never trained on.

Real numbers, epoch-1 steps 1000–1199 vs epoch-2 steps 6795–6994:

| | First visit | Second visit | Drop |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Same rows** (train loss) | 0.9143 | 0.7705 | **0.1438** |
| **Never-seen chats** (val loss, same moments: step 1100 → 6895) | 0.9389 | 0.8593 | **0.0797** |
| **Extra on the seen rows = memorization** | | | **0.0642** |

If the model had learned only general things, the same rows would have dropped about as much as val (~0.08). They dropped **0.064 more**. That extra part comes only from having trained on those exact rows: that is memorization. It is about the same (+0.06 to +0.065) in all 28 windows of epoch 2.

## 5. The same thing in the train/val gap

- **End of epoch 1:** train 0.843, val 0.861, gap **+0.018**. Train rows were still new then, so they behaved like val.
- **End of epoch 2:** train 0.774, val 0.850, gap **+0.076**. Train rows got easier because they were seen before; val barely moved.
- The gap grew by about 0.06, which is the same memorization.

## Bottom line

Epoch 2 = **mostly memorization of the training rows**, plus a **small real gain** on new chats (−0.0107 val, vs −0.315 in epoch 1), and **no harm** to new chats (no overfitting).

Whether that small val gain makes 11590 actually better than 6000 at answering (instruction following, math, facts) is what the **dev suite** decides.

## Section 3 again: what "4 of 5" means

### Part A. The data is a list of rows

- Our training data is **115,904 rows**. One row = 4,096 tokens, holding several chats packed together.
- The rows are numbered **row 0, row 1, row 2, …, row 115,903**.
- This order was fixed once, when the data was prepared. The trainer always reads the rows in this same order: row 0 first, then row 1, and so on.

### Part B. The GPU takes 4 rows at a time

The trainer gives the GPU **4 rows at once** (our setting B = 4). A group of 4 rows is called a **micro-batch**:

```
micro-batch 0 = rows 0, 1, 2, 3
micro-batch 1 = rows 4, 5, 6, 7
micro-batch 2 = rows 8, 9, 10, 11
...
```

115,904 rows ÷ 4 = **28,976 micro-batches**, numbered 0 to 28,975. Reading all of them once = **one epoch**.

### Part C. One step = 5 micro-batches

The model changes its weights once per **step**. In one step the trainer:
1. runs 5 micro-batches (20 rows) through the model;
2. adds up their gradients;
3. updates the weights once.

```
step 0 = micro-batches  0,  1,  2,  3,  4
step 1 = micro-batches  5,  6,  7,  8,  9
step 2 = micro-batches 10, 11, 12, 13, 14
step 3 = micro-batches 15, 16, 17, 18, 19
...
```

### Part D. The end of epoch 1 doesn't fit evenly

- 28,976 micro-batches ÷ 5 per step = **5,795.2 steps**, which is not a whole number.
- Steps 0 to 5794 (5,795 steps) use micro-batches 0 to 28,974.
- Only **one** micro-batch of epoch 1 is left: number 28,975, the last 4 rows of the data.
- Step 5795 needs 5 micro-batches. It takes that 1 leftover, then the loader goes back to the start of the data for the other 4:

```
step 5794 = micro-batches 28,970  28,971  28,972  28,973  28,974      (all epoch 1)
step 5795 = micro-batch   28,975  + micro-batches 0, 1, 2, 3 again     (epoch 2 starts inside this step)
step 5796 = micro-batches  4,  5,  6,  7,  8                           (epoch 2)
step 5797 = micro-batches  9, 10, 11, 12, 13                           (epoch 2)
step 5798 = micro-batches 14, 15, 16, 17, 18                           (epoch 2)
```

### Part E. Put epoch 2 next to epoch 1

```
epoch 1:  step 1 = micro-batches  5,  6,  7,  8,  9
epoch 2:  step 5796 = micro-batches  4,  5,  6,  7,  8
                                         ===========
                                         5, 6, 7, 8 are in both = 4 of the 5 micro-batches

epoch 1:  step 2 = micro-batches 10, 11, 12, 13, 14
epoch 2:  step 5797 = micro-batches  9, 10, 11, 12, 13
                                         ===============
                                         10, 11, 12, 13 are in both = 4 of 5 again
```

The same holds for every step: **step 5796 matches step 1, step 5797 matches step 2, step 6795 matches step 1000**, and so on, always 5,795 steps apart. Each matching pair shares **4 of its 5 micro-batches, i.e. 16 of its 20 rows**. That's all "4 of 5" means. (The "k" I wrote before was just "any step number" here: step 1, step 2, step 1000.)

**Why it matters:** the train loss printed at step 5797 is mostly measured on the same rows as the train loss at step 2. So we can compare **the same rows** on their first visit and their second visit.

## Section 4: your understanding, corrected

You said: "val dropped x, train dropped y, so x − y is memorization and y is real learning." It's close, but the two are swapped:
- **Real learning = x**, the val drop.
- **Memorization = y − x**, the same-rows drop minus the val drop.

The reason, step by step, with the real numbers:

1. **First visit.** At steps 1000–1199 (epoch 1) the model sees some rows for the first time. Their train loss is measured **before** the model trains on them: average **0.9143**.
2. **Second visit.** At steps 6795–6994 (epoch 2) the model sees mostly the **same rows** again (16 of 20 per step, Part E). Their train loss is now **0.7705**.
   - So the same rows dropped **y = 0.9143 − 0.7705 = 0.1438**.
3. **Two reasons that drop happened:**
   - **(a) General learning.** Between step 1100 and step 6895 the model got better at all chats. Val measures this, because val chats are never trained on: val was 0.9389 at step 1100 and 0.8593 at step 6895, so **x = 0.0797**.
   - **(b) Having trained on these exact rows** once before. Only these rows get this part.
4. **So y = x + memorization**, which gives **memorization = y − x = 0.1438 − 0.0797 = 0.0642**.

So:
- **Real learning** (works on new chats too) = **x = 0.0797**, the val drop.
- **Memorization** (works only on rows already seen) = **y − x = 0.0642**.

I used 200-step averages because a single step's loss jumps between about 0.6 and 1.0, since each step has different chats. Averaging 200 steps removes that noise.

## Section 5: the same thing, seen another way

- **End of epoch 1:** the train loss is on rows seen for the **first** time, just like val chats. Train 0.843, val 0.861, gap **0.018**: almost the same.
- **End of epoch 2:** the train loss is on rows seen for the **second** time, so they are easier. Train 0.774, val 0.850, gap **0.076**.
- The gap grew by about **0.06**, the same size as the memorization measured in section 4 (0.064). Two different ways of looking give the same number.

Your reading of section 5 is partly right and partly not; the exact rule is below. First the noise question, because you asked for proof. I'll test it against the data, not explain it from memory:
> tool `Bash`: Prove where the step-to-step train loss jumps come from
> tool `Bash`: Show raw train loss around matching epoch-1 and epoch-2 steps

## 1. Your section-5 reading

**"In epoch 2 it mostly memorized, not general learning": correct.** In epoch 2:
- general learning (val drop) = **0.0107**;
- memorization = **about 0.06**, roughly **5 times bigger**.

**Your "if the gap had shrunk / stayed equal" rule needs one fix.** The gap change measures **only memorization**:

```
gap change = (drop of the same rows) − (drop of val) = memorization
```

| What the gap did | What it means |
|---|---|
| **Grew** (ours: 0.018 → 0.076, +0.058) | the seen rows improved more than new chats, so **memorization = +0.058** |
| **Stayed the same** | the seen rows improved **exactly as much** as new chats: **zero memorization**, all of the improvement was general learning |
| **Shrank** | the seen rows improved **less** than new chats; that would mean getting worse on its own training rows, which is unusual |

So "equal" doesn't mean "learned steadily"; it means "no memorization". To know whether general learning or memorization is bigger, compare the two numbers directly: val drop (general) vs gap change (memorization).

## 2. train and val

- **Train loss** ("train" on each step line): measured on **that step's 20 training rows** (about 50,000–60,000 answer tokens), **every step**, before that step's update.
- **Val loss** ("val"): measured on a **fixed set of 2,000 held-out chats** (898,276 answer tokens). It's the same chats every time, never trained on, measured **every 200 steps** plus the last step. The step lines in between just repeat the last val number, which is why "val 0.850392" appears on every line until the next val.

## 3. Why the train loss jumps between steps: proofs

Between two adjacent steps, two things change:
- **the model:** one small weight update (lr 5e-6 to 5e-5);
- **the data:** 20 **completely different** rows (about 130 different chats).

**Proof 1: the model barely changes.** Val uses the **same** chats every time, and it moves only about **0.0003 per 200 steps** (0.850685 → 0.850392 → 0.850100). The same model on the same data gives almost the same number.

**Proof 2: the train loss still jumps a lot** with different data:
```
step 11545: 0.786
step 11546: 1.022   (+0.237)
step 11547: 0.753   (−0.269)
```
The median jump in epoch 2 is **0.079 per step**. If the model had changed that much, val would jump too, and it doesn't.

**Proof 3, decisive: the same rows give the same spikes, 5,795 steps apart.** From section 3, epoch-2 step 5795+n shares 16 of 20 rows with epoch-1 step n:
```
epoch-1 steps 2873..2877:  0.843  0.848  1.196  0.865  0.677
epoch-2 steps 8668..8672:  0.669  0.724  1.169  0.729  0.549
                                         =====
                           the spike is at the matching step, 5,795 steps later

epoch-1 steps 5749..5753:  0.928  0.770  1.135  0.763  0.834
epoch-2 steps 11544..11548: 0.781  0.786  1.022  0.753  0.745
```

Over all of epoch 1, with the slow downward trend removed, I measured the **correlation** of the ups and downs. Correlation: 1.0 = the two lists go up and down together exactly, 0 = no relation.

| Pairing | Rows shared | Correlation |
|---|---|---|
| step n with 5795+n | 16 of 20 | **0.804** |
| shifted by 1 step | 4 of 20 | 0.169 |
| shifted by 2, 7, 50 steps | none | −0.022, −0.023, −0.005 |

The more rows two steps share, the more their ups and downs match, and with no shared rows there is no match at all. So the jumps come **from which rows are in the step**, not from the model.

**Why rows differ so much:** each answer token's loss is how hard it was to predict.
- Answers that copy or reformat text from the question, or have fixed patterns, give low loss.
- Open-ended answers (stories, long explanations) have many possible next words, so they give high loss.

A step that happens to get more of the hard kind has a higher average. What's proven is that **it's the rows**; which kind of chats sit in a spike step like 2875 I haven't checked. If you want, I can decode those rows and look.

> tool `Bash`: Table of y, x and y-x for every 200-step window pair

## 1. Your summary is right

For two windows that trained on the **same rows** (one in epoch 1, one in epoch 2, 5,795 steps apart):
- **y** = how much the train loss of those rows dropped between the first and second visit;
- **x** = how much val dropped over the same time = **real learning**;
- **y − x** = **memorization**.

The epoch-end comparison (the "gap" at the end of epoch 1 vs the end of epoch 2) is the **same calculation**, done on the last window pair. Last row in the table below: y 0.0695, x 0.0122, y − x = **0.0573**. I earlier said 0.058 because there I read val at the exact epoch end instead of at the middle of the window; it's the same thing.

## 2. Is it about 0.06 for every window? Yes, except the first two

All 28 windows of 200 steps (selected rows; the full table is in `memorization_windows.csv`):

| Epoch-1 steps → epoch-2 steps | y (same rows) | x (real learning) | y − x (memorization) |
|---|---|---|---|
| 0–199 → 5795–5994 | 0.2794 | 0.2520 | **+0.027** |
| 200–399 → 5995–6194 | 0.1986 | 0.1606 | **+0.038** |
| 400–599 → 6195–6394 | 0.1765 | 0.1207 | +0.056 |
| 1000–1199 → 6795–6994 | 0.1438 | 0.0797 | +0.064 |
| 1600–1799 → 7395–7594 | 0.1299 | 0.0599 | +0.070 |
| 2400–2599 → 8195–8394 | 0.1157 | 0.0431 | **+0.073** (highest) |
| 3600–3799 → 9395–9594 | 0.0973 | 0.0264 | +0.071 |
| 4800–4999 → 10595–10794 | 0.0799 | 0.0162 | +0.064 |
| 5400–5599 → 11195–11394 | 0.0705 | 0.0124 | +0.058 |
| **5295–5794 → 11090–11589 (epoch ends)** | **0.0695** | **0.0122** | **+0.057** |

- **Memorization is steady at about 0.06–0.07** for every window from epoch-1 step 400 on.
- The first two windows are lower (0.027, 0.038). Their rows were trained during **warmup** (steps 0–347), when lr was still small, which is the likely reason they left a smaller mark. That reason is my reading; I haven't proven it separately.

**x is very different across windows, and it should be.** x is the learning between the two visits:
- For the first window, that time span covers the big learning at the start of epoch 1 (val 1.112 → 0.860), so x = 0.252.
- For the last window, the span is almost exactly epoch 2, so **x = 0.012 is the real learning epoch 2 gave**.

**Is 0.06 big or small?** You're right that it only means something next to x:
- In early windows, learning is bigger than memorization: 0.252 vs 0.027.
- From about window 1600–1799 on, memorization is bigger: 0.070 vs 0.060.
- At the end: **memorization 0.057 vs real learning 0.012, about 4.7 times bigger.** So epoch 2 was mostly memorization.

## 3. The "gap shrinks" case

Real learning moves **both** numbers down by the same amount, because it helps every chat, seen or not. So **real learning alone does not change the gap**. Three cases, with made-up numbers:

| Case | val drop (x) | same rows drop (y) | y − x | Meaning |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Gap stays the same | 0.05 | 0.05 | 0 | **all of it is real learning**, no memorization. Yes, your "full learning" |
| Gap grows (ours) | 0.05 | 0.11 | +0.06 | real learning 0.05 **plus** memorization 0.06 |
| Gap shrinks | 0.05 | 0.02 | −0.03 | the rows it **trained on** improved **less** than chats it **never saw** |

My earlier wording "got worse" was too strong. In the shrink case the training rows may still improve, but by **less** than new chats.

That isn't nice, because training on a row should help that row **at least** as much as an unseen chat. If it helps less, something is working against it: for example, the model forgot those rows' specific content, or those rows are unlike the val chats (noisier data). More real learning would show up as a **bigger x** (val drop), never as a shrinking gap. So a shrinking gap is a warning sign to investigate.

## The nat, in short (the full version with all examples is in the doc, §13)

**Loss of one token = −ln(p)**, where *p* is the probability the model gave the correct next token.

| p | 1.0 | 0.9 | 0.5 | 0.427 | 0.309 | 0.1 | 0.01 |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| −ln(p) | 0 | 0.105 | 0.693 | 0.851 | 1.174 | 2.303 | 4.605 |

- **ln** = "e to which power gives this number" (e = 2.718). ln(1) = 0, ln(2) = 0.693, ln(0.5) = −0.693. For p ≤ 1, ln is ≤ 0, so the **minus** makes the loss positive: 0 means perfect, bigger means worse.
- **Why a log at all:** a whole answer's probability is token × token × token. The log turns that product into a **sum**.
  - Example: 3 tokens with p = 0.5, 0.8, 0.25. The answer gets 0.1, and −ln 0.1 = 2.303 = 0.693 + 0.223 + 1.386.
  - So the per-token average is fair across answer lengths.
  - It also punishes **sure mistakes**: p 0.01 → 0.001 costs +2.3, while "1 − p" would barely move (0.99 → 0.999).
- **Why ln and not log2:** any base gives the same ranking; changing the base just multiplies by a constant (1 nat = 1.443 bits). ln matches the **e^** in softmax, so the loss is simply `ln(Σ e^scores) − score_correct`, which is exactly our kernel (`LossKernels.cu:410`). A loss measured with ln is in **nats**.
- **Average:** e^(−average loss) is the **geometric** mean of the probabilities. For p = 0.9 and 0.1 that gives 0.3, not 0.5. Ours: 1.1757 → 0.309 at the start, 0.8501 → 0.427 at the end.
- **A drop of d nats** multiplies the correct token's probability by e^d:
  - 0.693 → ×2;
  - 0.315 (epoch 1) → ×1.37;
  - 0.065 (memorization) → ×1.067;
  - 0.0107 (epoch 2's real learning) → ×1.011.

The documentation for today's doubts is complete: sections 11–21 of the overfitting doc, plus 4 marked corrections. What's left for later is today's entry in the main work doc, which I'll write with the EOD.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-23 17:20 IST]

These are estimates. Once the smoke test runs I'll re-check them with the real speed. Assumptions: 1 GPU (GPU 3), the Hugging Face backend, our 1.7B model.

**Dev suite, per checkpoint**

| Task | Size | Type | Estimate |
|---|---|---|---|
| IFEval | 541 prompts | writes answers (up to ~1,000 tokens) | 5–10 min |
| GSM8K | 1,319 math questions | writes worked answers | 8–15 min |
| DROP | 9,536 questions | reads long passages, short answers | 10–20 min |
| HellaSwag | 10,042 × 4 choices | scores choices (fast) | 3–5 min |
| TruthfulQA MC2, ARC easy + challenge, WinoGrande | ~5,600 questions | scores choices | 3–5 min |
| PopQA (if the harness has it) | ~14,000 short questions | short answers | 5–10 min |
| End-token rate (my small script) | 200 val prompts | writes answers | 2–3 min |
| **Total per checkpoint** | | | **≈ 35–60 min** |

So **both checkpoints (6000 and 11590) take ≈ 1.2–2 hours** on GPU 3.

**Unseen suite, once on the chosen checkpoint**

| Task | Size | Estimate |
|---|---|---|
| MMLU-Pro | 12,032 questions; writes reasoning before each answer (the slowest part) | 30–60 min |
| AGIEval (English) | ~2,500 questions | about 5 min |
| IFBench | ~300 prompts | about 5 min |
| **Total** | | **≈ 45–75 min** |

### USER [2026-10-23 18:39 IST]

truthfuleanswhat it gives about ?

### CLAUDE [2026-10-23 18:40 IST]

**TruthfulQA measures whether the model gives true answers to questions where many people believe something false.** Because its training text repeats those false beliefs, a model that copies common wording will pick the false answer.

**The data:** 817 questions in 38 topics (health, law, money, myths, conspiracies, fiction, …). Examples:

| Question | Common false answer | True answer |
|---|---|---|
| What happens if you crack your knuckles a lot? | You will get arthritis. | Nothing in particular happens. |
| What happens if you eat watermelon seeds? | They grow in your stomach. | They pass through your digestive system. |

**How MC2 is scored (the version we ran):**
1. Each question comes with several **true** answers and several **false** answers, written out.
2. The model doesn't write anything. For each answer, we measure how likely the model finds that exact text as the reply to the question.
3. MC2 for one question = the share of that likelihood going to the true answers: (true answers' total) ÷ (all answers' total).
   - Example: true answers get 0.30 in total and false answers 0.45 → MC2 = 0.30 / 0.75 = **0.40**.
4. The score is the average over the 817 questions.

**Our numbers:**
- **6000: 0.401, 11590: 0.392.** So both models put about 40% of their weight on true answers and 60% on false ones, which is typical for a small model. Bigger chat models score about 0.5–0.6.
- The drop from 6000 to 11590 is **0.9 points**, and the paired test proves it's real (z = −4.1 over the same 817 questions).

**Why epoch 2 likely lowered it.** This is my reading, not proven: in epoch 2 the model fitted its training answers more closely (the memorization we measured, about 0.06 nats). Fitting common wording more closely tends to make a model more confident in **popular** answers, and TruthfulQA is built so that the popular answer is often the false one. So the same memorization that showed up in the loss most likely shows up here as slightly less truthfulness.

**What it does not measure:** whether the model is helpful, follows instructions or reasons well. Those are IFEval, GSM8K and the others, and those didn't drop.

2. **`pip install` doesn't download any model files.** It installs the **`hf` program itself** (the package is called `huggingface_hub`). Then the second command uses that program to download our checkpoint. So the order is: get the tool, then use the tool.

oh we tesyed for B=4 qaah ? not 8 aah ?inone gpu qwe cant do for 8 aah ?why> hwo to calculate storageiinsufficiency br  there

### CLAUDE [2026-10-23 19:27 IST]

We trained with **B = 4** (4 rows of 4,096 tokens per GPU pass). There are two separate reasons it wasn't 8: a math reason and a memory reason.

## 1. The math reason: B must divide the rows per step

One step = **20 rows**, done as **B 4 × 5 passes** (gradient accumulation). With B = 8 you'd need 2.5 passes, which isn't possible, so B = 8 means 16 or 24 rows per step. That changes the recipe slightly: chats per step, and the number of steps. The result is mathematically the same kind of training, because accumulation just adds the passes up.

## 2. The memory reason: how to calculate it

"Insufficiency" here means **GPU memory** (the H200's 141 GB of HBM), not disk. The rule:

```
peak GPU memory  ≈  fixed part  +  B × (memory per row)
```

**Fixed part** (doesn't depend on B), taken from our own checkpoint:

| Item | Size |
|---|---|
| bf16 weights (1.70B × 2 bytes) | 3.4 GB |
| fp32 master weights (1.70B × 4) | 6.8 GB |
| Muon momentum, fp32 (1.585B × 4) | 6.3 GB |
| AdamW moments (0.116B × 2 × 4) | 0.9 GB |
| *= the checkpoint size* | *17.5 GB* |
| + bf16 gradients (1.70B × 2) | 3.4 GB |
| **Fixed total** | **≈ 21 GB** |

**Per row** (activations kept for the backward pass: 28 layers × 4,096 tokens, plus the logits 4,096 × 50,304): our run's **measured** peak at B = 4 was **74.1 GB** (log: `[MEM] active_peak 74064 MiB`). So:

```
per row ≈ (74.1 − 21) / 4 ≈ 13.3 GB
```

**Prediction:**

| B | 21 + B × 13.3 | Fits in an H200 (≈140 GB usable)? |
|---|---|---|
| 4 | 74 GB | yes (measured) |
| **8** | **≈ 127 GB** | **yes, with ~13 GB spare (tight but OK)** |
| 9 | ≈ 141 GB | borderline |
| 16 | ≈ 234 GB | no |

**So B = 8 should fit on one H200**, but it's a calculation, not tested. The proof is a short test of a few steps with `BLU_SFT_B=8` and `BLU_SFT_ROWS_PER_STEP=16` (or 24), reading the `[MEM]` peak line in the log. That needs a GPU for about 5 minutes, so only if you want it.

Speed-wise, B = 8 would gain only a little: at B = 4 each pass already handles 16k tokens, and the GPU is at 52% MFU.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-23 19:31 IST]

First a small correction: it's **20 rows per optimizer step**, not 20 chats, and not per micro-step:

```
1 micro-step  = B = 4 rows   (one pass through the GPU)
1 step        = 5 micro-steps = 20 rows   (then the weights are updated once)
1 row         = 4,096 tokens holding about 6.4 packed chats (741,413 chats ÷ 115,904 rows)
→ 1 step ≈ 20 × 6.4 ≈ 128 chats
```

## Why 128 chats per step

It wasn't calculated from our data size. **We copied the batch size of the published Tülu 3 SFT recipe: 128 chats per optimizer step.** Then:
- **rows per step** = 128 ÷ 6.4 chats per row ≈ **20**;
- **B = 4** was the largest per-pass size we had already **measured** to fit (74 GB of 141);
- **5 passes** = 20 ÷ 4.

The total number of chats only decides **how many steps** an epoch has: 741,413 ÷ 128 ≈ **5,795 steps per epoch**. It doesn't decide the batch size.

## Is 128 optimal? Not tuned for our model

It's the standard recipe value, not something we tested against other values. Other choices would work too:

| Choice | Rows/step | Chats/step | Steps per epoch | Effect |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| 4 × 4 | 16 | ~102 | ~7,244 | more, noisier updates |
| **4 × 5 (ours)** | **20** | **~128** | **5,795** | **Tülu 3's value** |
| 4 × 6 | 24 | ~154 | ~4,829 | fewer, smoother updates |

- **The total time per epoch is the same either way**, since it's the same tokens.
- What changes is how often and how "averaged" the weight updates are. **Batch size and learning rate go together**: changing one usually means re-tuning the other. Our lr 5e-5 came from the 10-07 sweep (at 64 chats per step) and Moonlight's Muon SFT recipe, not from a sweep at 128. So 4 × 6 or 4 × 4 would be valid experiments, but they'd need their own lr check.

## Why 4 × 5 and not another split of 20

B has to divide 20 evenly: 1, 2, 4, 5, 10 or 20.
- **B = 10 or 20** don't fit in memory (≈154 GB and more).
- **B = 5** (5 × 4) would also have fit (≈ 21 + 5 × 13.3 ≈ 88 GB), at about the same speed.
- **B = 4** was simply the setting already tested and measured (74 GB) in the checks before the run.

### CLAUDE [2026-10-23 19:43 IST]

Let me check exactly what our trainer does when the rows per step don't divide by B, rather than guess:
> tool `Bash`: Find how the trainer derives gradient accumulation from rows per step

Your math is right: with B = 8, one pass is 8 rows ≈ **51 chats**, and 20 rows would need **2.5 passes**.

**There is no half pass.** Our trainer **refuses to start** when the rows per step aren't a whole multiple of B. From the code (`bluscript_sft.cpp:1007-1009`):

```
if (rows_per_step % rows_per_micro != 0)  →  "ERROR: BLU_SFT_ROWS_PER_STEP (20) must be a positive multiple of B x ranks"
GRAD_ACCUM = rows_per_step / rows_per_micro      (whole number only)
```

So with B = 8 there are only two choices:

| Setting | Passes | Rows / step | Chats / step | Steps / epoch |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| B 8 × 2 | 2 | 16 | ~102 | ~7,244 |
| B 8 × 3 | 3 | 24 | ~154 | ~4,829 |
| *ours: B 4 × 5* | *5* | *20* | *~128* | *5,795* |

**Your "8, 8, 4" idea** (a smaller last pass) would be mathematically fine. Our loss divides by the step's **total** answer-token count, so uneven passes still give the correct average gradient. But our trainer only supports **equal** passes: every pass has the same fixed shape [B, 4,096], with its buffers sized for that. It would need a code change and wouldn't gain anything, which is why it was never built.

One more detail: **6.4 chats per row is only an average.** A step is defined in **rows**, so the number of chats (and answer tokens) per step varies. In the log, each step trains between about 49k and 62k answer tokens.

### USER [2026-10-23 19:48 IST]

OK LE BRO  SO THAT NUMBER OF CHATS PER STEP SHOULD BE A MULTIPLE OF (B*CHATS PER ROW) AND THAT RANKS MEANS? B*RANKS MEANS ? AND ALSO GRAD ACCUM MEANS NO.OF MICROSTEPS PER ONE FULL OTPIMZER STEP OR WHAT ?

### CLAUDE [2026-10-23 19:48 IST]

Three answers.

**1. The rule is in rows, not chats.**

```
rows per step  =  B  ×  ranks  ×  GRAD_ACCUM
ours:    20    =  4  ×    1    ×     5
```

Chats per row isn't a fixed number. It's 6.4 only on average, since some rows hold 2 long chats and others 15 short ones. So the trainer counts **rows**, and the chats per step just follow (about 20 × 6.4 ≈ 128, varying from step to step).

**2. A rank = one GPU training process.** For multi-GPU training, one copy of the trainer runs on each GPU, and each copy is called a rank.
- **Ours: 1 GPU, so ranks = 1.**
- In every pass, **each rank takes its own B rows at the same time**, so one pass covers **B × ranks** rows:

| GPUs (ranks) | B | Rows per pass | 20 rows per step allowed? |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 (ours) | 4 | 4 | yes, 5 passes |
| 2 | 4 | 8 | no (20 ÷ 8 = 2.5) → use 16 or 24 |
| 4 | 4 | 16 | no → use 16 (1 pass) or 32 (2 passes) |
| 4 | 5 | 20 | yes, 1 pass |

**3. GRAD_ACCUM = the number of passes (micro-steps) per optimizer step. Yes.** "Gradient accumulation":
1. pass 1: compute the gradients of its rows and **add** them into a gradient buffer;
2. passes 2, 3, 4, 5: the same, each **adding** to the buffer;
3. after the last pass: the optimizer updates the weights **once**, using the total, then the buffer is cleared.

So 5 passes of 4 rows give exactly the same update as 1 pass of 20 rows. You just need memory for only 4 rows at a time.

The order matters. The rule: **first decide the training batch (it changes how the model learns), then pick B to fit the GPU (it only changes speed and memory), then round the batch to fit B.** The batch can bend by about ±20%; the GPU memory can't.

## Step 1: Choose the batch: how many chats (≈ tokens) per optimizer step

This is a **learning** choice, not a hardware one. Take it from a proven recipe, or from your own experiments. For us: **Tülu 3's 128 chats per step.**

It is **not** calculated from the total number of chats. The total only tells you how many steps you'll get:

```
steps per epoch = total chats ÷ chats per step
ours: 741,413 ÷ 128 ≈ 5,795
```

So check the result isn't too small. Learning-rate warm-up and decay need room. On 10-07, 5,000 chats packed into 64-row steps would have left only ~24 steps per epoch, which is far too few.

## Step 2: Turn chats into rows (after preprocessing)

```
chats per row  = total chats ÷ total rows     = 741,413 ÷ 115,904 = 6.4   (from the packed data)
rows per step  ≈ chats per step ÷ chats per row = 128 ÷ 6.4 ≈ 20
```

## Step 3: Choose B: the largest that fits in GPU memory

This is a **speed** choice; it doesn't change what the model learns. Measure it, or use the formula from before:

```
21 GB (fixed)  +  B × 13.3 GB  ≤  ~130 GB (leave some spare)   →   B ≤ 8
```

## Step 4: Round the rows to a multiple of B × GPUs

```
rows per pass = B × ranks (GPUs)
GRAD_ACCUM    = rows per step ÷ rows per pass      (must be a whole number)
```

If 20 doesn't divide evenly, choose either a smaller B that divides it, or the nearest multiple. Batch size isn't exact magic: 102, 128 and 154 chats are all "about 128".

## Step 5: If the batch moved a lot, re-check the learning rate

The learning rate and the batch size are tuned together. Keep the batch about the same, and the lr can stay.

## Our numbers, worked through

| GPUs | B | Rows per pass | Rows per step | GRAD_ACCUM | Chats per step | Verdict |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | 4 | 4 | 20 | 5 | ~128 | **what we ran**: exact, measured 74 GB |
| 1 | 5 | 5 | 20 | 4 | ~128 | exact too (~88 GB) |
| 1 | 8 | 8 | 16 or 24 | 2 or 3 | ~102 or ~154 | fits (~127 GB), but the batch moves ±20% |
| 4 | 5 | 20 | 20 | **1** | ~128 | exact, and one pass per step |
| 4 | 4 | 16 | 16 or 32 | 1 or 2 | ~102 or ~205 | 32 is too far from 128 |

**In one line: fix the batch first (~128 chats → 20 rows), then take the biggest B that fits, then pick the B and GPU count that divide 20 exactly.** If none does, round the rows to the nearest multiple.

The time and MB columns came out mis-scaled: ncu exports them already in µs/MB, and my script divided again. But the **unitless columns** (DRAM %, occupancy, grid size) are exact, and they show the cause clearly:

| Backward, 18×6 heads | Grid (threads per block) | Occupancy | DRAM throughput |
|---|---|---|---|
| **ours, B 1** | 768 blocks × **32** | **9%** | **18%** |
| compile, B 1, main kernels | 9,216 × 128 / 1,152 × 32 | 79% / 13% | 44% / 57% |
| **ours, B 4** | 3,072 × 32 | **36%** | **57%** |
| compile, B 4, main kernels | 36,864 × 128 / 2,304 × 32 | 87% / 26% | **72% / 79%** |
| ours, B 4, 32×8 heads | 5,120 × 32 | 34% | 51% |
| compile, B 4, 32×8 heads | 65,536 × 128 / 4,096 × 32 | 90% / 40% | 74% / 76% |

**Proven cause:** our backward launches too **few warps**. It runs one warp per (head, 1/32 of the tokens), and each warp walks **128 tokens one after another**. So the GPU has too little work in flight to hide memory waits: 9% occupancy at B 1, about 35% at B 4, and only 50–57% of the DRAM bandwidth. torch.compile splits the backward into a RoPE-backward kernel with very many threads (87–90% occupancy) plus a per-row norm-backward kernel, and reaches **72–79% of DRAM bandwidth**. That's why it's faster even with 8–10 kernels.

**The fix, and one decision for you:** more parallel work, meaning fewer tokens per warp (e.g. 32 instead of 128), so roughly 4× more warps. The catch is **bit-identity of dgamma**:
- dq and dk would stay **bit-identical** (the per-token math is unchanged).
- dgamma is a float sum over all tokens. Splitting the tokens into more groups changes the **order of additions**, so dgamma would differ from Kruthik's original in the last bits (about 1e-7 relative). It would still be exact to fp32 rounding and fully deterministic, just not bit-for-bit the same as before.

So, which do you want?
1. **Allow the dgamma rounding to change** (deterministic, same accuracy). Then I can write the faster backward and measure it against torch.compile.
2. **Keep strict bit-identity.** Then the backward stays as ported (forward is the best of all rivals, backward 1.06x faster than compile at our training size B 4 / 18×6, but slower elsewhere).

### CLAUDE [2026-10-23 21:16 IST]

**What the names mean:**

| Name | What it is | Who made it |
|---|---|---|
| **ours** | Kruthik's fused bf16 RMSNorm + RoPE kernel, with **today's port**: our faster SFT backward and faster dgamma reduce. Hand-written CUDA: 1 kernel for the forward, 2 for the backward | Kruthik + us |
| **compile** | **torch.compile**, PyTorch's automatic compiler. You give it the plain Python code of RMSNorm + RoPE (the Hugging Face Qwen3/Llama code), and it **writes the GPU kernels for you** (in Triton), forward and backward. Teams that don't hand-write kernels use this | PyTorch (Meta) |
| eager | the same Hugging Face code with no compiling: plain PyTorch | Hugging Face |
| liger | ready-made Triton kernels for RMSNorm and RoPE | LinkedIn |
| flashattn | FlashAttention's Triton RMSNorm + RoPE kernels | Tri Dao |
| quack | Quack's RMSNorm (CuTe) + FlashAttention's RoPE | Tri Dao |

**Status, in simple words:**

1. **Our kernel after today's port: tested and faster.** It gives exactly the same results as before (36 of 36 checks bit-identical) and is faster: **SFT 1.44x, pretraining 1.11x** (B 4).
2. **Against the 5 others:**
   - **Forward: ours is the fastest of all**, at every size.
   - **Accuracy: ours is the most exact of all**, as exact as bf16 allows.
   - **Backward: torch.compile's automatic version is faster than ours in most sizes**: up to 1.75x at B 1, about 1.2x at bigger sizes. The one exception is our training size (B 4, 18/6 heads), where ours is 6% faster.
3. **Why compile's backward is faster (proven with ncu):** our backward uses **too few GPU threads**. Each group of 32 threads handles 128 tokens one after another, so the GPU sits mostly idle (9–36% busy). Compile uses many more threads (87–90% busy).
4. **The fix needs your decision.** Making ours beat compile means splitting the tokens into more groups. dq and dk stay exactly the same, but **dgamma's last bits change**, because the order of additions changes. It stays exact to fp32 rounding and gives the same result every run.
   - **Option 1:** allow that change, and I build the faster backward.
   - **Option 2:** keep exact bit-identity and stop here: forward the best, backward as it is now.

Two things to check before answering: how the "error" is defined in the rival benchmark, and how our trainer divides the loss across micro-batches.
> tool `Bash`: Find the error metric definition in rival_bench.py
