Written for: your colleague, as a record of every attention kernel optimization on H200 (10-10 to 10-21), forward and backward, kept or rejected, with timings.

## How everything was measured

- **GPU:** H200, head size 128, causal, bf16.
- **"Dense" shape:** our model's attention, B = 8 rows × T 4,096, 18 query heads / 6 KV heads. Some races also used 13 dense shapes.
- **"Packed" shape:** `real_rows_752`, 8 real packed SFT rows of typical chats, T 4,096.
- **Race:** two or more builds run one after another in the same session, 6–12 rounds, free clocks (as in training). A % is the paired mean change against the previous best (minus = faster). "8/8" means faster in 8 of 8 rounds. Larger |t| means a more certain result.
- **Correctness gate before every race:** the varlen test suite (144 / 296 / 605 checks). It includes "each packed chat = the same chat alone, bit for bit". A change that breaks this is rejected even if it is faster.
- **Scoreboards against FA3 / FA4 / cuDNN:** kernel time from nsys, free clocks, same box, steady state. A ratio is our time / their time, so below 1 = ours faster.

---

## Part 1 — Backward: Vj1d → Vj2

**Main kernel, dense:** 3,626 µs → 2,406.7 µs (**−33.6%**), from 1.46× FA3's time to 0.97×.

| # | Date | Change | Correctness | Speed result | Kept? |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| 0 | 10-12 | **Baseline Vj1d**: 64 keys per block, one warpgroup does everything | — | main kernel 3,626 µs; FA3 2,494 µs (1.46×) | — |
| 1 | 10-10 | Sync fix: one `__syncthreads` so all warps see the first LSE values (a race) | 289/289 | 12/4 heads −0.04%, 18/6 +1.71% (t 2.0) = noise | **Yes** (correctness) |
| 2 | 10-12 | **New kernel Vj2** in FA3's layout: 128 keys per block, loader + dQ-writer warps + 2 compute warpgroups, P/dS kept in registers, dS from the fp32 P | 605/605; dK/dV bit-identical every run | **5.2–13.0% faster than Vj1d** (mean 10.6%); kernel 3,615 → 3,197 µs | **Yes** |
| 3 | 10-12/13 | Memory path + descriptor fix: shared memory used as real shared loads/stores (they had compiled to generic loads); GEMM descriptors built once | 605/605, same values | **18–22% faster than Vj1d** (mean 20%); kernel 2,761 µs; instructions 1,096M → 840M | **Yes** |
| 4 | 10-13 | Phase 1.5 fix 1, dQ path: 128-bit stores in thread order + one 1-D bulk reduce-add per group (as FA3) | 144/144, same values | **−5.7%** (13/13); 2,778 → 2,599 µs; bank conflicts 56.3M → 18.3M | **Yes** |

**SFT packed-rows design, for reference (10-10/12):**

- Packed attention costs about half of dense on typical rows, and about a third on short-chat rows.

One correction to how I arrived here: when we built it on 10-21 I didn't record a citation. The design was modelled on CUTLASS: Nova's own code says the 232-register count is "CUTLASS's count", and the turn barrier was described as CUTLASS's ordered math barrier. It also followed Nova's existing FlashAttention-3-style turn in flash attention. Below is the proof, then the line-by-line check.
What "ping-pong" means, from primary sources
NVIDIA CUTLASS source, include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm90_gemm_tma_warpspecialized_pingpong.hpp, selected by the schedule tag KernelTmaWarpSpecializedPingpong:
Structure: NumMmaWarpGroups = 2, NumLoadWarpGroups = 1, "Pingpong kernel must have 384 threads in total".
Register split: LoadRegisterRequirement = 40, MmaRegisterRequirement = 232 (24/240 under heavy register pressure), applied with warpgroup_reg_dealloc / warpgroup_reg_alloc, which compile to setmaxnreg.
Ordering: OrderedSequenceBarrier with two stages: "// Order two Math WG's MMA one after the other, helps hide Epilogue", then "// Order two Math WG's Epilogue one after the other".
Tile assignment: the 2nd math warpgroup starts one tile ahead (advance_to_next_work()), and each warpgroup then steps advance_to_next_work(NumMmaWarpGroups).
NVIDIA CUTLASS docs (efficient_gemm.md, "Warp-Specialized Persistent Ping-Pong kernel design"): "The two consumer warp groups are assigned a different output tile… This allows for epilogue of one consumer warp group to be overlapped with the math operations of the other consumer warp group." The Cooperative design is the contrast: both consumers work on the same tile, split along M.
PyTorch's "Deep Dive on CUTLASS Ping-Pong GEMM Kernel" says the same independently: producers keep 40 registers and consumers get 232, which it shows in CUTLASS source and SASS; "each consumer works on separate C output tiles".
FlashAttention-3 (Shah, …, Vijay Thakkar, Pradeep Ramani (NVIDIA CUTLASS), Tri Dao), §3.1 "Pingpong scheduling": bar.sync barriers force one warpgroup's GEMMs before the other's, so one does softmax while the other does GEMMs.
cuBLAS is closed source, so the "pingpong" in its kernel names can't be read beyond its SASS. CUTLASS is the only public, inspectable definition.
Nova against CUTLASS
Checked on your current local tree (ac2ab83, which includes your later c54a485 "persistence, stream-k and ping-pong"), from a compiled ping-pong GEMM's PTX and from NovaGPUMapForallToGPU.cpp:

The two differences, and why:
The early hand-off is the v1 → v2 change. With CUTLASS-style strict ordering, our first version was 17–20% slower than cooperative. Handing on early, together with wait_group 1, is what turned it into a win (v2: −3.4% on the 26-layer step).
The unordered epilogue is safe because Nova's consumers don't share epilogue shared memory.
How to see it in SASS yourself: in any of our ping-pong kernels (or a CUTLASS ping-pong kernel), look for:
the register split: USETMAXREG dealloc 40 / alloc 232 (USETMAXREG.TRYALLOC);
384 threads per block;
named BAR.SYNC / BAR.ARV with 256 threads between the two consumer warpgroups.
A cooperative kernel has neither the register split nor the consumer-to-consumer barriers.
So yes: the structure Nova implements under the name ping-pong is CUTLASS's KernelTmaWarpSpecializedPingpong: one producer and two consumer warpgroups, 40/232 registers, a separate output tile per consumer alternating over the CTA's tiles, and an ordered barrier so one consumer's epilogue overlaps the other's MMA. It differs in two deliberate details, the earlier turn hand-off and the unordered epilogue, and uses FlashAttention-3's named-barrier primitive instead of CUTLASS's mbarrier-based one.

## Ping-pong: what the remote has, what our old research showed, and how much of the other Claude's reply holds

**Short answer.** The BLAS on remote BluTrain is Kota's code, not our hybrid. No version of our work has a ping-pong GEMM. The only ping-pong file on the remote is Kota's, and it is never compiled. The other Claude got the CUTLASS facts right, but made two real mistakes: the claim that cooperative kernels have no register split, and its SASS test.

### 1. What is on the remote (checked live today, read-only)

- BluTrain uses Tensor-Implementations as a submodule, and that uses BluBridge-BLAS as a submodule, on branch `master`.
- `git ls-remote` on BluBridge-BLAS shows **master = ea666ab**: "Merge pull request #3 from BlubridgeAI/production_blas", Kathir, 2026-08-31 14:35. That is exactly the commit in Harshini's screenshot.
- The code inside it was written by `dhanakumarK777` (email kotadhanakumar…), so it is Kota's.
- The repo has 17 branches. None of them is our hybrid or a branch of yours.
- Our hybrid exists only in your personal `GOUTHAM1926/blublas`. It was never sent as a PR to the team BLAS or to BluTrain.
- To read the remote I used your saved token in `~/.config/blubridge/github_pat`. It was never printed.

### 2. Where ping-pong exists, and where it does not

| Tree | Ping-pong? | Proof |
|---|---|---|
| Our SM90 template | No, cooperative only | [header lines 31-32](../blublas/src/level3/batched_gemm/BF16/SM90/Bgemm_sm90_warpspecialized_template.cuh#L31): "cooperative … not pingpong" |
| Our hybrid | No | Kota's file was deleted on 2026-09-02 in 713f0f7, recorded in [§H65](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L26731) |
| Remote BLAS (ea666ab) | Present but dead: no file includes it | [Bgemm_sm90_pingpong_template.cuh](../BluTrain_lottn/Tensor-Implementations/BluBridge-BLAS/src/level3/batched_gemm/BF16/SM90/Bgemm_sm90_pingpong_template.cuh#L112) |

**Kota's file is a real ping-pong design, not a mislabel.**
- Each consumer warpgroup takes alternating tiles.
- The register split is 24/240.
- It has a mainloop-turn and an epilogue-turn barrier, both modelled on CUTLASS.

**But it was never made to work.** Its own header (corrected 2026-08-24) says: it was run once and **hung**, then fixed, and the fix has **never been run again**. It is not in the build, so it was never part of his measured 98.4%.

The mix-up you remember:
- On 2026-08-31, [§H56](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L26272) called it "real".
- On 2026-09-02, §H65 found it was never compiled.

So if Harshini took a ping-pong reference from "BluBLAS in remote BluTrain", this unused file is the only one she could have found.

### 3. What our old research actually proved

You are partly right. We did find and quote the official definition: [§H24](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L6409) quotes CUTLASS `efficient_gemm`. What we could not do is see ping-pong in cuBLAS's machine code (SASS):

- **[§H23d](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L6352): cuBLAS's untagged kernels are ping-pong.**
  - All kernels use 384 threads.
  - Untagged kernels have blocks per warpgroup equal to the whole grid, so each consumer owns a whole tile. Cooperative kernels have half of it.
  - The relation "max register = blocks/WG × wgmmaN/2 + 26" is exact on 12 of 12 kernels.
  - This is proof from register arithmetic, not from an instruction.
- **§H24: the barrier mix is identical in both families.** Every kernel has 46 BAR.SYNC and no BAR.ARV. I marked that test inconclusive.
- **[§H25](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L6493): opcode census of all 18 kernels.**
  - Only 3 opcodes differ between kernels. **None of them tells ping-pong from cooperative.**
  - `USETMAXREG` (the SASS form of setmaxnreg) appears in 10 of 18 kernels, in **both** families, whenever max registers ≥ 154. The deciding factor is register pressure, not the schedule.
  - This also corrected H24's "no SETMAXNREG": H24 had searched for the PTX name, and the SASS name is different.
- **[R3](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L16762):** ping-pong could not explain V5's gap (it would need 288 accumulator registers; only 232 are available).
- **[§H158](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L31609):** "We have no Pingpong". It is the feature to build if BM=64 is ever needed.

If those lines exist, it is ping-pong-family. |

Short version: you are half right on the first point and wrong on the other two. Harshini's and Kota's designs both match the ping-pong definition. Kota's was never made to work. Harshini's is described but not shown.

## 1. "We could not find ping-pong in cuBLAS SASS, so we wrote that we didn't know and didn't build it"

**Right: we have the official definition.**
- §H24 quotes CUTLASS: the two consumer warpgroups get different output tiles, and one group's epilogue overlaps the other group's math. See [analyzations_h200.md:6411](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L6411).
- The same text is in local CUTLASS at [efficient_gemm.md:242-245](cutlass/media/docs/cpp/efficient_gemm.md#L242).

**Right: the SASS showed no ordering pattern.**
- [Line 6455](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L6455): "all kernels have identical barrier structure (46 BAR.SYNC … no BAR.ARV)", and I marked that test inconclusive.
- [§H25](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L6493): an opcode check of all 18 kernels found only 3 opcodes that differ between them, and none of them follows the schedule.

**But our check could not have found it.**
- CUTLASS orders the turns with an mbarrier: `using Barrier = cutlass::arch::ClusterBarrier` at [sm90_pipeline.hpp:1256](cutlass/include/cutlass/pipeline/sm90_pipeline.hpp#L1256). In SASS, mbarriers show up as SYNCS instructions, not BAR.
- H24 counted only BAR instructions.
- H25 only checked whether each opcode is present, not how many times. SYNCS is already present in every kernel for the TMA pipeline.
- So "not found" does not prove "not there".

**Wrong: we did not write "we don't know".**
- §H23d concluded: "NO SUFFIX -> PING-PONG: each consumer owns a whole tile" ([line 6382](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L6382)).
- The proof was register arithmetic, not an instruction: max register = blocks/WG × wgmmaN/2 + 26, exact on 12 of 12 kernels ([line 6427](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L6427)).

**Wrong: "not knowing" was not why we skipped it.** The recorded reasons are:
- [Line 5054](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L5054): it is UNDONE and only matters for matching performance, not for correctness.
- [Line 6787](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L6787): only 25 of 163 cuBLAS picks use ping-pong tiles, all of them small.
- [Line 9227](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L9227): it was priority #4, and "the uniform 10-14% gap … is worth more".
- [Line 31610](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L31610): build it only if BM=64 is ever wanted.

I cannot redo the SASS check on this laptop. The cuBLAS library here hides those kernels: 0 of its 1,597 sm_90 cubins contain an "nvjet" name. A proper check needs a SASS dump on an H200 and a count of SYNCS instructions per kernel. I will ask before doing that.

## 2. Harshini's: different from ping-pong?

**From its description, no. I cannot prove it either way.**
- The definition is about who owns which tile. Her claimed design matches it: each warpgroup owns a whole 128×192 tile, takes tiles w, w+2, …, and passes a turn barrier to the other.
- Her three differences (early hand-off, unordered epilogue, named barriers) are not part of the definition. FA3's ping-pong also uses named barriers.
- The "proof" it offered is not proof. 384 threads and the 40/232 register split are also in CUTLASS cooperative ([cooperative.hpp:150-151](cutlass/include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm90_gemm_tma_warpspecialized_cooperative.hpp#L150), lines 561 and 771). The PyTorch blog says: "cooperative kernel is largely equivalent to Ping-Pong, but both consumer groups work on the same C output tile".
- Real proof would be her code lines (`NovaGPUMapForallToGPU.cpp` 418-459) plus an A/B log against her cooperative version.
- It is not a copy of Kota's file. Kota uses mbarriers, an ordered epilogue, and hands off after the K-loop drains. Hers is described with named barriers, an unordered epilogue, and an early hand-off.

## 3. Kota's: different from ping-pong?

**No. His SM90 file is the real CUTLASS ping-pong.** All three parts match line for line:

| Part | Kota ([file](../BluTrain_lottn/Tensor-Implementations/BluBridge-BLAS/src/level3/batched_gemm/BF16/SM90/Bgemm_sm90_pingpong_template.cuh#L410)) | CUTLASS ([pingpong.hpp](cutlass/include/cutlass/gemm/kernel/sm90_gemm_tma_warpspecialized_pingpong.hpp#L558)) |
|---|---|---|
| Each consumer gets its own alternating tiles | 410-412: `task_id = blockIdx.x + g*gridDim.x; task_id += 2*gridDim.x` | 558-562: consumer 1 advances one tile; 952: `advance_to_next_work(NumMmaWarpGroups)` |
| MMA turn | 460 wait, 514 arrive for the other group | 850 wait, 877 arrive |
| Epilogue turn | 521 wait, 600 arrive | 899 wait, 936 arrive |
| Register split | 321 / 364: setmaxnreg 24/240 | 147-148: 24/240 under heavy register pressure |

**Why it still counts for nothing:**
- It waits for every MMA to finish at every k-step (`wgmma_wait_group<0>` at line 502). CUTLASS keeps several MMAs in flight. That makes his main loop slower, but the schedule is the same.
- Its own header (lines 112-118) says it "HUNG", was fixed, and the fixed version has "NEVER BEEN RE-RUN".
- Nothing at ea666ab includes it (checked with git grep), so it is never compiled.

**The "other thing" you remember is on B300.** In `Bgemm_sm103_cluster_dual_template.cuh` (lines 24-31 and 129-132), Kota uses "ping-pong" for `EPI_PIPE_DEPTH=2`. That means two TMEM accumulator buffers: the next tile's MMA starts while the previous tile's epilogue is still draining. The goal is the same, but the mechanism is different: there are no two math warpgroups taking turns. It is a different thing with the same name.

The memory note `project_pingpong_facts_1026.md` is updated with these points.

## 1. Did the compiler team build real ping-pong, as CUTLASS documents it?

**Yes.** The CUTLASS doc defines ping-pong with two points, and Nova's compiled kernel ([pingpong.ptx](reports_harshini_ping_pong/pingpong.ptx)) shows both.

**CUTLASS point 1:** "The two consumer warp groups are assigned a different output tile … epilogue of one … overlapped with the math operations of the other."
- [Line 86](reports_harshini_ping_pong/pingpong.ptx#L86): `w = tid >> 7`, so threads 0–127 are warpgroup 0 and 128–255 are warpgroup 1.
- [Lines 130](reports_harshini_ping_pong/pingpong.ptx#L130) and [137-141](reports_harshini_ping_pong/pingpong.ptx#L137): the CTA walks tiles t, t+132, …, and a warpgroup skips a tile unless `(tile number ÷ 132) & 1 == w`. So the two warpgroups take alternate tiles.
- Each warpgroup issues two sets of `m64n192k16` MMAs (registers `%r160…` and `%r256…`), which is the whole 128×192 tile. That needs 192 accumulator registers per thread; the highest register used is R215.
- After its K loop, a warpgroup writes its result with no wait on the other warpgroup. So its epilogue runs while the other warpgroup is doing MMAs.

**CUTLASS point 2:** "The producer … fill[s] buffers of the two consumer warp groups one after the other in order."
- There is one shared load ring, filled in tile order.
- The ring counter moves 36 steps for every tile, including tiles the warpgroup skips ([line 129](reports_harshini_ping_pong/pingpong.ptx#L129)).
- Turns: warpgroup w waits on barrier w+1 and signals barrier 2−w ([lines 92-93](reports_harshini_ping_pong/pingpong.ptx#L92)).

**It is not a line-by-line copy of CUTLASS's code.** There are three differences, and none of them breaks the definition:
- It passes the turn 5 K-steps before the end of the loop (after step 31 of 36). CUTLASS passes it after all MMAs are issued.
- It has no epilogue turn, because each warp has its own output buffer slots.
- The turn uses a named barrier (`BAR.ARV`), the FA3 style. CUTLASS uses an mbarrier.

## 2. Kota's version: is it also real ping-pong, and what went wrong?

**It is real ping-pong too, and closer to CUTLASS's code**: both turns, mbarriers, and the turn passed after the loop. The idea was right; the implementation was never finished. Three problems:

1. **It hung on its first run.** The first version left out the MMA turn and relied on the load ring to order the two warpgroups. That locked up at K ≤ 384. He added the turn, but the fixed version was **never run again** (his header, lines 112-118).
2. **It waits for every MMA to finish at every K step.** That is `wgmma_wait_group<0>()` at [line 502](../BluTrain_lottn/Tensor-Implementations/BluBridge-BLAS/src/level3/batched_gemm/BF16/SM90/Bgemm_sm90_pingpong_template.cuh#L502). Nova's own record names exactly this as the reason their v1 was 17–20% slower: "drains it every stage (… wait 0 …)". Nova fixed it by keeping one group in flight (`wait_group 1`, pingpong.ptx lines 446 and 544).
3. **It was never compiled or timed.** No file on any of the 15 branches uses it.

## 3. Did we ever build or test ping-pong?

**No. We never built it and never timed it.** The cuBLAS SASS was not the reason; our §H23d notes even concluded that cuBLAS *does* use ping-pong for small tiles.

| Evidence | Where |
|---|---|
| No commit implements it. The only "ping-pong" commit is 569cdaa, "fix slot ping-pong", which is an epilogue double buffer | git log |
| Our template is cooperative only | template header, lines 31-32 |
| R3 "ping-pong DEAD" was a calculation (288 registers needed vs 232 available), not a measurement | [line 16762](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L16762) |
| **Main reason recorded:** on our big shapes we were already at cycle parity with cuBLAS, with the tensor pipe 92–99% busy, so "neither regsplit nor pingpong adds math throughput" | [§H56, lines 26344-26348](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L26344) |
| Ping-pong was only needed for small tiles (64×64, BM=64), and was planned 4th | [line 9189](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L9189), [line 9227](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L9227), [§H158](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L31609), [§H159](../blublas/docs/analyzations_h200.md#L31732) |

For context: Nova's GEMMs took 1.27× cuBLAS's cycles before ping-pong (their 2026-10-10 note). That left a lot more room to gain than our kernel had.

I checked all 8 files locally on the CPU, without running anything of theirs:

Being the owner gives you permission to push. Git still has to prove who you are on every push, and over HTTPS GitHub has accepted only a token (or an SSH key) since 2021-08-13; your account password no longer works for git. So a token is always being used, even when you don't see one.

**What your laptop actually does.**
- Git is set to `credential.helper store` in `~/.gitconfig`. That saves logins as plain text in `~/.git-credentials`.
- That file has two saved logins for github.com. I identified them without printing them:
  1. User `GOUTHAM1926` with a classic PAT. This is **the same PAT that is written into the blublas remote URL**.
  2. User ID `133732634` with an OAuth token, which comes from an app or IDE sign-in.
- The experiment repo has no token in its URL, but its push still used a login from this file. That is why it worked "without PAT".

**Your Antigravity sign-in** (goutham64840@gmail.com) only feeds git commands run from inside the IDE: its Source Control buttons and its built-in terminal. In a normal terminal, git takes the login from `~/.git-credentials`. I couldn't confirm which saved login belongs to goutham64840@gmail.com, because asking GitHub with the saved tokens was blocked as credential exploration. Your GitHub settings page shows it.

**So the token in the blublas URL is not needed.** The same PAT is already saved in the credentials file. This command removes it from the URL, and pushes keep working:
```bash
git -C ~/Downloads/blublas remote set-url origin https://github.com/GOUTHAM1926/blublas.git
```

**One security step I'd still do.** That PAT is stored in plain text and was printed once in an earlier session. Revoke it on GitHub (Settings → Developer settings → Personal access tokens). After that, the next terminal push will ask for your username and a new token, or you can switch to an SSH key. If you revoke it without making a replacement, terminal pushes will fail until you do.
